title: விநாயகர் துதி
theme: Praise of Vinayaka (விநாயகர் துதி) opening the book: the elephant-faced god of the offerings, who drives off deeds and helped his younger brother win the hunter girl, and the poet's memory of Murugan's command to sing the Thiruppugazh.
structure_note: Both songs end at Ganapati, not Murugan. 1 is praise throughout; 2 opens with Murugan's emblems and his command to sing, then turns to Ganapati's food offerings.
source_issues: Song 2: one corrupt character in தன஧முலம் (line 12); probably தனிமூலம் (roots), but not certain.

reading: The poet worships with honey-dripping flowers the elephant-faced, pot-bellied son of Hara and Uma, who holds fruit, appam, aval and puffed rice in his hand and dwells like the wish-granting tree in the minds of devotees, so that their deeds flee. He praises him as the first to write Tamil on the first mountain, the hero who broke the axle of the chariot Siva rode to burn the three cities, and the one who became an elephant in the millet field so that little Murugan wed the hunter girl at once.
nuance: கற்பகம் எனவினை கடிதேகும்: for those who keep him in mind he is the kalpaka tree and deeds (வினை) leave quickly. முத்தமிழ் ... கிரிதனில் முற்பட எழுதிய points to the tradition that Ganapati wrote the epic on Meru with his tusk; the text says only that he first wrote the threefold Tamil on the mountain. The last lines name the hunter girl (குறமகள்) and the millet field, so Valli's story, in which the elephant drives her to Murugan.

reading: The poet says he will not forget the grace by which Murugan told him to sing, with love, an exalted Thiruppugazh that sets in it the saddled peacock, the kadamba garland, the vel that pierced the hill, the cock, the small feet, the twelve shoulders and the town of Seyppathi. The second half lists the offerings Ganapati takes as his own, sugarcane, fruits, sugar, dal, ghee, sesame, tender coconut, raw rice, pittu, cucumber and more, and praises him as the remover of obstacles, the son of the Lord with matted hair, the master with the tusk.
nuance: This is the book naming itself: திருப்புகழ் ... செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை, the grace of being told to sing it. The emblems listed (peacock, vel, cock, feet, shoulders, the shrine) are the furniture of almost every later song. செய்ப்பதி is usually taken as Vayalur. விக்கிந சமர்த்தன் is the one able against obstacles (vighna). One word in the offering list is corrupt.

title: விநாயகர்
theme: Songs to Vinayaka (விநாயகர்): prayers to the elephant-faced god for grace and a mind fixed on worship, one ritual offering ending in a battlefield, and a first confession of being sunk in women's love.
structure_note: 3 is a short plea and praise; 4 sets a worship scene against a battle scene; 5 has the book's usual two halves, a confession about women and a praise whose story is obscure. All three end at Ganapati.
source_issues: Song 4: one corrupt character in செற஧முளை (line 15); probably செறிமூளை (packed brain).

reading: The poet asks Ganapati to melt for him like the wish-granting tree, cow and gem of the gods, to let him drink the nectar of bliss many times, and to give his life grace. He praises him as the one who went to the forest for his younger brother's sake, who won the fruit by circling his father, the substance of those who love him, the five-handed elephant face.
nuance: தம்பிதனக்காக வனத்தணைவோனே recalls the elephant in Valli's forest (see 1). தந்தைவலத்தால் அருள் கைக்கனியோனே is the fruit won by going round the father, the story in which Murugan circles the world (30).

reading: The poet says he will never forget to worship the elephant-faced one with the single tusk, setting out fruits, appam, milk, honey, sugarcane, laddus, rice, dal, aval, sesame, plantains and tender coconut, with hymns, holding his ears, sit-ups and knocks on the temples, before the anklet-bearing lotus feet, so that he is given a mind that keeps the Lord's feet in thought. The second half is a battlefield: flies swarm on rivers of blood, flesh, bile, fat and brains, drums and tabors thunder, ghouls clap, Bhairavi dances in a ring, and the Lord offers the night-walking demons as sacrifice.
nuance: குழைபிடி தொப்பண குட்டொடு names the gestures still made before Ganapati: holding the ears, sit-ups (தோப்புக்கரணம்) and knocking the temples. The battle half is sung in drum syllables (தெனன, திமித, டிமுட), a device used again in 6 and 11. Whether the closing பெருமாளே is Ganapati, as the heading implies, or Murugan, the song does not settle.

reading: The poet confesses that, not knowing what deeds yield, he has drowned day and night in lovemaking on fragrant beds with women whose eyes are like the poison-filled sea, the gods' weapons, the trident and Vijaya's arrow, a base and ignorant wretch; he asks that he too be granted the Lord's anklets. The praise tells a story in which cowherds steal a little milk, a lord's daughter, not knowing the truth, cries out to 'my child, Ganapati', and the elephant-faced god gives understanding.
nuance: வினையின் விளைவு ஏதும் அறியாதே: the fault confessed is ignorance of what deeds bring. The second half's story is not one I can identify, and the lines (அகல்வதென் டாசொல் எனவுமுடி சாட) are hard to divide; the reading of the praise is a guess.

title: நூல்
theme: The opening song of the book proper (நூல்): Murugan named as Devayanai's lord, the seed of release and the guru who taught Siva the first of the Veda, with a plea for the day he will save the poet, and a battle in which demons are offered up.

reading: The poet calls Murugan the Shakti of the pearl-smiling daughter of the elephant's lord, Saravana, the one seed of release, the supreme guru, who taught the three-eyed Lord what comes before the Veda and whose feet Brahma, Vishnu and the thirty-three gods worship. He asks whether there will be a day when Murugan protects him with the meaning that Vishnu praises, Vishnu who loosed the arrow at the ten heads, churned with the mountain, made night at midday with his discus, and drove his devotee's chariot. The second half is a battle: Bhairavi dances, vultures and ghouls, the eight Bhairavas chant, owls cry, and the demons are cut down and offered as sacrifice while the great hill is pierced.
nuance: முக்கட் பரமற்குச் சுருதியின் முற்பட்டது கற்பித்து: what precedes the Veda is taken as Om, which the son taught the father. அத்திக்கிறை is the lord of the elephant, Indra, and his daughter is Devayanai. Vishnu's deeds are named by their details: Ravana's ten heads, the churning, the discus that hid the sun at midday, and the charioteer of Arjuna (பத்தற்கு இரதத்தைக் கடவிய). What 'the meaning Vishnu praises' (மெச்சத் தகு பொருள்) is, the song leaves open.

title: திருப்பரங்குன்றம்
theme: Songs at Thiruparankundram (திருப்பரங்குன்றம்): the poet confesses his bondage to women, courtesans who take a man's wealth with false hearts, his neglect of worship, his life from the womb to disease, and his begging from patrons, and asks for Murugan's feet, while the praise turns on the hunter girl, the vel against Sura, Vishnu as uncle and Murugan as teacher of Siva.
structure_note: All but 11 and 13 follow the two halves: confession and plea, then praise ending at the shrine. The confessions are mostly of women (7, 10, 12, 14, 16 to 20); 8 confesses neglected worship and asks for help at death, 9 runs through a life from conception, 15 confesses begging.
source_issues: Song 10: one corrupt character in மிடறு஡டே (line 9); probably மிடறூடே.
Song 12: one corrupt character in கி஡ணவ (line 16); probably கிரீவ (neck).
Song 18: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 12); clearly வயலூரா.
Song 20: one corrupt character in புண்ட஡ணகம் (line 12); clearly புண்டரீகம். The source's ஡ appears to stand for ஊ or ரீ in different songs.

reading: The poet describes, frankly and at length, lovemaking with proud women, from stroking their feet and loosening their clothes to biting, nail marks and the cries of birds, and asks whether he will ever give up delighting in it. He praises Murugan as Saravanabhava who told the Rig mantra to the seven sages, who wears on his shoulders Tamil poems that spread grammar and music, and as the holy child of the guru who gave grace under the kuruntham tree to the devotees of Sankara who danced in the hall.
nuance: தவிர்வேனோ, 'will I give it up?', is the whole plea: the confession is the bulk of the song. திருக்குருந்தடி அருள்பெற அருளிய குருநாதர் recalls Siva as the guru under the kuruntham tree, a story told of Manikkavasagar; the following lines (குருக்களின் திறம்) make Murugan the guru of gurus, and their syntax is not certain.

reading: The poet confesses that he has not worshipped Murugan daily, told his nature, bowed at his feet with flowers, done any austerity, sought out his devotees, gone round his hill or praised him with joy; and asks that when Death's men come on the bellowing buffalo with noose and club and his mind fails, Murugan come at that moment on the peacock and end his fear. The praise names the vel that slew the demons while ghouls leapt and vultures fed, the hunter girl's kumkum on his shoulders, and the sages of the four Vedas who worship him daily at Parangiri.
nuance: The confession is a list of omitted worship (தொழுதிலன், பணிந்திலன், வருகிலன்), and the plea is for one moment only, the hour of death. மறலிதன் உழையினர் are Death's servants, with the noose (கயிறு) and club (கதை) and Yama's buffalo (பகடு). This hour-of-death plea recurs through the book.

reading: The poet traces his life from the embryo ten months in the womb, through birth, washing, nursing, crawling and the child's ornaments, to youth, friendship with women and wandering in disease, and asks when he will gain the mind of Murugan's grace. The praise tells how the gods came to earth as Rama's monkey and bear army, the sun and Indra as monkey kings, Brahma as lord of the bears, Agni as Nila and Rudra as Hanuman, and names Murugan as nephew of Hari who defeated the asuras, and as the one who beat Brahma in anger and himself created the world.
nuance: The life is told as one breathless sequence that runs from womb to women to disease with no pause, so that youth and lust lead straight to sickness. அயனையும் புடைத்துச் சினந்து உலகமும் படைத்து is the story in which Murugan punished Brahma and took over creation.

reading: The poet describes how courtesans wound with kohl-dark eyes, catch a man with a smile and a net of talk, take him home with 'come in', and make love to him, and asks to be freed from the sorrow these deceiving young women cause. The praise is a battle in which the sea churns, the serpent's crowns crack and the demons' heads are heaped like mountains in fat and blood, and names Murugan as the younger brother of Ganapati and the son of the one who kicked Yama, at Parangiri.
nuance: சமன் உதைபட நிறுவிய பரன் is Siva who kicked Yama, the story of Markandeya; the song places it beside the poet's own fear without drawing the line. நஞ்சன சிறுமிகள் calls the women poisonous girls.

reading: A song mostly of praise: Murugan threw the blazing ball at the great golden mountain, was born as companion of the elephant, is nephew of the one who sleeps on the serpent and churned the sea, and son of the one who burned the three cities; with drums sounding he tore the bodies of the Suras and came on the peacock. In its middle the poet, small, base and a killer, troubled by many sorrows, asks Murugan to come and end his birth today, at Parangiri.
nuance: சிறியன் புலையன் கொலையன் is the self-description of the book: small, outcast, killer. The ball thrown at the mountain (செண்டை எறிந்திடு) is an allusion I cannot place with certainty.

reading: The poet tells how Kama, with eyes like carp, the five senses and the moon, attacks with his bow and how, deluded, he follows women and suffers in their embrace; he asks instead for the feet that devotees adorn with kadamba garlands. The praise names Murugan as the one who struck the lotus-dweller's head and fettered him and told the wealth of knowledge to Siva, whose twelve shoulders the conch-necked daughter of Indra and the hunter girl embrace, and who destroyed the clan of Nirudan, at south Parangundram.
nuance: மயல் (delusion) is the poet's word for his state. Brahma (போதிலுறைந்தருள்கின்றவன்) is struck and bound, and the knowledge he lacked is given to Siva (போதவளம் சிவசங்கரன் கொண்டிட மொழிவோனே), the same story as 6. One word is corrupt; கிரீவ, neck, is the likely reading.

reading: A short song: the poet asks whether, no longer wandering anxious in the chain of bonds, he will one day call on Kanda again and again, see him and love him. He names Murugan as the one joined to the elephant's daughter, the son of Sivai on Sankara's side, the vel at Senthil and Kandi, the lord at south Parangundram.
nuance: பந்தத் தொடர், the chain of bonds, and சஞ்சலம், agitation, are the condition; the cure is only the repeated name கந்தன். கண்டிக் கதிர்வேலா may point to Kathirkamam in Lanka; the reading is uncertain.

reading: The poet, sick with love, says that Kama's arrows, the burning moon, women's eyes, the south wind from the grove and the cuckoo singing night and day have kept his eyes from sleep, and asks whether a deceiver like him, wasted by infatuation, can now reach Murugan's blossoming feet. The praise names Vishnu who ate curd in the cowherds' homes and walked behind those who study Tamil, and Murugan as his nephew, at Parangiri where moon, sun and cloud move.
nuance: The love-sickness is told with the stock machinery of Tamil love poetry (moon, south wind, cuckoo, sleepless eyes), but its object is women in general and the speaker calls himself a deceiver (வஞ்சகன்). வண்டமிழ் பயில்வோர் பின் திரிகின்றவன் is Vishnu following a Tamil poet.

reading: The poet confesses that he has gone begging to people, praising them as lotus-handed, clouds in giving and the refuge of Tamil, his heart wounded and spinning like a top, and calls his body a swinging pot, a mass of suffering clay, a ship that sinks, a life of five senses; he asks Murugan to correct him in a moment and take him into service at his anklets. The praise names him the lone vel who set Brahma to create, Siva to destroy and Vishnu to protect, and ended the gods' fear, the son of Ganga at Parangundram, who folded his hands to the hunter girl in the millet field.
nuance: The confession is of a poet's trade: praising patrons in Tamil for gifts (தண்டமிழ்க்குத் தஞ்சம்). The plea is to exchange that service for தொண்டு, service at the Lord's feet. The body images (ஊசல் கடம், துன்ப மண் சடம், துஞ்சிடும் கலம்) stress its frailty. The praise also reverses rank: Murugan folds his hands before Valli.

reading: The poet describes the breasts, eyes and dark hair of women whom young men worship and confide in, women who undress and give the stronghold of pleasure, and calls himself a fool and madman caught by them; he asks for the lotus of Murugan's anklets to end the delusion of his mind. The praise names the vel that tore out the guts of the demon who hid in fear in the sea, the hunters' din in the millet field, and Murugan's embrace of the girl there, at Thiruparankundram.
nuance: இளைஞோர்கள் துதித்து முன் கும்பிட்டு: the young men worship the women, a reversal of worship that the plea sets right. The hunters' drum and horn syllables (குகுக்குகு, திதித்தி) fill two lines.

reading: The poet speaks of deceitful courtesans with mountainous breasts who take a man's wealth, quarrel and leave, and asks what he gains by wearing out his body after them, and whether Murugan's lotus feet will not love him. The praise names him Kandavel whom Brahma, Vishnu and Siva worship, the one of the Tamil mouth who set the hard Jains on great stakes, and the one who went to the hunter girl in the millet field, at Thiruparankundram.
nuance: பொருட்கவர்ந்து, taking wealth, marks them as courtesans. வன்சமணரைப் பெருந்திண்கழு மிசைக்கிடும் செந்தமிழ் அங்கவாயா identifies Murugan with the Tamil saint who defeated the Jains at Madurai (Sambandar, by tradition), a claim the book repeats.

reading: The poet speaks of women whose hair the bees follow and whose lips and breasts draw him until he falls into the pool of the navel, and asks to be joined to Murugan's feet with their anklets and bells. The praise names him the son of Siva who wears the boar's tusk, the tortoise shell, serpents and the gods' bones, the younger brother of the five-handed scholar, the lord of Vayalur who took the girl the hill people gave, at south Parangundram.
nuance: உந்தி என்கின்ற மடு, the pool called the navel, is the image of drowning. One word is corrupt; வயலூரா is clear from context.

reading: The poet describes courtesans who bewitch young men with breasts and smiles, invite them home, and while robbing them of wealth make them fall into their laps, and calls himself the small fool who trusted their false minds; he asks whether there is any thought of granting such a one grace. The praise names the vel, the hunter girl whom Murugan embraced, Rama who bridged the sea and slew Lanka's demons with one arrow as his uncle, and Murugan as Saravanabhava and guru, at Parangiri.
nuance: கணிகையர் தமதுபொய் மனத்தை நம்பிய: the fault is trusting, and the women's deceit and greed (வண்பொருள் கவர்பொழுதினில்) are the stock charge of the Kural and Naladiyar chapters on courtesans.

reading: The poet says that through women's breasts, bangled hands, eyes, lips and hair he has fallen into their power and is perishing like cotton in fire, and asks for Murugan's lotus feet with tinkling anklets so that he may cross the sea of bonds. The praise names the vel thrown at Sura, who harmed the gods and destroyed Indra's world, and at Krauncha, Vishnu with the conch as his uncle, and the hunter girl, at Thiruparankundram.
nuance: தொந்த வாரி, the sea of bonds, and கரையேற, to reach the shore: the feet are a crossing. One word is corrupt; புண்டரீகம் (lotus) is clear from context.

title: திருச்செந்தூர்
theme: First songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 1 of 6): the poet confesses his bondage to courtesans who invite, rob and expel, and to the body that rots and dies, imagines the hour of death and Yama's summons, and asks for Murugan's feet; the praise turns on Valli, Vishnu as uncle, Siva and Uma, and the shore of Senthil.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (21, 25 to 27, 29, 32, 33, 35), with 34 showing the same women aged; death songs (23, 28) and the decaying body (30); a love-lament in a mother's voice (24); and 22 and 31, which ask for inner vision and love rather than escape from women.
source_issues: Song 21: two corrupt characters, in வா஡ண (line 10, probably வாரீ, 'come') and வானு஡ (line 13, probably வானூடு); also the unflagged garble நநடுர் கேர்டுர் in line 22.
Song 33: unflagged garble மண்டுநநருர் (line 15); the source seems to use நந for a lost letter here and in 21.

reading: The poet gives the street talk of courtesans who stand at the crossroads pretending to fix their hair: 'Going without love? You came once and never again; what you gave before isn't enough, give today; come to my house', and asks not to fall in vain into these deceitful women's play. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Mayon, who became sky, wind, fire, water, earth, the seven worlds, you, I, Brahma, your Sankara and the gods, yet touches none of them, and the honey known to the hearts of those who live at Senthil.
nuance: The first half is reported speech, an unusual dramatic device: the courtesans' words are themselves the confession. In the praise, ஒன்றினும் கடை தோயா மாயோன, Vishnu who becomes everything without being touched by anything, is the pervasion of the Lord, here given to Vishnu as Murugan's uncle. Two words in the second half are garbled.

reading: The poet asks when, with Death turned back and the craving for women gone, the three gunas ended, day and night left behind and the senses' agitation cut, singing poems on the lotus feet and knowing Senthil and Kandan ever deeper, his mind will melt and dissolve, his speech end and his own action perish, so that he gains the vision of Murugan. The praise shows Indra crying 'refuge' and regaining his city, Devayanai gaining Murugan's arms, the demons dying, and the child Murugan toddling with bells and anklets ringing until Sankari's heart melts.
nuance: The plea moves by repeated doubled words (உணர்ந்துணர்ந்து, அறிந்தறிந்து, அழிந்தழிந்து), as if enacting the deepening it asks for. உரையொழித்து என் செயல் அழிந்து: the end of speech and of one's own agency is the goal, not escape from women alone. The praise ends with Murugan as a toddler (தளர்நடைச் சந்ததி), a tender picture rare in the battle-heavy praise.

reading: When the palm-leaf summons of Death, with his fanged and serpent-crowned retinue, arrives, the life faints, drums beat, kin wail, and the body is pushed through the streets; the poet asks whether his heart will not take fright at that departing path and, without the delusion 'this is ours', share even half a kunri seed or a grain of millet, instead of saying 'today, that day'. The praise shows Siva dancing with Uma, the crescent dripping nectar, the matted hair whirling and the drum sounding, and names Murugan the true guru whom that master of dance worships, at Senthil by the sea.
nuance: The remedy the plea draws from death is giving, not devotion: குன்றிப் பிளவளவு தினையளவு பங்கிட்டு உண்கை, to eat sharing even a split kunri seed or a millet grain. சமனோலை is Yama's written summons. In the praise Siva the dancer (பரதகுரு) worships Murugan the true guru (சற்குருநாதா).

reading: In the voice of a mother, the singer laments that her golden girl, wounded by Kama's lotus arrow, by the anril bird, the south wind and the crescent at evening, has given up all other joy and suffers from love; she asks whether those who bear daughters in this world should meet such a tiger of pleasure. The praise names Murugan the sweet one of the hunter girl, the one who prattled Tamil to explain the one thing to Siva of the konrai-hair, the vel that struck the golden peak, and the lord at Senthil dear to poets of fine speech.
nuance: This is akam poetry, a foster-mother's or mother's lament for a girl in love with the god, and there is no confession of the poet's own. The machinery is classical: the paired anril bird, the south wind, the crescent at dusk. கொன்றைச் சடையற்கு ஒன்றைத் தெரியக் கொஞ்சித் தமிழைப் பகர்வோனே: Murugan explains 'the one' to Siva in Tamil, again the teaching of 6 and 12.

tamil: அருணமணி மேவு பூஷித ம்ருகமத படீர லேபன
அளிகுலவு மாதர் லீலையின் முழுகியபி ஷேக மீதென
இருணிறைய மோதி மாலிகை சருவி யுறவான வேளையி
இரவுபகல் மோக னாகியெ படியில்மடி யாமல் யானுமுன்
தருணமணி யாட ராவணி குடிலசடி லாதி யோதிய
தருமுருக மேக சாயலர் தமரமக ராழி சூழ்புவி
செருமுதலி மேவு மாவலி யதிமதக போல மாமலை
திருமருக சூரன் மார்பொடு சிலையுருவ வேலை யேவிய
reading: The poet describes the bejewelled, musk-scented women in whose play he bathed as if in ritual, their hair loosened and ornaments slipping in the dark, and asks that, no longer deluded night and day, he be given fine words in his heart to sing Murugan's paired feet and live. The praise names Siva of the serpent and matted hair, source of the four Vedas, and Vishnu, the cloud-hued one who answered the elephant that first thought of him crying 'Root!', and calls Murugan the victorious Saravana whose vel pierced Sura's chest and the hill, at Senthil.
nuance: அபிஷேக மீதென: the poet calls his bathing in women's play an abhisheka, a sacred bath, an irony. The plea is for the gift of song (செஞ்சொல்), as in 2. The elephant crying மூலமே is the story of Gajendra. The lines on Vishnu gathering up the sea-girt earth and sharing nectar with the gods are hard to divide.

reading: The poet asks that he not end in the false play of embraces with women whose ear-ornaments wound like spears, and that, with birth ended, he think in his heart on the kadamba-adorned, anklet-bearing feet; he asks Murugan to look with love on the sorrow of one whose love and understanding have gone. The praise calls him the true guru who wondrously showed the form of Siva to the one who conquered with fire the Kama whose flower arrows frightened even ascetics, and the lord of Senthil where the sea casts conch-pearls and the sun's chariot stumbles.
nuance: The praise appears to tell of Siva burning Kama (தழலெழ வென்றார்) and of Murugan showing Siva his own form (சிவவடிவம் காட்டும் சற்குருபர); the phrases in between (தென்காற் கன்றில் திரிதரு கஞ்சாக் கன்று) are obscure and the reading is tentative.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women, hair loosened, faces sweating, nails and lips, and asks that, seeing clearly how to leave that embrace, he be given the cool lotus feet with anklets that those of Sivayoga who melt in jnana contemplate. The praise names Siva, son-giver, who drank the poison when Brahma, Vishnu the father of Kama, Indra and the gods cried 'Hara Hara Siva Sankara', and Vishnu who churned the sea as Murugan's uncle, at Senthil, a town of plantain, turmeric and ginger.
nuance: சிவயோகத்து உருகு ஞான பரம்பர தந்திர அறிவினோர்: the feet are those that yogis and jnanis hold in mind, so the plea sets the yoga of Siva against the embrace. இரதி வேள் பணி தந்தை is Vishnu, father of Kama (Rati's lord).

reading: The poet asks that Death, like fire, not call him while his mind fails, delusion grows, speech goes, eyes roll, the body's fire dies and its filth flows, and his mother and kin weep in fear by the bed; and that, with the two deeds, the instruments and the senses gone, he be given the boon of drawing near the high feet. The praise names Murugan the one who spoke sweet Tamil to delight the sage of Pothiyai, equal to Siva, the vel thrown at Nirudan whose rule harried the sun, moon, Yama, Indra, Agni, Nirruti, Kubera, Vishnu and Brahma, and the child who grew in the laps of Siva and Uma, at the shore of Senthil.
nuance: The death is told from the body outward, eyes rolling and filth flowing, then to the weeping mother at the bedside. இருவினை கரணம் மருவுபுலன் ஒழிய names what must fall away. பொதியவரை முநிவன் is Agastya, whom Murugan taught Tamil.

reading: The poet speaks of the tender-footed women with gem-set breasts and calls himself the sinner who presses his face to them, a wretch of deeds, an insulted fool who saw great wealth, a ruin who loves flesh, a deluded man who does not walk in dharma, and asks whether he will gain grace if Murugan calls him and gives him his sandals. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea and cut Ravana's heads with one arrow as his uncle, Siva who wears the moon, the serpent, Ganga and flowers as his father, and Murugan as Valli's lover, the champion at Thiruchendur.
nuance: The heap of self-abuse (வினைச் சண்டாளன், வீணன், நிர்மூடன், பாழன், மோக விகாரன், மூதேவி) is a set feature of the book. உன் பாதுகை நீ தர, 'that you give your sandals', recalls Rama's sandals, given just before in the praise. விடக்கு அன்பாய் நுகர் may mean loving to eat flesh, or the flesh of the body enjoyed in lust.

tamil: அனைவரு மருண்ட ருண்டு கடிதென வெகுண்டி யம்ப
அழுகுபிணி கொண்டு விண்டு புழுவுட னெலும்ப லம்பு
மனைதொறு மிதம்ப கர்ந்து வரவர விருந்த ருந்தி
மறைசதுர் விதந்தெ ரிந்து வகைசிறு சதங்கை கொஞ்ச
தினைமிசை சுகங்க டிந்த புனமயி லிளங்கு ரும்பை
ஜெகமுழுது முன்பு தும்பி முகவனொடு தந்தை முன்பு
இனியகனி மந்தி சிந்து மலைகிழவ செந்தில் வந்த
எழுகடலு மெண்சி லம்பும் நிசிசரரும் அஞ்ச அஞ்சு
reading: The poet speaks of carrying this wretched body, which stinks like a corpse, rots in disease, splits and rattles with worms and bones, while all who see it flee and Death follows behind, and of going from house to house speaking sweetly and eating whatever feast comes; he asks when, freed from that disgrace and knowing the four Vedas, he will bow at the flower feet with tinkling bells. The praise names the girl guarding the millet who chased away parrots, Murugan who circled the whole world on his golden peacock before the elephant-faced one and his father, and who told the frightened gods not to fear.
nuance: பிணநாறும் அழுகு பிணி ... புழுவுடன் எலும்பு அலம்பும் அவல உடல்: the body is already a corpse while alive. ஜெகமுழுது ... திகிரி வலம் வந்த is the circling of the world in the contest for the fruit (see 3).

reading: A short song: the poet asks not to tire himself and wander thinking night and day over a fitting woman praised in poetry and song, but to bathe in the sea of bliss of Murugan's high compassion and be given the love that knows him within. The praise names Murugan who bowed to and embraced the hunter girl guarding the millet field, the life of Senthil that is like Kailasa, the younger brother of the elephant-faced one.
nuance: உனை எனதுள் அறியும் அன்பு: the love asked for is one that knows the Lord inside the self. இயலிசையில் உசித வஞ்சி may also mean the deceit of poetry and song, so whether the first line speaks of a woman or of art is uncertain.

tamil: இருகுழை யெறிந்த கெண்டைகள் ஒருகுமி ழடர்ந்து வந்திட
இருளளக பந்தி வஞ்சியி லிருகலையு டன்கு லைந்திட
முழுமதிபு ரிந்த சிந்துர அரிவையரு டன்க லந்திடு
எரிவிடநி மிர்ந்த குஞ்சியி னிலவொடு மெழுந்த கங்கையு
இமவரைத ருங்க ருங்குயில் மரகதநி றந்த ருங்கிளி
அரைவட மலம்பு கிண்கிணி பரிபுர நெருங்கு தண்டைக
அகமகிழ்வு கொண்டு சந்ததம் வருகுமர முன்றி லின்புறம்
reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women whose eyes dart to their earrings and whose breasts are scented with sandal and kumkum, and makes an obscure request about the ill-fortune (முகடி) of mingling with them. The praise names Murugan the great treasure of Uma, the dark cuckoo of the Himalaya and green parrot whom Sankara loves, and the child who comes on the peacock with jingling bells, at the sea-washed courtyard of Senthil.
nuance: முகடியும் நலம் பிறந்திட அருள்வாயே: முகடி is the goddess of ill fortune (மூதேவி); the line may ask that even this ill fortune turn to good, or be divided otherwise. The praise centres on Uma (த்ரியம்பகி) more than on Murugan.

reading: The poet lists the courtesans' arts, loosening their hair, slipping their garments, looking from the corners of their eyes, asking for betel, laughing, calling 'come to our house', taking a man to bed and melting him while his wealth lasts, then, when it ends, beating him and driving him out if he enters; he asks when he will praise Murugan's feet and be rid of the blame of these one-sided unions. The praise is a long picture of the mountain stream in Valli's millet field, and names Murugan the life of Senthil, who gave the shastras to Siva with the crescent in his hair, the lord of ascetics.
nuance: ஒருதலை மருவு புணர்ச்சித் தூர்த்தர்கள்: the classical term for one-sided love is turned on the courtesan's bed, where only one side loves. வருபொருள் அளவில் ... வனைமனை புகுதில் அடித்துப் போக்கவும்: love lasting exactly as long as the money is the stock charge against courtesans. One word in the praise (மண்டுநநருர்) is garbled.

reading: The poet pictures the women once desired as they age: hair dark as a rain cloud turns grey like cotton, the spear-like eyes gather rheum like curdled sour curd and smell of flesh, the breasts that rivalled an elephant's temples become skin; he asks whether, understanding the state of women whose beauty perishes, he will not think of servanthood at Murugan's feet. The praise shows Brahma, Vishnu, Siva and Indra bowing to Murugan, who drank the milk-nectar from the breast of the Mother of all worlds, at Senthil where the conches roll in on the waves.
nuance: The argument against desire is decay rather than deceit: each charm is matched to its ruin (ஓதி நரை பஞ்சுபோல், விழி பீளை, கொங்கை தோல்). The plea names the remedy as வழியடிமை, hereditary servitude to the feet.

reading: The poet asks whether he will set his desire on women who talk tenderly, snatch coins, rage with rolling eyes, carry great blame, wound like serpents and measure the heart by the coin; he asks Murugan to rule him sweetly each day by grace, as one who calls his devotees with gracious eyes and talks with them. The praise names Siva who wears the aththi flower as his father, Vishnu the red light of the world whom ascetics and Vedic priests praise as his uncle, and the lord at Thiruchendur of rice fields, cane groves and plantains.
nuance: காசளவே மனம் உறைக்கும் தூரிகள்: their hearts are weighed exactly to the coin. The plea pictures the Lord's grace as intimacy, calling devotees and talking with them (அழைத்துஞ் சேதிகள் பேசிய).

title: திருச்செந்தூர்
theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 2 of 6): the poet confesses his bondage to women, many of them named as selling themselves for money, and to the body as a hut of guts and blood that ends on the bier, and asks for Murugan's feet, his company of devotees, and his coming on the peacock when Death's messengers arrive; the praise turns on the hunter girl, the vel against Sura, Vishnu as uncle and Murugan as Siva's teacher.
structure_note: Courtesan and lust songs (37, 39 to 41, 43 to 45, 47, 49, 50), the body and death (38, 42, 46, 48), and two self-accusing pleas (36, 40). 41, 42 and 49 are in a dense chiming rhythm of short syllables that is hard to divide; 43 gives its praise to Krishna's flute; 48 ends on சூராந்தகனே, not பெருமாளே.
source_issues: Song 47: corrupt character in கடலு஡டே (line 7), probably கடலூடே; the CORRUPT_CHARS field flags it. Also தட்முழ்கி (line 2), probably தடமூழ்கி, unflagged.
Song 39: unflagged garble மிக்முழ்கி (line 10), probably மிகமூழ்கி; the source seems to write ்மு for மூ here and in 47.
Song 48 ends சூராந்தகனே and song 50 தம்பிரானே rather than பெருமாளே; this is the text, not an error, but the shrine is named only within the praise.

reading: The poet heaps names on himself, one who joined women with arrow-like eyes, faulty, a fool who keeps to no path, base, wasted, wholly ignorant, dull, sick with diseases wrapped in great deeds, without truth, and asks Murugan not to scorn him but to give him one day his cool feet with jewelled anklets so that he may have a life. The praise names the leader on the peacock who sought out and joined in the forest the hunter girl of whom Narada spoke, the little son of the Devi, the supreme mother with honeyed speech, at Thiruchiralaivay (Senthil) under its high groves.
nuance: The plea is almost entirely a list of accusative self-names (ஏதனை மூடனை ... ஈனனை வீணனை ... ஏழையை மோழையை ... வாய்மையிலாதனை), each one the object of இகழாதே, 'do not scorn'. ஏடெழுதா முழு ஏழை may mean one who cannot write a single leaf, i.e. unlettered. Narada (நாரதனார் புகல் குறமாதை) is named as the one who told of Valli.

reading: In a run of clipped two-syllable words the poet speaks of wandering women who, without thinking or looking, come with their charms until life faints, sulk as if without goodness and give an unreachable delusion, and asks not to be shaken within by them but to be given grace without Murugan's word swerving. The praise names the unbeaten warrior who pierced the hill, the vel that made deceitful Sura flee to the eight directions, the one dear to the konrai-wearing father who rides the bull, and the sweet-spoken son easy to his lovers, at Senthil.
nuance: எட்டாமால் தந்திட்டு உழல்மாதர்: the women give a delusion (மால்) that cannot be reached or ended. The plea நின்சொல் கோடாது என் கைக்கு அருள் தாராய் may ask that the Lord's promise not bend; the clipped rhythm makes most of the first half hard to divide.

reading: The poet pictures the end: beauty gone, the body slack, the senses fail and it becomes a corpse; some lift the bier, great drums beat in order, the children follow rolling on the ground, and then leave it on the road; he asks whether he will escape this false life and know how to reach Murugan's feet. The praise is a battle scene: Krauncha split, the sea dried, the demons' crowns falling, headless trunks and vultures dancing in pools of blood, and Murugan at Senthil who saw the fruit of the knowledge of the true faith.
nuance: மித்தை is mithya, the false or unreal: the whole sequence of death and mourning is named as the illusion to escape. கிடஞ்சம் கிடஞ்சம் is the drum's own sound. சற்சமய வித்தைப் பலன் கண்டு, 'having seen the fruit of the learning of the true religion', may refer to Murugan's victory over other faiths.

tamil: கண்டுமொழி கொம்பு கொங்கை வஞ்சியிடை யம்பு நஞ்சு
கண்டுவளம்வ ருந்தி நொந்து மங்கையர்வ சம்பு ரிந்து
பண்டைவினை கொண்டு ழன்று வெந்துவிழு கின்றல் கண்டு
பண்புடைய சிந்தை யன்பர் தங்களினு டன்க லந்து
வண்டுபடு கின்ற தொங்கல் கொண்டறநெ ருங்கி யிண்டு
வஞ்சியை முனிந்த கொங்கை மென்குறம டந்தை செங்கை
திண்டிறல்பு னைந்த அண்டர் தங்களப யங்கள் கண்டு
reading: The poet confesses calling women's speech sugar-candy, their waists creepers and their eyes arrows and poison, and living night and day under their sway, burning in old deeds by fate; he asks Murugan, seeing him fall, to give his lotus feet and come saying 'fear not, fear not', so that he may join the loving devotees who sing his praise and gain their nature. The praise names the jewelled chest that the hunter girl embraced, the one who, seeing the gods' plea for refuge, rode the peacock to war, conquered the demons, married on the hill and came to Senthil.
nuance: The remedy asked is company: பண்புடைய சிந்தை யன்பர் தங்களினுடன் கலந்து பண்புபெற, to mix with devotees and so take on their nature. விதியாலே பண்டைவினை கொண்டு names both fate and old deeds as the force behind his bondage. குன்றிடை மணம் புணர்ந்து may be the marriage to Devayanai on a hill.

reading: The poet asks not to be deluded by women whom even Lakshmi cannot equal, with sandal on their breasts, eyes skilled in stealth and fragrant dark hair, but to reach a pure mind, learn and understand virtue, wealth and pleasure fully, and having left them, know grace itself; for this he asks the feet with ringing anklets. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess (Kumari, Kali, Sankari, Gauri, Ambika, Kundali, Uma) and of Ganapati with the mouse, and names Murugan as the younger brother whom the moon-crowned Siva delights in, at Senthil of plantain, turmeric and ginger.
nuance: அறம் பொருள் இன்பமும் அடைய ஓதி உணர்ந்து தணந்தபின் அருள்தானே அறியுமாறு: the three aims of life are to be learnt fully and then left, and only then is grace known, an order that sets the Lord's grace above and after the three. The Goddess's names include குடிலை and குண்டலி, Tantric names of her power.

reading: The poet describes women with breasts like elephant tusks and golden pots, swinging earrings and conch-like throats, whom he calls women for hire, who tire, then laugh, call a man and feign longing, and asks whether he must wander here suffering for their breasts. The praise names the vel that crushed the demons and broke the hill while the gods praised, the one who gives his devotees the virtue of the bowed head, the joined hands, the kadamba garland, Siva and austerity, and the lord at Senthil who sleeps on the breasts of the hunter girl and of Indra's daughter.
nuance: சம்பளமாதர், 'women of wages', names the courtesans as paid, and சண் பசப்பும் is their feigned pallor of love. சிரப்பண்பும் கரப்பண்பும் ... சிவப்பண்பும் தவப்பண்பும் தருவோனே: Murugan gives the marks of worship of head and hands as well as inner qualities. The chiming short-syllable rhythm makes many divisions uncertain.

reading: The poet speaks of the womb-born body of blood and sores, melted by women whom he follows, mingles with, quarrels with and is tangled with, reeling, until Yama comes with his staff and the world takes fright and he dies; he asks Murugan to see his confusion, save him, break the prison of the body of birth, and give the joy of his feet. The praise names the bright vel that killed the demon in the clear sea where the sun moves, Kumaresa at Senthil where waves cast up conches, the son of Sankari, of Sankara and of Ganga, who sleeps on the hunter girl's breasts.
nuance: பிறப்பங்கம் சிறைப்பங்கம் சிதைத்து: the body given by birth is a prison to be broken, not reformed. Ganga is named as one of his parents (கங்கையட்கும் சுதன்), from the story of Siva's sparks carried to the reed pool. The middle lines (செருத்தண்டம் தரித்தண்டம் ...) are hard to divide.

reading: The poet describes the courtesans: breasts flowing with sandal, eyes of poison mixed with nectar, quarrelsome with anyone, leading moneyless youths astray and leaving them spent, mocking all in the street, giving love by exactly the measure of the money, melting in bed for great wealth, ready to embrace even a corpse, drunk on liquor; he asks for grace to leave all ties with them. The praise is a picture of Krishna's flute, at whose music the tiger cub drinks the cow's milk and the calf the tigress's, mountains melt, dry trees sprout and birds come down, and names Murugan the nephew who delights that cloud-dark one, at the shore of Senthil.
nuance: பிளவு பெறில் அதில் அளவளவு ஒழுகியர்: given a scrap, they give just that much. பிணமும் அணைபவர், 'they would embrace even a corpse', turns the courtesan's indifference into an image of death. The Krishna passage, with its reversal of nature (கழை = flute, ஏழ் தொளை = seven holes), is the longest single myth in these songs and is given to Vishnu, not Murugan.

tamil: கனங்கள் கொண்ட குந்த ளங்க ளுங்கு லைந்த லைந்து விஞ்சு
கரங்க ளுங்கு விந்து நெஞ்ச கங்க ளுங்க சிந்தி டுங்க
பொனின்கு டங்க ளஞ்சு மென்த னங்க ளும்பு யங்க ளும்பொ
புணர்ந்து டன்பு லர்ந்து பின்க லந்த கங்கு ழைந்த வம்பு
அனங்க னெந்து நைந்து வெந்து குந்து சிந்த அன்று கண்தி
அடர்ந்த டர்ந்தெ திர்ந்து வந்த வஞ்ச ரஞ்ச வெஞ்ச மம்பு
சினங்கள் கொண்டி லங்கை மன்சி ரங்கள் சித்த வெஞ்ச ரத்தெ
சிவந்த செஞ்ச தங்கை யுஞ்சி லம்பு தண்டை யும்பு னைந்து
reading: The poet describes women born to name their price, hair loosened, eyes reddened, hands joined, hearts melting, joining with seeming love, friendship and kindness, uniting, tiring and mingling again, and asks whether he must forever suffer wandering so. The praise names the vel given by the dark-throated Siva who opened his eye and burnt Kama, Murugan the friend of devotees who fought the deceivers, the nephew of Rama whose arrow burnt the heads of Lanka's king, and Kandha who came to Senthil in red anklets.
nuance: பிறந்து விலைகூறி: the women are 'born to quote a price', and the love, friendship and kindness (அன்பு நண்பு பண்பு) they show are part of the sale. The praise sets Siva burning Kama (அனங்கன்) beside the plea against lust.

reading: The poet speaks of women whose eyes defeat the young deer, with lotus-bud breasts and night-dark hair, who bargain to strip a man of all his wealth and make him trust them, and asks Murugan to look with grace on one who, playing with them, wastes away like a frog that has eaten poison. The praise names Kumaresa, the guru, who rode the peacock with the red-eyed serpent in its beak and killed the demon army, at Senthil of areca, coconut and ponds where monkeys dance.
nuance: நன்று பொருள் தீர என்று விலை பேசி: the bargaining is aimed at the man's wealth running out. நஞ்சுபுசி தேரை: the frog that has eaten poison and wastes away is a fresh image for the lover.

reading: The poet asks that before Death's cruel messengers bind his feet with the noose and drag him off, and before loving sons and mothers follow wailing to the burning ground, Murugan come before him on the peacock, with trident, sword, club, red cock, bow, shoulders, chest and pure anklets, so he may see him with longing. The praise names Vishnu, who gave nectar to the gods when they feared the poison Siva took and who sleeps on the roaring sea, as his uncle, and Murugan the life of Senthil who hurled the vel so that Sura fell.
nuance: The plea is for sight at the hour of death (காண ஆர்வம் செயும்), and it lists the Lord's weapons and body one by one as what he wants to see. The cock (சேவல்) appears here among the weapons, as the banner.

reading: The poet confesses bowing to women, sinking in the pool of the navel, drinking the nectar of lily lips, and drowning in a sea of pleasure among those with cloud-dark hair and breasts scented with aloe and camphor, and asks Murugan gently to bring him to shore and give his golden anklets. The praise names him the one who told the one thing to Siva, whose measure Brahma could not find and who bathes in Ganga reaching to the sky's sphere, and the lord of Senthil where waves throw pearls onto towers, walls and streets.
nuance: The plea uses the sea of births image (இன்பக் கடலூடே அமிழுவேனை ... கரைசேர்த்து) for the sea of pleasure. கம்பர்க்கு ஒன்றைப் புகல்வோனே is the teaching of Siva (here as கம்பர், the lord of Kanchi), though Om is not named. The opening, குகர மேவு மெய்த் துறவினின் மறவா, seems to set the true renunciation of cave-dwellers against the poet's bowing to women, but its sense is unclear.

reading: The poet calls his body a rough hut of guts, fat, bone, water, filth, blood, nerves, pus and flesh wrapped in skin, which he carries about with fondness, wearying himself among women whose dark eyes are Kama's arrows until his understanding fails, and asks Murugan to remove that nature, give his paired feet and rule him. The praise names Murugan the lord of Senthil on whose arms the hunter girl lives, who circled the world on the peacock, who took up the vel in one hand to pierce the hill, and the destroyer of Sura who stood in the sea.
nuance: The list குடர் நிணம் என்பு ... குருதி நரம்பு ... தோல் is the stock anatomy of disgust, set against the poet's own fondness (குனகி மகிழ்ந்து) for this hut. The song ends on சூராந்தகனே, 'ender of Sura', without the usual பெருமாளே.

reading: The poet speaks of women with sandal and kumkum on their breasts and red carp eyes that call, and of himself toiling in the sorrowful pot of the body, eating and enjoying until the body-lump grows fat, and asks not to wander so but to be joined to the red feet with bells brighter than the rising sun. The praise names Siva with konrai on his golden hair, Sankari who shares his side, Murugan whose strong arms delight the elephant's daughter and the deer's daughter, and the lord at Senthil where conches roll from the sea.
nuance: உடற்பிண்டம் பருத்து: the body fattened by feasting is the image of waste. குஞ்சரக் கொம்பும் கலைக் கொம்பும் appear to be Devayanai, raised by the elephant, and Valli, born of a doe. Like 41, the song is in a chiming short-syllable rhythm and many divisions are guesses.

reading: The poet describes women with shaking breasts, bangles, bee-haunted hair, voices like cuckoos and parrots and eyes like fish, who infatuate even the vidyadharas, and asks that he, suffering in sickness and thoughts of birth, be ruled so as to reach Murugan's shining feet. The praise is a battle with drums and conches in which the Suras fall and the sea burns at the vel's smile, and names Murugan the king in whom the Vedas delight as the guru Sankara loved, who delights in the hunter girl at Senthil praised by Sambhu.
nuance: சங்கரன் உகந்த பரிவின் குரு எனும் சுருதி: the Vedas themselves call him the guru Siva loved, a reference to the teaching myth without naming Om. The song ends on தம்பிரானே rather than பெருமாளே.

title: திருச்செந்தூர்
theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 3 of 6): the poet asks to be freed from infatuation with women and courtesans who seek money, from the body of the five elements, from the kin who crowd the deathbed, and from praising petty patrons, and asks for the feet, for daily worship and service, and for Murugan to face Death on his behalf; he also scorns poets who sing love-sickness without naming Senthil.
structure_note: Courtesan and lust songs (51 to 54, 56 to 58, 65); the body and death (61, 63); the poet's craft, against praising men (55, 60) and against love poems that leave out Senthil (64); a doctrinal question in Saiva terms (59); and a song of longing to see Murugan's form (62). 57 and 58 share a run of epithets ending -க்கார.
source_issues: Song 53: corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 21), probably வயலூரா (Vayalur); flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS.
Song 57: corrupt character in வச்சிரகி஡ணடநிகர் (line 9), probably வச்சிர கிரீட நிகர் with ஡ண for ரீ; flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS.
Song 59: corrupt character in நீலக்஡ணபகலாபத் (line 11), probably நீலக்ரீப கலாப ('blue-necked, plumed') with ஡ண for ரீ; flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS.
Song 56: unflagged garble செர்ரு பம் (line 7), probably சொரூபம்.

reading: In clipped rhythm the poet speaks of women with breasts, cloud-dark hair, eyes like konrai arrows and carp and parrot speech, who meet men at the ends of streets, and asks not to be entangled with them but to have Murugan set his feet on his head. The praise is obscure: it seems to tell of the demon who left his army and fled into the sea, and names the lord at Senthil who keeps tenderness in his heart.
nuance: என்றன் தலையில் சந்தப் பதம் வைத்தருள்வாயே: the feet placed on the head, the gesture of the guru's initiation. சந்தப்படி may also mean 'in the rhythm of the song'. Most of the praise cannot be divided with confidence.

reading: The poet describes himself in a long series of names: one who drinks women's lips, wounded by their nails, a sinner, without knowledge, path or virtue, a man who never melts with love crying 'Senthil' and has given nothing, and asks whether Murugan will not give him his two small lotus feet with love. The praise names the peacock that tears the serpent, the vel that splits the demons joint by joint, and Siva the eight-qualitied, formless ancient Lord who burnt the three cities, with Ganga, konrai and crescent in his hair and the bull for his mount; and Murugan as the master of Tamil to whom Uma gave her breast, whom Sankara worships.
nuance: கவுரி உமை கொங்கை தந்து அன்புறும் தமிழ் விரக: the Tamil master who drank Uma's breast milk is Sambandar's story, here given to Murugan. எண்குணன் for Siva is the Kural's epithet for the Lord. Several words in the first half (செஞ்செநீடும், அண்டுஞ்சகன்) are unclear.

reading: The poet asks not to be dazzled by women's breasts with sandal, kumkum and ornaments and their hair with water-lily garlands, but to sing daily 'Lord of the gods, namo nama; my Lord, namo nama; lover of the bangled one, namo nama', do proper worship with love and not waste his days. The praise names the Goddess, who danced like a spinning top, queen of ghouls, Kali, Yogini, holding the trident, who saw the war with drink-sodden Sura and blessed her son with the victorious vel, and Murugan as lord of Vayalur, Visakha, and the life of Senthil who saves the poet.
nuance: The plea contains its own litany: the நமோநம lines are the praise the poet asks to be able to sing. The vel is given by the Goddess (எம்புதல்வா வாழி வாழி எனும்படி வீறான வேல்தர), which ties it to Shakti. Vayalur, another shrine, is named among the epithets.

reading: The poet calls himself a dog who drank the lips of women with breasts like a killer elephant's temples and melted in infatuation, and asks whether, with the cares that destroy him ended and the eye of grace on him, he will hold Murugan's flower feet in mind and come to cling to him. The praise names the child of red words graced by Siva whose bow is the northern mountain, the vel that killed the demon from the sea, the lover of the hunter girl and the rider of the emerald peacock.
nuance: நின் பற்று அடைவேனோ: the plea is for attachment, but attachment to the Lord, after attachment to women. செஞ்சொல் சிறுபாலா may point to Sambandar, again identified with Murugan, but that is uncertain.

reading: The poet asks not to wander praising women's conch-necks, coral mouths, pearl teeth and mountain breasts, nor to go to the men of the world telling them like a mother 'you are the noble Vel, you are the golden cloud of red hands', but, his sorrow and disease scattered, to say one word of service: 'good Kanda Vel'. The praise names Siva who took the poison and gave the gods nectar and dances in the great hall, before whom red-eyed Vishnu won the bright discus, and Murugan the red-Tamil lord of Senthil whom that moon-crowned Siva loves.
nuance: The patron is flattered as Murugan himself (துங்கவேள்) and as a cloud for his giving: the poet asks to keep those names for the Lord alone. செங்கண்மால் பங்கயக் கண் ... கதிராழி appears to be Vishnu offering his lotus eye to Siva and receiving the discus, though the line is compressed.

reading: The poet calls himself a deceiver without shame, his heart full of agitation, puffed with the pomp of sandal and kumkum, and asks not to suffer in vain from the body's infatuation with women's breasts, but that Guha come with the splendour of his own form and rule him with love. The praise names the son of the Ganga-bearing lord, Kandha, who saved Indra's worlds from trembling, the hero of Indra's cause, the vel that killed Sura, and the lord at Senthil whom Vishnu and Brahma worship.
nuance: நின் சொரூப ப்ரகாசம் கொடே வந்து: the plea asks for the Lord's own form shining, a vision rather than a gift. The opening (சங்கைதான் ஒன்றுதான் இன்றியே) could mean without doubt or without shame, and the self-description is uncertain.

reading: The poet heaps comparisons on women's eyes, the seven roaring seas, honey, arrows, the shakti spear, the mango slice, the lily, lotus, poison and the leaping fish, and on their breasts, like a rutting elephant's temples, hung with pearls; he asks when, the delusion laid on them gone, Murugan will come on his diamond peacock for this poor servant to do him devotion. The praise is a chain of epithets ending -க்கார: holder of the vel in twelve hands, lord of the devotees' hymns, lover of the hunter girl, scourge of the demons, protector of the good, speaker of words that free devotees, expert in the three Tamils, lord at sea-girt Senthil.
nuance: The plea is a catalogue: piling the conventional comparisons is the infatuation itself, which the poet then asks to leave (வைத்த கொடிதான மயல் விட்டு). அடியார்கள் முத்திபெற வேசொல் வசனக்கார: Murugan is the one whose word gives release to devotees.

reading: The poet describes women scented with sandal, civet, camphor, kumkum and musk, in silk and diamonds, who seek money with great desire, cruel and deceitful at heart, whose glance of feigned longing withers his mind, and asks when Murugan will think to come and take him into service. The praise, again a chain of -க்கார epithets, names the guardian of Indra's city, the rider of the peacock, the ever-young, the lover of the hunter girl, Uma's son, the master of the four kinds of verse, the strength of the vel, the one easy for devotees, the glory of mantra teaching, at Senthil.
nuance: பொருள் தேடுமதி நிட்டூர வஞ்சக விசார இதய: money-seeking, cruel and deceitful hearts, the courtesan named by her motive. நாலுகவிதைக்கார, master of the four kinds of poetry, and மந்த்ர உபதேச மகிமைக்கார, glory of teaching the mantra, make Murugan both poet and guru.

reading: Rather than a plea, the poet asks a question: why do some, without loving the lotus feet the endless Vedas proclaim and without care for virtue, waste away in lust, anger and greed, in the changes of the elements, in the body of maya, in the bonds of soul and fetter? The praise names the warrior of the kadamba on the blue-necked peacock, whose war raised dust from Meru, son of the Mother who gives Sivaloka to those who keep the fire rite, the master who taught the way of yoga, lord of the silent gods.
nuance: The vocabulary is Saiva Siddhanta: பசு பாசம், மாயாகாயம், and the three faults காம க்ரோத லோப. The song asks a question (அது என்கொலோ தான்) instead of confessing. ஓமத் தீ வழுவார்கட்கு ஊர் சிவலோகத்தே தரு names the fire rite as a path to Sivaloka. ஊமைத் தேவர்கள் is unclear.

reading: The poet speaks of craving women with fragrant hair and golden breasts, joining them and leaving mantra, faith and prayer, and asks whether, ceasing to praise impure fools who wander the earth deceiving, he will adorn himself with Murugan's flower feet and worship. The praise is given in drum syllables for the dancing peacock and names the vel that destroyed the demons, the son of the mountain's daughter, and the lover of the hunter girl, at Senthil.
nuance: புநிதமிலி மாந்தர் தங்கள் புகழ்பகர்தல் நீங்கி: the poet gives up praising patrons, as in 55. The lines on studying Sangam Tamil poems (தாந்த்ரி சங்கத் தமிழ் பனுவல் ஆய்ந்து) may describe the poet himself or the men he praised; the reference is unclear.

reading: The poet calls himself a dog whose heart is set on women with cloud-dark hair full of honey and bees, and asks Murugan to come and give his golden feet before this false hut of earth, water, fire, wind and sky falls apart and goes to the harsh burning ground. The praise names Kumaresa who killed famous Sura, the lord of the fragrant hill where bees sing, and Kandha the son at Senthil.
nuance: மண் தோயம் தீ மென்கால் விண் தோய் வண் காயம் பொய்க் குடில்: the body is a false hut of the five elements, which come apart at death. Parts of the praise (கண்டா கும்பால் உண்டாய்) are unclear.

reading: The poet asks whether Murugan will not appear before him, so that his eyes are cooled, with anklets and bells ringing, as when he once danced with joy and embraced his father, with kadamba, crowns, lotus hands, vel, eyes and faces. The praise names the form that grew like a golden mountain to fill the worlds in battle until even Brahma's father (Vishnu) was amazed, the dance he dances at Senthil and before the poet himself, and the lord whom Agastya worships.
nuance: There is no confession here, only longing for sight (கண்குளிர என்றன்முன் சந்தியாவோ). செந்திலிலும் என்றன் முன் கொஞ்சி நடனங் கொளும்: the poet says Murugan dances before him, a claim of vision. The cosmic form (பொன்கிரியெனச் சிறந்து எங்கினும் வளர்ந்து) is Murugan's, not Vishnu's.

reading: The poet lists the kin who gather at death, mothers who fed and stroked him, brothers, servants, sisters, nephews, sons and wives, with their claims, and asks that when Death himself comes pressing on a buffalo, Murugan come on the strong peacock saying 'fear not' and tell that Death, 'Kandha says this man is our devotee'. The praise names the warrior whose peacock delights Uma, and the lord at Senthil of Siva who wears the moon, the serpent and the river.
nuance: அந்த மறலியொடு கந்த மனிதன் நமது அன்பன் என மொழிய: the plea is not only for Murugan to come but for him to speak to Death and claim the man as his own. The kin are pictured with the debts and claims they bring (கடனுதவு), so they offer no help.

reading: The poet scorns some who sit singing a few poor poems about a girl whose garment slips, who pines struck by Kama's arrows and is bewildered by the little southern breeze and burnt by the crescent, and do not know to speak of Thiruchendur and be saved. The praise names Murugan the guru who gave grace both to Siva, whose feet and crown Vishnu, Brahma and the Vedas could not know, and to the sage Agastya, and the lord who destroyed the demon's kin.
nuance: The love-sickness of the girl, with Kama's arrow, the south wind and the crescent, is the stock of akam verse; the complaint is against poems that spend these devices without naming the shrine. அரற்கும் ... கும்பநன் முநிக்கும் க்ருபை வரிக்கும் குருபர: Murugan as teacher both of Siva and of Agastya.

reading: The poet asks not to go near the agitation of women, which leaves the body wasted and suffering and love and goodness forgotten, but to be given the lotus feet the gods worship, so he may cry 'refuge' and do service forever. The praise names the younger one who, seeing the feet of the hunter girl who shares his side, cried 'refuge', stood behind her and bowed, and the lord at Senthil where valampuri conches throng the golden shore.
nuance: தஞ்சம் is said twice: the poet asks to cry 'refuge' at the Lord's feet, and the praise has the Lord crying 'refuge' at Valli's feet and bowing (கும்பிடும்). The devotee's surrender is mirrored in the god's surrender to his beloved.

title: திருச்செந்தூர்
theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 4 of 6): the poet confesses bondage to courtesans who lure, rob and expel, the decay of the old body and Death's coming, and his own trade as a poet who praises patrons for gifts and prides himself on titles; he asks for the feet, the six-letter name and the gift of song, and the praise turns on Rama and Vishnu as uncle, Siva burning Kama, and Murugan as Siva's teacher.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (66, 67, 73, 74, 77, 78, 79, 80); the aged and dying body (68, 72, 75); the poet's own art misused or made a source of pride (69, 71, 76); and 70, a song on the body of nine gates and the wish to recite the books of knowledge.
source_issues: Song 70: one corrupt character in மதனு஡டே (line 2); probably மதனூடே.
Song 72: the source lists a heading variant (திருச்செந்தூர்) in brackets; it matches the chapter's shrine.

reading: The poet describes the women who lure men from the street, shaking their breasts and laughing, who set their minds on rich men, take them up to the upper floor, lie with them by lamplight and coax coins from them, demand more as owed, strip even the jewels from their hands, and drive them out exhausted; he asks to be kept from their company. The praise names Vishnu, who in anger struck down the demon of twenty mountain-like arms and ten heads, as the loving uncle, and calls Murugan the Guha of Senthil who also lives in glory at Thiruttani, where fish leap over the field ridges onto heaped pearls.
nuance: The sequence is a small drama of the courtesan's house: the street, the upstairs room, the lamp, the coaxing (பசப்பி), the claim 'this is owed for that' (இதுக்கு அதுக்குக் கடப்படாம்), and the expulsion (இளைக்க விட்டுத் துரத்துவார்). A Senthil song names Thiruttani in its last lines (திருத்தணிக்குள் சிறப்பில் வாழ்) before ending at Senthil. The phrase பண்டைகூளமென வாழ் and the closing epithet வயத்த நித்தத் துவத்தனே are hard to divide.

reading: The poet speaks of women who draw men to the bed of burning pleasure, gather the gold and ornaments they bring, and when a man is spent tell him to go today; he asks that his mind, which goes so sweetly to them, be given love for Murugan's feet and the power to praise him in poetry and song. The praise recalls Kama, whose arrows made even great ascetics wilt, falling into the fire of Siva who burned him with a slight thought, and the vel that removes the gods' distress, at Senthil where striped bees hum his praise.
nuance: அற்றனை என இன்று ஓட்டு என்று: the woman's dismissal once the man has nothing left, the same charge as in 33 and 66. The plea is to redirect the same mind (இனிமையில் ஒன்றாய்ச் சென்று உட்படு மனம்) rather than to kill it. The dense rhythm makes the first eight lines and the phrase திடமுறு அன்பால் சிந்தைக்கு அறிவிடமும் சேர்த்து hard to divide.

reading: The poet pictures his old age, belly sagging, hair white, teeth loose, back bent, lips hanging, one hand on a stick, while women laugh 'who is this worn-out old man', his cough rattles, speech slurs, eyes go blind and ears deaf; a physician comes, his young sons ask about property and debts, his wife weeps and falls, and Yama's servants stand by as his filth flows: at that hour, he asks, come quickly on the peacock. The praise is a long lullaby of Kausalya calling the child Rama, 'come, my father, come, lord of the Raghus, come, my son, my eye, my life, come and drink at the breast, come and wear flowers', and calls Murugan the nephew who delights that Mayan's heart, Valli's lover and son of Siva who wears the moon, the serpent and the river, at Senthil.
nuance: தொண்டு கிழவன் here means a decrepit old man, not a servant: the same word the book uses for service is turned into mockery in the women's mouths. The deathbed is social as well as bodily: the doctor, the sons asking உடைமை கடன் ஏது, the falling wife. The Kausalya passage, ten repetitions of வருக, mirrors the plea: the poet calls the Lord to come as Kausalya called her child.

reading: The poet confesses that, trusting this hut thatched with skin and full of women's deceitful play, he ran after wealth composing new தூது, நான்மணிமாலை, கோவை, உலா and மடல் poems and entering the doors of worthless patrons, and calls himself idle, unjust, a liar and slanderer, shameless, cruel, miserly and reviled; he asks whether grace will not grant a little of the stainless sea of true knowledge and austerity, so that all the sorrow of the world of cause and effect ends. The praise tells of Rama, borne on Hanuman's shoulders, who cut off Ravana's heads and gave Vibhishana his kingdom, and of Narada coming to say 'this is the field where she lives', so that Murugan went to Valli, at Seeralaivay.
nuance: The plea names the prabandha genres the poet used to win gifts (தூது, நான்மணிமாலைப் பிரபந்தக் கோவை, உலா, மடல்) and the doors of patrons (தோமுறு காளையர் வாசல்தொறும்): the confession is of poetry sold, not only of lust. தோலொடு மூடிய கூரை, a roof covered with skin, is the body. Narada's part in the Valli story is named outright (நாரதர் வந்துற்று ஈது அவள் வாழ் புனமாம்).

tamil: நாலு மைந்து வாசல் கீறு தூறு டம்பு கால்கை யாகி
நாத மொன்ற ஆதி வாயில் நாட கங்க ளான ஆடி
நூல நந்த கோடி தேடி மால்மி குந்து பாரு ளோரை
நோய்க லந்த வாழ்வு றாமல் நீக லந்து ளாகு ஞான
காலன் வந்து பால னாவி காய வென்று பாசம் வீசு
காம னைந்து பாண மோடு வேமி னென்று காணு மோனர்
ஆல மொன்று வேலை யாகி யானை யஞ்சல் தீரு மூல
ஆர ணங்கள் தாளை நாட வார ணங்கை மேவு மாதி
reading: The poet speaks of the body of four and five gates, a bush of sinew and bone with arms and legs, in which sound joins at the first gate and its plays go on unnoticed, and asks that before it grows old in seeking endless books and speaking clever words to men he be given a life of reciting fully the books of knowledge in which Murugan is mingled. The praise names the primal one who cried 'refuge' when Death came casting his noose for the boy's life, the silent dark-throated one who looked at Kama and his five arrows and said 'burn', to whom Murugan spoke the Veda, and Vishnu with the discus who ended the elephant's fear, at Senthil where the Vedas seek the feet.
nuance: நாலும் ஐந்து வாசல் is the body of nine openings. The plea sets two kinds of learning against each other: the endless books sought with delusion and the clever words that breed harm, and the ஞான நூல் in which the Lord is present. The boy whose life Death came for, with the cry ஓலம், points to the story of Markandeya; whose the cry is, the boy's or Siva's, depends on the division. Several phrases (நாரி என்பில் ஆகும், நாதம் ஒன்ற ஆதி வாயில்) are uncertain.

reading: The poet confesses that he compared men to Kubera for wealth, Indra for rank and Kandan for beauty, cried to them that they were his refuge in his great hunger, and sang new verses daily while pouring out his distress; he asks Murugan to break the agitation of the senses in which the body perishes and give him love that unites him to his feet. The praise names Siva, who laughed and burned the strong cities and dances in the hall with the axe, to whom Murugan gave a Tamil verse in rhythm, the splitter of the hill at Senthil, and Murugan who joined his red hands and bowed to the golden creeper of the hunters in the field.
nuance: The begging poet even compares patrons to Kandan (நிறத்திற் கந்தன்), the god he should be praising: the flattery borrows Murugan's own name. In the praise Murugan bows to Valli (செங்கரம் குவித்துக் கும்பிடும்), the lover humbling himself. மழுக்கைக் கொண்ட சங்கரர்க்குச் சென்று வண்டமிழ்ச் சொல் சந்தம் ஒன்று அருள்வோனே: the teaching to Siva is given here as Tamil verse.

reading: The poet confesses that, taking impermanent things for himself, he wasted long days until his strength went, he grew deaf and blind, full of disease, his senses faltering, swollen on a bed of filth and water, on the way to the burning ground, and asks for the lotus feet that spread as a light the Vedas cannot praise. The praise names the boiling vel that dried the sea like a pond and split the old mango tree of the demons, and calls Murugan the Kumara of Alaivay who showed the highest meaning to Siva of undying pure form, easy for his devotees to reach.
nuance: நிலையாப் பொருளை உடலாக் கருதி: the error is taking the passing thing for oneself, and the decay that follows is its result. மறைபோற்ற அரிய ஒளியாய்ப் பரவு மலர்த்தாள் makes the feet a pervading light. The mango tree (சூதம்) is Sura's last form. அடியார்க்கு எளிய: the Lord is easy of access for devotees, the closing note. மடுவேற்கு உரிய நெறியாக is obscure.

reading: The poet describes women who make love-pellets ground with sugarcane juice and feed them to men, rub on many scents, hide something inside the betel they give on the bed, then complain 'you never think of me', and so drag men into the net of desire; he asks not to wander in their ways but to be granted daily vision in his heart of the fragrant six letters, the kadamba garland and the radiance of Murugan's face. The praise names Siva of the dark throat and Rama of the bow as kin, lists the shrines where Murugan dwells (Sikkal, Valanchuzhi, Thiruchengodu, Idaikkazhi, Thandalai, Kalar, Chengadu, Kurukkai, Purambayam and others), and the vel that pierced the chest of the deceitful Sura and drank his life, at Thiruchendur.
nuance: The deceit named here is the love-charm: கருப்பஞ் சாறொடு அரைத்துள உண்டைகள் and something hidden in the betel (வெற்றிலையின் புறம் ஒளித்து), the courtesans' magic rather than their price. ஆறெனும் அக்கரம், the six letters, is Murugan's six-syllable mantra, set against those potions. The list of shrines in the praise is unusual. The opening phrase நிறுக்கும் சூதன மெய்த்தன முண்டைகள் is hard to divide.

reading: The poet asks that, stumbling in the darkness of defiled birth and its bonds, wounded by Kama's five arrows, he not waste away in doubt and delusion in the embraces of deceitful, showy common women, but be given Murugan's flower feet with anklets and bells, and his love. The praise names the vel that broke the demon's power and gave the world back to Indra, a picture of Siva's red matted hair with the moon, konrai, datura and tulasi, and Murugan of fine Tamil at Senthil, where the southern breeze blows through the groves.
nuance: பிறப்பு அந்தகாரம், the darkness of birth, and பந்த பாசம, the binding bonds, set the women within the larger bondage of birth. Tulasi (துழாய்), Vishnu's plant, appears among the flowers in Siva's hair; what the peacock (தோகை) in that hair stands for is unclear to me.

reading: The poet draws Yama in full, with the five great sins, crescent fangs, fiery hair, poisoned eyes, trident and noose, black as a rain cloud on his graceless buffalo, and asks that at the hour of his coming Murugan come before him, his servant who praises the feet with a love received from generation to generation, on the peacock whose dance cracks the cosmic sphere and shakes the eight directions. The praise dwells on Valli's beauty, her cloud of hair, nectar speech and moonlit smile, with Murugan as the bridegroom asleep on her breast, and names him the king among kings who conquered every direction, worshipped at Siva's shrines and struck Mount Meru with a ball, at Senthil where devotees find the path from age to age.
nuance: வழிவழி அருள்பெறும் அன்பினால் உனது அடிபுகழ் அடிமை: the claim on the Lord at death is hereditary service, the வழியடிமை of 34. மகமேரு செண்டு மோதின அரசருள் அதிபதி points to the story of the Pandya king who struck Meru with a ball, which is told of Murugan born as Ugra Pandya; the text gives the deed but not the name.

tamil: வகை வகையி லாசு சேர்பெ ருங்கவி ...... சண்டவாயு
அதிபெல கடோ ர மாச லந்தர ...... னொந்துவீழ
reading: The poet sets out his learning and fame as a poet: he has read the Sangam songs and books, stories and kavyas, the sixty-four arts, the truthful word of Thiruvalluvar and the proverbs, has made garlands of many rhythms, madal, parani, kovai and kalambakam, crores of prabandhas and extempore verse like a storm, and goes about as king of sweet poetry with white umbrella, titles, flags, drums and palanquin; he asks whether this pride will not be removed. The praise tells how Vishnu, unable to defeat the fierce Jalandhara, worshipped Siva with a thousand lotuses a day, and when one flower was missing offered his eye, and received the discus that cut Jalandhara's body; Murugan, son of that Mahesa, married Indra's daughter and came to rule the poet at Senthil.
nuance: The song is a self-portrait of a court poet and a confession that the honours (வெண்குடை, விருது, கொடி, தண்டிகை) are pride (மால் அகந்தை). Among the learning listed is திருவள்ளுவ தேவர் வாய்மை, the Kural named as a classic. In the myth, Vishnu offering his eye to make up the missing lotus is my reading of கோ அணிந்திடு செங்கண்மால் and is not certain.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women, bowing at their lotus feet, breasts thrilling, large dark eyes clashing with gold earrings, sweet lisping words, hair falling, new nail-marks and sweat on the brow, and asks whether he will not give up the 'love' of these women of wealth that makes men lose their sense in the snare of Kama, whom Siva burned to ash. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, with the demons bowing their heads to Murugan's feet and begging for his grace, and names him the Kumara of Seyppathi and Senthil by the sea.
nuance: பொருளின் மகளிர்: women of wealth, the Kural's phrase for courtesans, and their அன்பு is the love the poet asks to give up. In the praise the defeated demons themselves ask for grace (எங்கட்கு உன் கட் க்ருபை தா), not only the gods. செய்ப்பதி, the field town, is probably Vayalur.

reading: A short song: the poet, bewildered by women of fragrant sandal-dressed breasts, by eye-corners they whet like weapons and by dark hair humming with bees, asks Murugan to grant him grace with joy and love. The praise names the nephew of Hari with the kadamba garland, the vel that made the sea boil, and the true guru whom the burner of the three cities worships, at Senthil.
nuance: மறுகிடு மருளனை: the poet names himself the bewildered one; the remedy asked is grace given with joy (இன்புற்று அன்புற்று அருள்வாயே), as if the Lord's pleasure in giving were part of the gift. திரிபுர தகனரும் வந்திக்கும் சற்குருநாதா: Siva worships his son as teacher.

reading: The poet speaks of women with breasts like a tusker's, whose red eye-corners hold a man until he grows weak, and calls himself one who never suspected the mind that cuts him; he asks Murugan to rule him by giving Tamil words that string together the meaning of his golden feet. The praise names Murugan who answered the gods' distress at Sura's hands and slew Sura with his vel for love of Indra, and who rebuked the lotus-born Brahma, struck him, and as Siva's true calf lisped that meaning to him, at Thiruchendur.
nuance: எனக்கு என்று அப்பொருள் தங்கத் தொடுக்கும் சொல் தமிழ் தந்து: the plea is for the gift of song, as in 2 and 25. In the praise, திருக் கஞ்சத்தனைக் கண்டித்து ... குட்டி and சற்சிவக் கன்று அப்பொருள் கொஞ்சிப் பகர்வோனே give the Om story without naming Om. The dense rhythm makes much of the first half uncertain.

reading: The poet describes the courtesans' charms from anklets to hair, their cuckoo voices welcoming whoever looks, 'come home', their bed where they seem loving, and their play with sweat and kisses, and asks whether union with them is fitting. The praise is a battle in drum syllables in which Sesha, Meru, Sura and Taraka fall and the gods dance, names the face that whispered into the father's ear, and ends with Murugan embracing Valli, 'my doll, our girl', at Senthil of tall screwpine.
nuance: அன்புளார் போல், 'as if loving', and வாரும் வீடே, 'come home', are the two marks of the courtesan here. தாதை காதில் அங்கு ஓது is the teaching of Siva, whispered in his ear. என் பாவை வள்ளி எங்கள் மாதை sounds like the voice of Valli's own people, which suggests the praise briefly takes another speaker.

title: திருச்செந்தூர்
theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 5 of 6): beside the confessions of bondage to courtesans and the decay of the old body, several songs ask for something higher, the One that the gods seek, the yogi's absorbed vision and the breath's ascent to the nectar of the moon, and others confess the poet's begging at patrons' doors; the praise turns on Valli, Siva taught by his son, and Vishnu as uncle.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (83, 85, 88, 89, 90, 92); the dying or aged body (84, 86, 93); the passing goods of household life (87); begging with poetry (86, 91); songs of inner attainment (81, 82, 94); and 95, mostly a battle of Rama with a short plea for release.
source_issues: Song 88: one corrupt character in கி஡ணட (line 23); ஡ண for ரீ, so கிரீட (crown), as in songs 12 and 20.
Song 94: two corrupt characters, in லு஡டு (line 8, probably லூடு, 'through') and லு஡றுங் (line 9, probably லூறும், 'wells up'); also unflagged முலபர (line 6), probably மூலபர.
Song 82: unflagged garble காலுட லுடி (line 9); the second word is unclear.

reading: The poet asks to be given the One that Indra on his spotted elephant amid the clouds, Brahma who expounds the Vedas, and Vishnu of the discus asleep on the serpent all wander in search of, so that, the waves stilled, he may taste it and grow clear within. The praise names Murugan who rides the ram and dwells in the lotus pool, who gave joy to the young hunter girl, and whose vel shattered the golden peak, at coral-walled Senthil.
nuance: ஒன்றைத் தரவேணும்: what is asked for is named only as 'the one', the thing the three great gods fail to find. திரை அற்று, with the waves gone, and தெளிதல், becoming clear, make the goal a stilled and clarified mind. The identifications of the three gods rest on epithets (புகர், புயல், சுருதிச் சங்கப் பொருள், திகிரி) and the first lines are hard to divide.

tamil: பூரண வார கும்ப சீதப டீர கொங்கை
மாதர் விகார வஞ்ச லீலையி லேயு ழன்று
போதவ மேயி ழந்து போனது மான மென்ப ...... தறியாத
பூரிய னாகி நெஞ்சு காவல்ப டாத பஞ்ச
பாதக னாய றஞ்செ யாதடி யோடி றந்து
போனவர் வாழ்வு கண்டு மாசையி லேய ழுந்து ...... மயல்தீரக்
காரண காரி யங்க ளானதெ லாமொ ழிந்து
யானெனு மேதை விண்டு பாவக மாயி ருந்து
காலுட லுடி யங்கி நாசியின் மீதி ரண்டு ...... விழிபாயக்
காயமு நாவு நெஞ்சு மோர்வழி யாக அன்பு
காயம்வி டாம லுன்ற னீடிய தாள்நி னைந்து
காணுதல் கூர்த வஞ்செய் யோகிக ளாய்வி ளங்க ...... அருள்வாயே
ஆரண சார மந்த்ர வேதமெ லாம்வி ளங்க
ஆதிரை யானை நின்று தாழ்வனெ னாவ ணங்கு
மாதர வால்வி ளங்கு பூரண ஞான மிஞ்சு ...... முரவோனே
ஆர்கலி யூடெ ழுந்து மாவடி வாகி நின்ற
சூரனை மாள வென்று வானுல காளு மண்ட
ரானவர் கூர ரந்தை தீரமு னாள்ம கிழ்ந்த ...... முருகேசா
வாரண மூல மென்ற போதினி லாழி கொண்டு
வாவியின் மாடி டங்கர் பாழ்பட வேயெ றிந்த
மாமுகில் போலி ருண்ட மேனிய னாமு குந்தன் ...... மருகோனே
வாலுக மீது வண்ட லோடிய காலில் வந்து
சூல்நிறை வான சங்கு மாமணி யீன வுந்து
வாரிதி நீர்ப ரந்த சீரலை வாயு கந்த ...... பெருமாளே.
reading: The poet confesses that, wandering in the deceitful play of women with breasts like full cool pots, he lost his wisdom and did not know shame, became base, left his heart unguarded, did no dharma and sank in desire even watching the lives of those who had died; to end that delusion he asks that cause and effect fall away, the self that says 'I' break, both eyes rest on the tip of the nose with breath and fire held, body, speech and heart go one way, and that, thinking of the feet, he shine as a yogi of seeing. The praise names Murugan, full of perfect knowledge, to whom Siva bowed saying 'I am lower', the slayer of Sura risen from the sea in a vast form, and the nephew of Mukunda who hurled the discus at the crocodile when the elephant cried 'Root!', at Seeralaivay where conches give birth to pearls on the sand.
nuance: The remedy for infatuation is a yogic programme: யானெனும் மேதை விண்டு (the 'I' broken), நாசியின் மீது இரண்டு விழிபாய (the gaze on the nose tip), காயமும் நாவும் நெஞ்சும் ஓர் வழியாக (body, speech and mind made one). ஆதிரையான் is Siva, whose star is Thiruvathirai; his saying நின்று தாழ்வன் makes the father bow to his son as teacher. A garbled word in line 9 (காலுட லுடி) is unclear.

reading: The poet asks that, agitated, grieved, without sense or livelihood, he not lie in the laps of common women who call him with pretended love and bind him; instead, he asks, give your feet to protect me, the title of a poet who sings fine Tamil so that service flourishes, and the renown that comes to the mind.
