The praise names Murugan who fell at the hunter girl's feet in the millet field, cut off Sura's head and struck the hill, and spoke into the ear of the father of Thiruchitrambalam, apparently the five letters.
nuance: The plea asks for honours (புலப்பட்டம், புகழ்ச்சி) but for the sake of service: எனக்குத் தொண்டுறப் பற்றும் புலத்துக் கண் செழிக்கச் செந்தமிழ் பாடும். In 76 the poet's titles are pride; here they are asked for as tools of devotion. சிறக் கற்கும் அஞ்செழுத்து அத் தந்து, if so divided, makes Murugan teach Siva of Chidambaram his own five-letter mantra; the division is uncertain. As in 71, Murugan prostrates before Valli (தெண்டனிட்டு).

reading: The poet pictures his death, wife, children and kin wailing, the body burning in the fire, what is left cast into water, and the life in the hand of cruel-eyed Death, and asks Murugan to come so that he, his servant, may worship his victorious feet. The praise names Murugan who went into the forest of lions and tigers and lived with the hunter girl, the one at Senthil whom devotees praise, the ever-young lord whom women with faces like moon and lotus embrace.
nuance: The scene runs past the moment of death to the cremation and the casting of the ashes into water (விண்டு புனலில் வஞ்சம் ஒழிய விழ), an unusual length for the plea. ஒரு பாச விஞ்சை விளைவும் அன்று is obscure; it may say that what happens is no work of magic or bond, or be divided otherwise.

reading: The poet gives a head-to-foot catalogue of women, cloud hair, crescent brow, bow-like eyebrows, eyes that shame the carp, the bee and the lotus, earrings, pearl teeth, areca-like neck, breasts like hills, coral lips and thighs like plantain stems, and asks whether he will trust these deceivers in eye, hand, foot and act. The praise is a battle in drum syllables with conches and trumpets proclaiming the son of Sambhu, the poet, Kandan, as Sura's host and his hill burn and Indra takes refuge, and names Murugan who delights at Senthil with the girl of the Kurinji hut.
nuance: The whole first half is the conventional blazon of beauty, each part matched to its comparison, and the question only comes at the end: செயல் வஞ்சரை நம்புவேனோ. Among Murugan's titles proclaimed by the drums is புலவன், the poet.

reading: The poet asks that before Death, his flower-red eyes blazing, raises his club and tears him away, before the kin who live here wear out their love quarrelling 'this is mine, why yours?' over their shares, and before the body passes, Murugan end the sorrow of his base trade of begging with sung Tamil and give him joy. The praise names Murugan who gave the true meaning to Sambhu while Vishnu, conch in hand, slept and Brahma's wisdom failed, who wears the hunter girl's kumkum on his golden arms, at Senthil of moats and sandalwood groves.
nuance: இசைக்கும் செந்தமிழ்க் கொண்டு அங்கு இரக்கும் புன்தொழில்: the poet's Tamil is named as the means of his begging, the confession of 69 and 71. The kin dividing the dying man's goods (எனக்கு என்று இங்கு உனக்கு ஏன்று) is a sharp detail. The opening lines on the senses are hard to divide.

reading: The poet lists house, gold, sons, beautiful wife, strength, family standing, town and name, youth, ornaments, ranks and kin, and asks whether it is right to take the pleasure of this passing dream as his own, lie with women, join many bodies and fall again into the womb. The praise names Murugan who removes the old deeds of devotees who think of him, whose vel split the great mountain, who stays at Senthil, and who embraced the hunter maiden.
nuance: மாயக் கனவுநிலை இன்பம் அதனை எனது என்று கருதி: the error is the claim 'mine' over a dream. The list moves from goods to people to rank, then to women, and ends at the womb (கருவில் விழுகின்றது): attachment's end is rebirth.

reading: The poet heaps names on the courtesans: women who open the cloth over scented breasts, whimper at every door, feign a childhood love for old lovers, sell remedies for love-sickness, want whatever wealth comes, coldly drop men without money, have mothers who play the dark-goddess drama, drink palm toddy and mix with the low, and asks whether kinship with them is fitting. The praise names Murugan as the younger brother of the elephant-faced one who wrote the Bharata on Meru, Valli's lover, the nephew of Vishnu who came as a lion and tore open the demon king's chest and wore his entrails, and the lord of the gods given by Sankara, at Senthil.
nuance: The catalogue of abuse (மழுங்கிகள், சிணுங்கிகள், வம்பிகள், சண்டிகள், மிண்டிகள், பறம்பிகள், தொண்டிகள், கடம்பிகள்) runs on one suffix, a set feature of the book. அவர் தாய்மார் நீலி நாடகமும் பயில் மண்டைகள: the mothers are part of the trade, as in Naladiyar's courtesan chapter. The praise names Ganesa writing the Mahabharata on Meru and the Narasimha story outright.

reading: The poet speaks of women with doe eyes and breasts like golden peaks, whose speech drips like cane juice, who on the flowered bed say 'first give the gold and coins' and, once given, talk as sweet as milk and honey, and asks whether kinship with these fools of pleasure is fitting. The praise names Vishnu, Achyuta, who fought the demon king with bow and arrows, as uncle, Murugan as the son born to Kali for those who have left behind talk sweet as milk, syrup and sugar, and as honey at Senthil where devotees swarm.
nuance: பொற்பணம் முதல் நீ தா, ஈந்தால் ... பால் தேன் போல செப்பிடும்: the payment comes first and the sweet words after, the sequence the Kural's courtesan chapter condemns. The rhythm, with long syllables at every foot, splits words heavily and much of the praise is uncertain.

reading: The poet lists what the young women show, cloud-like hair, moon-like brow, budding smile, nectar speech, creeper eyes, lotus face, breasts like hills, creeper waist, bangled hands and jewelled hips, and above all the practised arts, and confesses that he wallows in the mire of infatuation with them, without asking for anything. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva who burned Kama's form with a smile, who shows love so that his union with the elephant's maiden never slips, and who showed refuge to Indra on Airavata's back and protected him wholly.
nuance: Each line repeats காட்டி, 'showing', so that the women's beauty is a display, and the confession ends without a request: மயலின் சேற்றில் உழல்வேனே. இபமின், the elephant's maiden, is Devayanai, raised by Airavata.

reading: The poet asks that, no longer wandering to the doors of fools singing crores of rhythmic Tamil garlands, with past deeds gone and love of women far away, he, the old servant, be ruled by Murugan, who will come at the decisive hour on the golden peacock that dances to the drum. The praise is a long string of titles ending in காரன்: guardian of the Vedic sacrifice, master of Tamil verse, helper of the gods, lord of the cock, lover of those who fold hands over their heads, wielder of the vel that pierced the hill, lover of the elephant's maiden and of the hunter girl, friend of devotees of fine speech, and destroyer of Sura, at Senthil.
nuance: முந்து தமிழ் மாலை கோடிக் கோடி ... முஞ்சர் மனை வாசல் தேடித் தேடி: the confession of begging with poetry again, now with the poet's verse called garlands. The praise answers it: Murugan is himself செந்தமிழ் சொல் பாவின் மாலைக் காரன், the one to whom such garlands belong.

tamil: முலைமு கந்தி மிர்ந்த கலவை யுந்து லங்கு
முருக விழ்ந்து திர்ந்த மலர்க ளுஞ்ச ரிந்த
சிலைமு கங்க லந்த திலத முங்கு ளிர்ந்த
தெரிய வந்து நின்ற மகளிர் பின்சு ழன்று
மலைமு கஞ்சு மந்த புலவர் செஞ்சொல் கொண்டு
வளர்பு னம்ப யின்ற குறம டந்தை கொங்கை
அலைமு கந்த வழ்ந்து சினைமு திர்ந்த சங்க
அளிக லந்தி ரங்க இசையு டன்து யின்ற
reading: The poet pictures women with sandal-dressed breasts, smiles, red lips, flowers falling from their hair, spear eyes, tilaka on the brow and beads of sweat on the face, and asks whether he will wander after them, his acts undone. The praise names the vel that opened a way out for the poets shut in the mountain at their fine words, the arms embraced by the hunter girl's breasts, and Senthil, where conches cry from the waves onto the lotus and bees sing.
nuance: செயல் அழிந்து உழன்று: infatuation undoes one's own agency, where in 22 the undoing of one's agency was the goal. மலைமுகம் சுமந்த புலவர் செஞ்சொல் கொண்டு வழிதிறந்த செங்கை வடிவேலா points to the story of Nakkirar and the poets held in a mountain cave, freed by the vel when he sang; the text gives the details but not the name.

reading: The poet pictures old age, hearing gone, heavy breathing, faltering acts, harsh words, vomiting, phlegm in the nose, and asks that before his life wanders out of its cage, Murugan remove the reality of Death, join him to the golden feet and grant a little grace. The praise names Murugan as guru to Siva who bent the golden mountain against his foes, the one who spoke many sly words to the hunter girl in the forest, the Murugan in whose mouth lies the meaning of the Tamil way, at Senthil of the holy waters.
nuance: கூற்றத் தத்துவம் நீக்கி: what is asked is not only rescue at death but the removal of Death's principle. வாய்ப்புற்ற தமிழ் மார்க்கத்து இட்பொருள் வாய்க்குச் சித்திர முருகோனே makes Murugan the master of Tamil's meaning.

reading: The poet, who has done no just deed and enjoyed delusion amid the illusions of the five elements, asks when the one day will come when, taking up the root yoga that the gods cannot find, the breath driven fast through the fire, rising to the moon in the head where the nectar of bliss wells, going up through the nadi to the space beyond, he will live where there is neither you nor I nor even the nadi. The praise is given to the goddess, the drinker of poison, Matangi who speaks the Veda, the dark Nili, Chamundi who struck down Death with her feet, the one who dwells in fire, wind and sky, the dancing Kali, partner of the rider of the bull and Vishnu's younger sister, and names Murugan as her son, who went to the towns of his devotees and played there, the peacock hero of Senthil.
nuance: The plea is a full account of yogic ascent: வாசி (breath) through அனல் (fire) to மதி (the moon), where the இன்ப அமுது ஊறல் flows, and then மேலைவெளி, the space above. The goal, நீ இன்றி நான் இன்றி, is beyond the duality of devotee and Lord. The praise, nearly all of it on Uma as Shakti, gives her the deed of kicking Death (காலன் விழ மோது சாமுண்டி).

reading: Most of the song is a battle: Ravana comes with his army of horses, chariots and elephants, boasts and fights, the monkeys hurl rocks and trees, the demons are torn apart, Yama's messengers drive them south and ghouls feast on flesh and marrow, and Vishnu wins with his arrows. The poet then calls 'refuge, refuge', asks the Lord to give his small mind grace little by little and to grant the house of bliss, at Senthil of ponds full of conches, lotuses and fish.
nuance: The plea comes only at the end and is brief: தஞ்சம் தஞ்சம் ... இன்பம் தரு வீடு அது தருவாயே. Uncommonly, the battle in the praise is Rama's against Ravana rather than Murugan's against Sura.

title: திருச்செந்தூர்
theme: Last songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 6 of 6): the poet asks for Murugan's feet at the hour of death and at the fading of house, wife and child, confesses his capture by women's eyes and his voyages abroad for money to win them, and traces his body from seed through many burnings; one song speaks for a lovesick girl of the hills. The praise turns on Brahma imprisoned, the vel against Sura and the hill, Siva who drank the poison, and the shore of Alaivay and Senthil.
structure_note: All eight end at Senthil or Alaivay. 96 and 97 set the plea at life's end (Death's coming; the fading of child, house and wife); 98, 99, 102 and 103 confess women; 100 asks for release from births in Saiva terms; 101 is in another voice, for a girl sick with love.
source_issues: Song 100: one corrupt character in விந்ததினு஡றி (line 1); clearly விந்ததின் ஊறி.
Song 103: சுழ்தரு (line 15) should be சூழ்தரு; not flagged as corrupt.

reading: The poet pictures his death: women who think many things in one deceitful heart, the sons and the kin gathered at evening crowd round wailing, the worm-like body wrapped in cloth goes to be food for the fire, and victorious Yama comes near to terrify; on that day, he asks, give your pair of feet. The praise names the peacock hero who made lotus-born Brahma suffer and imprisoned him, the chest that the sweet-voiced lady embraces, Senthil where poets of fine speech weigh the Tamil of the Sangam, and the one who fought so that the golden northern mountain scattered into the sea.
nuance: The plea is the pilot's hour-of-death formula: அண்டிப் பயமுற வென்றிச் சமன் வரும் அன்றைக்கு அடியிணை தரவேணும். The wailing wife, sons and kin (மடவார், புதல்வர், கிளைஞர்) are the household that cannot help at death, and the body is பஞ்சிப் புழுவுடல் அங்கிக்கு இரை, a worm-body for the fire. Brahma's imprisonment appears without the Om teaching. The line on the chest (கண்டொத்த அனமொழி அண்டத் திருமயில் கண்டத்து அழகிய) is hard to split; 'a woman with speech like sugar candy' is the likely sense.

reading: The poet names what a man holds to, the baby that crawls up again and again crying for him, the house of golden halls that seem to split the sky, the wife with curled hair and kumkum on her breasts taken as refuge, and asks for Murugan's lotus feet with their anklets and kadamba at the time when these fade. The praise names Senthil of sandal, mandara, sugarcane and plantain, Murugan who crossed the cool forest into the millet field and bowed to the girl with sweet words, and the lord whom Siva, Indra and the gods trust.
nuance: மங்கு காலம், the time of fading, is the key: the child, the house and the wife are listed with delight before the turn. The song is set in very short rhythmic units, so many words are split; the last six lines (அந்தகன் கலங்க வந்த ... கும்பர் நம்பு தம்பிரானே) can be divided more than one way, and I have given only their outline.

reading: A short song: the poet asks that he not waste away morning and evening in the bond of desire for dark-eyed women and for children, and that Murugan give him love for his two feet. The praise names him the protector, the son of Parameswara's grace and the nephew of Hari Kesava, at Alaivay.
nuance: மடமாதர் மக ஆசை தொந்தம்: the bond (தொந்தம்) joins desire for women and for children in one phrase. The plea is not for release but for love (இருதாளின் அன்பு).

reading: The poet speaks of women whose eyes press like fate and whose foreheads are like the moon, who join young men's minds, offer pleasure to drink its fill and say 'rule us sweetly', and asks whether the dark sorrow and delusion of maya that come to tear him will never end. The praise names Siva who wears the moon, drank the rising poison so the gods might live, rides the bull and comes to the side of devotees who never forget, and Murugan his son, who fought the Suras of great sorcery with the vel, on the peacock at Alaivay.
nuance: விதிபோலும் உந்த விழி makes the women's eyes press on a man like fate. மருள் மாயை, delusion and maya, names the poet's condition in doctrinal terms, and the Suras who are defeated are themselves அதிமாயம், great maya, so the praise answers the plea.

reading: The poet says his body came from seed and has burned a crore of times, and asks that from now on, like the knowing ones who never part from Murugan's feet, he too may have his ruin and old sin ended, take the form of Siva-knowledge, rise to the strong state and rest, and be given the flower feet. The praise names Siva, the one red flame within the poet, with fire in his eye and flame-coloured hair, helper of devotees, and Murugan his son, who embraces the beautiful hunter girl of wisdom, at Senthil.
nuance: விந்ததின் ஊறி வந்தது காயம் வெந்தது கோடி: the body comes from seed and has been burned on the pyre countless times, so the plea is against rebirth itself. சிவஞான வடிவு and எந்தன் உளே ஏக செஞ்சுடர் give the song a Saiva Siddhanta cast. விஞ்சையர் may be the Vidyadharas or simply the wise; ஞானம் என் குறமாது makes Valli herself wisdom.

reading: Spoken for a girl of the hunters' hill who is sick with love: Kama's five flower arrows scatter, the moon burns like the sun, the soft breeze comes like fire and spiteful women speak blame, and the speaker asks Murugan to come near with his cool garland to end her cruel infatuation. The praise names him the wise one whom Siva, holder of the leaping deer, worshipped with joy, the hero who threw the vel so that the hill and the mango scattered and the sea feared, and the one who removes the troubles of devotees, at Alaivay.
nuance: This is an akam song: குறவாணர் குன்றில் உறை பேதை is spoken of in the third person, by her mother or friend, and the cure asked is Murugan's garland, the lover's token. The moon, breeze and gossip (வினைமாதர் தம்தம் வசைகூற) are the stock torments of the separated woman. மறிமான் உகந்த இறையோன் ... வழிபாடு தந்த makes Siva the worshipper of his son.

reading: The poet says that taking women's eyes for cruel black arrows and fish, their speech for cuckoos' song and their hair as soft as it seems, he went seeking wealth as far as Bengal, Sonam and China to join their soft shoulders, and asks whether he must suffer such hard pain; he asks the strong-shouldered young lord to come and rule him at this hour. The praise names Murugan sweet to the hill girl, who fought in anger so that the hill, the seas and Sura were lost, and the son of Siva who bears the skeleton, lord of the gods, at Senthil.
nuance: பொருள்தேடி வங்காளம் சோனம் சீனம் போய்: the price of women is paid with wealth earned by voyages to distant lands, a merchant's confession rather than a poet's. சோனம் is not certain (perhaps a land to the east). The song is set in heavy monosyllabic beats (வெங்காளம் பாணம் சேல் கண்), so the splits are not all sure.

tamil: வெஞ்ச ரோருக மோகடு நஞ்ச மோகய லோநெடு
வெந்து போன புராதன சம்ப ராரி புராரியை
தஞ்ச மோயம தூதுவர் நெஞ்ச மோவெனு மாமத
சங்கை யோர்விரு கூதள கந்த மாலிகை தோய்தரு
பஞ்ச பாதக தாருக தண்ட னீறெழ வானவர்
பங்க யாசனர் கேசவ ரஞ்ச லேயென மால்வரை
செஞ்ச டாடவி மீமிசை கங்கை மாதவி தாதகி
செண்ப காடவி நீடிய துங்க மாமதிள் சுழ்தரு
reading: The poet asks of a woman's eye whether it is a fierce lotus, harsh poison, a fish, a sea of pleasure, a slice of mango, the arrow of the burnt Kama that defeated Siva, a dark flower, a refuge or the heart of Yama's messengers, and, sunk in such women's breasts and in doubt, asks whether a day will come when Murugan gives his feet with their anklets and garlands. The praise names the vel that turned Taraka of the five great sins to ash, let the gods return to Amaravati as before and told Brahma and Vishnu not to fear, and Murugan as the treasure of Siva who wears Ganga, flowers and the moon in his matted hair, at Senthil.
nuance: The opening is a chain of doubting comparisons (ஓ ... ஓ ...), ending with தஞ்சமோ யமதூதுவர் நெஞ்சமோ: is the eye a refuge or Death's servants' heart? The poet's own state is சங்கை, doubt. Kama the enemy of Sambara (சம்பராரி) is said to have defeated Siva before he was burnt.

title: பழநி
theme: First songs at Palani (பழநி, 1 of 7): the poet confesses courtesans who sell love, take wealth and embrace without regard to caste, his begging from patrons, and a life run from birth through lust to the pyre, and asks for Murugan's feet, grace, the meaning of the mantra and the work of worship; the praise turns on Murugan as Siva's teacher, as the Tamil saint who defeated the Jains, as the all-pervading tradition, and on the goddess of Palani.
structure_note: Most follow the two halves. The confessions are of women (104, 108, 111 to 113, 117, 118), of a whole life (110, 115) or of household ties (109); 106 is a hymn to Murugan as what fills all things, 107 a short prayer for the guru's mantra, 114 a song on those who chant the six faces, and 116 an akam song for a lovesick girl.
source_issues: Song 106: line 20 runs two lines of the stanza together (அகில நிசிசரர் ... துங்ககாளி), breaking the stanza's layout.
Song 115: முழ்கி (line 12) should be மூழ்கி, and பிணியமுடிச் (line 12) and வாழவுக் (line 47) look garbled; none is flagged as corrupt.

tamil: அகல்வினை யுட்சார் சட்சம யிகளொடு வெட்கா தட்கிடு
அகில்கமழ் கத்து ரித்தனி யணைமிசை கைக்கா சுக்கள
பகலிர விற்போ திற்பணி பணியற விட்டா ரெட்டிய
பழநித னிற்போ யுற்பவ வினைவிள கட்சேர் வெட்சிகு
புகலிவ னப்பே றப்புகல் மதுரைமன் வெப்பா றத்திகழ்
பொருதச மர்த்தா குத்திர துரகமு கக்கோ தைக்கிடை
இகல்படு நெட்டூர் பொட்டெழ இளநகை யிட்டே சுட்டருள்
றிடரற முப்பால் செப்பிய கவிதையின் மிக்கா ரத்தினை
reading: The poet calls himself a witless man who joins the followers of the six sects without shame and keeps friendship with women who give their favours for coins on beds scented with agil and musk, and asks when he will go to Palani and grasp Murugan's feet, worn with vetchi and kuravu flowers, which end the deeds of birth. The praise names him the one who, for the glory of Pugali, cured the fever of the Madurai king and sent the Jains with their grass mats to the stakes, who helped Nakkirar among poets against the horse-faced demoness, the son of Siva who burned the cities with a smile, and the one who wrote a poem and cast it on the water.
nuance: The praise makes Murugan the Tamil saint of Sirkazhi (புகலி) who cured the Pandya's fever with holy ash (பொடி) and impaled the Jains, the story told of Sambandar; the closing lines (கவிதை ... எழுதி வனத்தே எற்றிய) seem to recall the palm leaf thrown into the river in the same contest. துரகமுகக் கோதை and நக்கீரர் point to the story of the poet Nakkirar rescued from a horse-faced demoness. முப்பால் செப்பிய may name the Kural, but the phrase's syntax is not clear to me.

reading: The poet says that by the arrows of women's eyes and the flower arrows of Kama, son of Vishnu, he is struck with disease, loses his senses, wastes away and, taking on what Yama takes, dies, and asks for grace to leave the sea of births and reach the high good state. The praise names Murugan who took a seer's form and won the fruit of the hill, who imprisoned lotus-born Brahma over the meaning of the Pranava, and who, when Siva bowed and bowed again and praised him, told him the one word lovingly, at Palani with walls of coral, white and gold.
nuance: ப்ரணவத்து உரையைக் கருதிச் சிறைவைத்திடுவோனே and பணியப் பணியப் பரமர் பரவ ... ஒருசொல் பகர்வோனே tell the pilot's Om story in full: Brahma jailed for the meaning of Om, Siva bowing to receive one word. கணி நற் சொருபத்தை எடுத்து மலைக் கனியைக் கணியுற்றிடுவோனே is unclear; it may be Murugan taking a fortune-teller's form to win Valli.

tamil: அகில நிசிசரர்ந டுங்கக்கொ டுங்கழுகு பரிய குடர்பழுவெ லும்பைப்பி டுங்கரண ...... துங்ககாளி
reading: The poet describes Murugan as the one tradition that stands filling everything, the nether worlds, the earth, the gods' worlds, the cosmic egg, the seas, the eight directions, fire, sun and moon, the twilight mantras, the Veda, the tattvas and the atom within the atom, and says that Murugan came and first gave him the experience in which, as dark breaks at sunrise, the lotus of the heart opens; holding to sweet poems of crafted Tamil, will his rightful servant trust any world but him? The praise is a battle sung in drum syllables, with Kali dancing and foxes and vultures feeding, ending at Palani as lord of the gods.
nuance: The plea is unusual: no confession, only a grateful refusal to trust the world (ப்ரபஞ்சம்) after an experience already given (அநுபவம்). அணுவில் அணு, the atom within the atom, and the long list of worlds and elements make Murugan the all-pervading Lord, as Tirumular says of Siva. உரிய அடிமை is the poet's title for himself, service and not bondage.

reading: A short song: the poet asks whether, no longer wandering in harm and slander and no longer seeking out ignorant deceivers, he will think of Murugan through the meaning of the mantra of instruction and gain grace. The praise names him the younger brother of the elephant-faced god, the son of Himavan's excellent daughter, the true guru who gave the rosary, at Thiruvavinankudi.
nuance: உபதேச மந்திரப் பொருள் is the meaning of a mantra given by a guru, and ஜெபமாலை தந்த சற்குருநாதா makes Murugan the guru who gave the rosary; the song does not say to whom, but it reads like the poet's own initiation. Thiruvavinankudi is the shrine at the foot of the Palani hill.

reading: The poet describes courtesans at their toilet, bathing in turmeric and scent, dressing in many saris, combing and knotting their hair, setting their earrings, putting a camphor dot on the forehead, smearing agil and musk on their breasts, darkening their eyes for love's glances and wearing lily ear-flowers, then laughing so that young men and even ascetics weaken; he asks for Murugan's golden feet to end the desire and sorrow he has given to these women who take wealth. The praise names the vel that churned the sea of the Suras' blood so the gods survived, Murugan who wears the hunter girl's feet on his head and gives his shoulders to Devayanai, the peacock rider with the cock banner, at Palani.
nuance: The whole first half is the courtesan's preparation, step by step, and its end is பொருள்கவர் மாதர், women who take wealth. துறவினர் சோர claims that their laughter loosens even renouncers. குறமகள் பாதச் சேகர reverses rank as in 15: Murugan wears Valli's feet as a crown.

reading: The poet asks that instead of thinking real the wife who delights in a life of desire, the kin, those close to him, the children who please him, the rich land and the town he holds, he be given the work of praising and worshipping Murugan. The praise names him the tongue that spoke instruction into the ear of the lord who rides the bull, the head that bears the hunter girl's feet on her watch-platform, the twelve-shouldered one to whom Indra gave Devayanai, at Palani.
nuance: மெய் என மனம் நினைவது நினையாது: the fault is taking household and possessions for real, and the cure is a task, வழிபடு தொழில். Siva receiving instruction in his ear (செவிபுக உபதேசம்) is the Om story without the word Om.

tamil: அவனிதனி லேபி றந்து மதலையென வேத வழ்ந்து
அருமழலை யேமி குந்து குதலைமொழி யேபு கன்று
சிவகலைக ளாக மங்கள் மிகவுமறை யோது மன்பர்
தெரிவையர்க ளாசை மிஞ்சி வெகுகவலை யாயு ழன்று
மவுனவுப தேச சம்பு மதியறுகு வேணி தும்பை
மனமகிழ வேய ணைந்து ஒருபுறம தாக வந்த
பவனிவர வேயு கந்து மயிலின்மிசை யேதி கழ்ந்து
பரமபத மேசெ றிந்த முருகனென வேயு கந்து
reading: The poet traces his life from birth through crawling, walking, lisping speech and growing to sixteen, saying that he never praised the feet of devotees who recite the Siva texts, Agamas and Vedas but wandered in many cares with growing desire for women, and asks Murugan to join him to his feet. The praise names Siva who taught in silence and wears the moon, arugu and thumbai on his crown, the mountain's daughter who came as his half, and Murugan her son, the vel who walked on the peacock so the earth shook, the Murugan who is the supreme state, at Palani.
nuance: The omission confessed is not worship of the Lord but praise of his devotees' feet (அன்பர் திருவடிகளே நினைந்து). மவுன உபதேச சம்பு is Siva teaching in silence, the Dakshinamurti form.

reading: The poet describes women who learn a life without virtue, send cruel vel-like glances, put away a man's understanding, bargain a price, lay him on the bed, give the nectar of coral lips and hold his body tight with bangled arms, women like wax in the furnace, and asks for a release that ends the madness of love's play that melts him with them. The praise names Murugan whose chest the hunter girl embraced, whose fierce vel made the demon's hill melt and fall, and his mother, Rudri who loves drums, the dark-haired Shakti beside Siva, old Parvati, Kotri and Periyanayaki, at the great hill of Palani.
nuance: விலைபேசி, bargaining a price, marks the women as courtesans. மதன நாடக பித்து, the madness of Kama's drama, calls the affair a performance. The praise gives as many lines to the goddess as to Murugan, ending with பெரியநாயகி, a name of the goddess at Palani.

reading: The poet names the women's lively eyes, nectar speech, smile, drum-like waist, scented hair, deceitful young breasts and earrings, and asks for grace so that the trouble of ties with women who give an unfailing infatuation does not close round him. The praise names Murugan who killed Sura, who would not circle his feet or respect him and fought him, crying 'wait, wait, you will not escape', the son graced by the one whom Brahma and Vishnu could not know, the vel at Palani, lord of the gods.
nuance: The plea is built as a list of the women's charms, each ending ஆலே, 'by', and the danger is called சோரா மயல், infatuation that does not slacken. The meaning of ஆதாளிகள் and of புரிவரு in the last lines is not clear to me.

reading: The poet describes women whose eye-corners, keen as a killing vel and deadly as poison, rouse desire in young men, who swear oaths, hold them back, catch the men worth having, take all the wealth in their hands, then quarrel and bewilder them, and embrace without regard to caste; he asks for grace to leave their pleasures and, as Murugan's servant, praise and think of his feet daily. The praise names him the wonder given by the lord of Alavay who wears the moon, datura, erukku, arugu and pulai flowers, the nephew of Vishnu who shot the magic deer and pierced Vali's chest, the one who sought out the hunter girl in the forest Narada told of, and the lord holding the full-wisdom spear at Palani.
nuance: கைப்பொருள் மாள and சாதி பேதம் அறத் தழுவி: the women spend a man's wealth and embrace any man regardless of caste, the charge Parimelazhagar also makes on Kural 913. உனக்கு அடியான் sets the poet's service against his bondage to them. ஞான பூரண சத்தி names the vel as Shakti, full of wisdom.

reading: The poet speaks of devotees who chant 'Arumugam' six times with holy ash, take as their aid the feet of those who wear the feet of great ascetics, and say daily 'Guha who rides the peacock, Saravana, my lord, my honour is yours', and asks: if you only ask what these poor ones' trouble is, who will praise you, and what will the Veda not say? The praise names Murugan with a body like gold under ash, son of Uma, the lion-like vel thrown to end the poet's evil deeds, the companion of the elephant-faced god who took the life of the raging asura, at Palani, boon-giver to Brahma.
nuance: ஆறுமுகம் repeated six times opens the song with the chant itself. The question in the second quatrain seems to bind Murugan's fame to his care for devotees: if he neglects their distress, who will praise him? Its syntax (ஏழைகள் வியாகுலம் இது ஏது என வினாவில்) allows other readings.

reading: The poet tells a whole life: a human seed is born crying, crawls on the lap, toddles with dancing steps, runs in the streets, is taught the arts, at sixteen joins with young girls, weakens to Kama, sings poems in praise of patrons, runs to every quarter for wealth, melts in pleasure on scented beds and sinks in women's breasts until disease ruins his mind; then Yama chases him with the noose, parents and kin weep, they say Brahma's leaf has run out and carry him with drums to the burning ground, and those who embraced him bathe and leave the bond. Before that, he asks Murugan to come now and give the love that bows at his true lotus feet and melts singing Tamil poems. The praise, after drum syllables, names the vel that pierced the sea and split the seven hills, Murugan the guru-child of Uma, the nephew of Rama who felled Lanka's heads, who knew the Vedas and tested Tamil, at Palani, the lord who moves within his devotees' lives.
nuance: The cremation is told in detail (நவப்பறைகள் கொட்டா, சுடலை, சடம் பெரிது வேக), and the last act of the mourners, நீரில் படிந்து விடு பாசத்து அகன்று, is that they wash and let go. The leaf by which Brahma set the span of life (ஓலைப் பழம்படி) is the summons the pilot calls சமனோலை. The plea, இனி வரவேணும், is to come before this ending.

reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love: the moon climbs the sky like the sun, the submarine fire and poison, Kama shoots his arrows and the cuckoo calls, the drum of the seas, the flute and the bull's bell pierce her ears like iron, and women blame her; she cries 'Hara, Hara', longs for the peacock's rider and quarrels with everyone, and has grown faint. Though it is fate written on her head, the speaker says, taking her into his service is his burden; let him come on the horse that is Om to embrace her in her loneliness. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Krishna who kicked the cart, felled the twin trees and held up the hill against the rain, the son of the goddess under many names, the peacock hero whose vel turned the demon army to dust, and the delight of the hunter girl, at Palani.
nuance: The speaker calls her அகுதி இவள், this helpless one, so the voice is a mother's or friend's. அடிமைகொள உனது பரம், 'to take her as your servant is your charge', fuses the akam lover with the devotee. ஓகார பரி, the steed that is the syllable Om, is the peacock.

reading: The poet asks whether women's young breasts are two golden Merus, nectar pots, tender coconuts, elephant-hill peaks or the crown of Kama, says he fell into the maya of desire for them, praised as equal to the five heavenly trees men who never gave a coin, sang great Tamil and begged daily without finding a footing, and asks whether, trusting this diseased and ruined body and seeking life in vain, he will wander again in birth. The praise names his mother, Uma, sister of Vishnu and Kali who contended with Siva, the one who showed love to the Kaveri chieftain of Kalisai, the Kumaresa who came on the peacock so the asuras fell in the sea and Indra's heart was eased, and the lord whom the gods and Siva himself worship at Palani.
nuance: The confession joins two of the book's subjects, desire for women and begging from patrons in Tamil (ஒரு காசே கொடாதவரை ஐந்து தருவை நிகரே யாக ... புகழ்ந்து), and the begging is plainly in order to pay for the first. கலிசைவரு காவேரி சேவகன் seems to be a patron or devotee named in the praise; I cannot identify him.

reading: The poet describes women whose breasts are like caskets and hills, and the act with them, the hair loosened, the lips drunk, the embrace on the bed, the struggling and fondling, and asks whether he must wander so without any austerity. The praise names Murugan as the holy kinsman dear to Brahma, Vishnu's son, the one with the cock banner who fought the asura clan, and the one who lovingly told Siva the good meaning so he might know its fruit, at Palani.
nuance: தவமற்று உழல, wandering without tapas, is the whole plea. அரனுக்கு அருள் நற்பொருளைப் பகர்வோனே is the Om story without naming Om. அரிபுத்திர சித்த அஜனுக்கு ... மைத்துன வேளே makes Murugan Brahma's brother-in-law, perhaps because his consorts are counted Vishnu's daughters; the reading is uncertain.

title: பழநி
theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி), second part: the poet confesses infatuation with women and courtesans who swear lasting love and take a man's wealth, the bonds of kin and body, neglected worship and the coming of Death, and asks for Murugan's feet; the praise names Murugan as the child born of Siva's grace, as Siva's teacher, and, in 126, as the boy Uruttiracanman who judged the Tamil of the Sangam poets.
structure_note: Most songs keep the two halves. 127 is praise alone. 122, 123, 124 and 129 confess something other than women: the bonds of kin and body (122), worship never done (123), the sects and the round of births (124), and the hour of death (129). 126 and 130 are built on catalogues of comparisons for a woman's eyes and body.
source_issues: Song 126: one corrupt character in பவனு஡ணாக் (line 3); probably பவனூணாக், the beggar's food.
Song 133: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 18); clearly வயலூரா.

reading: The poet describes women who smear themselves with sandal paste and musk, chew betel and in lovemaking pass it from their mouths into their lovers', women of many minds, and asks Murugan to tell him on what day he will let go of his attachment to them. The praise names him lord of the hunter girl of the millet field, whose breasts he embraced, the one who delighted in the vel that ended the murderous asura clans, and the guru who dwells always at Palani.
nuance: பலபல சிந்தை மாதர்கள், women of many minds, is the charge of divided hearts. The word கசனை, which carries the plea, I take as attachment from context; I cannot confirm the word.

reading: The poet, caught by infatuation with women's sleepless eyes, their humming-bee hair, budding breasts and Kama's sugarcane bow, says his body burns in the moonlight and his life loosens in pain, and asks whether he must die with the thought of these women living in his heart. The praise names the vel wet with flesh and hung with bells and fresh flowers, the chest whose garland was crushed by the hunter girl's breasts, and Guha on the many-coloured peacock, at Palani hill.
nuance: அவர் குடிபுகுந்த நினைவொடும் இறந்துபடலாமோ: the fear is not death itself but dying with the women settled (குடிபுகுந்த) in the heart, where the Lord should be. The love-sickness uses the stock moonlight and Kama's bow (மதவேள்) of Tamil love poetry.

reading: The poet describes courtesans (விலைமாதர்) who swear that until life leaves the body they will never once slacken in their union with a man, then turn against those they joined before, strip them of their wealth, go out to meet the next ones and talk sweetly to them night and day; he asks Murugan to come on the peacock and free him from their net. The praise names Hari who danced with the cowherd women when mocked as a curd thief, the Lord of Kazhi, Marudur, Maraikkadu, Marugal and Dhanushkodi whose gift Murugan is, and Palani where carp leap up to fight the stars.
nuance: The song turns on the false oath (சூள்): உயிர்க்கூடு விடுமளவும், until the body's nest is left, is the promise; திரவியம் அதுடைத்து, wiping out his wealth, is the outcome. The shrine list names Siva's Tamil temples (சீகாழி, மருதூர், மறைக்காடு, மருகல், தனுக்கோடி) as one Lord's.

reading: A short song: the poet names the bonds of the world, pasu and pasam, kin, mother, father, home and children, and the agitation of the body's filth and breath, and asks for grace so that his mind's balance is not destroyed by them. The praise names Murugan as the son adorned with Ganga, arugu grass, poolai and thumbai flowers, Saravanabhava, nephew of Mukunda, who studies the many arts and the Siva Agamas, at Palani.
nuance: உலக பசு பாச தொந்தம் uses the Saiva Siddhanta terms pasu and pasam for the ordinary ties of family. The flowers of சலம் அறுகு பூளை தும்பை are Siva's; the line can make Murugan wear them or make him the son (சேய்) of the one who does. பலகலை சிவாகமங்கள் பயில்வோன் makes Murugan a student or master of the Agamas.

reading: A short song: the poet confesses that he has never once known the god with love for his two feet, never worshipped at Palani, never set his aim on the rare life, and asks whether he will not give up the burden of desire and think of ending birth. The praise calls Murugan, in four rhyming lines, the plunderer of the demons' city, the guardian of devotees who worship him, the one who delights in giving and in honoured verse, and the bodyguard (வேளைக்காரன்) of the hunters' little girl.
nuance: The four epithets end in காரப் பெருமாளே, and the last makes the Lord a servant: வேளைக்காரன் was a king's sworn bodyguard, here in Valli's service. ஆசைப் பாடை may be the burden or suffering (பாடு) of desire, or desire as a bier; the split is uncertain.

tamil: ஒருவரை யொருவர் தேறி யறிகிலர் மதவி சாரர்
உடலது சதமெ னாடி களவுபொய் கொலைக ளாடி
வருமொரு வடிவ மேவி யிருவினை கடலு ளாடி
மருவிய பரம ஞான சிவகதி பெறுக நீறு
திரிபுர மெரிய வேழ சிலைமத னெரிய மூரல்
திருசரஸ் வதிம யேசு வரியிவர் தலைவ ரோத
சுரர்பதி யயனு மாலு முறையிட அசுரர் கோடி
சுககுற மகள்ம ணாள னெனமறை பலவு மோதி
reading: The poet describes sectarians who cannot recognise one another's truth, men of the senses on no single path, who think the body permanent, steal, lie and kill, fall into Death's hell and are born again to swim the sea of the two deeds; he asks Murugan to give him holy ash and his feet, so that he may gain the supreme knowledge and the path to Siva. The praise names the guru of true knowledge who burned the three cities and Kama with a smile and an eye, the Lord whose dance Saraswati and Maheswari praise, and Murugan's vel of true knowledge that powdered crores of asuras when Indra, Brahma and Vishnu cried out, at ancient Palani where the Vedas hail him as the hunter girl's husband.
nuance: மதவிசாரர், the sect-disputers, open the song, and the remedy is not a better doctrine but a sign and a gift: நீறு வடிவுற அருளி, grant the ash to take form on me. The vel is called மெய்ஞ்ஞான அயில், the lance of true knowledge. The line மறைவரின் அனைய கோலம் is unclear to me.

reading: The poet describes women whose maids run back and forth to call men and coax them, women who dress their hair, tuck in betel rolls and smear agil and civet on their breasts before embracing with a show of love, and asks whether a bond with such hussies is fitting. The praise names Palani in Vaikavur country, where bees drink from lotus pools in the fields and sing and the conches spill pearls, and Murugan who embraced the faultless hunter girl.
nuance: சேடிமார்கள் பசப்ப, maids who coax, is the household of a courtesan, but the song does not name money. சிறுக்கிகள் உறவாமோ, is a bond with such hussies fit, makes the confession a question of the company he keeps.

reading: The poet describes women's eyes as having defeated every standard of comparison, imprisoning the sea, branding the bee, leaving poison fit only for the beggar-god's food, sending the carp into the pond and the deer into the forest, putting the mango slice in salt, the spear in the fire, trampling Yama and breaking the sword, and asks whether he will fall to the eye-corners of these wily women. The praise names Murugan as the one born, by Siva's command, in a merchant family under the name Rudrajanma, who taught Sanaka, Agastya, Pulastya and Sanatkumara, and made the forty-nine poets of the plank understand without fault the sense of the three Tamils, grammar and literature; he is the true guru, at Palani.
nuance: The first half is a single conceit: each thing a poet compares eyes to has been beaten and put away. The second names the story of the dumb child Uruttiracanman (ருத்ரஜன்மப் பெயர்), born to a merchant (செட்டி), who judged the commentaries of the Sangam's poets (சதுபத்துநவப் புலவர், the forty-nine on the plank, பலகை). Murugan is thus the judge of Tamil itself. Several lines of the first half are compressed, and my split of them is not certain.

reading: A song of praise only: Murugan is the brother of the pot-bellied, small-eyed elephant-faced god who eats gram, puffed rice, beans, fruit and sugarcane; the hero whose emerald peacock circled the northern mountain in an instant, shaking its peak; the bridegroom of Indra's daughter and the hunter girl; and the lisping child given by the grace of Pasupati, who wears the moon, konrai and the river, who came to Palani.
nuance: The song is a family portrait: the brother, the two wives, the father. The peacock circling the mountain in a moment may allude to the race round the world for the fruit that tradition ties to Palani, but the text names no fruit. மழலை மொழி மதலை, the lisping child, is Murugan as an infant.

tamil: கதியை விலக்கு மாதர்கள் புதிய இரத்ன பூஷண
கவலை மனத்த னாகிலும் உனது ப்ரசித்த மாகிய
அதிபல வஜ்ர வாகுவும் அயில்நுனை வெற்றி வேலதும்
அதிர வரற்று கோழியும் அடியர் வழுத்தி வாழ்வுறும்
இரவி குலத்தி ராசத மருவி யெதிர்த்து வீழ்கடு
இளையவ னுக்கு நீண்முடி அரசது பெற்று வாழ்வுற
பதினொரு ருத்தி ராதிகள் தபனம் விளக்கு மாளிகை
பரிமள கற்ப காடவி அரியளி சுற்று பூவுதிர்
reading: The poet says that though his mind is anxious and infatuated with the jewelled breasts of women who block the way to release, he will not forget Murugan's golden body, six faces, twelve mighty arms, the victorious vel, the peacock that holds the snake, the cock whose cry shakes the seven worlds, and the new lotus feet in which devotees thrive. The praise names Raghava, who gladly gave the long crown to the younger brother when the elder of the sun's line fell fighting, as Murugan's uncle, and Palani where the eleven Rudras keep the lamps and flowers fall from the kalpaka forest.
nuance: The song is a vow, not a plea: மறவேனே, I will not forget, answers ஆகிலும், even though, so the remembered form is set against the infatuation. கதியை விலக்கும் மாதர்கள், women who turn one from release, names what is at stake. The brother given the crown is Sugriva, son of the Sun, by the details.

reading: The poet asks that the cruel trident-bearer who drives the great black buffalo, rushing in with his tightening noose when lives end, and the jackals and fire that claim the body, not come near him, and that Murugan give him his feet, which shine with closeness, knowledge and kinship. The praise names him the son born of the grace of the Lord joined to the mountain's daughter, dwelling at old Palani where the ploughmen's shares write in the fields, the one who pierced the hard mountain with the vel so that even Mayan feared, and the Lord with lance, peacock, valour, colour and beauty.
nuance: Death here is திரிசூலன், the trident-bearer, with buffalo and noose; the jackal and fire (நரியும் எரியும் உரிமை) are the claims on the corpse, earth burial or burning. செறிவும் அறிவும் உறவும் lists what the feet give; the meaning of each word there is not certain.

reading: The poet asks a run of questions about women: is the hair a black cloud or darkness, the face the full moon, the eyes arrows or a vel, the breasts golden Meru or pots, the belly the banyan leaf on which Vishnu sleeps, the waist a thread; seeking such women like golden peacocks, he calls himself worthless and asks that after his hundred years pass his life may come to Murugan's two lotus feet. The praise names him son of Mahesvara who burned the three cities and Kama with his eye, the vel that freed the gods from Sura's prison, nephew of Narayana, and son of the merciful goddess, at Palani praised by the fourteen worlds.
nuance: The comparisons are put as questions (மேகமதோ இருளோ), the infatuated man's own way of seeing. கசடன், the worthless one, is the self-judgement. வயதாய் ஒரு நூறு செல்வதனின் மேல் I read as asking for the feet when the full life is over; it could also mean before.

reading: The poet describes courtesans who sway their breasts, talk of money with carp-eyed glances, tug at clothes, laugh, cause infatuation and confusion and then embrace, women who snatch a man's wealth; he asks that, without falling into their ways in this Kali age, Murugan fix him in devotion to Siva's state. The praise names him son of the god who burned the three cities with a small smile, the vel that made the sea cry out and the thieves flee, and the bridegroom of the hunter girl at Palani, where monkeys tear open fragrant fruit and play.
nuance: கயல்விழிப் பார்வையில் பொருள் பேசி, talking of money with the eyes, and பொருட்பறி மாதர், women who snatch wealth, name the trade. The plea places the poet in the Kali age (இக்கலியுகத்தே) and asks for சிவபதம், Siva's state, from Murugan. The split of சிவபதபத்தே is uncertain.

reading: The poet says that, praising women's dark, wide eyes as carp and swallowing the poison of the waist where the garment gathers, he has passed many days in a body of fierce deeds driven by passion, and asks that he not falter on the way fate set but gain Murugan's high feet fragrant with garlands. The praise names Muruga of the kadamba with the hunter girl at his side, whose vel defeated the deceitful asura who came with the old sea when the gods cried for justice, and who settled at Palani after seeing the shaven-headed Jains on rows of stakes.
nuance: விதிவழி நின்று, standing on fate's path, sets the confession inside fate and deed (வினை உடல், the body of deeds). பறிதலைக் குண்டர் கழுநிரை கண்டு, having seen the hair-plucked Jains in rows on stakes, is again the Madurai story told of Sambandar, now given to Murugan.

reading: The poet asks not to be bewildered by the infatuation that women stir with sidelong eyes like the arrows Kama shoots from his sugarcane bow and with breasts that rival a rutting elephant, and asks whether he, a servant who praises Murugan, will have the day when Murugan, by grace, teaches him the meaning of the Veda, as he did when Rudra came near asking for grace. The praise names the Lord on the great peacock that shook mountains, giant demons and the seven seas, with twelve jewelled arms like hills, lord of Vayalur, the guru who defeats poverty and enmity for those who recite and read the Thiruppugazh, at Palani where hunters' smoke rises among the clouds.
nuance: உருத்திரனும் விருத்திபெற ... மறை அடுத்து பொருள் உணர்த்து நாள்: the poet asks for the teaching Murugan gave Siva, and asks it as அடிமை, a servant. The song names its own book: திருப்புகழை உரைப்பவர்கள் படிப்பவர்கள் are promised victory over want (மிடி) and enmity. The syntax of the Rudra line is not certain.

title: பழநி
theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி), third part, two of them at Thiru Avinankudi at the hill's foot: the poet confesses a life spent on women and courtesans who sell themselves, begging at patrons' doors, the foul and diseased body, and the clamour of rival schools, and asks for Murugan's feet and teaching; the praise makes Murugan the Tamil child of Pukali whom Parvati fed, the lover of Valli, Siva's teacher, and the form of A, U and M.
structure_note: All follow the two halves. The confessions are mostly of women (135 to 137, 139 to 144, 147, 148); 134 runs from the womb to begging, 138 is about the rival schools, and 145 and 146 dwell on the body's filth and disease. 143 and 144 end at Thiru Avinankudi (திருவாவினன்குடி), 140, 145 and 146 at Sivamalai or Sivagiri, named for the Palani hill. 141 has a long passage of drum syllables, and 147 is a word-play song repeating one word in different senses.
source_issues: Song 135: one corrupt character in பா஡ண (line 9); possibly பாரீர் (look!), taking ஡ண for ரீ, but uncertain.
Song 135: a stray character ஧ in மாயையி ஧ல்முழ் காதே (line 10); probably மாயையில் மூழ்காதே.
Song 146: one corrupt character in உடலு஡டே (line 3); clearly உடலூடே.

tamil: கருவினுரு வாகி வந்து வயதளவி லேவ ளர்ந்து
கரியகுழல் மாதர் தங்க ளடிசுவடு மார்பு தைந்து
அரகரசி வாய வென்று தினமுநினை யாமல் நின்று
அசனமிடு வார்கள் தங்கள் மனைகள்தலை வாசல் நின்று
உரகபட மேல்வ ளர்ந்த பெரியபெரு மாள ரங்கர்
உபயகுல தீப துங்க விருதுகவி ராஜ சிங்க
பரவைமனை மீதி லன்று ஒருபொழுது தூது சென்ற
பகையசுரர் சேனை கொன்று அமரர்சிறை மீள வென்று
reading: The poet traces his life from the womb through growing up and learning many arts, then being kicked on the chest by dark-haired women's feet and wasting in grief, never thinking daily 'Hara Hara Sivaya', knowing nothing of the six religions, and standing every day without shame at the gates of those who give food; he asks whether he will perish so. The praise names Murugan as nephew of Ranganatha on the serpent and of Vishnu who measured the world, the lamp of both lines and lion of honoured poets who came to Pukali that day, and Kumaresa raised by the grace of the Lord who went once as messenger to Paravai's house, at Palani.
nuance: The life runs from கருவின் உரு to begging at food-givers' doors (அசனமிடுவார்கள் ... தலைவாசல்), with women in the middle. உபயகுல தீப ... விருதுகவி ராஜசிங்க ... புகலியூரில் அன்று வருவோனே identifies Murugan with Sambandar, born at Pukali (Sirkazhi). The messenger to Paravai is Siva sent by Sundarar to his wife, so the praise gathers the Tamil saints round Murugan.

reading: The poet repeats the questions men ask about women, whether the eyes are vel or carp, the words honey or milk, the hair cloud or forest, the breasts Meru or tusks, the waist a thread, and whether the Creator did not draw them so; he asks not to drown in the maya of such women's eyes, and promises to study Murugan's poems if given a life free of trouble. The praise is a string of rhyming names: Visakha, joy of the elephant-reared girl, husband of the hunters' daughter, younger brother of Vallabha's husband, ageless god, lord of sweet knowledge, Kumara of Palani on the peacock.
nuance: இருகண் மாயையில் மூழ்காதே: maya here is the enchantment of the eyes. The cure offered is reading: உனது காவிய நூல் ஆராய்வேன், I will study the poems about you. Two words are corrupt, and the women's or the man's voice in the questions is not clear to me.

reading: The poet speaks of courtesans whose quarrelsome carp eyes make war as Kama's army, sinful, angry women who speak ever so sweetly, and asks for grace so that his mind will not wander daily thinking union with them is sweet. The praise names Murugan the lover who embraced Valli till she melted, the giver of favours to Vedic Brahmins, the teacher who spoke the Pranava into the ear of the moon-crowned Siva, the enemy of the demons, and the pure guru whose twelve eyes give grace and who delights in his devotees, at Palani Sivagiri among groves and fields.
nuance: செவியிற் பிரணவம் ஓதிய தேசிக names the Om story outright. The praise calls Murugan himself காமுகன், the lover, for Valli, in the same song that confesses desire for courtesans; I read the contrast as deliberate, love given to the god against love sold.

reading: The poet describes at length lovemaking with women ready to sell their breasts, drinking from their lips, hair loosening, the waist bending and the forehead mark smudged, and asks whether he must fade in the great pool of cruel infatuation. The praise names Kandavel who bowed at the lotus feet of the hunter girl, the vel that dried the seven seas and shattered the mountain, and Murugan who gladly accepted the milk of the mountain's daughter, bidden to sing Tamil praised in every direction, at Palani.
nuance: கனதனம் விற்கச் சமைந்த, ready to sell their breasts, marks them as courtesans. The milk from the breast of the mountain's daughter given with செந்தமிழ் பகர் is the story told of Sambandar, fed by Parvati before he sang; the song gives it to Murugan. As in 15, Murugan bows before Valli (பதம் பணிந்தருள்).

tamil: கலைகொடு பவுத்தர் காம கருமிகள் துருக்கர் மாய
கலகமிடு தர்க்கர் வாம பயிரவர் விருத்த ரோடு
சிலுகியெதிர் குத்தி வாது செயவுமொரு வர்க்கு நீதி
தெரிதர விளக்கி ஞான தரிசந மளித்து வீறு
கெலையுற எதிர்த்த கோர இபமுக அரக்க னோடு
குறையுட லெடுத்து வீசி யலகையொடு பத்ர காளி
பலமிகு புனத்து லாவு குறவநிதை சித்ர பார
படைபொருது மிக்க யூக மழைமுகிலை யொட்டி யேறு
reading: The poet lists the schools that clamour with their many books, the Buddhists, the ritualists, the Turks, the followers of Kapila and Kanada, the materialists, the quarrelling logicians and the left-hand Bhairavas, and asks whether there will be a day when Murugan makes clear the teaching that is hard for anyone to discern, gives him the vision of knowledge and grants him his feet. The praise names the vel thrown at the elephant-faced demon and the horse-faced and lion-faced warriors while ghouls and Bhadrakali danced, the chest that rests on the hunter girl's breasts, and Palani, which rises to the rain clouds.
nuance: The list names Islam (துருக்கர்) beside the Indian schools, as one more voice in the dispute. The plea is for உபதேசம் and ஞான தரிசனம்: not to win the debate but to be taught past it. காம கருமிகள் may be the ritualists of desire-rites; that identification is mine.

tamil: களபமுலை யைத்தி றந்து தளவ நகை யைக்கொ ணர்ந்து
கரியகுழ லைப்ப கிர்ந்து மலர்சொருகு கொப்ப விழந்து
முழுமதி யெனச்சி றந்த நகைமுக மினுக்கி யின்ப
முதலுளது கைப்பு குந்து அழகுதுகி லைத்தி றந்து
இளமதி கடுக்கை தும்பை அரவணி பவர்க்கி சைந்து
இபமுகவ னுக்கு கந்த இளையவ மருக்க டம்ப
குழகென எடுத்து கந்த உமைமுலை பிடித்த ருந்து
குடிலொடு மிகச்செ றிந்த இதணுள புனத்தி ருந்த
reading: The poet describes courtesans who bare their sandal-smeared breasts, show a jasmine smile, let flowers fall from loosened hair like stars, stand and name a price, and once the money is in their hands open their garments and press close, and asks whether he will waste away for them. The praise names Murugan the guru who told the sweet meaning to Siva of the crescent, konrai and serpent, brother of the elephant-faced god, the one who grants his feet on the poet's head, the child who drank at Uma's breast when she lifted him, and the lover of the hunters' daughter at Sivagiri.
nuance: விலைகூறி, naming the price, and முதல் உளது கைப்புகுந்து, once the capital is in hand, make the trade plain. எனது தலையில் பதங்கள் அருள்வோனே, who grants his feet on my head, is the poet speaking of a gift already given, the feet set on the devotee's head.

reading: The poet describes women with flowered hair, brow-mark, arrow-eyes, conch necks, breasts and a creeper-thin waist, cuckoo voices and the gait of peahens and swans, women who seize a man's wealth and spread nets, and asks whether he will give up the base pleasure of following them in the burning mire. The praise names Murugan the guru of Sambhu, who holds axe and deer and wears konrai, thumbai, moon, river and snake; the vel that boiled the sea and laid the demons and mountains to sleep; the feet on the whirling peacock; and the husband of the hunter girl, daughter of Lakshmi and daughter-in-law of Uma, at Sivamalai.
nuance: பொருள்பறி, seizing wealth, and புலையவர் வழி இன்பு, the pleasure of the base path, carry the judgement. திருமகள் ... குறத்தி மகள், making Valli Lakshmi's daughter, follows the tradition of her birth. The opening words of Siva's description (பறித்த விழி) I cannot place, and the long description of the women has compressed lines.

reading: The poet describes women who stand every day at the doorway with breasts like golden pots, setting a price so that all may have their pleasure, and confesses that, bewildered by their tricks, he has wasted in desire on the bed and drowned in a sea of pleasure; he asks Murugan to remove his deceitful heart and give him the refuge of his feet. The praise is a long passage of drum syllables, the peacock dancing so that the elephants of the eight directions and the cosmic sphere tremble, and the vel that killed the demon's kin, at Palani.
nuance: அனைவரும் கொளும் என்று மேவு இலையிடும், setting a price so that all may take, is the common woman of Kural chapter 92. The deceit confessed is the poet's own (வஞ்சக நெஞ்சு) as well as the women's (தோதகம்). The drum syllables (தனதனந்தன, டிகுகு, டுண்டுடு) are rhythm.

reading: The poet describes the breasts of women who delight in fine garments, and says that, melting like wax in fire for them and sunk in the sea of birth with debased words, he is like a fool to be laughed at; he asks whether he must be bound to the shame of this infatuation. The praise names Guha whose shoulders bear the scent of the hunter girl's breasts, the lord who gave delight to the mountain king's daughter, consort of the ascetic Siva with the river in his hair, the vel that destroyed the demons in an instant, and Kumara of Palani.
nuance: அனற்குள் மெழுக்கென, like wax in fire, and பவக்கடல், the sea of births, set the infatuation within the round of births. The song's syllables are packed tightly into its rhythm, and several word-splits in both halves, especially the last two lines, are my guesses.

reading: The poet says that after embracing women with breasts rising like mountains and anointed with camphor, he lost the wealth in his hand and grew weary, his mind failing, hiccups rising, dried out like ginger, and asks whether, leaving this wasting disease, he will praise Murugan as his treasure. The praise names him the old man who loved the golden hunter girl given by the forest hunters, the fierce hero whose vel shattered the seas, the mountain and Sura's heads, the gracious one whose small feet ring with anklet bells, and the son of Sankari, at Thiru Avinankudi.
nuance: கைப்பொருளே இழந்து, losing the wealth in the hand, links the women to the man's ruin. சுக்கதுபோலே, like dried ginger, is the body after. அக்கிழவோனே, that old man, is Murugan's disguise as an old man to win Valli.

reading: The poet says that, his heart wavering with a love bound to deeds and bearing a false body of flesh, blood, skin and fat, he has bowed at the feet of women with flowered hair, sharp eyes and bow brows and desired their golden shoulders, and asks whether it is right for him to sink so low and perish. The praise names the vel that fought until Sura fell and the waters dried while the gods stood worshipping, the one who roams the hill field where the pure hunter peahen stood, the one dear to the Lord who drank the poison, whom Brahma and Garuda-bannered Vishnu worship, at Thiru Avinankudi among sugar mills and groves.
nuance: தாள் பணிந்து, bowing at their feet, is worship given to the wrong feet, and தாழ்வடைந்து உலைய, sinking and perishing, is its result. பொய்க் காயம், the false body, is listed as flesh, blood, skin and fat.

reading: The poet calls the body a hut of excrement, urine, fat, bone, flesh, guts, hair and blood, and those who live in it cruel, ignorant and pathless; calling himself hellish and wretched, he says he will not forget the smiling faces, shining eyes and two flower feet of Murugan, who came on the peacock so that he might hold in his mind 'Saravana' and the light of Siva. The praise names Murugan lord of the land of Puliyur, where cuckoos and bees sound in the groves and peacocks dance, the one who sent the asuras with their elephants and horses to Yama's city, guru of the Lord whose dancing feet Brahma, sages, gods and Rambha hail with 'Hara Hara Siva Siva', and the lover of the hunter girl at Sivamalai.
nuance: குரம்பை, the hut, is the body, as in Saiva poetry generally. The string of names for himself (நரகனை, கலியனை, சடலனை) is the poet's self-abuse before the grace. புலிநகர் is Puliyur, Chidambaram, the dancer's city. The middle lines are hard to construe, and whether the cruel ones are all who live in bodies or the women is my reading.

reading: The poet describes the body, oozing blood, filth and urine, with worms writhing, flesh, marrow and phlegm, as a house whose tenants are diseases, fits, colic, headache and stomach-ache, and confesses he has cherished it and been infatuated with women; he asks that his grief and deeds be scattered and that Murugan place his feet on his head. The praise names the vel that pierced the mountain and burned the sea, the peacock rider whom gods and sages hail as guru and refuge, the son of the mountain's daughter, sister of Hari, and the one whom the hunter girl embraced in fear when Ganapati came as an elephant, at Palani.
nuance: குடிகள் எனப் பல ... பிணி: the diseases are the body's tenants. The plea is the same as 139's, the feet on the head (எனது தலை பதம் அருள்வாயே). The elephant that frightened Valli into Murugan's arms is told outright (கணபதி ... மதகரி வடிவு கொடு வர).

reading: The poet lists the things women's hair, brows, lips, teeth, ears, words, breasts and eyes are compared to, and asks whether he, a dog, should go on telling women false ways and be uselessly troubled. The praise is word play: Murugan the peacock hero by whose grace the deeds of those who bow at his anklets come loose, the nephew of Lakshmi's lord, the vel that pierced the mountain and the demons, Muruga Visakha of the Palani hill, lord of the gods whom the sea-coloured Hari praises.
nuance: The second half is a yamakam: கழல், கமலை, பழநி மலை and பரவை are each repeated three times with different word-splits and senses (கழல் as anklet and as coming loose). பழநி may play on பழம் நீ, the fruit story, but the text gives only the repeated word. நாயேன், I the dog, is the self-abuse. Several of the splits are uncertain.

tamil: குலவு கிகிகி கிகிகி எனவு மிடறி லொலிகள்
இளநி ரெனவு முலைக ளசைய உபய தொடையும்
இனிய அமுத ரசமும் வடிய உபரி புரிவர்
மிளிரு மதுர கவிதை யொளிரும் அருண கிரிசொல்
விமலி அமலி நிமலி குமரி கவுரி தருணி
பழைய மறையின் முடிவி லகர மகர உகர
பழன வயல்கள் கமுகு கதலி பனசை யுலவ
reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women whose hair slips, words falter, eyes roll, throats make sounds, breasts and thighs sway and who take the upper place, and asks whether he will be troubled in that infatuation. The praise names Murugan as the one who wears the bright, sweet poetry spoken by Arunagiri, son of the pure virgin goddess Gauri who walks in the forest, and the one whose form is the A, U and M at the end of the ancient Veda, at Palani among fields, areca, plantain and jack.
nuance: அருணகிரி சொல் ... அணிவோனே: the poet names himself, and his poem as Murugan's ornament. பழைய மறையின் முடிவில் அகர மகர உகர படிவ வடிவம் makes Murugan the form of Om, the end of the Veda. விஜயகிரி is perhaps another name of the poet or of Palani.

title: பழநி
theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி, 4 of 7): the poet confesses bondage to courtesans who sell their bodies and take a man's wealth, the rotting body and its burning, and his own faults, and asks for Murugan's feet, grace and liberating knowledge; the praise turns on Murugan as Siva's teacher, as the Tamil saint who defeated the Jains, on Vishnu as uncle, and on the shrine's patron from Kalisai.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (149, 150, 152, 154, 155) and songs of women's charms (151, 161, 163); death and the body (154, 157, 158); a list of self-accusations (159); and three songs of doctrine and yoga rather than confession (156, 160, 162). Two songs (149, 152) name Seypathi (Vayalur) as the place where Murugan took the poet into service; three (149, 150) cast Murugan as the saint who impaled the Jains.
source_issues: Song 150: the long run of names in lines 44 to 46 of the praise (துங்கன் வஞ்சன் சங்கன் மைந்தன் தருமகன் முநி தழல் வருதகர்) does not split cleanly; possibly garbled.
Song 156: தெவயானை (line 13) for தேவயானை, probably a lost vowel sign.
Song 161: one corrupt character in மதனு஡லே (line 2); clearly மதனூலே (Kama's treatise).
Song 162: சீரங் னெனது (line 10) looks garbled, a letter lost after சீரங்.

reading: The poet describes women who arrange their clothes and hair, chew betel, call a man to bed, cloud his sense, embrace him with nail-marked breasts and take the wealth of proud men while binding them in lust, and asks Murugan to end the delusion that drives his mind to the senses and give him his holy anklets. The praise makes Murugan the poet-king who impaled the Jain teachers on heated stakes, spread holy ash, and set his weighty word into fire and water; whom the moon-crowned Siva honoured as 'father'; and who stopped the poet at Seypathi and made him his servant, at Palani.
nuance: கைப்பொருட் கவர, taking the wealth in a man's hand, marks the women as courtesans; ப்ரமம், delusion, is the poet's word for his state. கனற்புனலிற் கனத்த சொலைப் பதித்தெழுதி points to the ordeals of fire and water by which, in tradition, Sambandar's written verses defeated the Jains of Madurai. தகப்பன் மதித்து உகப்பன் எனச் சிறக்க has Siva honour his son as a father, the teacher's rank. செய்ப்பதிக்குள் எனைத் தடுத்து அடிமைப் படுத்த is the poet's own story: he was stopped and taken into service at Vayalur.

reading: The poet describes women with musk-smeared breasts and moon-bright faces who coax, plead and deceive in one trade, claim a man as their right and charmingly take every possession, and asks that, through the sorrow and infatuation they cause, he may still come to praise Murugan's flower feet and gain grace, joy and kinship with him. The praise runs through Vishnu's deeds (the demoness Kamsa sent, the lion that devoured Hiranya, the one who drove Arjuna's chariot), a battle in drum syllables against an elephant-faced foe, the Jains impaled, the leaf that went against the river and the poem that brought a girl back from her bones, at Sivagiri.
nuance: பொருளுள தெவைகளு நயமொடு கவர்பவர், those who charmingly take whatever wealth there is, is the courtesan charge. உரை நதி எதிர்பட and என்பின் அரிவையை எதிர்வர விடுகவி are the leaf floating upstream in the Vaigai and the poem that raised a girl from her bones, both told of Sambandar, here credited to Murugan. Many runs of the rhythm (the list of Vishnu's names before மருகோனே, துங்கன் வஞ்சன் சங்கன் மைந்தன் தருமகன்) split uncertainly.

reading: The poet runs through a woman's beauty as a string of questions (is her hair darkness or cloud, her brow a bow or a crescent, her speech nectar or fruit, her breasts elephants or hills), says he gives his heart to such dancing sinful women, and asks instead for the glory of a scripture that thinks only of Murugan's two red feet. The praise names the vel that cut down the asura chief, the gods and sages who serve him, Ganapati's brother, the hunter girl's husband and Kathirkamam, at Palani.
nuance: The doubting similes (இருளோ புயலோ, சிலையோ பிறையோ) are the stock catalogue of beauty, and the dance syllables (திந்தித் திமிதிமி) belong to the women's dance, not to battle. மறையாகிய சீர் may mean the glory of scripture or of a secret; the sense of the plea is not certain. Kathirkamam (கதிர்காமா) is named in a Palani song.

reading: The poet describes courtesans adorned with saffron, camphor, sandal, coral and garlands who sell their breasts for a price, and asks not to delight in their sinful words sweet as milk, sugar and honey, but to keep the love Murugan gave him at Seypathi of singing Thiruppugazh daily with his lotus feet held within. The praise names the vel that dried the sea, bowed the eight hills, burst Krauncha and crushed Sura, and the guru loved by the father who drank the poison and dances in the burning ground wearing the gods' bones, at Avinankudi with its golden-pot towers.
nuance: பணைத்தனம் விற்கும் பொதுமாதர், women who sell their breasts, is the plainest courtesan charge of the book. The song names its own book: ஓதுகின்ற திருப்புகழ் நித்தம் பாடும் அன்பு, the love of singing Thiruppugazh daily, given at Seypathi (Vayalur), where by tradition the poet received his calling.

reading: The poet describes in detail lovemaking with women, from the sweating face and loosened hair to the bird-cries of the throat and the sound of bangles and anklets, and says that even if he falls into that river of pleasure he, Murugan's servant, will never for a moment forget his feet. The praise names the war against the asuras in the sea, Murugan's courtship of the hunter girl in the millet field, and the peacock that circled the world while the elephant-faced one circled Siva, and the lord in the heart of the servant from Kalisai, at Veerai and Palani, the hill of knowledge.
nuance: The plea is unusual: not to be freed from women but, even while falling (வீழுகினும்), not to forget the feet (மறவேனே). ஆனைமுகர் அரனை ஓடி வலம்வரு முன் ... உலகை வலமாக வரு மயில் is the race round the world for the fruit, told fully in 176. கலிசை வரு சேவகன், the servant from Kalisai, recurs in the Palani songs (158, 159) as a devotee in whose heart Murugan lives.

reading: The poet describes adorned women who clutch a man, then his life after them: worry, wealth gone, stammering speech, a staff, disease, exhaustion and the sickbed, until many bind the body, beat their heads, lay it on the cremation logs and burn it to ash, and asks whether he will become a mere corpse. The praise, after a battle in drum syllables, names the deeds of Siva who burned the cities and Kama and the punishment of Brahma, Murugan as the true guru who taught the meaning to the supreme dancer, and his union with the parrot-voiced girl, at Palani.
nuance: The confession moves in one breath from the women's embrace (கொளுமாதர் சுகமுற்று) to ruin, old age and the pyre, so that lust leads straight to the burning ground; சடமாமோ, 'shall I become a corpse?', is the whole plea. பரமர்க்குச் சற்குருவொத்துப் பொருளைக் கற்பித்தருள்வோனே is Murugan teaching Siva. Who does the acts before it (knocking out the sun's teeth, burning the cities, burning Kama, striking Brahma) depends on how the run is parsed; most are Siva's deeds.

reading: The poet describes priced women who sing in the street, call out 'who has come?', bathe, take a man to the cotton bed, rouse lust with charms and, when he begs, shut the front door, and asks Murugan to remove his desire for them and give his golden feet. The praise names Krishna, who had Arjuna drive the chariot as a eunuch and gave the Pandavas Kurukshetra through friendship, as uncle, and Murugan as the guru who spoke the quality into Siva's ear, at Palani of cool Tamil.
nuance: பொன் பறி விலைமாதர், priced women who snatch gold, and முன்றலை வாயில் அடைத்து, shutting the door, mark the courtesan: the door closes when the money ends. ஒரு பேடி இன்கன தேரை நடத்தி recalls Arjuna as Brihannala. சங்கரனார் செவி புக்கப் பண்பு does not name Om, so `gnaanam` stands for what was taught.

reading: A short song: Murugan, the guru who spoke the instructing mantra into both of Siva's ears to cool his heart, the son of Sivakama Sundari, is asked to come and say 'do not fear' to one who, not loving his deeds, wanders the world in vain in base illusion, and to give the bliss of grace-knowledge so that understanding grows and trouble ends. The praise names Krishna who stole butter and was tied to the mortar, Rama as uncle, Devayanai and the hunter girl, at Thiruvavinankudi.
nuance: The song opens with the teaching (உபதேச மந்த்ரம் இரு செவிமீதிலும்) and asks for the same gift for the poet: அருள்ஞான இன்பம். அவமாயை, base illusion, is the condition. செகமேல் மெய் கண்ட may mean 'who saw the truth in the world' or allude to Meykandar of the Siddhanta; I can't tell.

reading: The poet pictures death: drums beat, Death's men seize him and drag him with a rope, kin wail, the body is burned and the ashes sent to the sea; before this hut is gone, he asks that, as the Veda describes the final state of release, body, life and faculties be passed beyond and the three gunas brought under, and that Murugan come dancing on the peacock and give him Siva's feet. The praise tells how Siva praised him, how the worlds shook as he chased the serpent, his union with the hunter girl in the millet hut, and how he taught Agastya the ways of knowledge and penance in Tamil, at Palani.
nuance: The plea is for release while still in the body (படிக்குடிலை ஒழியாதே, before the earthly hut is gone), described in Vedantic terms: மறைமுறையின் இறுதிநிலை முத்தி, கரணவெளி, குணத்திரயம். குறுமுநிவன் is Agastya; Murugan as his Tamil teacher recurs through the book. The middle lines of the plea split uncertainly.

reading: The poet describes the body as an illusory mass of filth, pus, blood, worms, skin, flesh, bone and nerves, food for jackals, vultures and crows, that stinks the moment the life passes to Yama's hand, and confesses that, cherishing it as lasting, he desires women and is dying in that sorrow; he asks Murugan to love him. The praise names Krishna who broke the two tusks of the elephant sent by Kamsa and herded cows with his flute, the vel that broke Krauncha, and the servant from Kalisai who bows to Murugan, at Veerai and Palani.
nuance: The catalogue of the body (சீ, உதிரம், புழு, தோல், தசை, எலும்பு, நரம்பு) is the Naladiyar's method, turned on the poet's own body and set beside his desire: he knows what the body is and still cherishes it (பேணி நிலையென்று). The elephant whose tusks Krishna broke (வாரண இரண்டு கோடொடிய) is Kuvalayapida, by its details.

reading: The poet lists his own faults: an angry fool, a wrongdoer without order, a deceiver who seeks the disease of birth, without justice or worth, a liar to all, cruel, a talebearer, ignorant, rubbish who does not cherish Murugan's feet; and asks that even so he be joined to Murugan's devotees. The praise names the victory garland of the war, the peacock as horse, the servant from Kalisai in whose heart he lives, at Veerai and Palani.
nuance: The whole confession is self-abuse without a story (சீறல் அசடன், கபடி, கோளன், கூளன்), and the plea is modest: not release but company, உனடியரொடு கூடும் வகைமை.

reading: A song of doctrine: Murugan is addressed as the one life that is the silence at the crown of the Veda, Siva as knowledge, the non-dual supreme flame and the formless nature; the poet confesses that, not knowing how to reach the lotus feet of bliss known to the liberated who have seen turiya, he takes as real the body formed in the womb from seed and breath, divided by the three gunas and stirred by deeds, a cave of illusion, and asks for grace to rule this worthless thing. The praise names him as root, crown and middle of the six religions and the Veda, the cosmic egg and space, the guru who came as the pranava mantra, the dancer on the peacock and Saravanabhava, Subramanya on Palani hill.
nuance: The vocabulary is Vedanta and Siddhanta together: சுருதிமுடி மோனம், அத்துவிதம், நிட்கள சொரூபம், துரியநிலை, முக்குண விபாகம். The body is born in the womb (கருவில் உரு, சுக்கில நிதானம், வளி பொரும) and is called refuse (குப்பைமல வாழ்வு) and a cave of maya. உருபிரணவாம் மந்த்ர ... குருநாதா makes Murugan the pranava in person. Several compounds split uncertainly.

tamil: சுருளளக பார கொங்கை மகளிர்வச மாயி சைந்து
சுருதியென வேநி னைந்து அறிவிலிக ளோடி ணங்கு
அருமறைக ளேநி னைந்து மநுநெறியி லேந டந்து
அகிலபுவ னாதி யெங்கும் வெளியுறமெய்ஞ் ஞான இன்ப
பருதிமகன் வாசல் மந்த்ரி அநுமனொடு நேர்ப ணிந்து
பரவியவி பீஷ ணன்பொன் மகுடமுடி சூட நின்ற
எரிபுகுத மாறி லண்டர் குடிபுகுத மாறு கொண்ட
இளையகுற மாது பங்க பழநிமலை நாத கந்த
reading: The poet confesses that, enslaved to women, he took Kama's treatise of lovemaking as if it were scripture and mixed with fools, and asks that, like Murugan's devotees, he may meditate on the scriptures, walk Manu's path, know understanding by understanding, become full, and drink unceasingly the nectar of true knowledge and bliss. The praise tells the Rama story through Sugriva, Hanuman and Vibhishana's crowning and Ravana's burning with his kin, and names Murugan Rama's nephew, the hunter girl's lord, at Palani, the joy of the mountain's daughter.
nuance: மதனூலே சுருதியென நினைந்து, taking the love-treatise for the Veda, is the poet's sharpest self-mockery: the wrong book taken as scripture, set against அருமறைகளே நினைந்து. அறிவை அறிவால் அறிந்து, knowing knowledge by knowledge, is the goal.

tamil: ஞானங்கொள் பொறிகள் கூடி வானிந்து கதிரி லாத
நாவின்ப ரசம தான ஆநந்த அருவி பாய
ஊனங்க ளுயிர்கள் மோக நானென்ப தறிவி லாம
ஓரந்த மருவி ஞான மாவிஞ்சை முதுகி னேறி
தேனங்கொ ளிதழி தாகி தாரிந்து சலில வேணி
சேர்பஞ்ச வடிவி மோகி யோகங்கொள் மவுன ஜோதி
கானங்கள் வரைகள் தீவு ஓதங்கள் பொடிய நீல
காமன்கை மலர்கள் நாண வேலம்பெ ணமளி சேர்வை
reading: A song of yoga: the poet asks that his senses gather and reach the land without moon or sun, climb the mountain of Namasivaya, let the bliss of the tongue fall like a waterfall, play among the nadas, forget body, souls, delusion and 'I', become one end with the Lord, and ride on great knowledge around the worlds. The praise names Siva with konrai, moon and river in his hair, 'my father', and his consort as the pure lord's half, Murugan on the peacock that shattered forests and seas, and Kama's arrows shamed, at 'our Palani'.
nuance: The plea is a yogic ascent, not a confession: வான் இந்து கதிர் இலாத நாடு (where neither moon nor sun shines), நமசிவாய வரை, நாவின்ப ரசம், நாதங்களொடு குலாவி, நான் என்பது அறிவிலாமல். ஓமங்கி உருவமாகி and இருவோரும் ஓரந்த மருவி (the two joining in one end) are uncertain splits; who the two are is not said. The last lines of praise are hard to parse.

reading: The poet says that fate, written on his head, drove him into houses with fragrant-haired women whose eyes are nets, and that he sinks in a burning sea of attachment to sons, mother, father, wives, friends and cattle; he asks for the meaning that is first as A is first, to join his hands and melt crying 'Hara', and for Murugan's feet, coming on the emerald peacock with vel and cock banner. The praise runs through Krishna's deeds (the hill as umbrella, Vidura's house, the stolen butter, Vamana, the dance on the serpent) as uncle, and Murugan who brought the elephant to frighten the girl among the deer, guru, son of the mountain's daughter, at Palani.
nuance: விதி தலையில் எழுதியும் places the poet's lust under fate.
