The bonds of kin (தனயர் அனை மதர் மனைவியர்) are a sea of fire (தவன சலதி). அகர முதல் உள பொருள் echoes the Kural's first line and points, as in 173, to the meaning of the first letter. வனிதை வெருவ முன் வர is the elephant that frightened Valli into Murugan's arms.

title: பழநி
theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி, 5 of 7): the poet confesses lust and courtesans who take a man's property, his faults and sins, disease and Death's rope, and the vain praise of patrons and court poets, and asks for Murugan's feet, service and knowledge; the praise turns on Murugan as Siva's child guru who spoke the pranava, the race for the fruit that brought him to Palani, the Tamil saint who cured the Pandya, and Vishnu as uncle.
structure_note: Courtesan and love songs (169, 172, 177, 178, and 164, a love-lament in another voice); lists of self-accusation (167, 174) and of diseases (166); Death and rebirth (165, 168); two songs against patrons and court poets (171, 175); the litany 170; and 176, a song of praise alone that tells the Palani story of the fruit.
source_issues: Song 166: one corrupt character in தா஡ணர் (line 6); probably தாரீர் ('give').
Song 169: one corrupt character in தா஡ணரெ (line 5); probably தாரீரே ('give').
Song 170: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 18); clearly வயலூரா. Also the unflagged garble அர்ருரர் (line 19), probably ஆரூரர் (Sundarar).
Song 171: the unflagged garble மல்ருபம் (line 21); a letter seems lost, perhaps மலரூபம்.
Song 174: one corrupt character in கடலு஡டு (line 3); clearly கடலூடு.
Song 176: one corrupt character in தன஧முவ (line 6); the word cannot be restored with confidence.

reading: A love-lament, apparently in a mother's or companion's voice: through Kama's bow, the dark roaring sea with its rolling pearls and the evening when the light fades, the creeper-like girl has lost speech and sense and her life grows faint, and Murugan is asked to give her his garland. The praise names him the hero who imprisoned the lotus-born Brahma, the one who melted for Devayanai, and the one who told a word to Siva of the radiant matted hair, at Palani.
nuance: The speaker never says 'I': the girl is கொடி, the creeper, and the plea is for Murugan's garland (நற்பிணையல்) for her, the stock request of akam poems addressed to a god. The metre and machinery (Kama's arrows, the sea, the evening) match 24. The first lines split uncertainly.

reading: The poet asks that before fierce-eyed Death throws his twisted rope around his head, when kin, friends, house, wealth and power become strangers, Murugan grant him thought of his two feet, end his loneliness and give him knowledge. The praise names Kumara of war, the lord of Palani hill, the hunter girl's bridegroom, the destroyer of the asuras who troubled the gods, the owner of dharma, colour, the peacock and the vel.
nuance: அயலாக, become strangers, is the point: at Death's coming everything owned turns foreign, and the poet names his state தனிமை, loneliness. மயிலும் அயிலும் is a play on peacock and vel.

reading: The poet lists the diseases (headache, jaundice, anaemia, fever, eye pain, colic, asthma) and asks that they not come near, nor the indignity of physicians who name remedies, turn deaf, and demand payment for failing age; and asks that, like the sages who gather flowers for garlands to adorn his feet and hold them in their hearts, he may be given the feet, with Murugan coming on the peacock that lifts the snake. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea, cut Ravana's crowns and brought back Janaki, as uncle; Siva who danced in the hall to shame Kali, to whom Murugan came as a father; and the hunter girl on her platform, at Palani.
nuance: The list of illnesses (தலைவலி, காமாலை, சோகை, சுரம், சூலை, காயாசுவாசம்) is unusually medical. The physicians' lines are hard to parse: who turns deaf and who is asked to give (தாரீர்) is not certain. மாதாதையே எனவும் வருவோனே again makes Murugan father to his father, the teacher's rank.

reading: A short song of self-accusation: the poet says he has no firmness, no good quality, no skill, no wonderful deed, no true penance, no japa, no place in heaven, no giving hand and no fit speech, and asks that he may sing good Tamil, reach the two feet, be rid of both kinds of deeds and gain the destined state. The praise names the vel against the asuras and Murugan as son of the dancer whose matted hair wears the crescent, arugu, konrai and crane feather, at Palani.
nuance: The confession is built of negatives in -இலி (திடமிலி, சற்குணமிலி, தவமிலி, கொடையிலி); the remedy is first to sing Tamil (நற்றமிழ் பாட) and then to be rid of இருவினை, good and bad deeds alike.

reading: The poet asks that if Murugan leaves him in birth, which is like a dark sea of hell, he not be deaf, blind, deformed or the least poor, but have a fine form, high family, knowledge and fullness, and that Murugan give his grace and come to take him, mind and all, into service. The praise names the vel that made the asuras' heads roll, the sea wail and the mountain break, Vishnu on the serpent bed as uncle and the dark-throated Siva as father, at Palani.
nuance: The plea is conditional and practical: if rebirth must come (விடுவாயேல்), let it be a whole and fortunate one, then service. It does not ask for release outright.

reading: The poet quotes his own wooing of women (peacock, lotus, deer, honey who knows every art of love, come to my breasts, give me your lips, I swear I will be your slave) and says he wandered so, a great sinner without justice, infatuated, and never chanted Murugan's name, joined his devotees or wore ash; yet he asks for the anklets so that the servant may be saved. The praise tells the churning of the ocean, Siva taking the poison and Vishnu as the enchantress sharing the nectar, as uncle, and the generous lord of Kalisai on the Kaveri, at Veerai and Palani.
nuance: Unusually the poet's own pleading speech to women is quoted (என் ஆணை மொழி சோர்வதிலை, யான் அடிமையாவேன்): he offers them the servitude (அடிமை) he owes Murugan, and the song turns on that word. The omissions are worship's marks: chanting, devotees, ash on the forehead (நீறு நுதல்மீதிடலிலன்). The patron of Kalisai is praised as a cloud in giving.

reading: A litany of homage (நமோநம): Murugan beyond nada, bindu and kala, the form of Vedic mantra, the scholar of knowledge, son of Sambhu, lord of the serpent-bound peacock, the one who split the Suras, the lamp of auspicious light, Devayanai's lord; the poet asks never to forget giving, worship with many rites, recitation, good conduct, kindness and service at the guru's feet. The praise names him lord of Vayalur in the Chola land of the Kaveri and recalls the Chera king who rode with Sundarar to Kailas and sang the Ula, at Avinankudi in the Kongu land.
nuance: நாத விந்து கலாதீ puts Murugan beyond the tattvas of Saiva cosmology. The plea is a short list of practice (ஈதல், பூஜை, ஓதல், குருசீர்பாத சேவை), not a confession. The last lines recall Cheraman Perumal's ride to Kailas with Sundarar (ஆரூரர் தோழமை, the horse, the Ula).

reading: The poet attacks court poets who learn petty verses, call them Veda, boast daily, win titles, palanquins, umbrellas, rings and earrings, but whose learning breaks and changes colour when tested, and asks that he may stand before Murugan and speak fine words with full devotion. The praise tells how a pinch of ash from a small hand cured the Pandya of the fever the Jains had set on him and the Jains were impaled, and how Murugan took as his hereditary servant a fool who embraced women without limit and a sinner dazed by impurity, at Palani.
nuance: The target is professional learning: titles and regalia (சத்ர சாமர, மோதிரம், குண்டலம்) without substance. The cure of செழியன் with ash from a child's hand (சிறிய கர பங்கயத்து நீறு) is Sambandar's story, credited to Murugan as in 149 and 150. The poet calls himself the one taken into வழியடிமை, inherited service. Some lines of the confession are unclear.

reading: The poet describes kohl-eyed women who stand in the street with sweating foreheads and swaying breasts, delude men daily on flower beds, take every possession under friendship and invent new tricks each day, and asks that, instead of their company, Murugan give him a cool mind of true devotion. The praise names Siva who gave paddy to a learned Tamil poet, Devayanai whom the elephant of heaven raised, Vishnu with the conch as uncle, and Palani where the drummers' mridangam sounds like thunder.
nuance: மெத்தவும் நட்பொடு பறித்து, robbing under friendship, is the courtesan charge. மெய்ப்படு பத்தி, true devotion, and உட்குளிர் புத்தி, a cool mind, are what is asked. The story of Siva giving paddy to a poet (நெல் பல அளித்த) I cannot identify with certainty.

tamil: பகர்தற்கரி தான செந்தமி ழிசையிற்சில பாட லன்பொடு
பவளத்தினை வீழி யின்கனி யதனைப்பொரு வாய் மடந்தையர்
சகரக்கடல் சூழ மம்புவி மிசையிப்படி யேதி ரிந்துழல்
தகதித்திமி தாகி ணங்கிண எனவுற்றெழு தோகை யம்பரி
நுகர்வித்தக மாகு மென்றுமை மொழியிற்பொழி பாலை யுண்டிடு
நுதிவைத்தக ராம லைந்திடு களிறுக்கரு ளேபு ரிந்திட
அகரப்பொரு ளாதி யொன்றிடு முதலக்கர மான தின்பொருள்
அமரர்க்கிறை யேவ ணங்கிய பழநித்திரு வாவி னன்குடி
reading: The poet confesses that he has not learned a few songs of fine Tamil in music or known the epics, and that through women with coral lips he wanders the sea-girt earth like a dry leaf; before his body thins he asks Murugan to come on the dancing peacock. The praise names him as the child who drank the milk Uma poured, Vishnu who came in a moment to save the elephant from the crocodile as uncle, and the guru who told Hara the meaning of the first letter, at Thiruvavinankudi in Palani.
nuance: The confession sets neglected Tamil learning beside lust. உமை மொழியிற் பொழி பாலை உண்டிடு பாலன் is Sambandar, fed by Uma, again identified with Murugan. அகரப் பொருள் ஆதி ஒன்றிடு முதல் அக்கரம் is the meaning of the first syllable, the pranava, told to Siva.

reading: The poet lists his sins: guilty of the five great crimes, a total fool, deceitful, a miser, a gambler, a killer, seeking women, house and gold, held by the five malas and bonds and by the five elements, who never joined the devotees of grace; and asks to be granted to play in Kanda's world, where the consort of the moon-crowned Siva, the light Vishnu and Brahma could not find, plays. The praise names the vel against Sura's army, the sea and Krauncha, Murugan as son of Uma, Rama's sister, called Sivakami, Kali and Mangala, and the hunter girl, at Palani.
nuance: பஞ்ச பாதகன் (guilty of the five great sins) and பஞ்ச மாமலம் (five impurities) set the confession in Siddhanta terms. The goal named is கந்த நாடு, Kanda's world, a heaven rather than union. Uma as Rama's sister (ரகுராமர் இட தங்கை) follows the tradition that makes Vishnu Uma's brother.

reading: The poet describes singing great poems to patrons, praising them as Pari in giving, a cloud, mighty-shouldered, famed in seven worlds, the light of the world and Indra's equal, only to be met with anger and no pity and to wilt at their doors in vain, while others carry off the poem and waste it; he asks whether those who do not think of Murugan can come near him. The praise names Vishnu, who saved the elephant crying 'first cause' from the crocodile, as uncle, Murugan with twelve hands on the peacock, and the servant from Kalisai, at Veerai and Palani.
nuance: The patrons are flattered with the stock comparisons (பாரியான கொடை, கொண்டலே), the very praise the poet now regrets (சீறுவார் கடையிற் சென்று). The closing question turns the complaint: men who do not think of Murugan are unworthy of praise. Vishnu saving the elephant (மூலமென் ஆரவாரம்) parallels 173.

reading: A song of praise alone: Siva, who burned the cities with a smile, is made clear in mind when the child guru speaks the secret of the pranava into his golden ear; Murugan fights the asuras until the mountains turn to dust and blood overflows the sea. When Siva gave the fruit to the elephant-faced one for circling his feet while Murugan circled the world, Murugan grew angry that it was not given to him and came to dwell at Palani, Sivagiri.
nuance: This is the Palani legend: பொற்கிரியைத் தனி வலம் வர (circling the golden mountain, the world), அக்கனியைத் தரவிலை என வெகுண்டு (angry that the fruit was not given). The anger is told plainly and the shrine is its result. பொற்செவியுட் பிரணவ ரகசியம் ... உரைசெய் குழந்தைக் குருநாதா names the pranava. One line is corrupt.

reading: The poet confesses that, embracing women's adorned breasts daily, he has become helpless, chaff in understanding, a worthless fool, and asks Murugan, with incomparable grace, to speak one word to his servant. The praise names him the younger brother of the elephant with temples like pots and the vel that rushed on the asura army, at Palani with its dripping banana clusters and sugarcane fields.
nuance: அறிவிற் பதடி, chaff in understanding, and அசடன் are the self-names. The plea for 'one word' (ஒருசொல் புகல்வாயே) echoes the word Murugan spoke to Siva, asked now for the poet.

reading: The poet describes women with breasts like tusks, crescent brows, vel eyes and night-dark hair, who question those who come with property at their houses and carry it away, deceitful at heart, and says that, infatuated, he melted, wasted and whirled in deeds; he asks for the bliss of knowledge to worship Murugan's feet. The praise names the vel that restored the gods, Murugan circling the earth on the peacock in a moment with devotees crying 'Hara', and Krishna who was tied with a rope and ate curd from the hanging pot, at Palani by the great river.
nuance: உரியதோர் பொருள்கொடு வந்த பேர்களை மனையிலே வினவியே கொண்டுபோகிய: the women take the property men bring, and the verse calls them வஞ்ச மாதர்கள். The poet's state is மயல், and the result is bodily wasting (உடலற வெம்பி).

title: பழநி
theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி, 6 of 7), many naming the shrine at its foot, Avinankudi: the poet confesses capture by women's charms and by courtesans who take a man's money, and asks for the Lord's feet, for jnana, or simply not to forget him; between these stand a namo-nama litany, a song of kundalini yoga, a positive plea to live by scripture in service, and a self-indictment that lists the virtues he lacks.
structure_note: Confessions of desire (180, 183 to 187, 190, 191, 193), the courtesan's trade named in 180, 183 and 193; birth to infatuation (181); praise only, in litany form (179); a plea for disciplined service (182); the yogic ascent (188); a list of missing virtues with the Sambandar story (189); a brief prayer through the six-syllable mantra (192). 184 gives its whole praise to the Goddess.
source_issues: Song 181: செறிவுடன் றிந்து (line 6) looks damaged, probably செறிவுடன் அறிந்து.
Song 179: ஆவல் கொண்டுவி றாலே சிராடவெ (line 22) is unclear and may be garbled.
Song 180: செந்தமிழ் லுனையே (line 21) is ungrammatical, probably செந்தமிழில் உனையே.
Song 192: ருளும்வோலா (line 6) is probably ருளும்வேலா, 'vel-bearer'; the letter is not flagged as corrupt.

reading: A litany of praise ending each line with நமோநம: Murugan is hailed as the king who gives teaching, the god in whom justice dwells, the form of the rare Veda mantras, the master of jnana, the one in love with the hunters' creeper and the treasure of the heavenly girl, and is asked for grace. The second half tells how his sharp vel killed sinful Sura so the gods regained heaven, praises Siva of Kailash, and names Uma by many titles, Ambika, Manonmani, Sundari, Narayani, Abhirami, as the mother who fondles him, at the shrine of Avinankudi.
nuance: There is no confession here; the song is a string of invocations, a form of worship by naming. போதகந்தரு கோவே and ஞான பண்டித நாதா make Murugan the giver of knowledge, and வேத மந்திர ரூபா makes him the mantra's form. The phrase ஆவல் கொண்டு விறாலே சிராடவெ, apparently the mother's fond play with her son, is unclear.

reading: The poet describes women with turmeric-scented breasts who walk the fragrant streets, bend passers-by with their eyes, embrace those who come, state their trade, win full trust and then snatch their wealth, and asks that his mind not wander seeking the houses of these women who sell pleasure, but that Murugan come today, give him abundant love and rule him. The praise names him Uma's son and Kanda the guru, lover of the Kurava girl, whose lotus feet poets worship, and to whom the sage of the southern-breeze mountain bowed in fine Tamil and received grace, on southern Palani.
nuance: தொழில்கூறி and விலைமாதர் name the trade plainly: these are women who sell. The plea asks for the Lord's love (அன்புடைமை) to replace theirs. தென்றல்வரை முநிநாதர் is the sage of Pothigai, Agastya, here worshipping Murugan as guru in Tamil, the claim the book repeats that Murugan taught Tamil to Agastya.

tamil: மருமலரி னன்து ரந்து விடவினைய ருந்த அந்தி
வகைதனைம றந்தெ ழுந்து முலைதனைய ருந்தி யந்த
இருமயல்கொ டுந்து வண்டு பொதுவையர கம்பு குந்து
இருவினைபொ திந்த இந்த ஜனனமர ணந்து றந்து
திருவொடுபெ யர்ந்தி ருண்ட வனமிசைந டந்தி லங்கை
திடமுளமு குந்தர் கஞ்சன் வரவிடுமெல் வஞ்ச கங்கள்
பரிவொடும கிழ்ந்தி றைஞ்சு மருதிடைத வழ்ந்து நின்ற
பதுமமிசை வண்ட லம்பு சுனைபலவி ளங்கு துங்க
reading: The poet traces his life from Brahma's sending him out to eat his deeds, through birth, the breast and childhood, to a grown body that enters the houses of common women and spends night and day there until it turns foolish, and asks when, leaving this birth and death bound up with two kinds of deed, he will worship the Lord's paired feet. The praise is given to Vishnu as Murugan's uncle: Rama who walked the dark forest with Sita and whose monkey burned Lanka, and Krishna who saw through Kamsa's tricks and crawled between the marudha trees, and ends at Palani of lotus pools.
nuance: The song is a small autobiography of the soul: மருமலரினன் துரந்துவிட, sent off by the one on the flower (Brahma), வினை அருந்த, to consume deeds. பொதுவையர் அகம் are the houses of women common to all. The opening lines (அந்தி மதியொடு பிறந்து முன் பெய்வதையாலே) are hard to divide, and செறிவுடன் றிந்து looks damaged.

tamil: மனக்கவலை யேது மின்றி உனக்கடிமை யேபு ரிந்து
வகைப்படிம னோர தங்கள் தொகைப்படியி னாலி லங்கி
வினைக்குரிய பாத கங்கள் துகைத்துவகை யால்நி னைந்து
வெகுட்சிதனை யேது ரந்து களிப்பினுட னேந டந்து
மனத்தில்வரு வோனெ என்று னடைக்கலம தாக வந்து
வரர்க்குமிமை யோர்க ளென்பர் தமக்குமன மேயி ரங்கி
தினைப்புனமு னேந டந்து குறக்கொடியை யேம ணந்து
செழித்தவள மேசி றந்த மலர்ப்பொழில்க ளேநி றைந்த
reading: Unusually, the plea confesses nothing: the poet asks that, free of anxiety and serving Murugan, not straying from the rules of the Manu texts, seeking the meaning the Vedas hold and following the Agamas in order, trampling the sins deeds bring and driving out anger, he walk in joy and come to worship him. The praise names him the one who enters the mind, who pitied the sages and gods who took refuge at his flower feet and defeated Sura with the vel, and who married the Kurava creeper in the millet field, at fertile Palani.
nuance: உனக்கடிமையே புரிந்து is service, and it is joined to an orthodox programme: மநுநூல், the Veda and the ஆகமங்கள் முறையாலே. The rhythm makes வகைப்படி மனோரதங்கள் தொகைப்படியினால் இலங்கி hard to construe; it seems to ask that his wishes be fulfilled in due order.

reading: In a long chain of phrases each ending in இலே, the poet names what caught him: a woman's flowered hair, the pride of her sweet words, the twist of her cruel heart, her hips and breasts, her coming close uninvited, the net of her eyes, the jingle of her bangles and the pose that snatches great wealth, so that joined to her for a moment he lost his wits and wanders in thought and dream; he asks that, fool and deceiver as he is, he may worship the golden feet with flowers by Murugan's glance. The praise pictures Murugan wearing gold pendants and kadamba garlands and the Tamil of those who call themselves his servants, dwelling in love at Palani.
nuance: The anaphora (கொண்டைச் சொருக்கிலே, செருக்கிலே, இருக்கிலே) makes the list itself the snare. கனநிதி பறி அந்தப் பிலுக்கிலே, the pose that plucks away great wealth, marks her as a courtesan. In the praise the devotee's Tamil is one of Murugan's ornaments, worn with rose-water and the kadamba garland. The lines on the mountain and hills before Palani are unclear.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking at length, flowers in the hair, nail-marks, sweating faces, reddened eyes, musk on breasts, bodies joined as one life on the couch, bangles ringing, and asks whether this love of rising infatuation will not end. The whole praise is given to the Goddess: Sankari who bore the world, dwelling in devotees' minds and in one half of Siva, the green one, Parai, Ambika beyond day and night, Tripura, Parabrahmi, the faithful wife, the girl born on the mountain, who gave Murugan, Lord at Palani.
nuance: The plea is only a question (அன்பு ஒழிந்திடாதோ), asking for no gift. The praise is a hymn to Shakti in her cosmic titles, and Murugan appears only in the last word, தம்பிரானே, which here replaces பெருமாளே. Several compounds in the Goddess's titles (பசங்கியம் பண கரதலி, இரண்டொடு ஒன்று அலர்) are obscure.

reading: The poet confesses sinking into women's arms and pleasure, heedless of the world calling him a worthless man, falling headlong and drinking the nectar of their smiles until he perishes, and asks Murugan for jnana, so that he may drink instead the nectar of the Lord's two feet. The praise names him the one whose vel churned the sea, who rode the peacock against the asura army, and the young one whom Siva, said to be beyond speech, holds in his heart as supreme guru, at Palani whose peaks touch the moon.
nuance: விழலன் என உலகோர்கள் மொழியும் அது மதியாமல்: he heard the world's blame and ignored it. The two nectars are set against each other, the smile's (நகையமுதம்) and the feet's (இருதாளின் அமுது). உமைகொழுநர் உளமேவு பரமகுரு alludes to Murugan as Siva's teacher without telling the story.

tamil: முதிர வுழையை வனத்தில் முடுகி வடுவை யழித்து
முரண வளரும் விழிக்குள் மதன விரகு பயிற்றி
மதுர அமுத மொழிக்கு மகுட களப முலைக்கு
மனதை யுடைய அசட்டு மனிதன் முழுது புரட்டன்
சதுரன் வரையை யெடுத்த நிருத னுடலை வதைத்து
தழையு மரமு நிலத்தில் மடிய அமரை விளைத்த
அதிர முடுகி யெதிர்த்த அசுர ருடலை வதைத்து
அரிய புகழை யமைத்த பெரிய பழநி மலைக்கு
reading: The poet describes women whose eyes outdo the deer, the mango slice and the carp, teaching Kama's arts and destroying propriety, and whose sweet speech and sandal-pasted breasts force men into slavery, and asks that he, a foolish, false-minded cheat, be given Murugan's feet to rejoice in. The praise is for Vishnu as uncle, who killed the demon that lifted the mountain, kicked the cart and the marudha trees and drew the bow that felled trees, and for Murugan who freed the gods from prison and makes his peacock walk at Palani.
nuance: வலிய அடிமை புகுத்திவிடும்: here அடிமை is bondage to the women, not service to the Lord, the sense the concept adimai names. The eyes are praised by the old conceit of defeating deer, mango and carp. The poet calls himself அசட்டு மனிதன் முழுது புரட்டன, a foolish man and a cheat through and through.

reading: In a dense, doubled-consonant rhythm the poet lists a woman's adornments, the pearl tassel and coiled hair, the green mark and jewelled pendant on the forehead, the three-layered bodice, the sweet words, coral lips and poisonous eyes, and asks whether he must go on wandering, caught by such seductresses and their breasts, his life snared and ruined; he asks that his great sorrow be removed and that, with devotion in his mind, he be given the supreme consciousness. The praise names Murugan the master of knowledge, son of the three-eyed Siddha, wearing the red vetchi garland, worshipped with flowers by siddhas of the eight directions, devotees in nishtha and gods at Palani.
nuance: The sound is the point: almost every word doubles a hard consonant (முத்துக்குச் சிட்டுக் குப்பி). பற்பல லச்சைக்குட்பட்டு, falling into many shames, names his own disgrace. சிற்பரம் is the supreme of consciousness, and பத்தத்தொடு seems to stand for bhakti; the splitting of many lines is uncertain.

reading: A song of yoga: the poet asks that the breath, run through the channels from the root (ida, pingala and the middle way) up the pillar through the six centres, reach the feet of the Supreme in the radiance of Jnana Sadasiva, and that he become one with the nada and the ringing anklets of the dancing foot. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva who bears the trident, deer, axe, drum and Brahma's skull, the vel that reduced Sura to dust, the dancer whose anklets sound through the ages, and the lover of the forest deer-girl, at Palani.
nuance: The vocabulary is technical yoga, as in Tirumular: மூலம், பிங்கலை நாடி, வாயு, மூலந்திகழ் தூண் (the spine as pillar), பால் அங்கு இளர் ஆறு (the six centres), ஞான சதாசிவம். The goal is heard, not only seen: the sound of the nada is the anklet of the Lord's dancing foot. The measurements (நாலங்குலம்) and the சிகாரம் of the sixth line are obscure.

reading: The poet lists what he lacks, the chanting of the root mantra, giving, love, silence and jnana, and what he has, lust for women, great thirst, transgression and offence and the name of a dumb fool, and confesses he wanders in this body while thinking of falling into the burning hell Kumbhi; he asks for the sharpness to keep company with those of jnana-filled heart. The praise tells of the Jains, their peacock-feather fans burnt, who argued, of the palm leaf that went against the river, the Pandya cured of illness and the deceivers sent to the stake, as Murugan's work, and names him Sankari's son, the jnana master of the Vedas, at Avinankudi.
nuance: The opening is a catalogue of negations (ஓதல் இங்கு இலை, ஈவது இங்கு இலை, மோனம் இங்கு இலை, ஞானம் இங்கு இலை) followed by a catalogue of possessions, with மூகன் (dumb one) as his name. The remedy asked is fellowship: ஞான நெஞ்சினர் பால் இணங்கிடு கூர்மை. The praise identifies Murugan with Sambandar, by tradition the saint whose leaf floated against the Vaigai and who cured the Pandya (மாறன்) before the Jains were impaled.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking in full detail, loosened hair, thrilling breasts, jingling bangles, sweat, faltering words, drinking the lips' nectar, and says that even lying on that flower-bed he will not forget Murugan's lotus feet. The praise names the vel that crushed Nirudan's chariots and elephants, the guru with form and without, the Kumara who dwells at the top of the sky, and the lover of the Kurava girl at Palani where waterfalls scatter gems over the areca palms.
nuance: Unlike most such songs this one does not ask to leave the embrace: துயிலுகினும் அலர்கமல மலரடியை மறவேனே, 'even if I sleep there, I will not forget the feet'. It reads as a vow of remembrance inside desire rather than a plea for escape. நிகழ் அகள சகள குரு names the Lord as both formless and formed.

reading: The poet confesses that he described women in the poets' figures, hair as cloud, breasts as lotus buds, smile as jasmine, gait as a swan, waist as a drum, face as the moon, and then melted like wax in a furnace in the union they gave; he asks that he, a fool sunk in the sea of births, be given the Lord's anklet feet. The praise tells how, when poison rose with the nectar from the churned sea and Vishnu, Brahma and Indra cried for refuge, Siva who took it fathered Murugan, whose vel shattered the asuras, who embraced the Kurava girl and was born in the lotus of Saravana, worshipped as supreme guru at Palani.
nuance: The confession is partly a poet's: உருவக உரைசெய்து, having made metaphors of women's forms, the very figures the song lists. The list is the stock catalogue of Tamil love poetry, so the poet indicts his own craft. உவகை தரு கலை பல உணர் பிறவியின் உவரி: the sea of births is the place where he learned the many arts of pleasure.

reading: A short song asking that the poet, not forgetting to speak Murugan's praise and not wandering in the river of the mind's sorrow, gain fortune in this world and the next through the six-syllable mantra set to song. The praise names Murugan the one who knows Siva's own word, the vel-bearer enthroned on Palani, who withered the asuras and freed the gods.
nuance: இசைபயில் ஷடாக்ஷரம், the six syllables practised in music, is the Murugan mantra (by tradition சரவணபவ). இகபர செளபாக்யம் asks for good in both worlds, not release. பசுபதி சிவாக்யம் உணர்வோனே may allude to Murugan knowing the word he taught Siva; the sense of வசனமிக ஏற்றி is uncertain.

reading: The poet heaps abuse on deceitful courtesans who torment those who come, talk of love without knowing friendship, show the wonders of passion on the couch, speak harshly, never melt despite sweet words and only act at union, and asks whether he must waste his body delighting in the pleasure they give. The praise tells of Krishna killing Sakatasura sent by Kamsa and climbing the kurundham tree before the cowherd women, as Vishnu, Murugan's uncle, and of Murugan embracing Devayanai and Valli, Lord of Avinankudi and of every hill.
nuance: வஞ்சனை மிஞ்சிய மாய வம்பிகள், இன்சொல் புரிந்து உருகாத தொண்டிகள், சங்கமம் என்பதையே புரிந்தவர்: the deceit is that the sweet words and the union are performance. The abuse is coarse (வேசை முண்டைகள்). குன்றுகள் எங்கினுமே வளர்ந்தருள் makes Murugan lord of all hills. Some words (கடம்பிகள், மண்டைகள், லண்டிகள்) are abusive terms whose exact sense is unclear.

title: பழநி
theme: Last songs at Palani (பழநி, 7 of 7), several at Avinankudi: the poet sets knowing Murugan above alchemy, traces his life from the womb to ruin among women, lists the body's diseases and the cheats around it, sees women's beauty as maya in form, and asks for the feet, for tears of devotion and for the simple rite of pouring Ganges water on them.
structure_note: A short song against alchemy (194); a life from womb to waste (195); disease and the false body (196); desire seen as maya (197); confessions of desire with pleas for the feet (198 to 200), 200 asking for puja. Murugan as Siva's or Brahma's teacher appears in 196, 197 and 200.
source_issues: Song 196: one corrupt character in தொணு஡றறு (line 8), probably தொண்ணூற்றறு, 'ninety-six'.

reading: A short song: if one realises that Murugan, the giver of boons, is the gem, what will not come; it does not come by mercury and the like, for the nine metals put in turn to charcoal, so what use is that? The praise names him the son of the supreme Goddess whom the Vedas, Brahma, Vishnu and all the Agamas do not know, Lord of Palani.
nuance: இரதாதிகளால் நவலோகம் இடவே கரியாம் seems to reject the alchemist's art: mercury (இரதம்) and the nine metals give only charcoal, while the true gem is Murugan himself. The reading depends on how the clipped short lines divide, so it is tentative.

tamil: வனிதையுடல் காய நின்று வுதிரமதி லேயு ருண்டு
மனிதருரு வாகி வந்து அநுதினமு மேவ ளர்ந்து
கனகமுலை மாதர் தங்கள் வலையில்மிக வேயு ழன்று
கனபொருளெ லாமி ழந்து மயலில்மிக வேய லைந்த
புனமதனில் வாழு கின்ற வநிதைரகு நாதர் தந்த
பொருமதனை நீறு கண்ட அரியசிவ னாரு கந்த
பனகமணி மாம தங்கி குமரிவெகு நீலி சண்டி
பகையசுரர் மாள வென்று அமரர் சிறை மீள வென்று
reading: The poet traces his life: heated in a woman's body, rolling in blood, long in the womb, born in human form, growing daily to sixteen, then wandering in the nets of women, embracing them, seeking wealth and losing it all, lost in infatuation, and asks Murugan to rule him by grace. The praise names him the lover of the millet-field girl given by Vishnu (Raghunatha), son of Siva who burned Kama and of the Goddess called Matangi, Kumari, Nili and Chandi, who destroyed the asuras and freed the gods, at Palani.
nuance: The life runs in a single sentence from the womb (வனிதை உடல் காய நின்று உதிரமதிலே உருண்டு) to ruin, with sixteen as the age when the body takes its shape and the trouble begins. பொருள்தேடி... கனபொருள் எலாம் இழந்து: the wealth he gathered was lost in the women's nets. புனமதனில் வாழுகின்ற வநிதை ரகுநாதர் தந்த புதல்வி makes Valli Vishnu's daughter.

reading: The poet lists the body's diseases, wind, bile, phlegm, colic, dropsy, eye disease, piles, cough and vomiting, and the ninety-six tattvas and the cheats who live around a man, and confesses that, with the three cravings, he took this thieving, false hut for happiness and ran in fine cloth and gold chains as if to outrun the seven worlds; he asks to reach the feet of the Lord's pure devotees. The praise sounds the battle drums as the vel shakes Adisesha, the seas and the asura hill, tells how Murugan struck Brahma's golden head and as true guru spoke in Siva's ear the gain of the detached, and how he went in disguise after Valli, at Palani.
nuance: பொய்க்குடில், the false hut, is the body, and the list of diseases is the evidence. தத்துவகாரர் தொண்ணூற்றறுவர் treats the ninety-six tattvas as agents who crowd the body. The teaching myth is told in full except for the word Om: வேதன் பொற்சிரம் மீது கடாவி, நல் ஈசன் சற்குருவாய் அவர் காதினில் மேவும் பற்றிலர் பேறு அருள் ஓதிய. The opening lines on the drums (தீதந் தித்திமி, டுடுண் டுட்டுடு) are rhythm, not words.

reading: The poet describes a woman, breasts like an elephant's brow under necklaces, face like the young moon, long carp eyes, nectar lips, plantain thighs, thread-thin waist, the gait of a peacock and swan, and asks that the understanding arise in him that this deceit is great maya itself standing in form. The praise names the vel that destroyed the night-walkers so Indra could rule, the son of Siva who drank the poison for the gods, the one who argued with Brahma, asked him for one word he could not give, and broke his pride by confinement, at towered Avinankudi.
nuance: தோதகந்தனை மாமாயையே வடிவாக நின்றது: the plea asks not to escape the woman but to see her charm as maya embodied, a doctrinal turn on the usual confession. The Brahma story (ஆரணன்றனை வாதாடி ஓர் உரை ஓதுகின்றென வாராது) is told without naming Om.

reading: The poet describes women with flower-garlanded hair who speak of love, generosity and their own pride, with golden, Meru-like breasts that seek battle, walking swan-like in the street and deluding all with the net of their eyes, and asks that his mind not wither but that one day Murugan rule him by his two lotus feet. The praise names the vel that split Sura in two, the son of Uma called Narani, Gauri, Syamala, Parvati, Mauna Sundari and Yogini, who circles the seven worlds in an instant on the peacock, at Palani, said to surpass Kasi, shining like ten million suns.
nuance: எனை யாள்வதும் ஒருநாளே: the plea is put as a hope for one day. காசியின் மீறிய பழநி, Palani above Kasi, claims for the shrine more than the holiest pilgrim city.

tamil: விரைமருவு மலர ணிந்த கரியபுரி குழல்ச ரிந்து
விழிபுரள முலைகு லுங்க மொழிகுழற அணைபு குந்து
இரவுபக லணுகி நெஞ்ச மறிவழிய வுருகு மந்த
எனதுதலை மிசைய ணிந்து அழுதழுது னருள்வி ரும்பி
அரவில்விழி துயில்மு குந்த னலர்கமல மலர்ம டந்தை
அடலசுர ருடல்பி ளந்து நிணமதனில் முழுகி யண்ட
பரவைவரு விடம ருந்து மிடறுடைய கடவுள் கங்கை
பரமரரு ளியக டம்ப முருகஅறு முகவ கந்த
reading: The poet describes women in the bed of desire, hair falling, eyes rolling, words faltering, whom he sought night and day until his heart's knowledge was gone, and asks that, the darkness lifted, he wear Murugan's anklet feet on his head, weep and weep for his grace and proclaim his sweet praise. The praise names him nephew of Vishnu sleeping on the serpent beside Lakshmi, the vel that plunged into the asuras' fat and freed the gods, and son of Siva who drank the poison and bears the Ganga, at Palani.
nuance: அழுதழுது உன் அருள் விரும்பி: the remedy is tears, devotion shown in the body that desire had seized. The feet are asked for on the head (எனது தலைமிசை அணிந்து), as a crown.

reading: The poet confesses that he embraced women with bamboo-like shoulders, did sins in vain, wandered far, his mind scattered and his life withered, and asks that, his delusion gone, he pour Ganges water on Murugan's two lotus feet, bow to them and perform some puja. The praise names Rama who burned Lanka and cut off Ravana's heads as his uncle, the vel that killed Sura so the gods could rule, the Goddess as Sundari, Nili, Kundali and Veda Tantri on Siva's left, and Murugan who gladly gave a teaching when Siva, who drank the poison, bowed to him, at Avinankudi.
nuance: The plea is modest and ritual: some puja (பூசையும் சிலவே), with Ganges water poured on the feet. ஆலமுண்ட அரனார் இறைஞ்ச ஒர் போதகந்தனையே உகந்து அருள் is the teaching of Siva, without naming Om.

title: சுவாமி மலை
theme: First songs at Swamimalai (சுவாமி மலை, also called Tiruverakam and Gurumalai; 1 of 3): pleas against craving and courtesans, against a life spent at patrons' gates and against Death's hour, and several prayers in Siddhanta vocabulary for jnana, union without difference and a silence beyond breath-yoga; the praise keeps to Murugan as guru, as Valli's lover, and as giver of Tamil verse.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (202, 204, 213, 215); doctrinal pleas (203, 205, 211, 216); life's passing and Death (208, 212); initiation and the devotees' cry (207, 214); poetry and patronage (209, 210). Song 206 has no text in the source.
source_issues: Song 206 has no text (marked missing); the chapter runs 201-216 with 15 songs.
Song 203: the source's printed number is 202, duplicating song 202; one corrupt character in ப்஡ணதி (line 23), possibly ப்ரணதி or ப்ரீதி.
Song 211: two corrupt characters, அனலு஡தி (line 3, அனலூதி) and புண்ட஡ணகம் (line 12, புண்டரீகம், consistent with ஡ண for ரீ).
The source drops ஊ and leaves a stray virama, unflagged: இத்ழுறல் (202, இதழூறல்), மல்முட (205, மலமூட), மல்ருடே (210, மலரூடே).

reading: The poet confesses that, not seeing that a life spent in the fire of craving for women is ruin, he grew deluded and never once thought of the name 'Sivaya', and asks Murugan to call him in his darkness and give him the feet that great ascetics meditate on, where the veiling impurity ends. The praise names the twelve-armed, six-faced son of Siva who rides the peacock with the vel in hand, the lover of the hunters' doe, and the lord of Swamimalai to whom Indra, Brahma and Vishnu bow.
nuance: The first word, அவா (craving), sets the theme, and every line opens on a long syllable of the same pattern (அவா, அரா, சிவா, உவா, உலா, துவா, சுரா). திரோத மலம் is the veiling (tirodhana) counted among the impurities in Saiva doctrine. The opening words are hard to divide.

tamil: ஆனனமு கந்து தோளோடு தோளிணைக லந்து பாலன
ஆதரவி னுண்டு வேல்விழி பூசலிட நன்று காணென
மானனைய மங்கை மார்மடு நாபியில்வி ழுந்து கீடமில்
வாரிஜப தங்கள் நாயடி யேன்முடிபு னைந்து போதக
ஈனவதி பஞ்ச பாதக தானவர்ப்ர சண்ட சேனைகள்
ஏவல்கொளு மிந்த்ர லோகவ சீகரவ லங்க்ரு தாகர
சோனைசொரி குன்ற வேடுவர் பேதைபயில் கின்ற ஆறிரு
சூளிகையு யர்ந்த கோபுர மாளிகைபொ னிஞ்சி சூழ்தரு
reading: The poet describes embracing women and drinking their lips' nectar, and asks that his craving for the pleasure of sinking like a worm into their navel cease, and that one day Murugan set his lotus feet as a crown on this dog-like servant's head and rule him with a word of teaching. The praise names the conqueror of the demon armies who commands the gods' host, twelve-armed Kanda whom the hunter girl of the rain-wet hill loves, the life of Vayalur, and the lord of Swamimalai of towers and golden walls.
nuance: கீடம்: the lover as a worm dying in a pit. The feet set on the head and a word of instruction (போதக வாசகம்) are the marks of a guru's initiation. Vayalur is named inside a Swamimalai song, as in 203.

reading: A doctrinal plea: the poet asks when, the fetter of earth and the darkness of great maya gone, he will reach the supreme light of consciousness, vast as space, which lies beyond the thirty-six tattvas and beyond turiya and which no master of yoga attains, and join with joy the unchanging, supportless Sthanu of bliss. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea and killed the ten-headed sinner as uncle, the son of Vayalur's Agnisvara, and the lover of the hunter girl, and asks for grace that ends the sense of 'mine'; the shrine is Swamimalai on the Kaveri's north bank.
nuance: ஆறாறின் அதிகம், beyond the thirty-six; பர துரியாதீதம், beyond turiya; பரை, the supreme Shakti; தாணு, Siva as the immovable. The whole plea is in Siddhanta's technical words, close to Tirumular's. The lines on the hunter girl and the eye-arrows that pierce the heart may speak of Murugan's love for Valli or of the poet's own heart; they are hard to divide.

reading: The poet lists women whose dark hair, eyes like Rama's arrows, musical speech, heavy breasts and vanishing waists wear down young men's hearts morning and evening while they name a price no one can meet, and asks that he not suffer in their love but be given the beginningless word of jnana that seeks the Lord's feet. The praise names Murugan whom devotees hail daily as Kumara in the shade of the kura tree, the vel that split Sura's hooded heads, and Swamimalai, where ascetics gather before whose good jnana deeds flee like straw before fire.
nuance: அடாத விலை கூறும்: naming an impossible price is what marks these women as courtesans. துரால் மிக தீ முன்: deeds burned like straw before fire, a common figure for knowledge destroying karma. அநாதி மொழி, 'the beginningless word', may mean the Veda or Om; the text does not say.

tamil: இருவினை புனைந்து ஞான விழிமுனை திறந்து நோயி
விருளற விளங்கி யாறு முகமொடு கலந்து பேத
பரிமள சுகந்த வீத மயமென மகிழ்ந்து தேவர்
பரிவுகொ டநந்த கோடி முநிவர்கள் புகழ்ந்து பாட
அரியய னறிந்தி டாத அடியிணை சிவந்த பாதம்
அழலுறு மிரும்பின் மேனி மகிழ்மர கதம்பெ ணாகம்
மருவலர் கள்திண்ப ணார முடியுடல் நடுங்க ஆவி
வளைகுல மலங்கு காவி ரியின்வட புறஞ்சு வாமி
reading: The poet asks Murugan to come so that, the two deeds broken, the eye of jnana opened at its tip and the dark of impurity cleared, he and the six faces may mingle and the two become one without difference, while the gods bow, the women of heaven strew flowers and countless sages sing. The praise names Nataraja, whose red feet Vishnu and Brahma could not find, Siva of the three cities, whose body is like red-hot iron with the emerald woman at his side, and the vel that gave the enemies' lives to Death, at Swamimalai on the Kaveri's north bank.
nuance: பேதம் இலை என இரண்டு பேரும்: the goal is union without difference with the Lord, not only escape. அழலுறும் இரும்பின் மேனி ... மரகதம் பெண் ஆகம் அயல்: red Siva with green Uma at his side, the half-woman form. The first lines are partly garbled.

reading: The poet says he roamed, no one knowing anyone, tormented in the troubles of his two deeds, melting like wax in a furnace, dancing like a puppet on strings and vanishing like lightning, and asks Murugan, who came in form, spoke in his ears 'this is the supreme thing' and burned his karma and impurity to ash, to come on the peacock with his six compassionate faces and ringing anklets and rule him. The praise names Siva who burned the three cities and Kama, the dancer on the young bull, Arunagiri in form, the cause in Sivayanama, and calls Murugan the son of Uma, the poet's mother, the Kumaraguru the thousand Vedas hail, who joined Valli and Devayanai on Gurumalai.
nuance: என் செவியிணையின் அருளி உருவாகி வந்த: the song speaks of an initiation already given, the Lord coming in form and teaching in the poet's ears. Three images of a life driven by deeds: wax, a string-puppet, lightning. Siva is called அருணகிரி சொருபன், the form of Arunachala, which is also the poet's name.

reading: The poet sets out how uncertain life is: Yama on his buffalo, the messenger he sends whose path never fails, a story played in a dream, the wealth hunters hoard without giving; seeing that life does not stay, he asks Murugan to see that he too may chant him with sweet words morning and evening, today. The praise names Siva, lord of grammar, who dances daily with Pidari, the vel that ended Sura, and Swamimalai where ascetics in good jnana gather.
nuance: கிராதர் பொருள், wealth hunters gather and never give, stands beside the dream as a figure for what will not stay with you. வியாகரண ஈசன்: Siva as lord of grammar. The closing lines on breath and the five senses may describe the ascetics' restraint; the song shares its last line with 204.

tamil: கடிமா மலர்க்கு ளின்ப முளவேரி கக்கு நண்பு
கனமேரு வொத்தி டும்ப னிருமாபு யத்த ணிந்த
வடிவார் குறத்தி தன்பொ னடிமீது நித்த முந்தண்
வளவாய்மை சொற்ப்ர பந்த முளகீர னுக்கு கந்து
அடிமோனை சொற்கி ணங்க வுலகாமு வப்ப என்று
அடியேனு ரைத்த புன்சொ லதுமீது நித்த முந்த
செடிநேரு டற்கு டம்பை தனின்மேவி யுற்றி டிந்த
திறமாத வர்க்க னிந்து னிருபாத பத்ம முய்ந்த
reading: Mostly praise: Murugan wears the kadamba garland on twelve arms like Meru, bows his crown daily at the hunter girl's feet, delighted in Keeran's poems of true speech and taught him grammar, and by grace gives verse whose alliteration fits; the poet asks that grace grow daily on the mean words he speaks, and asks whether he must suffer here, lodged in this body like a nest in a bush. The shrine is Tiruverakam.
nuance: கீரன் is Nakkirar; the song makes Murugan his teacher of grammar (இலக்கணங்கள் இயல்பு ஓதி). அடிமோனை: the poet credits even his alliteration to grace. Murugan bowing his crown at Valli's feet reverses the usual order of worship.

tamil: கதிரவனெ ழுந்து லாவு திசையளவு கண்டு மோது
கணபணபு யங்க ராஜன் முடியளவு கண்டு தாள்கள்
இதமிதமி தென்று நாளு மருகருகி ருந்து கூடு
இசையொடுபு கழந்த போது நழுவியப்ர சண்டர் வாச
மதுகரமி டைந்து வேரி தருநறவ முண்டு பூக
வகைவகையெ ழுந்த சாம வதிமறைவி யந்து பாட
அதிரவரு சண்ட வாயு வெனவருக ருங்க லாப
அடைவொடுல கங்கள் யாவு முதவிநிலை கண்ட பாவை
reading: The poet asks whether he must wander, deluded, to the edges of the directions where the sun rises, the shores of the sea and the crown of the serpent king, wearing out his feet, never tiring of saying 'this is the place to sit near', and, when the powerful men he praised with music slip away, go to their gates night and day and wilt. The praise pictures bees in the areca blossoms and Sama singers at Swamimalai where the moon casts its shade, Murugan riding the peacock like a storm wind, and the son of the Mother who set all worlds in place.
nuance: இசையொடு புகழ்ந்த போது நழுவிய ப்ரசண்டர் வாசல்: the gates of patrons who slip away once they are praised in song, the same complaint as 220. The first lines may also describe wandering for wealth in general.

reading: The poet asks that the mind given to the anxious fancies of yoga go away, the yoga that refuses to think this stained body will not last, turns back the breath with ritual words and fans the inner fire; that the quarrelling five senses be uprooted and his own action end, so that he enters the full silence beyond qualities and reaches release; and he asks whether he will know, as the true guru of Gurumalai, the lotus feet on which he strews fresh flowers crying 'Kumara, refuge'. The praise tells of the war in which Murugan freed the gods to their city, burned the peaks and dried the sea, punished Brahma and kept him under guard, and married the elephant-raised Devayanai.
nuance: The participles (கருதுதல் ஒழிந்து, வாயுவை மறித்து, அனல் ஊதி, கவலைபடுகின்ற) appear to describe the yoga the poet wants to be rid of: a yoga of breath and fire aimed at keeping the body, set against the silence (மோனம்) beyond the gunas. Brahma's punishment (பிரமனை முனிந்து காவலிட்டு) is told without naming Om. Two corrupt glyphs.

reading: A short song: the poet asks not to waste away in desires nor die in the hands of Death's men, but, with love for the letter Om welling up, to be given the end 'in the painting'. The praise names the vel that drove off Sura, the hero on a peacock high as the golden mountain, and the lord at Erakam.
nuance: ஓவியத்தில் அந்தம் is obscure: it may be the stillness of a painted figure, an image for absorption. காமியம் may mean desire or rites done for desired ends. தூமமேய்க் கணிந்த in the praise is hard to read.

reading: The poet laments that he did not melt daily chanting Murugan's names, but wandered after cuckoo-voiced women who melt men with their eyes, walk the street as if lost in thought, seize their lovers' belongings, stand mid-street with garments slipping, net the penniless with their eyes and, having taken all, made him their slave doing whatever they bid; he asks for grace to praise the feet. The praise is a long battle with Virabhadras, Kali drinking blood, ghosts, jackals and vultures, and names Murugan of the Saiva faith, of Palani and Kathirkamam, dwelling at Tiruverakam.
nuance: அவர் அடிமை என மாதர் இட்ட தொழில் தனில் உழலும் அசடன்: the poet calls himself the women's slave, the bondage the other songs turn into service of the Lord. சிவசமய அறுமுக places Murugan within the Saiva faith. The battle is in drum syllables (திமிதமிட).

reading: The poet asks whether Murugan does not hear the cry for refuge of his devotees, crushed by cruel deeds, who chant him daily, 'Kumara, Guruparan, Muruga, Saravana, Guha, Shanmukha, younger brother of the elephant one, son of Siva, jewel of a guru', as gods once cried out at the sea. The praise names the peacock hero who felled the Suras, the guru of Siva whose feet took the life of Death and whose hair holds the river, and the lord of Gurumalai praised by the Vedas.
nuance: The plea is a litany of names, as if the song were itself the devotees' cry. நமனை உயிர்கொளும் இணைகழல்: Siva's feet that killed Yama, though the text names only the deed. The simile of the gods at the sea (அமுத இமையவர் திமிர்தம் இடு கடல்) is obscure.

reading: The poet asks whether he should keep company with courtesans who melt men's hearts, sell their lips daily, learn the calls of peacock, quail, cuckoo, dove and cock to bewitch with sidelong eyes, lie on flower beds, call anyone into their house, loosen their garments, embrace and snatch coins, and act out a learned art of deceit. The praise names the vel that cut down Sura, and lists the shrines where Murugan grants devotees all they wish, Kathirkamam, Palani, Tiruttani, Tiruchendur by the sea and Swamimalai called Erakam.
nuance: தோதக வித்தை படித்து நடிப்பவர்: deceit as a learned art and a performance. காசு பறிக்க மறித்து முயக்கிகள்: the embrace is for the coin. The praise is a pilgrim's list of shrines.

tamil: சரணகம லால யத்தை அரைநிமிஷ நேர மட்டில்
சடகசட மூட மட்டி பவவினையி லேச னித்த
கருணைபுரி யாதி ருப்ப தெனகுறையி வேளை செப்பு
கடகபுய மீதி ரத்ந மணியணிபொன் மாலே செச்சை
தருணமிதை யாமி குத்த கனமதுறு நீள்ச வுக்ய
தகைமைசிவ ஞான முத்தி பரகதியு நீகொ டுத்து
அருணதள பாத பத்ம மதுநிதமு மேது திக்க
அதிசயம நேக முற்ற பழநிமலை மீது தித்த
reading: The poet calls himself a dull, foolish wretch, born of worldly deeds, who never knew how to fix meditation on the lotus feet even for half a moment, and asks whether he must stay confused by poverty and what fault keeps Murugan from compassion now; he asks for great wealth, yoga, a life of greatness, Siva-jnana, release and the supreme state together. The praise names the son of Kailasa's lord who gave rare Tamil so the poet could praise his feet daily, and Murugan of Palani and Tiruverakam.
nuance: The plea sets worldly gifts beside final ones without embarrassment: wealth and yoga beside Siva-jnana and mukti. அரியதமிழ் தான் அளித்த: the gift of Tamil verse to praise the feet, as in 209. மிடி is poverty.

title: சுவாமி மலை
theme: Swamimalai (சுவாமி மலை, 2 of 3): courtesans and the arts of 'Kama's scripture', the diseased and ageing body, poems wasted on patrons, a lovesick girl's song, and pleas for the release the Agamas teach, for servanthood among devotees, and, uniquely, for Murugan to be born as the poet's own child; the praise returns again and again to Murugan teaching his father Siva.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (219, 224 to 227, 230); the body and age (217, 229); patronage (220); an akam song (221); Death (228); devotion and doctrine (222, 223, 231); and 218, which brings the Lord into household life.
source_issues: Song 218: corrupt character in உடலு஡றி (line 2, probably உடலூறி).
Song 224: corrupt character in மதனு஡லின் (line 4, probably மதனூலின், 'Kama's treatise').
Song 229: corrupt character in சிலையி னு஡டோ ளித்த (line 3, probably சிலையினூடு ஒளித்த).
Song 217: unflagged garbles சங்முளை (line 3) and வங்க்முடே (line 6), apparently the same dropped ஊ (மூளை, அங்கமூடே).
Song 225: unflagged garble உனதிரு வடிவியினி (line 4).

reading: The poet catalogues the body, nerves, bones, flesh, fat, phlegm, the cave of blood, semen, worms, filth and hair, and its diseases, leprosy, abscess, swelling, colic and bile, and asks whether he must fade in the world, taking up again and again this hut of five elements with all its thoughts, cravings, pride and deceits, birth after birth. The praise is a battle in drum syllables at the Krauncha hill, and tells how Murugan seized the lotus-born by his tuft and rapped his head; he is the merchant who came to Valli's millet field and the guru of Siva whom the freed souls praise.
nuance: The fullest anatomy of disgust so far in the book. கமலத்தனை மணிக்குடுமி பற்றி ... பல குட்டி: Brahma punished by Murugan, though Om is not named here; செட்டி வடிவு: Murugan disguised as a merchant to woo Valli. Some disease names and two garbled words (சங்முளை, வங்க்முடே) are uncertain.

reading: The poet asks Murugan to come into the household life that the world's maya has given him, as the child his wife carries ten months and brings forth, so that he may play with him on his head, at his eyes and face and on his shoulders, take him on his lap, and receive kisses from his jewelled mouth every day. The praise names the one who came to embrace the hunter girl, the guru who told the one great meaning within the ancient Veda, Murugan of Erakam who let the poet see his feet, and the lord with the battle-vel on the Kaveri's north bank.
nuance: மணிவாயின் முத்தி: முத்தி is the child's kiss (முத்தம்) and also mukti, so the plea asks for both at once. The Lord is asked into household life, as the poet's son, rather than as an escape from it.

tamil: சேலுமயி லுந்த ரித்த வாளையட ருங்க டைக்கண்
சீலமறை யும்ப ணத்தி லாசையிலை யென்ற வத்தை
காலுமயி ரும்பி டித்து மேவுசிலு கும்பி ணக்கு
காமகல கம்பி ணித்த தோதகமெ னுந்து வக்கி
ஏலமில வங்க வர்க்க நாகம்வகு ளம்ப டப்பை
யாவுமலை கொண்டு கைத்த காவிரிபு றம்பு சுற்றும்
சேலைமடல் கொண்டு சக்ர மால்வரைய ரிந்த வஜ்ர
சூர்முதிர்க்ர வுஞ்ச வெற்பும் வேலைநில மும்ப கைத்த
reading: The poet describes women with eyes like fish and spears, who say they have no wish for money and cling like a wife, then seize a man's legs and hair and quarrel, and asks whether he, the Lord's servant, should be thrown into turmoil in this snare of deceitful lust. The praise pictures the Kaveri carrying cardamom, cloves and areca around Erakam, the vel that Indra, holder of the thunderbolt, worships, and the lord who split Krauncha, the sea and Sura.
nuance: பணத்தில் ஆசை இலை என்ற: the protest that she does not want money belongs to the trick. The second and third lines are hard to divide, so the picture of the women is tentative.

tamil: தருவரிவ ராகு மென்று பொருணசையி னாடி வண்டு
சரசகவி மாலை சிந்து கலிதுறைக ளேச லின்ப
மருவுகையு மோதி நொந்து அடிகள்முடி யேதெ ரிந்து
வருமதுவொ போது மென்று வொருபணமு தாசி னஞ்சொல்
உருகிமிக வாக வெந்து கவிதைசொலி யேதி ரிந்து
உபயபத மால்வி ளங்கி யிகபரமு மேவ இன்ப
குருகினொடு நாரை யன்றில் இரைகளது நாடி டங்கள்
குரைகடல்க ளேய திர்ந்து வருவதென வேவி ளங்கு
reading: The poet describes singing for patrons: thinking 'these men will give', he made bee-messages, envoy poems, garlands of verse, sindhu and kalitturai for love of wealth, praising their hands and heads, only to be told 'come another time' and tossed a coin with contempt by fools; he asks that this wandering end and that he be given the love that rules him with joy here and hereafter under Murugan's two feet. The praise pictures Gurumalai's waters, where storks, herons and anril birds startle at leaping vaalai fish as if the sea had roared in.
nuance: A poet's complaint about patronage that names the genres he wasted on men (வண்டு விடு தூது, கவிமாலை, சிந்து, கலித்துறை). The remedy is not to give up song but to turn it to the Lord. A few lines (வருமதுவொ போதும்) are hard to divide.

reading: In the voice of someone close to a girl in love, the song asks whether she, her breasts thrilling, should be left wavering and worn in mind by the taunts of the women who gather in the street, by the moon rising red over the sea like the sun, and by the arrows of Kama. The praise names the vel that split a hill in two, Murugan who stands at Tiruverakam, the poet who tells the Vedas and Tamil works in order, and the lord who frees the fettered feet of Vishnu, Brahma and the gods.
nuance: Akam conventions throughout: the street's gossip, the evening moon that burns like the sun, Kama's bow. The speaker is not named; it reads as a mother or friend, as in 24. அருமறை தமிழ்நூல் அடைவே தெரிந்துரைக்கும் புலவோனே: Murugan as poet of Veda and Tamil alike.

tamil: நாசர்தங் கடையதனில் விரவிநான் மெத்த நொந்து ...... தடுமாறி
ஞானமுங் கெடஅடைய வழுவியா ழத்த ழுந்தி ...... மெலியாதே
மாசகந் தொழுமுனது புகழினோர் சொற்ப கர்ந்து ...... சுகமேவி
மாமணங் கமழுமிரு கமலபா தத்தை நின்று ...... பணிவேனோ
வாசகம் புகலவொரு பரமர்தா மெச்சு கின்ற ...... குருநாதா
வாசவன் தருதிருவை யொருதெய்வா னைக்கி ரங்கு ...... மணவாளா
கீசகஞ் சுரர்தருவு மகிழுமா வத்தி சந்து ...... புடைசூழுங்
கேசவன் பரவுகுரு மலையில்யோ கத்த மர்ந்த ...... பெருமாளே.
reading: The poet asks that he not stumble, worn out, mingling at the doors of the wicked, nor lose his knowledge and sink deep, but, speaking the words of those who praise Murugan, live in joy and stand worshipping the two fragrant lotus feet. The praise names the guru whom Siva praised for telling the word, the bridegroom moved by Devayanai whom Indra gave, and the lord in yoga on Gurumalai, worshipped by Kesava.
nuance: நாசர் தம் கடை அதனில் விரவி: the doors of the wicked may be those of patrons, as in 220, or the company of bad men generally. The guru 'for the word' (வாசகம் புகல) is the Swamimalai teaching of Siva.

tamil: நாவேறு பாம ணத்த பாதார மேநி னைத்து
நாலாரு மாக மத்தி னுலாய ஞான முத்தி
நீவேறெ னாதி ருக்க நான்வேறெ னாதி ருக்க
நீடார்ஷ டாத ரத்தின் மீதேப ராப ரத்தை
சேவேறு மீசர் சுற்ற மாஞான போத புத்தி
தேரார்கள் நாடு சுட்ட சூரார்கள் மாள வெட்டு
காவேரி நேர்வ டக்கி லேவாவி பூம ணத்த
கார்போலு மேனி பெற்ற மாகாளி வாலை சத்தி
reading: The poet asks for the jnana-release that runs through the twenty-eight Agamas and their four ways, as he has spoken it daily in songs on the Lord's feet, so that, with neither the Lord saying 'you are other' nor he saying 'I am other', he may live in union, and that Murugan tell him 'see' the Supreme above the six supports. The praise names the guru who taught Siva and his circle the understanding of jnana, the bridegroom of the hunter girl, Murugan of Swamimalai by the Kaveri, and the son of Kali, Bala, Shakti, the left half of Kama's foe.
nuance: நாலாறு நாலு: twenty-eight, the number of the Saiva Agamas; the 'four' may be the four paths. நீ வேறு எனாதிருக்க நான் வேறு எனாதிருக்க: non-difference asked from both sides. ஷடாதாரத்தின் மீதே பராபரம்: the Supreme above the six centres of yoga. The counting is the likeliest reading, not a certain one.

tamil: நிலவினி லேயி ருந்து வகைமல ரேதெ ரிந்து
நிகரறு வேலி னங்கள் வரிதர வாச கங்கள்
கலபம னோக ரங்க ளளவற வேபு ரிந்து
கலவியி லேமு யங்கி வனிதையர் பால்ம யங்கு
உலகமொ ரேழு மண்ட ருலகமு மீசர் தங்கு
உயிரொடு பூத மைந்து மொருமுத லாகி நின்ற
குலைபடு சூர னங்க மழிபட வேலெ றிந்த
கொடுமுடி யாய்வ ளர்ந்து புயனிலை போலு யர்ந்த
reading: The poet describes women who sit in moonlight choosing flowers for their hair, whose spear-eyes reach their ear-rings, whose words drive out thought, and who practise without measure the arts of Kama's treatise, and calls himself the deceiver deluded in lovemaking with them; he asks for grace to rule him. The praise names Uma, who stood as the single source of the seven worlds, the gods' worlds, Kailasa, Meru, life and the five elements, as the one by whose grace Kumara grew, and the vel against Sura, at Gurumalai rising like a peak.
nuance: மதன் நூல் (garbled in the source): Kama's treatise as the women's discipline, as மதனாகமம் in 230. கபடன், deceiver, is the poet's name for himself. The praise gives Uma the place of first cause.

reading: A short song: the poet asks whether the love of women whose faces shine like the full moon and whose eyes are arrows can be a true bond, and asks for Murugan's holy feet now. The praise names Vishnu's nephew, death to the demon clans, Valli's bridegroom, at Gurumalai.
nuance: உனதிரு வடிவியினி is garbled; it most likely reads உன திருவடி இனி, 'your holy feet now', though திருவடிவு, 'holy form', is possible.

reading: The poet asks whether he must wander as great infatuation rises for women whose breasts carry ornaments, whose eyes are swords, whose hair is full of flowers and whose smile is like moonlight. The praise centres on Uma, the light on the left side of Siva who wears the serpent, named Dakini, Tripurai and Narani, and names Murugan Saravana the teacher, Guha the treasure of compassion, at Gurumalai.
nuance: மாமயல் நிலையெழவே அலைவது: infatuation as a state that rises and drives him wandering. As in 32, the praise dwells on the Mother more than on Murugan.

reading: The poet asks whether the false lovemaking of women who sell themselves can be sweet: they promise many loves for one hour's gain, praise many men, talk away shame, give poison and snatch great wealth. The praise names Rama, whose arrow felled the demon who lifted the mountain, as uncle, Murugan who hears with delight the Tamil of those who know the kavyas, and the lord at Tiruverakam who gave Siva the teaching due to him.
nuance: விலைமாதர் பொய்க்கலவி: the courtesan's love called false, in the Kural's own terms. விடமே கொடுத்து may be a love-drug or poison. சிவனார் தமக்குரிய உபதேச வித்தை: the teaching to Siva, the Swamimalai myth.

reading: The poet asks that Death not come near him but that he worship at Murugan's holy feet. The praise names the son given by Siva of the crescent, river and flowers, the bridegroom who pressed the hunter girl's feet, the nephew of Vishnu who showed grace to the crow that lost one eye, the young one who freed the gods from prison and comes on the peacock, at Swamimalai, whose vel dried the sea.
nuance: காதும் ஒருவிழி காகம் உற அருள் மாயன்: the crow that lost one eye to Rama's arrow and was spared, an act of grace. Murugan pressing Valli's feet (பாதம் வருடிய) matches 209.

tamil: மகர கேத னத்த னுருவி லானெ டுத்து
மலைய வேவ ளைத்த சிலையி னு஡டோ ளித்த
இகழ வாச முற்ற தலையெ லாம்வெ ளுத்து
இடைவி டாதெ டுத்த பிறவி வேர றுத்து
அகில மேழு மெட்டு வரையின் மீது முட்ட
அசுரர் சேனை கெட்டு முறிய வான வர்க்கு
மிகநி லாவெ றித்த அமுத வேணி நிற்க
விரைய ஞான வித்தை யருள்செய் தாதை கற்க
reading: The poet describes women whose eyes are arrows hidden in the bow of the bodiless Kama, and asks whether one day, before they scorn him as his scented hair whitens and youth slips away, Murugan will cut the root of the births he has taken without pause and give his sweet feet. The praise names the peacock that shakes the seven worlds and eight mountains, the young one who gave the gods back their life, Murugan of Swamimalai, and the lord who taught the jnana his father asked to learn.
nuance: The argument against desire is the women's scorn when he ages, not their deceit (compare 34). தாதை கற்க வினவ ஓதுவித்த: the father asks and the son teaches.

reading: The poet confesses that he was deluded by women with fragrant hair through the arts of Kama's scripture, drank their lips and was bound to their breasts, and asks Murugan, not forgetting his favour to this lonely one, to bear with his faults and grant the great life that holds to his feet. The praise names Guha who gave the teaching to Siva as guru, the bridegroom of the hunter girl, the young one of the Kaveri from the western hills, and Vishnu's nephew who cut off the demons' heads.
nuance: மதனாகமம்: Kama's Agama, a pointed phrase in a Saiva poet, as if love had its own scripture. பிழையே பொறுத்து: the plea is for forgiveness, not reward.

tamil: முறுகு காள விடம யின்ற இருகண் வேலி னுளம யங்கி
முழுகு காதல் தனைம றந்து பரம ஞான வொளிசி றந்து
அறுகு தாளி நறைய விழ்ந்த குவளை வாச மலர்க ரந்தை
அவச மாகி யுருகு தொண்ட ருடன தாகி விளையு மன்பி
தறுகண் வீரர் தலைய ரிந்து பொருத சூர னுடல்பி ளந்து
தரள மூர லுமைம டந்தை முலையி லார அமுத முண்டு
மறுவி லாத தினைவி ளைந்த புனம்வி டாம லிதணி ருந்து
மருவு ஞாழ லணிசெ ருந்தி யடவி சூத வனநெ ருங்கி
reading: The poet asks that, forgetting the love that drowned him in women's breasts, with the light of supreme jnana growing and longing for the six faces without tiring, he strew arugu, thali, kuvalai and karandai flowers on the feet, and be given the one way of servanthood that grows from love among devotees who melt beside themselves. The praise names the vel that dried the sea, the peacock hero who drank Uma's milk and circled the seven worlds, Valli's bridegroom, at Swamimalai of groves.
nuance: அவசமாகி உருகு தொண்டருடன் அதாகி: the poet asks to become one with the melting devotees; அடிமையாகு முறைமை is devotional service here, the opposite of the bondage to women in 213.

title: சுவாமி மலை
theme: The last songs at Swamimalai (சுவாமி மலை, also called Eragam): the poet confesses the diseases of a sinful life, his spending on women's jewels, and courtesans who dance in the street, drug a man and take his gold, and in the last song his refusal to share with the hungry before Death comes; the praise returns to Murugan as teacher of Siva and Brahma's humbler, and to the Rama story.
structure_note: All eight follow the two halves. 234 to 238 are confessions of women and courtesans; 232 is a catalogue of diseases, 233 of spending on women, 239 of hoarding before death. Five songs name the shrine Eragam (ஏரகம்) or the Mantra-guru hill rather than Swamimalai.
source_issues: Song 232: one corrupt character in வெற஧முடி (line 12); the intended word is unclear to me.
Song 234: one corrupt character in துண்டக்஡ணவ (line 3); ஡ண probably stands for ரீ (க்ரீவ, neck), as in song 12. Also unflagged சங்மாக (line 15), probably சங்கமாக.
Song 239: filed under சுவாமி மலை but ends at தணியிற் குமரப் பெருமாளே, which appears to name Thiruthani; the heading may be wrong, or தணி may be read otherwise.

tamil: வாதமொடு சூலை கண்ட மாலைகுலை நோவு சந்து
வாயுவுட னேப ரந்த தாமரைகள் பீன சம்பின்
பாதகவி யாதி புண்க ளானதுட னேதொ டர்ந்து
பாதமல ரான தின்க ணேயமற வேம றந்து
ஏதமுறு பாச பந்த மானவலை யோடு ழன்று
ஈடழித லான தின்பின் மூடனென வோது முன்புன்
சூதமகிழ் பாலை கொன்றை தாதுவளர் சோலை துன்றி
தோரணநன் மாட மெங்கு நீடுகொடி யேத ழைந்த
reading: The poet lists the diseases that have come on him, wind, colic, scrofula, swellings, cough, ringworm and the sores he calls the ornaments women give, which keep him to his bed; through them he has forgotten the love of Murugan's flower feet and drunk sin like liquor. Caught in the net of bonds in a low birth, he asks Murugan to come with grace and rule him before he is ruined and called a fool. The praise is only of Swamimalai, its groves of mango and konrai, its walls reaching the clouds and its flags.
nuance: மாதர்தரு பூஷணங்கள், 'ornaments women give', is bitter irony: the diseases caught from women are the jewels they return for the jewels given them. பாதகவியாதி, 'diseases of sin', ties illness to fault. The word in line 12 is corrupt and its sense uncertain.

tamil: வார முற்ற பண்பின் மாத முற்ற நண்பி
வாலை யிற்றி ரிந்து கோல மைக்கண் மங்கை
ஆர மிக்க பொன்க ளால மைத்த மர்ந்த
ஆட கொப்ப மைந்த வோலை முத்த முங்கொ
சூர னைத்து ரந்து வேர றப்பி ளந்து
சூக ரத்தொ டம்பு தானெ டுத்து வந்த
ஏரெ திர்த்து வந்து நீர்கள் கட்டி யன்று
யேமி குத்து யர்ந்த மாவ யற்கள் மிஞ்சு
reading: The poet tells how he grew old in friendship with women, wandering from youth after kohl-eyed girls and seeking wealth to buy them gold ornaments, earrings and pearls, and asks whether he must go on wandering in such pain of spirit. The praise names the hero who drove off Sura and split him to the root, the nephew of the charioteer Vishnu, and Eragam among high paddy fields where farmers raise water.
nuance: The confession is of spending: பொருள்தேடி, 'seeking wealth', for women's ornaments (மாபணிக்கள், ஓலை, முத்தம்). The epithet சூகரத்தொடு அம்பு தானெடுத்து வந்த சூதன் may join Vishnu's boar form to the charioteer Krishna; the reading of the opening lines and of this epithet is uncertain.

reading: The poet describes at length the beauty of dancing women like Rambha, from their hair, earrings, teeth and lips to their breasts, waist and thighs, who sing in cuckoo voices and twist, smile and dance in the street, and asks whether it is fit to keep company with these deceivers who serve Kama's bed. The praise is a battle in which the sea roars, jackals and vultures feed, the mountain is struck and the elephants of the directions shake as Murugan sends the vel with a smile; he weds Indra's daughter and the hunter girl and stands at Eragam.
nuance: The whole charge sits in the last line of the confession: குத்திரர், deceivers, and சந்தமாமோ, 'is it fitting?'. Dancing in the street (நற்றெருமீதில் ... நடிப்பவர்) suggests temple or street dancers, but no payment is named. The final epithet, லக்ஷுமி பெற்றருள், is unclear to me.

tamil: வார்குழல் விரித்துத் தூக்கி வேல்விழி சுழற்றிப் பார்த்து
வாசக முரைத்துச் சூத்ர பாவையெ னுறுப்பைக் காட்டி
சீர்கலை நெகிழ்த்துப் போர்த்து நூலிடை நெளித்துக் காட்டி
சேருற அழைத்துப் பார்த்து சார்வுற மருத்திட் டாட்டி
சூரர்கள் பதைக்கத் தேர்க்க ளானைக ளழித்துத் தாக்கி
தூமொழி நகைத்துக் கூற்றை மாளிட வுதைத்துக் கோத்த
ஏரணி சடைச்சிப் பாற்சொ லாரணி சிறக்கப் போற்று
ஏடணி குழைச்சித் தூர்த்த வாடகி குறத்திக் கேற்ற
reading: The poet describes courtesans who loosen and toss their hair, roll their spear eyes, laugh 'come', show their bodies like puppets on strings, slip their garments, dance and sing like cuckoos, draw a man close, dose him with a drug and strip him of his wealth, and asks whether a bond with these false dancers is right. The praise names the vel that burned Sura's hill, the father who kicked Death, Uma as mother, and the hunter girl, at Eragam.
nuance: மருத்திட்டு ஆட்டி, 'dosing him with medicine', and சீர்பொருள் பறி, 'snatching his wealth', make these women thieves as well as lures; பொய்க் கூத்தர், false dancers, joins the two. The lines on Siva who kicked Death (கூற்றை மாளிட உதைத்து) and wears a skin may say that Murugan taught him (எனப்பர்க்கு ஏற்றி), but the syntax is not clear to me.

reading: The poet describes women's eyes, like poison, the vel and Kama's arrows, their musk-scented breasts like the northern mountain, their anklets, flowered hair, moon faces and swan gait, and asks whether he may melt and waste in union with them. The praise tells the whole Rama story, the golden deer, Kara, the seven sala trees, Vali's chest, the demon army and the ten crowned heads of Lanka's king, and names Murugan as that Rama's nephew, who mounted the peacock and circled the world in an instant, at Swamimalai.
nuance: The plea is one question, கலவியில் நைந்துருகிடலாமோ, 'may I melt in union?', after nine lines of description. உலகை வலமாக நொடியினில் வந்து, circling the world in a moment, recalls the story of the fruit contest, but the text gives only the circling.

reading: The poet describes the hair, carp eyes, earrings, brow, smile and breasts of courtesans who dance in anklets, and asks whether his drowning in infatuation with these deceivers and enchantresses will never end. The praise names Siva who wears the flayed elephant and tiger skin and shares his body with Uma, and Murugan as the guru Siva bows to; the vel that broke the seven seas; Vishnu as uncle; and Murugan who came to the millet field as an old man and beguiled the hunter girl, at the Mantra-guru hill.
nuance: கணிகையர் சழக்கர் விஞ்சையர் piles three names on the women: courtesans, deceivers, sorceresses. அவர்பணி குருபர, 'the guru whom he serves', puts Siva at Murugan's feet. மந்திர குருமலை, the hill of the mantra-guru, names Swamimalai by that teaching.

tamil: விழியால் மருட்டி நின்று முலைதூச கற்றி மண்டு
விலையாக மிக்க செம்பொன் வரவேப ரப்பி வஞ்ச
மொழியாத சொற்கள் வந்து சிலுகாகி விட்ட தொந்த
முடியாது பொற்ச தங்கை தருகீத வெட்சி துன்று
பொழிகார்மு கிற்கி ணைந்த யமராஜ னுட்க அன்று
புருகூத னுட்கு ளிர்ந்த கனகாபு ரிப்ர சண்ட
செழுவாரி சத்தி லொன்று முதுவேதன் வெட்க அன்று
திரளாம ணிக்கு லங்கள் அருணோத யத்தை வென்ற
reading: The poet tells how women bewitch with their eyes, slip their breast-cloths and drown a man in the fire of lust, agree to deceitful play once red gold is spread before them as the price, and after a few days quarrel with unheard-of words, and asks for Murugan's ever-fresh feet with golden anklets and vetchi flowers. The praise names Siva who raised his foot against Yama, Murugan's marriages, and the Murugan who once told the truth so that the old Veda-knower Brahma was ashamed, at Eragam.
nuance: விலையாக மிக்க செம்பொன், gold 'as the price', and the quarrel that follows (சிலுகாகி) are the courtesan story in brief, and the bond is called முழுமாயை, wholly illusion. முதுவேதன் வெட்க ... திருவாய்மை செப்பி is the story of Brahma's ignorance, here without naming Om. The epithets for the two consorts (புருகூதன், ம்ருகக் கரும்பு) are uncertain to me.

reading: The poet asks whether he must fail and perish, having refused to share food with the hungry who came to him, kept his wealth for his hands and his youth, strayed from grace and suffered in pride, and taken this body to be lasting until kin surround it weeping, drums beat and Death takes the life. The praise names Murugan as the one who spoke agreeably to Siva, who gave half his body to Uma, who fed his foes to vultures, and who seeks out those who leave the quarrels of religions for austerity; the song ends at Thani.
nuance: The confession is of not giving: பசியுற்றவருக்கு அமுதைப் பகிர்தற்கு இசையாதே, refusing to share food with the hungry, set against the funeral (தமர் சுற்றி யழப் பறைகொட்டியிட). சமயச் சிலுகிட்டவரைத் தவறி, leaving those who quarrel over religions, is unusual praise: Murugan seeks those who go beyond sect.

title: திருத்தணிகை
theme: The first songs at Thiruthani (திருத்தணிகை): beside the usual confessions of courtesans who take a man's wealth, the poet catalogues his diseases, the body as a house of filth, the begging poet's humiliation and a child's plea to his father, and three songs name the Thiruppugazh itself; the praise dwells on Murugan as teacher of Siva and on Thani's blue-lily pool and fields.
structure_note: 240 is praise only. Courtesan confessions: 241, 252, 253, 254, with 242 on women's delusion. Diseases: 243, 250. The body and its tattvas: 244 (the pervading Siva), 247, 248. 245 confesses begging, 246 asks to worship, 249 to live among the singers of Thiruppugazh, 251 argues as a child to his father. 242, 249 and 254 name the Thiruppugazh.
source_issues: Song 243: one corrupt character in லு஡ர்தி (line 13); clearly ஊர்தி.

Song 244: nine corrupt characters; ஡ stands for ஊ in the repeated ஊடு (னு஡டு, வானு஡டு, யாறு஡டு), and ஡ண for ரீ in வா஡ணச (line 9), probably வாரீச (lotus). Also unflagged நநருடு (line 3), probably நீருடு, the sign seen in songs 21 and 33.
Song 247: one corrupt character in கொலு஡னை (line 4); probably கொல் ஊனை. Also unflagged த்ததகுரு (line 7), unclear.

reading: A song of praise: Siva, Vishnu and Brahma praise Murugan daily as six-faced Saravanabhava; he sent the vel like fire against the asuras, dwells by his anklet-ringed feet in devotees' hearts, was born of Uma, and as guru told Siva, to his delight, the meaning that ends the one word Pranava. All worlds, gods and sages praise him at Thanigai, where he comes with the hunter girl and the daughter of the heavenly tree at either side.
nuance: பரமன திருசெவி களிகூர உரைசெயு மொருமொழி பிரணவ முடிவதை: the teaching is spoken into Siva's ear and is the end (meaning) of Om, not the syllable alone. The song opens with the three gods as worshippers.

reading: The poet speaks of women who laugh softly, melt a man and wipe out his thought with dark eyes, draw him in and take all his wealth, and of men bound to them who boast of a tattva-knowledge found nowhere else; he asks whether he must slip again into this birth, lying down and rising in an instant. The praise names the vel that split the sea and the demons' mountain of illusion and took pity on Indra's city, the hunter girl, the cock banner, and the famous lily pool of Thiruthani.
nuance: ஒட்டறப் பொருட் பறிப்பவர், those who strip wealth entirely, are courtesans. The middle lines (தத்துவப் ப்ரசித்தி ... ஞானம் சமைத்துரைத்து) seem to mock those who contrive and proclaim a knowledge of the tattvas, but how they connect to the women, and the sense of the birth line, depend on a word split I am not sure of. உற்பலச் சுனை is the blue-lily pool of Thani.

reading: The poet recalls that those who read the Thiruppugazh with love are said to be freed of their troubles, and that men keep and recite the four kinds of poetry in music, dance, grammar and literature; without learning to recite it, he asks, must he fall into the delusion of clever women who melt men with breast, face and mind? The praise names Siva who burned Kama with the fire of his forehead eye, lives on Kailasa and gave half of himself to Uma, and Murugan as their son at Thiruthani.
nuance: The song names its own book: திருப்புகழ் விருப்பொடு படிப்பவர் இடுக்கினை அறுத்திடும், reading the Thiruppugazh with love cuts affliction. The burning of Kama (மதவேள்) in the praise answers the women of the plea. The opening word இருப்பவல் is unclear to me.

reading: The poet lists diseases, cough, epilepsy, wind, burning fevers, poison, urinary flux, headache, anaemia, scrofula, dropsy, phlegm and colic, and asks for Murugan's feet so that they do not torment him in birth after birth. The praise names the vel thrown while a crore of asuras died and Bhairavas danced, the husband of the girl given by Indra, and Thani hill with its lotus pool.
nuance: The plea is not to be cured now but to be spared the diseases in every birth (பிறவிகள் தோறும்), so the list stands for embodied life itself. முயலகன் is the epilepsy demon of the Siva story.

tamil: உடலி னு஡டு போய்மீளு முயிரி னு஡டு மாயாத
டுலவை யூடு நநருடு புவியி னு஡டு வாதாடு
சுடரி னு஡டு நால்வேத முடியி னு஡டு மூடாடு
தொலைவி லாத போராசை துரிச றாத வோர்பேதை
மடல றாத வா஡ணச அடவி சாடி மாறான
மதகு தாவி மீதோடி யுழவ ரால டாதோடி
கடல்பு காம காமீனை முடுகி வாளை தான்மேவு
கடவுள் நீல மாறாத தணிகை காவ லாவீர
reading: The poet speaks of the light of lone knowledge that runs through the body, through the life that goes and returns, through awareness, sky, fire, wind, water and earth, through the crown of the four Vedas, the turiya state beyond, the form of Siva that does not join those who argue; and asks the Lord to tell a fool of endless desire and unremoved faults some means of touching it. The praise is a long scene of Thani's fields, where fish leap the sluices and flee the farmers into lotus pools, and names Murugan the guard of Thanigai, the mountain of compassion.
nuance: The repeated ஊடு, 'through', builds the pervasion line by line, from body and breath to the five elements and the Veda's end (நால்வேத முடி, Vedanta) to துரிய ... அதீத. வாதாடும் ஒருவரோடும் மேவாத, not joined to any who dispute, sets the truth apart from debate. The plea asks only for an உபாயம், a means. The text has nine corrupt glyphs, but ஊடு is clear throughout.

reading: The poet confesses that he searched out who the rich were, sang them extempore verses saying their fame was as great as Mount Meru, and walked back and forth until they said 'go, come tomorrow' and turned their faces; he asks for Murugan's two lotus feet before he is worn down. The praise names Siva with bull, trident, moon, vilva, skull, river and serpent in his matted hair, and Murugan who came in the toddling steps of wisdom while Siva watched and Uma rejoiced, at Thani hill of blue lilies.
nuance: ஆசுகவி, the quick verse made to order, is the poet's trade, and நாளை நடவும், 'go, tomorrow', its reward. ஞான தளர்நடை, the toddling child of wisdom before Siva and Uma, may point to Sambandar, whom the book identifies with Murugan; the text does not name him.
