reading: The poet asks whether, never leaving the path of saving knowledge and reciting through the Veda, so that the darkness of delusion in the heart breaks and grace becomes his kin, he will worship Murugan at the hill of lilies with fresh vilva sprouts and scattered flowers. The praise names Murugan as son of Siva's consort and of Ganga, lord of the hunters, nephew of Vishnu, and plays on Devayanai's name: younger than the divine elephant, lord of the white elephant, dear to Devayanai.
nuance: The closing line puns three times on தெய்வ யானை: Ganapati the divine elephant, Indra's white elephant, and the goddess Devayanai. Much of the plea depends on how the rhythmic syllables split (மோகப்பொருளை, பழைய வல்ல), and I offer the reading only in outline.

tamil: எத்தனைக லாதி சித்தங் கெத்தனைவி யாதி பித்தங்
எத்தனைவி டாவெ ருட்டங் கெத்தனைவ லாண்மை பற்றங்
பித்தனைய னான கட்டுண் டிப்படிகெ டாமல் முத்தம்
பெற்றியுமொ ராது நிற்குந் த்ததகுரு தார நிற்கும்
தத்தனத னாத னத்தந் தத்தனத னாத னத்தந்
தக்குகுகு டூடு டுட்டுண் டிக்குகுகு டீகு தத்தந்
சித்தர்கள்நி டாதர் வெற்பின் கொற்றவர்சு வாமி பத்தர்
செக்கணரி மாக னைக்குஞ் சித்தணிகை வாழ்சி வப்பின்
reading: The poet runs through his bondage: how many arts, diseases, madnesses, inert things moving and unmoving, terrors, powers and attachments, and the daily satisfying of hunger with the flesh of killing; and asks that a madman so bound not perish thus but gain release, for the feet that stand beyond bondage. The praise is drum syllables and Thanigai, ringed by eight mountains, home of siddhas and hunters, red as the evening sky.
nuance: முத்தம் is release (mukti) and பெத்தம் bondage, Siddhanta terms set against each other. கொல் ஊனை நித்தம் பசியாறல, eating killed flesh daily, is the one concrete fault in the list. The lines on Murugan's seat (ஆசனத்தின் செயல்) and the garbled த்ததகுரு are beyond me.

reading: The poet calls the body a house of bones, nerves, blood, filth, brain, fat and worms, inhabited by many cheating tattvas, and describes the people who live in such houses, gamblers, householders in samsara, villains in the net of lust who never think of austerity, traitors to friends and killers, beset by fevers; he asks whether he must desire and carry this house and wander. The praise names the vel against Sura, Vishnu who slew Ravana, imprisoned Mahabali and cast the filed pestle into the sea, and Murugan as guru of his father after humbling Brahma, at Thiruthani.
nuance: The body is a வீடு, a house, and the tattvas within it சதிகாரர், conspirators. உலக்கை ராவி நடுக்கடல் விட்டவன் recalls the pestle ground to powder and thrown in the sea in the Yadava story. வலிக்க வேதனை குட்டி, knocking Brahma on the head, joins the Om story to பரப்ரமருக்கு அருள் குருநாதா.

reading: The poet confesses that he has gathered everything for himself, wearied without rest, and that the body he took dies without shame; to end his births he asks to live among those who speak of Murugan daily through the Thiruppugazh and never to part from the knowledge they teach, so that he too may worship his feet. The praise names the slaying of an opponent, the Veda Murugan told that pleased Brahma, the vel that took Sura's head, and the hunter girl, at Thiruthani.
nuance: திருப்புகழாலும் உரைத்திடுவார் தங்குழி மேவி asks for the company of Thiruppugazh singers, so the book is again named within itself as a means of grace. The first line of the praise (வேள் கொன்றவன்) and the Brahma line are uncertain to me.

tamil: எனைய டைந்த குட்டம் வினைமி குந்த பித்த
இகலி நின்ற லைக்கு முயல கன்கு லைப்பொ
மனைகள் பெண்டிர் மக்கள் தமைநி னைந்து சுத்த
மருவி யின்றே னக்கு மரக தஞ்சி றக்கு
நினைவ ணங்கு பத்த ரனைவ ருந்த ழைக்க
நிலைபெ றுந்தி ருத்த ணியில்வி ளங்கு சித்ர
தினைவி ளங்க லுற்ற புனஇ ளங்கு றத்தி
திசைமு கன்தி கைக்க அசுர ரன்ற டைத்த
reading: The poet names leprosy, bile, fever, pain, epilepsy and cough, and asks not to die with his mind confused by thoughts of house, wife and children, but that Murugan come today on the emerald peacock and give him release. The praise names the vel that stands on the path to protect devotees, the chest that embraces the hunter girl, and Murugan who opened the prison where the asuras held the gods, at Thiruthani.
nuance: The disease list joins the family list: மனைகள் பெண்டிர் மக்கள் தமை நினைந்து, and both are what the mind should not be clouded by at the end. முத்தி தரவேணும் asks for release directly.

reading: The poet argues with Murugan as a son: what wisdom has he, whom else can he seek, must he die in vain; Murugan is father and mother to him, and if he refuses to set his feet on him the world will laugh, for when a child runs crying before its father, who else picks it up, and would a father leave it to cry? The praise names the vel that drove off the villains of the eight directions like milk boiling over, Siva who danced with deer and axe, and Valli, at Thiruthani.
nuance: The plea is a lawyer's argument from kinship: பார் நகைக்கும், the world will laugh, if a father abandons his crying son. The grace is claimed as a father's duty, not begged as a favour.

reading: The poet describes women with palm-leaf earrings, picture-like colour, arrow eyes, sugared speech, bird voices, drum waists, garlands and pearl-hung breasts, whose deceitful delusion destroys the mind, who call a man into a dark room and, seizing his wealth, embrace him, and asks whether his suffering over them will not ease. The praise tells how Rama dried the sea, cut down Ravana's ten heads and freed Lakshmi from prison, names Murugan as his nephew and as son of Uma the parrot of dharma, the true guru who gives love to those who wear the ash, at Thiruthani.
nuance: இருட்டறை வாவெனப் பொருள் பற்றி முயக்கிடு, 'come into the dark room', seizing wealth and embracing, is the Kural's image of the courtesan's embrace almost word for word. நீறிட்டு நினைப்பவர், those who wear the ash and think of him, are the ones the true guru blesses.

reading: The poet describes women with bodiced breasts, pearls and jingling bangles who speak of infatuation and take the wealth in a man's hand, and calls himself a slave of desire, melted and ignorant, who does not know the one thing that has no remainder; he asks for Murugan's fragrant feet now. The praise names Krishna who stole curd from the cowherd women and came on Garuda, and Vishnu who sleeps on the serpent as uncle, at Thani hill praised by Siva.
nuance: கைப்பொருள் கவர்தரு, taking the wealth in hand, marks the courtesans. எச்சமில் ஒருபொருள், the one thing without remainder, names what the poet does not know against what the women take. The line on the bird (குற்கிர வினியொடு) is unclear to me.

reading: The poet describes women who trouble those who come near with a sidelong glance, call them, speak the arts of love, melt the heart with bird cries, loosen their silk, take a man to bed, kiss, bind him in their hair, mark him with nails and teeth and keep him in their laps, and asks whether he must delight in them. The praise names Murugan who gave life to the Thiruppugazh that tames adversity, the vel of the millet hill, the cock banner, and the true guru who taught the Unborn Siva and ended false babble, at Thiruthani of paddy heaps.
nuance: மெய்ப்பொருள் திருப்புகழ்க்கு உயிர்ப்பளித்து makes Murugan the giver of the book's life, the third song of the chapter to name it. பிறப்பிலிக்கு உணர்த்து சற்குரு, the true guru who taught the Unborn, is the Siva-teaching story without naming Om.

title: திருத்தணிகை
theme: Songs at Thiruttani (திருத்தணிகை, 2 of 5): the poet turns from women who deceive and rob, from the false pot of the body, and from sectarians who chase gods and gold back into the womb, and asks for the feet, release and the gift of praise; four songs are love laments for a girl wasting for Murugan, and one, 269, praises the Thiruppugazh itself as fire. The praise returns often to Murugan as teacher of Siva and as Sambandar who routed the Jains.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (255, 260, 264, 266, 267); the body and birth (258); sectarians and false company (257, 261); the gift of praise and the poet's lowliness (263, 269); akam laments in another voice asking for Murugan's garland or arm (256, 259, 262, 265); and 268, a thanksgiving for a teaching received in which Murugan writes Valli's beauty on the madal.
source_issues: Song 255: மினுக்யும் (line 4) has lost a letter, probably மினுக்கியும்.
Song 256: புமணி (line 4) probably பூமணி; கநவன (line 6) is garbled, probably a lost letter as in songs 21 and 33.
Song 261: one corrupt character, in கருக்கடலு஡டே (line 6), read as கடலூடே.
Song 266: one corrupt character, ஡ணங்கிசை (line 9), probably ரீ, giving இட்டவரீங்கிசை (இட்டவர் ஈங்கு இசை).
Song 267: one corrupt character, in கானு஡ர் (line 8), read as கானூர்.
Song 268: two corrupt characters, சஞ்ச஡ண (line 10), probably சஞ்சரீக (bee), and செம்பொனு஡புற (line 18), probably செம்பொன் நூபுர (golden anklet).

reading: The poet describes women who loosen their dark hair, glance with fish eyes, jingle bangles and chains and shimmer their garments, and the deceitful ones (கவட்டர்) who bow only to destroy the heart; he asks Murugan to look on him so that, free of their company, he may bathe in the sea of austerity, become his servant and live in his shrine with a glad mind. The praise names Murugan the guru of his father Siva, who burnt the cities, flayed the elephant and wears ash, the poet of nectar-praise in a kadamba garland, and the vel that dusts the demons' horses and elephants, at Thiruttani where the hunter girl rejoices.
nuance: உனக்கு அடிமையுற்று உன் தலத்தினில் இருக்கும்படி: the remedy asked is to live at the shrine itself as the Lord's servant, a concrete hope beside the inward bath in தவக்கடல். எனப்பன் குருநாதா calls Murugan 'guru of my father', the poet claiming Siva as his own father.

reading: In the voice of one watching over a lovesick girl, the singer asks that the creeper-waisted girl not perish under the women's taunts and the noise of bangles, the dark cloud and swelling water on the shore, and the many killing arrows of Kama, and that Murugan graciously give her his cool garland of kura and kadamba flowers. The praise names the vel that the lords of Uma, Saraswati and Lakshmi worship, the chest where Valli of the millet field and the heavenly deer Devayanai dwell, and the lord who rides his peacock daily at Thanigai so that the loneliness of the lonely ends.
nuance: The request for the god's garland is the akam convention of the girl asking for her lover's token. கலைமடவார் தஞ் சிலை may be the women's gossip (சிலை as sound) or their bow-like brows, so whether this is அலர் is uncertain. தனியவர் கூருந் தனிகெட: the god rides out to end the solitude of the lonely, which turns the praise back to the girl.

reading: The poet asks why the deceitful siddhas and those confused by the six sects, who consecrate many gods, fix names and set up images, and seek wealth for necklaces, signet rings, bangles and chains, should wander dividing themselves only to enter the womb again; will they not understand a little the fame of the Lord's feet, which stand one with everything and yet apart? The praise is of the vel that churned the eight peaks and the sea, cut Surapadman and bathed in his blood, of Valli bowing in shame in the millet field, and of Thiruttani with its golden walls, lord of Sruti and Tamil poetry.
nuance: சகலத்தும் ஒற்றைபட்டு அயல்பட்டு நிற்கும்: the Lord is at once one with all things and other than them, the doctrine of pervasion with transcendence, set against the sects' many installed gods. The jewels named (சவடி, இலச்சினை, சரி, சரப்பளி) make the sectarians' religion a trade. Whether the wanderer of the first lines is the poet or the sectarians depends on how உழல்வானேன் is taken.

reading: Not knowing how to draw near the anklet feet, his mind on women with heavy breasts and dark kohl eyes, the poet asks Murugan to cut off this birth that bears the false pot of flesh, skin and semen, a bellows that is home to the troop of diseases, and to give him release every day. The praise names the vel that fought the elephant-borne demon, the Kumaresa of the cock banner whose feet trample the pride of mountains, and the embrace of the hunter girl, at Thiruttani of pearls.
nuance: இனப்பிணிக் கணத்தினுக்கு இருப்பு, துருத்தி, பொய்க் கடம்: three images of the body in one line, a lodging for diseases, a bellows of breath, a false pot. The plea asks for release daily (நித்தம் முத்தி), as if it must be renewed.

reading: A short love lament: the singer asks whether, because of the roaring dark sea, the moon that rises red as fire, and the arrows Kama shoots from his sugarcane bow, a girl should be stopped here and her body grow slack. The praise names Murugan the husband of the girl who once guarded the millet, Kandavel shining on the hill of Thiruttani, and the lord of the three gods who create, protect and destroy.
nuance: The torments are the classical night machinery, sea, moon and Kama's cane bow, as in 24; the moon is called hot (சிவத்து அங்கி வாய்த்து எழு திங்கள்), the cool moon turned to fire by longing. ஒருத்தி is in the third person, so the speaker is a mother or friend. பனைக்கரக் கயத்து அண்டர் போற்றிய மங்கைபாகா is hard to place: it may name Siva or Murugan.

reading: The poet lists the courtesans: actresses of deceit who drop their garments, bodies full of disease, sweet talkers who embrace on the bed until the heart melts for money, who fight with loveless infatuation, embrace whoever gives more as if he were an old friend, and steal like arrows with their eyes; he asks whether a day will come when, not thinking of them, he thinks of Murugan coming on the peacock to tell him the way to the state of release. The praise names the vel that dusted the demons who harried Vishnu, Brahma and the gods, the husband of the hunter girl, and the lord at Thanigai whose lotus feet are reached by those of dharma, Veda, patience, unwavering austerity and wisdom.
nuance: அதிகமா ஒரு பொருள் தருபவரொடு பழைய பேரென இதமுற அணைபவர்: the courtesan treats the highest payer as an old friend, the stock charge of money for love. The praise ends with a long list of who reach the feet, the devotees' virtues answering the women's vices.

reading: The poet asks whether, having fallen in with liars, followers of the senses, blind fools whose eyes do not look to end birth, thieves and sectarian disputants, knowing nothing, weary and sinking in the sea of the womb, he will rise in understanding and reach the paired feet. The praise identifies Murugan with Sambandar, the poet of the Kaundinya line at Pugali who spread holy ash to cure the Pandyan's fever and crushed the Jains, and names him the son of Siva who burnt the cities with a laugh, lord at Seruttani where the kuvalai blooms daily in the spring.
nuance: The plea turns on company: the bad are named in a string of types (கிருதர், பொறிவழிச் செறிஞர், குருடர், திருடர், சமயதர்க்கிகள்), and to keep company with them is already to sink. The praise is Sambandar's story told of Murugan: the Pandyan (செழியன்) freed of fever by holy ash at Madurai and the shaven-headed Jains (பறிதலைப் சமணர்) defeated.

reading: A love lament: the cuckoo torments the cuckoo-voiced girl, Kama's flower arrows kill, the cool white moon and the fire of her breasts burn, the wind and the roaring sea and the women's gossip assail her, and her arm grows weak; the singer asks whether she may not be given Murugan's own arm to embrace. The praise names the hero who fought until the mountain shook, the chest that joins the hunter girl's breast, Thanigai where the crescent bows in the cool groves, and Murugan of Sengazhani who told the meaning to the Supreme when he bowed.
nuance: பொருமங்கையர் உக்கு அலர்: the women's gossip is one of the torments, alongside cuckoo, moon and sea. பரமன் பணியப் பொருள் அன்று அருளிற் பகர்: Siva bowed and Murugan told him the meaning, the teaching of 6 and 24, here without naming Om. The speaker may be the girl or one who watches her.

reading: The poet asks not to wander born as sparrow, kite, jackal, forest beast, worm, fish, elephant and tree, nor to bathe at Kumari with a sorrowing mind and be mocked by many as a diseased wretch; he will not seek ornaments, elephants, horses, silks and golden vessels, and asks instead that, as Murugan's feet suffice for his dwelling, he be given the Thiruppugazh that dwells in them. The praise, after drum syllables of battle, names Siva who burnt the cities with his eye and cut Brahma's head, and Murugan who impaled the Jains and dances at Thiruttani with Valli and Devayanai.
nuance: The list of creatures reads as the births the poet fears (திரி உறவாகா), though it may be a list of insults the crowd would throw. உனது பதச்சரண் மருவு திருப்புகழ்: the poet asks for his own book's name, praise that rests in the feet. அமணர் உடற்கெட வசியில் அழுத்தி is again the impaling of the Jains, Sambandar's story told of Murugan, as in 261. The lines on the feet and the waterfall (வரிய பதத்தினில் நருவி) are hard to divide.

reading: The poet asks whether it is fit to be kin to the common women who loosen their hair, roll their gemmed breasts, whirl their fish eyes, arch their crescent brows, laugh, kindle infatuation, sway as they walk and, feeding his desire, destroy his austerity. The praise names Siva who bent the bow and burnt the three cities, wore the axe and the tiger and elephant skins, and held the poison in his throat so the gods survived, and calls Murugan the one who told the meaning to that matted-haired god, and the hero bathed in infatuation for the hunter girl at Thiruttani.
nuance: பொதுமாதர்: common women, but money is not named, so the charge is desire, not trade. தவத்து அழிப்பவர்: what they destroy is austerity. சடைக் கடவுட் சிறக்கப் பொருட் பகர்வோனே is the teaching of Siva, without naming Om.

reading: A love lament: the singer asks that this girl not weaken under the crescent moon, the umbrella-crown of Kama who shot the kuvalai arrow, and under the cuckoo, and that Murugan, who has drawn her close and embraced her shoulders in love, give her his sweet garland of compassion to wear in peerless beauty. The praise names the vel that fought the golden mountain until the eight elephants cried, the chest that rises to embrace the girl, and Thiruttani where heaps of coral and pearls lie like hills by the fields and conches crowd.
nuance: இவளை: 'this girl', so the voice is a mother or friend pleading for her. The garland is called கருணைக்கு இனிமைத் தொடை, a garland of compassion: the love token is also grace. The crescent as Kama's royal umbrella (குடை) is a striking image.

reading: The poet describes courtesans who loosen and retie their hair, paint their eyes and deal double, press their breasts on a man's shoulders, leave crescent nail-marks, speak desire for many days to get the money given, cry as if forsaken, and when the money ends leave him groaning at the door; he asks how, without the compassionate feet that would take him from their side, he can enter the good state. The praise names Murugan nephew of Achyuta of the Gandiva and of Rama with the monkey army, younger brother of the elephant-faced god who ate fruits and sugar, and the one who stood as the vengai tree to unite with honey-voiced Valli, at the Thiruttani hill of sugarcane and kuvalai springs.
nuance: பொருள்தீரில் ஏங்கியிடக் கடையில் தளிவைப்பவர்: the man left groaning at the door once his money ends, the formula of 33. ஈந்திலை: 'you have not given', a reproach to the Lord, not only a plea. In the praise Vishnu is named as Krishna with Arjuna's bow (காண்டிப அச்சுதன்).

reading: The poet describes women who bewilder with eyes sharper than spears, call with their breasts, draw a man to the flower bed, drink from his lips, loosen their hair and scold while their ear ornaments fall in play, and asks whether the strife of dwelling rejoicing among these infatuating women, as in Yama's forest-town, will not end. The praise names the vel that killed Sura amid drums and the sound of Vedas and Agamas, the guru who gave the great teaching in the holy ear of Siva who burnt Kama with a laugh, and the lord who embraces Valli, given by Vishnu, at Thiruttani.
nuance: நம கானூர் உறைக் கலகம் is uncertain: it may be the turmoil of dwelling in Yama's town (நமன் கானூர்) or be split otherwise. தாதா திருச்செவியில் மாபோதகத்தை அருள் குருநாதா: the teaching whispered in Siva's ear, the Om story, though Om is not named. மாலோன் அளித்த வளி makes Valli Vishnu's daughter.

reading: The poet thanks the guru who dwells at the foot of the kura tree, in the lotus of devotees' hearts and at the crown of the Vedas, who told him the way that sectarian disputants cannot reach and others never meet, 'this is the tradition', and gave the great grace of his anklet feet; he will not forget it in dream or waking. The praise names Murugan son of Siva of the matted hair, and the lord who painted on the madal Valli's lotus feet, bamboo arms, moon face, musk-dark breasts, honey speech and smile, red as the cochineal insect and green as emerald.
nuance: A song of thanksgiving rather than plea: the poet speaks of a teaching already received, தனது என வரும் ஒரு சம்ப்ரதாயம், a tradition that comes as one's own, beyond the reach of சமய விரோத தந்த்ர வாதிகள். குரவடி may recall Siva teaching under the kura tree. The ending makes Murugan the lover who rides the madal, painting the beloved's form on it, the akam convention turned on the god. கொந்து காவென is obscure.

reading: The poet declares that the Thiruppugazh is fire to the heads of the angry, the clans of enemies, the lives of destroyers, and to those who laugh and those who blame; it grants what one thinks, melts the mind, cuts the womb of darkness so that one is not born, burns fire itself and breaks mountains, and he asks for the act of speaking that full praise. The praise, in drum syllables, shows the vel that destroyed the Suras and burnt the mountain with a laugh, and Murugan delighting in the hunter girl at Thiruttani.
nuance: The book praises its own name: திருப்புகழ் is given the powers of a mantra, to burn enemies, fulfil desire and end birth. நெருப்பையும் எரிக்கும்: it burns even fire. The plea is not for the praise itself but for the act of speaking it (உரைக்கும் செயல்).

title: திருத்தணிகை
theme: Songs at Thiruttani (திருத்தணிகை, 3 of 5): the poet counts his numberless births and deaths, takes apart the body as a pot, bellows and bag of humours, turns from courtesans, flattering court poetry and barren book-learning, and asks for the feet as the raft over the seas of desire, birth and learning; the praise names Murugan as the southern guru who told Siva the meaning of Om, and Thiruttani as Sivaloka, where he is physician of the disease of birth.
structure_note: Births and deeds counted (270); the body and the humours (274, 275, 280); courtesans and desire (273, 276, 281, 282, 283); self-abuse and the plea not to be cast off (272); against court poets who flatter patrons (271) and against learning that scorns the wise (279); samsara and the gift of praise (277); short prayers for grace (278, 284).
source_issues: Song 272: தவ்முழ்குந் (line 3) and மற்றவ்ரு தாவனை (line 7) look damaged, perhaps for தவம் மூழ்கும் and வ்ருதாவன், though not flagged.
Song 276: அனைததையும் (line 13) is a typo for அனைத்தையும்.
Song 277: one corrupt character, in அதனு஡டே (line 2), read as அதனூடே.
Song 278: மதித் முத்தமிழிற் (line 6) has lost a letter, probably மதித்த.
Song 284: three corrupt characters, in கடலு஡டும் (lines 4, 5 and 6), each read as கடலூடும்.

reading: The poet asks how many bodies, countless as grains of sand, he has filled, how many lives born in the sea like shoals of fish, on hills and in springs, how many times infatuation for women held him and Death snatched his life, how many deceits he thought, families he ruined and lives he killed like a beast; and he asks Murugan to grace this fool, rough and wretched, to melt at the flower feet. The praise, in a long run of drum syllables, shows the vel in the battlefield where kites and jackals feed, and Thiruttani where Siva's devotees and sages worship with honeyed flowers.
nuance: The plea is a catalogue built on எத்தனை, 'how many', closing with அளவேதோ and அளவிலை, 'what measure? there is none': the poet counts his births and his sins alike. The first words (சினத்திலத்தினை) are hard to divide, and விதிகர may be the deeds fate ordains.

reading: The poet asks to leave the delusion of the poets who praise base patrons as equal to the rain cloud, the treasure of Kubera, the wish-cow and the wish-tree, melting their own minds before them, and who steal and twist old verses of rare meaning to make poems, so that he may sing instead of Murugan's kuvalai hill. The praise shows Murugan himself, wounded by the poison-tipped blue arrows of Valli's eyes under her dark bow-brows, falling at the feet of the doe's daughter crying 'refuge' and melting in infatuation to embrace her.
nuance: A satire of court poetry: the patron is likened to cloud, padma-nidhi, Kamadhenu and kalpaka tree, the stock comparisons for a giver, and the poems are plagiarised (பழைய மொழியைத் திருடி நெருடி). The praise reverses the plea: the god falls at a girl's feet crying அபயம், as the poet will not fall at a patron's. உழையின் மகள் is Valli as a doe's daughter.

reading: The poet heaps names on himself: a rat-snake for quarrels, one who eats without witness, far from the shastra of holy ash, a sinner without the meaning of austerity, a dog barking Tamil who does not think of Murugan with love as poets do, a traitor who does not honour the wise, a wretch flowering with the three malas; he asks whether it is Murugan's duty to cast him off, and whether there is no state to be gained by going with the devotees. The praise tells at length of Surpanakha's nose cut off and Ravana carrying Sita away, and names Murugan nephew of Rama the archer who destroyed him, at Thiruttani with its long spring of kazhuneer.
nuance: போக்கிவிடக் கடனோ: 'is it your duty to throw me away?', a challenge as much as a plea. அடியாரொடு போய்ப் பெறுகைக்கு இலையோ கதி: the hope is to be saved in the company of devotees, not alone. Several of the epithets (சாரை, சாக்ஷியறப் பசியாறி, வ்ருதாவன்) are obscure, and the source seems damaged in தவ்முழ்குந்.

reading: The poet asks whether he will wander caught in the winking ways of lust, bewildered by thieving, hollow, proud women who dance daily, sway their bodies and cast the net of their eyes, letting what is good run out of his mind. The praise names Murugan the able child who told the meaning of the great Om (மாகுடிலை) to the ash-smeared, babbling madman Siva, the supreme who comes in compassion to the wise, the southern guru skilled in a thousand yogas, the slayer of Sura in a field of ghouls, and the lord of Thiruttani, whose spring holds a lily that blooms three times a day.
nuance: குடிலை is a name for the pranava, so the Om teaching is explicit here. தெக்ஷிண குருநாதா, the southern guru, gives Murugan the title of Dakshinamurti, Siva's own teaching form. Siva is called பித்தன், the madman, a devotional epithet.

reading: The poet asks not to be born again in the world through desire for this sinful body, steeped in the delusion of the three gunas, wrapped in skin and soaked in Kama's sickness, and to be given the grace that neither cheats nor the proud can reach. The praise names Murugan who removes the deeds of those who sing and serve without fail, who destroyed Sura, the true wisdom of Thanigai, the one who embraces the girl of candied-milk speech, and calls him father, eternal, free and knowing.
nuance: The song is in clipped syllables (துப்பா ரப்பா டற்றீ), so the first lines are hard to divide and the reading of the body's description is tentative. அத்தா நித்தா முத்தா சித்தா: four titles in a rhyme, father, eternal, freed, knower. எத்தார் வித்தாரத்தே கிட்டா அருள்: grace is beyond both deceivers and the learned show-offs.

reading: The poet asks whether a day will come when this body falls: a hut of skin, the pot of pleasure and pain, of mala and maya, of the humours, of babbling speech, unable to grasp the many sect books, bound with flesh and blood, loathsome, in which he wanders seeking. The praise names Murugan worshipped by gurus who wear rudraksha and ash, lord of the twelve hills and Thanigai, son of Parvati and the river, who helps the ascetics, easy to reach for those who praise him in Tamil verse and hard for those who do not.
nuance: சட்டவாக்கு அழிவது ஒருநாளே: the plea is for the body's end, not its health. The praise closes on a paired rule, எத்திடார்க்கு அரிய, முத்த பாத் தமிழ் கொடு எத்தினார்க்கு எளிய: the Lord is hard for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise in Tamil. The crowded first lines (காற் பதலை, கைக்கொளாக் கதறு) are hard to divide.

reading: The poet heaps names on the women who sell their breasts for a price, shaking, scheming, blind, deceitful, slippery, and asks not to enter their net, nor to play with those who call men coral-red and bangled; he asks whether a day will come when the states of consciousness and the tattvas perish, the darkness is cleared, a single light spreads, grace is fed to him and the paired feet given. The praise names Uma the emerald-formed, who creates all and with the dancer removes it, as Murugan's mother, Vishnu with discus and conch who swallowed the earth as his uncle, and the peacock that circles the world in a moment, at Thiruttani with Valli and Devayanai.
nuance: விலைமுலை: breasts sold for a price, which makes these courtesans in the trade sense. The plea is in the language of Saiva doctrine: அவத்தை தத்துவம் அழிபட, இருள் அறை விலக்கு, ஒரு சுடரொளி பரவ. The praise gives Uma the dance at the summit of the Supreme (பரத்தின் உச்சியில் நடம் நவிலும் உமை).

tamil: நிலையாத சமுத்திர மான சமுசார துறைக்கணின் மூழ்கி
நெடுநாளு முழைப்புள தாகி பெரியோர்க ளிடைக்கர வாகி
தலையான வுடற்பிணி யூறி பவநோயி னலைப்பல வேகி
தவியாமல் பிறப்பையு நாடி யதுவேரை யறுத்துனை யோதி
கலியாண சுபுத்திர னாக குறமாது தனக்குவி நோத
களிகூரு முனைத்துணை தேடு மடியேனை சுகப்பட வேவை
பலகாலு முனைத்தொழு வோர்கள் மறவாமல் திருப்புகழ் கூறி
பதியான திருத்தணி மேவு சிவலோக மெனப்பரி வேறு
reading: The poet asks for grace so that, instead of plunging into the unstable sea of samsara and calling it real, labouring long, hiding from the great, failing to praise the feet, steeped in bodily disease and the sickness of birth and maddened, he may seek out and cut the root of birth, chant Murugan's name and be saved; he asks Murugan to keep him, a servant who seeks him as companion, in joy, since that is his duty, and to let those who worship him live praising him with the Thiruppugazh. The praise names Murugan Valli's bridegroom, and the lord of Thiruttani, which is like Sivaloka, the physician of the disease of birth.
nuance: பவரோக வயித்திய நாத: Murugan as Vaidyanatha, physician of the disease of becoming, which matches the plea's பவநோய். கடனாகும் இது: as in 272, the poet tells the Lord that saving him is his duty. The song names its own book (திருப்புகழ் கூறி).

reading: A short prayer: the poet asks that whatever he thinks not fail, that he not be parted from the steadied mind, that he not perish in the great tattvas, and that he be given the eternal consciousness that rises. The praise names Murugan easy for men and devotees, great in the three Tamils, the youngest of the sons born to Siva, at Thiruttani.
nuance: நித்திய சித்து: eternal consciousness, the soul's goal named in a single phrase. மிலைத்த புத்தி may mean the mind that has been crowned or fixed; the sense of the first two lines is uncertain.

reading: The poet, who feeds his body day and night through the senses, has read some old Vedas, new books and many Puranas, and calls those settled in the reality whose breadth and length cannot be measured 'fools and dumb', asks whether he must perish without knowledge. The praise shows the vel thrown so that the mountain broke, Brahma was humbled, Indra freed from prison, the dark sea cried out and the great mango tree scattered, and names the chest adorned with kazhuneer, jasmine and kadamba at Thanigai.
nuance: The confession is of learning that breeds contempt: reading some Vedas and Puranas, the poet mocked the silent knowers as அசடர் மூகர், fools and mutes, when their silence was the knowledge. அகல நீளம் என்று அளவு கூறரும் பொருள்: the Reality whose breadth and length cannot be told.

reading: The poet takes apart his body: a head of big teeth, hands and feet that bear it, a false pot, a place of blame, a belly-pot for hunger, an artificial bellows full of bile, bound by the three humours and the five senses, a bag of disease; he asks Murugan to give him the purpose that would cut off its birth. The praise names the hero who sets on his true feet those devotees who speak from the heart, the embracer of the hunter girl, the golden son of Siva who burnt the three cities with a laugh, at Thiruttani, renowned for the Tamil of dharma.
nuance: பசிக்குடற் கடம், கிருத்திமத் துருத்தி, இப்பிணிப்பை: pot, bellows and bag, the same images as 258. முக்குற்றம் is probably the three humours of medicine (wind, bile, phlegm), which would make பித்து bile rather than madness. The plea asks not for health but for the end of the birth that makes such a body.

reading: The poet describes women who recall old intimacy, call sweetly, embrace, leave nail-marks, press face to face, feed a man with their spittle and work base magic, women who say they are many men's; he asks whether a day will come when Murugan sets him, a fool who longed for their ruinous work, disgraced and lost, at his red-gold feet, which make all powers and the eight siddhis easy and plain. The praise shows ghouls dancing in the battlefield and Sura vomiting blood, and Murugan stroking the feet of Valli in her leaf skirt, touching the tilaka on her round face and fastening a golden bodice over her breasts on the Thani hill.
nuance: குத்திர வித்தை: base arts, probably love-charms or drugs, the deceit of the women. The praise inverts the plea: the poet asks to be set at the Lord's feet, and the Lord himself strokes Valli's feet (பதத்துணை வருடி). The feet that make the siddhis easy suggest the siddhis are a by-product, not the goal.

reading: The poet calls himself the foolish wretch who rolls embracing women with knitted brows, sweating and thrilled, caught in their eyes, the evil base man who has lost the guru's word and abandoned the way of release, and asks whether Murugan will not think to let him praise the victorious lotus feet. The praise names the vel that ended the false race of demons, the chest joined to Valli, and the beautiful lord (சொக்கப் பெருமாள்) on the pure Thani hill where drums sound daily.
nuance: குருமொழி அற்று: what the poet has lost is the teacher's word, so desire is cast as a failure of instruction. The question turns to the Lord: கருதாதோ, will you not think of it, rather than asking what the poet should do.

tamil: பூசலிட் டுச்ச ரத்தை நேர்கழித் துப்பெ ருத்த
போலமுட் டிக்கு ழைக்கு ளோடிவெட் டித்தொ ளைத்து
ஆசைவைத் துக்க லக்க மோகமுற் றுத்து யர்க்கு
ஆரணத் துக்க ணத்து னாண்மலர்ப் பொற்ப தத்தை
வாசமுற் றுத்த ழைத்த தாளிணைப் பத்த ரத்த
வாழ்வுறப் புக்கி ரத்ன ரேகையொக் கச்சி றக்கு
வீசுமுத் துத்தெ றிக்க வோலைபுக் குற்றி ருக்கும்
வேலெடுத் துக்க ரத்தி னீலவெற் பிற்ற ழைத்த
reading: The poet speaks of women whose eyes, like a sharpened sword, rush to the ears, cut and pierce and steal pleasure, and asks that he not perish exhausted in desire, confusion and sorrow over them, but be granted to praise the fresh-flowered golden feet of the Vedas and be happy. The praise names Murugan who comes on the gem-necked peacock so that the devotees of his fragrant feet do not perish in the prison of women's eyes, the husband of the golden hunter girl, and the lord at the blue hill.
nuance: The whole song is about the eyes: in the plea they are a sword that cuts to the ears, in the praise a prison (மாதர் கண் சிறை) from which the Lord comes to free his devotees. சொற்கருத்தர் at the close may mean the lord of those who hold his word in mind.

reading: The poet asks not to whirl in the sea of desire for the breasts of scheming women, in the unending sea of the womb, or in the sea of the many arts, but to be given the raft of Murugan's kadamba-garlanded, anklet-bright feet. The praise shows Brahma imprisoned, the fourteen worlds living, the seven seas and seven mountains shaken, and the vel taken up in war on the proud peacock, at Thiruttani of wisdom and the three Tamils.
nuance: Three seas, of desire (ப்ரியக்கடல்), birth (கருக்கடல்) and learning (கலைக்கடல்), and one raft, the feet (கழற்புணை). Learning is placed beside desire and birth as something to drown in.

title: திருத்தணிகை
theme: Songs at Thiruthanigai (திருத்தணிகை, 4 of 5): love-laments for a girl wasting with longing for Murugan, the poet's confessions of infatuation with women and courtesans, of book-babble and begging praise of patrons, and a death song that lets go of wife, children and goods before the buffalo comes; the praise turns on Valli, Vishnu as uncle, Parvati, Murugan as Siva's teacher and as Sambandar, and the hill of Thanigai.
structure_note: Four akam laments in another voice for a lovesick girl (285, 286, 294, 297); confessions of women and lovemaking (287, 289 to 291, 293, 295, 296, 299), with courtesans named by money in 287 and 299; 288 confesses book-learning without devotion, 292 begging praise of patrons, and 298 is a death song. 291 and 292 give most of their praise to Parvati.
source_issues: Song 289: one corrupt character in வன்பில஧முகன் (line 10); the intended word is unclear.
Song 297: one corrupt character in லதனு஡டே (line 12), probably லதனூடே; also the unflagged garble மலாணனும் (line 15), perhaps மலரயனும்.
Song 299: unflagged garble மிக்முள (line 4), probably மிகமூள ('flares up').
Song 287 ends with வேளே rather than பெருமாளே; the shrine is named only in தணிக்குமரேசா.

reading: In the voice of one who watches over a girl, the singer says that with her pearl strings scorched and buried in the dust on her breasts, and Kama of the fish banner fierce against her, she has melted and lost all power to act; she asks that, without her chastity perishing, the dear girl be given back her senses so that she may sleep on her bed. The praise names Murugan who gives the gods of the kalpaka city their rights, who told the meaning of the Veda to the god of golden Kailasa, and whose single long vel destroyed the asura armies, at Thanigai of white conches and pearl-strewn fields.
nuance: This is akam poetry for a girl in love with the god, not the poet's own confession. கற்பழியாதே, that her chastity not perish, sets the girl's steadfastness against the love that is wasting her. The praise repeats Murugan the teacher of Siva: சுடர்பொற் கயிலைக் கடவுட்கு இசையச் சுருதிப் பொருளைப் பகர்வோனே. The opening lines (தெரிவைக் கரிவைப் பரவைக் குருகி) are hard to divide.

reading: Again for a lovesick girl, the singer tells how Kama's new lotus arrow, the south wind that makes her breasts pour fire, the women in the street who quarrel angrily over her, and the rising moon have left her helpless, sleepless and afraid on her bed, and asks Murugan to give her his kuravam garland. The praise names him easy of reach for the hill folk who sow millet, the Kumaresa who took up the vel and gave the gods their realm, and the one who went to the city of the gods' tree and embraced its Lady, at Thanigai of the red lilies.
nuance: உன் குரவைத் தரவேணும்: the girl asks for the god's garland, a classical token of the lover. தெருவில் பெண்கள் மிகக் கறுவிச் சண்டையிட is the town's gossip (அலர்) at its harshest, women in the street quarrelling over her. The திரு embraced in the city of the tree is probably Devayanai, Indra's daughter.

reading: The poet speaks of women who sway breasts like golden pots, babble bird-call arts so that the money in a man's hand passes to them, wear the pottu on the forehead and loosen the cloth about their small waists, and calls them base and worthless; he asks that the mind caught in the net of their eyes be made to cease. The praise names Murugan of Thanigai, Kumaresa gracious to Siva who wears crane feathers and datura, to the sound of drums, and the lord who rests his heart on the breasts of the hunter girl whose speech is like sugar and the three fruits, and who smashed the heads of the rakshasas.
nuance: கைப்பொருள் புக்கிடவே தான் புட்குரல் விச்சை பிதற்றும்: their sweet talk, likened to the cries of birds, is a skill for getting the money out of a man's hand. அக்கண் வலைக்குள் அகப்படு புத்தி: the eyes are a net. The song ends with வேளே, not பெருமாளே.

tamil: பொற்ப தத்தி னைத்து தித்து நற்ப தத்தி லுற்ற பத்தர்
புத்த கப்பி தற்றை விட்டு வித்த கத்து னைத்து திக்க
முற்ப டத்த லத்து தித்து பிற்ப டைத்த கிர்த்ய முற்றி
முட்ட விக்க டைப்பி றப்பி னுட்கி டப்ப தைத்த விர்த்து
வெற்ப ளித்த தற்ப ரைக்கி டப்பு றத்தை யுற்ற ளித்த
வித்தை தத்வ முத்த மிழ்ச்சொ லத்த சத்தம் வித்த ரிக்கு
கற்ப கப்பு னக்கு றத்தி கச்ச டர்த்த சித்ர முற்ற
கைத்த ரக்கர் கொத்து கச்சி னத்து வஜ்ர னுக்க மைத்த
reading: The poet confesses that he has not learned to melt in praise of devotees who praise the golden feet, has not left the babble of books to praise Murugan with skill and an untroubled mind, and wanders always, born and acting out deeds whose seed was sown before; he asks whether a day will come when Murugan ends his lying in this base birth and gives him a little release. The praise names Murugan the peacock hero, son of the wise one who gave his left side to the daughter of the mountain, who dwells on Thanigai hill where knowledge, tattva and the three Tamils in word, meaning and sound are unfolded, and who embraces the hunter girl.
nuance: புத்தகப் பிதற்றை விட்டு: book-learning is the babble that stands in the way of praise, a confession of the learned rather than of the lustful. முத்தி சற்று எனக்கு அளிப்பது: he asks only for 'a little' release. The last lines of praise (வஜ்ரனுக்கு அமைத்த கைத்தொழுத்து அறித்துவிட்ட) seem to tell of Indra's hand, but the allusion is unclear.

reading: The poet says he befriends the delusion of women with fragrant hair, fruit-red mouths and foreheads like the half moon, without seeking the skill to sing Murugan's flower feet, and calls himself proud, without a shred of generosity, a miser, one who never comes to the shrine to bow; he asks to be given the company of those dear to Murugan. The praise names Vishnu, envoy for the king of the Kuru line, the dwarf, the lover of butter with Lakshmi on his chest and lord of the three gunas, as his uncle, and Murugan at Thanigai, life of the sea-girt earth.
nuance: The plea is for a place in the assembly of devotees (இனியார் தம் சபை), not for the feet alone. Among the self-reproaches, the miser who gives nothing (உதாரம் துணுக்கிலி லோபன்) stands out. One word (வன்பில஧முகன்) is corrupt.

reading: The poet describes women with mountain breasts, carp eyes, moon faces, peacock gait and cuckoo speech who melt the heart and loosen their clothes on the bed, and calls himself dross and a fool drooping in an incurable sickness of union; he asks whether a day will come when Murugan sets him in the state of refuge. The praise names the vel that pierced the Krauncha, the Kumara who joined the hunters' little girl, the gracious one who removed the troubles of the gods who took refuge, at Thanigai hill of groves.
nuance: கலவியில் துவள் பிணி தீரா: union itself is an incurable disease. கசடனைக் குண அசடனை: dross, and a fool in character, the stock self-abuse.

reading: The poet heaps names on women who gloss their faces, deceive, frighten with their eyes, steal and beguile in speech, and calls himself the witless, pathless servant who stared and was deluded and took the worm-filled body for a thing of worth; he asks that the six-faced Saravana appear with his peacock and vel, and that, singing poems in padigams night and day, he be given the one thing that comes to erase what Brahma wrote. Most of the praise is for Parvati, who dwells in the side of Siva who laughed and burned the triple cities, the fisher girl, the daughter of the Himalaya, Abhirami, Gauri, the one who raises dharma and gives Tamil, whose little son Murugan dances on the peacock at Thanigai.
nuance: விதித்தன் எழுத்தினை: Brahma's writing on the forehead, fate, which the 'one thing' (ஒருபொருள்) is asked to erase. புழுக் குடலைப் பொருளென மிக எணி: the confession is of valuing a worm-filled body. The long list of Parvati's names (வலைமகள், அபிராமி, பகவதி, கவுரி, அறத்தை வளர்த்திடு பரசிவை) is the heart of the praise; several of its compounds are hard to divide.

reading: The poet confesses that he has sung praises of poor men, likening them to the cloud, the sun, Kama, the bountiful son, Kubera, the kalpaka tree, Vishnu who saved the elephant in the crocodile pool, the six-faced Murugan himself, Arjuna and Meru, and walking from door to door; he asks that this begging end, that he reach the two feet, and that devotees come into austerity. The praise names Parvati of the Himalaya who with the mountain as bow burned the cities at Athigai in an instant, and Siva of the old Tamil who dances beyond Vishnu and Brahma, whose wealth Murugan is, and a battle in which the asuras' crowns were crushed, at Thanigai.
nuance: The list of comparisons is the patron-poem itself, quoted to be renounced; it even includes comparing the patron to Murugan (முகமும் அறுமுகம் உடையவன் இவன்), the god the poet should have praised. இரவு தவிர: the plea names begging. Several comparisons (முதிய கனன், சயில பகலவர்) are uncertain.

reading: The poet speaks of women with bound hair, refined speech and bright eyes, whose cloth sways over their breasts and whose waists are thin, and asks that, infatuated, he not wander daily on earth with those he embraced in bed, but that Murugan give him the paired lotus feet whenever he thinks of him on the stout peacock. The praise names Raghu-Rama, whose arrow felled the ten-headed one's crowned heads, and Vishnu who measured the world in a step, as his uncle, at Thanigai of fish-filled tanks and bending plantains.
nuance: நினைத்த பொழுது உன பதத்து மலரிணை அருள்வாயே: the feet are asked for at whatever moment he thinks of the Lord, a simple and complete plea.

reading: For a lovesick girl, the singer says that through the flowers shot by Kama with his sugarcane bow and the moon that rises from the sea scattering pearls, this golden creeper is wasting, and asks Murugan to come today to Thanigai, famed in every direction, so that she does not droop. The praise names the bright vel that pierced the northern mountain, the jewelled chest that melted embracing the hunter girl, and the feet kept in the heart of Siva who wears datura and the river, and the lord who cut down the one who opposed him in the sea.
nuance: இற்றைத் தினத்தில் வரவேணும்: the plea is that the god come today, as a lover is begged to come. The line எத்தத்தையர்க்கும் இதம் மிக்குப் பெருக்க is unclear.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking on the bridal bed, breasts thrilling, bangles chiming, hair loosened, speech faltering, eyes closing, faces sweating, clothes slipping and bodies made one as hearts melt, and asks whether he will gain Murugan's love so that the care of being tossed on the shoreless waves of union's pleasure ends. The praise names the vel that fought when the sea burned and the gods cried 'refuge', Siva who wears the moon, the river, thumbai, arugu and konrai in his matted hair as father, and Murugan at Thanigai hill where the five-headed serpent worships.
nuance: கலவி கரை அழி இன்ப அலை: the pleasure of union is a sea without shore, and what he asks for against it is love (நினது அன்பு), not escape. ஐந்து தலை அரவு தொழுகின்ற தணிமலை: a serpent's worship at Thanigai, probably the local legend of Vasuki.

reading: The poet gives a long and elaborate scene of lovemaking with women like lotus-peacocks on a bed sprinkled with agil, musk and rose water, according to the law of love, and asks whether, when strength, form and beauty have rotted in that pride, his hair has greyed and his body ripened and fallen, Murugan will not think of him and let him enter and stay in the one supreme light. The praise is a battle sung in drum syllables, at which the ancient Bhairavi's heart trembled in wonder, and Murugan dancing on the peacock at Thanigai.
nuance: உடல் ஒக்கப் பழுத்து விழும் அளவில்: the hour of death is pictured as fruit ripening and falling, and the goal as entering a light (பரம ஒளியில் புக்கிருக்க), not as reaching the feet. The praise is almost all rhythm syllables.

reading: For a lovesick girl, the singer says that by the waves beating on the sea and by Kama, firm in deceit, loosing his five arrows, this one creeper, soft as cotton and like a peacock, has her golden body marred and her heart on fire, and asks Murugan whether he will not think of her loneliness that is wasting her. The praise is a picture of Thanigai, its coconut and plantain groves where bees hum and peacocks dance, its springs full of blue lilies, where Murugan stands.
nuance: பொன்றும் தனிமையை நினையாயோ: the girl's loneliness, the pain of separation, is what she asks the god to think of. The praise is almost all landscape. The closing lines are garbled (லதனு஡டே, மலாணனும்) and their sense is uncertain.

reading: The poet asks that, before the fools who drive the goring buffalo bind him and call him away, his wife, his babbling children at the breast, his old mother, his town and land, the garden he kept, his house, gold, earned wealth and all the rest become alien to his mind, and that he be given the two feet that make one free so that he may draw near release. The praise names Murugan the bridegroom of the daughter of the four-tusked white elephant, the one who joined the hunter girl at Thanigai, whose vel shook the eight elephants and eight mountains of the directions, hard to reach for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise in pure Tamil verse.
nuance: The list of what must become alien (மனைச்சி, குதலை மக்கள், தாய்க் கிழவி, பதி, நாடு, தோட்டம், மனை, அத்தம்) is the whole household, given in order of nearness; the plea is detachment before death rather than rescue at death. The bride of the elephant (இபத்தின் பிடி) is Devayanai, raised by Airavata. One word (அசுருதிக்கு) is unclear.

reading: The poet confesses that, infatuated with women whose glances bewitch young men, he lost his wits, gave them all his money and became destitute with hunger burning in his belly, befriending one, quarrelling with another, chasing a third, and calls himself a wretched sinner; he asks for the noble character to sing Murugan's feet. The praise names Murugan who delights when the garland of Tamil spoken by Arunagirinathan is recited, the poet whose Tamil sent the Jains to the stake and brought back a woman's husband, and the vel that destroyed Sura's clan, at Thanigai with its spring of the one blue lily.
nuance: விரித்து அருணகிரிநாதன் உரைத்த தமிழ்: the poet names himself, and his songs as a garland Murugan enjoys. வெடித்த அமணர் கழுவேற ஒருத்தி கணவனும் மீள: Murugan is the Tamil poet who impaled the Jains and revived a woman's husband, i.e. Sambandar. The confession runs from infatuation to money to hunger, a sequence of ruin.

title: திருத்தணிகை
theme: Last songs at Thiruthanigai (திருத்தணிகை, 5 of 5): two confessions of infatuation with women, one asking for Murugan's feet before knowledge and life are lost, the other for the art of singing his praise instead of falling into womb after womb; the praise dwells on the town of Thanigai, whose towers clear the deeds of those who worship from afar and where those who chant Thiruppugazh gather.
source_issues: Song 301: unflagged garble புநக்முள (line 12), perhaps புகைமூள ('smoke rising'); the same க்மு appears in song 299 (மிக்முள) where மூ is likely meant.

reading: The poet describes the women on the street with bound breasts, long dark hair, speech like a young cuckoo, carp eyes and swinging earrings, seducers skilled in enchantment, and asks that, before he, lacking true knowledge and learning, fades in infatuation, loses his understanding and dies, Murugan grant him the feet, bright as a crore of suns, that the wise praise, coming on the peacock with the rooster banner. The praise names the vel that cut down Sura's warriors for the ghosts to drink their blood, and Thanigai with its areca, plantain and paddy, its groves on the slopes, its towers and halls whose golden dust scatters the deeds of those who worship from afar, and its festooned streets circled by the chariot.
nuance: தூரத் தொழுவார் வினை சிந்திடு ... கோபுர மண்டபம்: the shrine's towers remove the deeds even of those who bow from a distance, a claim for the place itself. மோகன விஞ்சையர்: the women are 'enchanters', practisers of a spell.

reading: The poet speaks of women whose breasts are kin to evil deeds and whose eyes rival Kama's arrows, and asks that, after going among them and sinking in sorrow, he not fall face down into every womb-pit where heavy care and birth sink, but be given the art of chanting the praise of the feet that learned poets set to music. The praise names Murugan who went to the millet field and embraced Valli of the bow-bearing hunters, whose vel split the mountain, dried the sea and opened Sura's chest, at Thanigai where those who are minded to chant Thiruppugazh gather.
nuance: கருக்குழி தோறும் கவிழாதே: each birth is a fall headlong into a womb-pit. திருப்புகழ் ஓதும் கருத்தினர் சேரும் திருத்தணி: the song names the book's own title as the chant of Thanigai's devotees. The battle line has an unflagged garble (புநக்முள).

title: குன்றுதோறாடல்
theme: Songs of Kundruthoradal (குன்றுதோறாடல், 'dancing on every hill'), Murugan of all the hills: a lovesick plea in the poet's own voice and one for a girl wasting with longing, a short prayer for refuge, a plea for the samadhi beyond yogis and sages, and a renunciation of praising miserly patrons for one word from Murugan's mouth; the praise names Murugan as the poet of Sambandar's victory over the Jains and as the one who settled the meaning of Pandya Tamil.
structure_note: 302 and 304 are love songs to Murugan (the first in the poet's own voice, the second for a girl); 303 is a short prayer; 305 sets women against yogic samadhi and is sung to the hill of Thirisiramalai; 306 renounces patron-praise. 302 names Thanigai and 305 Thirisiramalai, both gathered here under the heading of all hills.
source_issues: Songs 302 and 305 name shrines (Thiruthanigai, Thirisiramalai) other than the heading குன்றுதோறாடல், which may be a collective heading for the hill shrines.

reading: The poet asks that he not perish under the arrows of Kama's victorious cane bow, the moon spreading fiery light over the open street, the many parrot-tongued women skilled in slander, and the sounding wheel, but that Murugan, giving him devotion and granting release, come on the green peacock. The praise names the hero whose anklets are held in the heart of the dancer whose forehead eye burned, the chest that daily embraces the hunter girl, Murugan who always stands at Thiruthanigai, and the lord who freed the gods from the asuras' prison.
nuance: The poet borrows the lovesick girl's afflictions (Kama's arrows, the moon, the women's slander) for his own voice, and asks for பத்தி and முத்தி as the lover's cure. இசைபட்ட திகிரி is unclear; it may be the sounding conch or the moon's wheel. The shrine named is Thanigai, though the heading is Kundruthoradal.

reading: A short song: the poet asks when he will see the state in which he, bowing at Murugan's ringing anklets, takes refuge in him, and asks Murugan to dwell in his heart with compassion so that his troubles and doubts dissolve. The praise names him the son of Uma, who is part of the Lord who dances with none to rival him, and the one who plays in every town and dwells on many hills.
nuance: இடர் சங்கைகள் கலங்க: doubts as well as troubles are what grace should scatter. பலகுன்றிலும் அமர்ந்த: the song's close names the heading's sense, Murugan on every hill.

reading: Mostly praise: Murugan circled the seven worlds on his peacock in an instant, threw the vel for the gods, and spoke the one meaning of the Pandyas' Tamil so that it was honoured; within it the singer asks whether it is fitting that the girl who bows to his flower feet should droop with pallor and infatuation. The praise goes on to the old hill where the hunter girl pours out gems, pearls and coral from the stream, Murugan the guru who dwells in the hearts of those immersed in grace, and the lord of many hills.
nuance: வழுதியர் தமிழின் ஒருபொருள் அதனை வழிபட மொழியும்: Murugan declares the one meaning of the Pandyas' Tamil, perhaps the story of his judging the true commentary at the Madurai assembly, though the text names no more than this. The love plea is a single line set in the middle of the praise.

reading: The poet speaks of deceitful flirting women for whom men on earth write the madal, and asks whether he, a weak dog of a servant, should wilt and be deluded by their hair, breasts, waist, gait, speech and eyes; he asks Murugan to come and give him the samadhi and dissolution of mind, the secret bindu and nada reached by the swift filling of the breath, which true jnanis and silent sages cannot approach and which cannot be spoken, reached or thought. The praise names Murugan the hero on Thirisiramalai by the cool Kaveri from Kudagu, lord of the kurinji hunters, younger brother of the first Vinayaka, lord of the gods, guru of Gauri's lord, the master who dwells on all hills.
nuance: The plea is in the language of yoga: பவன பூரகம் (filling the breath), விந்து நாதம், சமாதி, மனோலயம். Yet the song says even jnanis and munis cannot reach it and asks it as a gift. மடல் எழுதும்: the women are those for whom men write the madal, the desperate lover's public plea. The praise is a litany of நாயக.

tamil: வஞ்சக லோப மூடர் தம்பொரு ளூர்கள் தேடி
வண்புகழ் பாரி காரி யென்றிசை வாது கூறி
செஞ்சர ணாத கீத கிண்கிணி நீப மாலை
செந்தமிழ் நாளு மோதி உய்ந்திட ஞான மூறு
பஞ்சவ னீடு கூனு மொன்றிடு தாப மோடு
பண்பறு பீலி யோடு வெங்கழு வேற வோது
குஞ்சரம் யாளி மேவு பைம்புன மீது லாவு
கும்பிட நாடி வாழ்வு தந்தவ ரோடு வீறு
reading: The poet asks that he not perish in vain like the court bards who seek out the wealth and towns of deceitful, miserly fools, praising them in manjari, kovai, thoothu and many verse forms and arguing they are as generous as Pari and Kari, but that, chanting daily in Tamil Murugan's feet, anklets, kadamba garland, vel, peacock and six faces, he be given one word from the red mouth where wisdom springs. The praise names Murugan the learned one who gave the holy ash of wisdom that cured the Pandya's hunch and fever and sent the mute Jains to the stake with their peacock feathers, and the lord of Kundruthoradal whom the hill tribes worship with frenzied dance.
nuance: பாரி காரி என்று இசை வாது கூறி: the poet mocks the bard's stock claim that a miser is Pari or Kari, the legendary patrons. ஓர் சொல் அருள்வாயே: he asks for a single word, the guru's teaching. The praise identifies Murugan with Sambandar at Madurai: the Pandya's hunch (கூன்) and fever (தாபம்) cured by the ash, and the Jains (சமண்) impaled.

title: ஆறு திருப்பதி
theme: A song of the six shrines (ஆறு திருப்பதி): the poet confesses his bondage to courtesans who sell their arts and ruin young men's families, and asks for Murugan's feet; the praise names him the guru, Siva's son, and the lord abiding in all six shrines.
source_issues: Song 307: line 8 reads நி முடனை, with a letter lost; probably நிர்மூடனை ('utter fool').
Chapter 27 is a single song under the heading ஆறு திருப்பதி.

reading: The poet speaks of courtesans who cast nets with eyes like the wave-tossed sea, deceitful great sinners full of tricks, who flirt with fools, sell their arts for a price and ruin the families of young men, and calls himself the cheat and utter fool who falls on their breasts; he asks to be granted now the paired feet. The praise names Murugan son of Pasupati who bears the river, the six-faced form of grace and guru, the hero whose vel ruined the asuras and gave the gods back their city, the Sivaguru whom Brahma did not know, whom devotees on earth hold in mind, and the lord on the peacock abiding in the six shrines that are the source of all.
nuance: விலைமாதர்கள் ... இளைஞர்கள் குடிகேடிகள்: the courtesans sell and ruin households, so the charge is money and family, not desire alone. தலை அயன் அறியா ஒரு சிவகுருபரன்: Murugan as the teacher whom Brahma did not know recalls the Om story without naming it. சகலமும் முதலாகிய அறுபதி: the six shrines are themselves the first of all things.

title: காஞ்சீபுரம்
theme: First songs at Kanchipuram (காஞ்சீபுரம், 1 of 3): in dense rhythms the poet asks to stand beyond the tattvas and the quarrels of the sects, confesses flattering patrons, the prison of the body, old age and his own worthlessness, and asks for the feet and a poet's speech; the praise dwells unusually long on the Goddess of Kanchi, who did penance by the Kampa and keeps the thirty-two charities, and on Siva and Vishnu worshipping Murugan at Kachi.
structure_note: A short opening song (308) that ends at the six shrines rather than Kachi; then songs in a heavy four-line rhythm (309 to 320) whose second halves often praise the Goddess (313 to 315, 317, 318) or the myths of Siva and Vishnu (309, 310, 312, 316, 319); two songs in another metre (321, 322) share the closing line on the lord of Thirukkottam.
source_issues: Song 308 is under the Kanchipuram heading but ends at the six shrines (ஆறு திருப்பதியில் வளர் பெருமாளே) and does not name Kachi.
Song 318: one corrupt character, in கம்பையினு஡டே (line 268), probably கம்பையினூடே.
Song 321: last line has இநதிரர், a typing slip for இந்திரர் (322 has the correct form).

reading: A short song: the poet asks that base birth not come near him, that he become Murugan's servant, and that he be given the grace of jnana so that his deeds end, with a compassion that takes away his shame. The praise names Murugan who excels in gift and penance, the companion of an excellent consort, the young one who gave the sacred padhigams, and the lord who grows in the six holy shrines.
nuance: ஆன திருப்பதிகம் அருள் இளையோனே: 'the young one who gave the holy padhigams' identifies Murugan with Sambandar, the child poet of the Thevaram padhigams. சாரதி உத்தமி துணைவ is unclear: சாரதி may name the Goddess or a consort, and the line may be divided otherwise. நாணம் அகற்றிய கருணை could also be the compassion that ended Valli's shyness.

reading: The poet praises Murugan as the one who, for the parrot of the hunters' forest, melted, went and bowed at her feet and swooned in infatuation, and the one who ends the sorrow of pure devotees, and asks that, worshipping him so with desire quenched and singing his fame, he be looked on and made to stand beyond the end where the Vedas' rows of devotion, the turiya state and all the tattvas vanish. The praise tells of Daksha's sacrifice, where the god of the discus and Brahma were struck in fear, the sun's teeth knocked out, the bird's wings cut and the guardians' army scattered, after Daksha's daughter, keeping her vow, entered the fire; Siva, who raged that day, worships Murugan at Kachi.
nuance: The plea reverses the usual roles: the first half gives Murugan's own infatuation (மயற்கொண்டு அயர்பவன்) for Valli, and asks for the poet's desire to be quenched (இச்சை தணித்து). துரியமும் தப்பித் தத்வம் அனைத்தும் தொலையும் அந்தத்துக்கு அப்புறம்: the goal is beyond turiya and the tattvas, as in 203. The sacrifice is named by its details: Daksha (தக்கன்), his daughter in the fire, the sun's teeth, the wings cut off the bird (குயில், here perhaps Agni in bird form).

reading: The poet confesses that, though he learned the poetry that worships Murugan of the golden arms and the red vel that reduced the mango in the sea to dust, he went to the people of the world, fawned on them, called a man a kalpaka tree for his giving, the sinless one, a Kumanan who gives whatever is wished, and, blind with begging, stole all the words of meaning and strung them to suit; he asks whether this confusion will not clear. The praise names Rama, who for Janaka's daughter of matchless chastity burned the whole kin of Lanka and cut the ten crowned heads with a single arrow, and names the sun, Indra, Sukra, the moon, the guardians, Agastya, Brahma, Vasishtha, the Vedas, the pure devotees whose action has ceased, and Siva himself as worshipping Murugan at Kachi.
nuance: The confession is the poet's trade again: the patron is flattered as the wishing tree and as குமணன், the Sangam chieftain famed for giving. இரவான குருடு, 'the blindness that is begging', and சத்தம் அனைத்தும் திருடி, stealing every word, make the flattery a theft from the poetry owed to the Lord. The long list of worshippers at Kachi ends with those whose action has ceased (செயலொழிந்து).

reading: The poet calls the body a stinking frame of bones and blood bound with nerves, a prison of karmic bonds, a raft whirling in the dark-waved sea of birth's sorrow, a hollow dwelling of the instruments that carries the filth of death and stumbles in all eight directions, and asks to escape the crowd of sects who learn the world and shout themselves weary and to reach the quality of staying within, at one. The praise names Murugan whom the three-eyed Goddess, wishing tree of chastity, delights in, the guru whose feet Siva worships, he who gives siddhi to devotees reciting the syllables daily, and the one whose heart melts for Valli's hands, waist, hair, lips and breasts, worshipped by the gods at Kachi.
nuance: The body images pile up as in 30: frame (சட்டம்), prison (சிறை), raft in the sea of birth (செனன ... துக்கக்கடல் ... தெப்பம்), hollow house (பொக்கப் புக்கில்). The remedy is not only escape from the body but from the sects that 'learn and shout and tire' (கற்றுக் கத்தி இளைக்கும் சமய சங்கம்). எட்டக்கரம் may be eight syllables or a misdivision; it is left unexplained.

reading: The poet strings Murugan's names, the one who threw the sakti at the golden Krauncha, knocked Brahma on the head and fettered his hands, the god whom Siva loves, the one whose hand Ganesa held, the patron who spoke his desire to the young parrot of the millet field, and asks whether, having learned these names, his clinging will go and he will gain the one meaning hidden in every thing. The praise tells of Ravana, who fought the eight elephants of the quarters and pulled up golden Kailasa by its roots, then had his twenty arms crushed under one toe, and of Siva who afterwards gave him a sword; Murugan stands at Kachi, having that god and his consort, Kailasa and the southern hill of the true guru.
nuance: பசை ஒழிந்து ... பொருள் தொறும் பொத்தப்பட்டது ஒர் அத்தம்: the plea is for the meaning enclosed in every object once attachment has gone, a pervasion read through the names. Brahma knocked and fettered (குட்டிக் கைத்தளையிட்டு) is the Om story, though Om is not named here. தெற்குச் சற்குரு வெற்பு, the southern hill of the true guru, is Swamimalai.

reading: The poet confesses that he has no great poetry of devotion to worship Murugan as the child of Ganga who freed the imprisoned gods, that his mind was never purified, that he learned many tattvas only to fall into argument, and that he has not gained the high vow by which those who reach the supreme state stand rapt and free of all attachment; he asks how else his sorrow can go. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess, Siva's consort with the trident and cane bow, Bhadra, the great thing unknown to anyone, the lotus-handed creeper, whose child Murugan is, and of the sakti that split the mountain touching Brahma's egg, at Kachi.
nuance: பரவசம் பற்றிப் பற்று அற நிற்கும் பரவ்ரதம்: the devotee's rapture is what frees from attachment, not learning; தத்வம் பலவையும் கற்றுத் தர்க்க ம(த)த்துவம் sets learned argument against it. Much of the litany of the Goddess is hard to divide.

reading: The poet asks to see the meaning the devotees praise as Murugan, the common ground that holds all the ninety-six tattvas yet stands free of them, the truth hard to know for the six sects who argue and quarrel in anger every day, and, having seen it, to sing his deeds and teach it in every direction; he asks for the small anklets and golden lotus feet. The praise lists Ganesa's offerings, sesame, puffed rice, appam, fruit, roots, cane, sugar, gram and pittu, names him the elephant-faced brother, and names their mother Gauri, who bore the old universe and rescues worshippers from the waves of birth, at the side of the naked Siva, at Kachi.
nuance: எண்பத்தெட்டு எட்டு இயல் தத்வம்: eighty-eight and eight, the ninety-six tattvas of the Saiva count. சகலமும் பற்றிப் பற்று அற நிற்கும் பொது: the Lord holds all and clings to none, the formula used again in 320; பொது, 'the common', makes him what all the quarrelling sects share. The plea ends in teaching (திசைதொறும் கற்பிக்கை), a rare missionary note.

reading: The poet names Murugan Saravana of the fierce sakti, the thief who hides in the mind, the lord of the cock, the lord of the serpent hill, of Palani, of Kachi and of Vanji, and asks whether, singing him so in Tamil with flawless love, forbearance growing, pride left, his own qualities ended and having reached the quality that has no other, free of all attachment, he will not get even a little grace to attain the guru's feet where pure devotees abide. The praise is of the Goddess, worn at Siva's side with his crescent, karandai, serpent, datura, skull and konrai, Tripura, Durga, Sakti, the pure green-hued woman, whose son gives siddhi to his servants.
nuance: சித்தத்துக்குள் ஒளிக்கும் கரவடன், 'the thief who hides in the mind', is a bold epithet for the indwelling Lord. குணம் அடங்கக் கெட்டு குணம் அற்று ஒன்று இலதான குணம் அடைந்து: the goal is a quality beyond the qualities. குருபதம் is both the guru's feet and the guru's state.

reading: The poet asks for the ripeness to reach the state attained when the mind's action ceases, through a love that opens as he learns of Murugan's hills, his vel that split the peak and his arms, and through the clear knowledge that sees the world, where delusion grows like an anthill, as a bubble; he names Murugan the god who told his father what he lacked, who cuts the fear of devotees, at Kachi. The praise tells of Vishnu, the dwarf who became greater than all while Sukra trembled, and the man-lion who tore out the entrails of Hiranya when the little boy Prahlada spoke the truth, the Murari who sleeps on the serpent with the discus, father of the world, whom Murugan grants siddhi.
nuance: ப்ரபஞ்சத்தைப் புற்புதம் ஒக்கும்படி நாடும் அறிவு: the world seen as a bubble. பக்வம், ripeness, is the soul's readiness for grace. அத்தற்கு அற்றது செப்பும் கடவுள, 'the god who told his father what he lacked', points to the teaching of Siva. The Vamana and Narasimha stories are named by their details (குறியவன், சுக்ரன், சிறுபாலன் குதலை, கனகன்). The last lines on who receives siddhi are unclear.

reading: The poet asks whether, thinking of the lotus of the sakti that fought, while Vishnu and Brahma showered flowers, the gods worshipped and a crore of ghosts danced to the drums on the battlefield where the Asuras were pierced, and praising Saravana the beautiful one of Kachi, he will reach the boon of service in his mind. The praise is a long picture of the Goddess's body, her sandal-dressed breasts, slender waist, a voice holding the notes kaikkilai, tuttam and kural, the navel that bore the worlds, cloud-dark hair, tilak and pearl-hung neck, and her compassion that gives siddhi to devotees: Murugan is the son of Gauri Amba and lord of all.
nuance: The first half is almost all battle, sung in drum syllables, with the plea folded into its last line (சித்தத்துக்கு வரத் தொண்டு அடைவேனோ). The Goddess's voice is described with the names of the Tamil musical notes (கைக்கிளை, துத்தம், குரல்).

reading: Not a plea but thanks: the poet calls himself one who never spoke even in dream of Murugan's mango of Kachi, the serpent hill, Palani, the southern hill of the true guru, Kathirai and Thiruchendur, who stole all that suits this body and whirled in fancies, who never melted and worshipped him as the jewel in Amba's hand, the new pearl of old Ganga and the treasure of the destitute, and asks what words could compare with the forbearance by which Murugan bore his faults and placed him among devotees. The praise names the Goddess of southern Kachi, sweeter than candy, mother of all worlds, the young woman who did penance in the waters of the Kampa, took the measures of grain and nurtures the thirty-two charities, and Murugan who told the truth to her consort.
nuance: பிழையுடன் பட்டுப் பத்தருள் வைக்கும் பொறை: the forbearance here is the Lord's, who bears with the poet's faults. The Kanchi legend of the Goddess is told by its details: penance in the Kampa (கம்பையினூடே தவமுயன்று), the measure of grain (படி) and the thirty-two charities (அறம் இரண்டு எட்டு எட்டு எட்டு, read as a count). சத்யம் உரைக்கும், telling the truth to Siva, is the teaching of 6 and 12.

reading: The poet pictures himself old: the skin hanging loose on its frame, hair white as a crane, head and body worn, bones and joints slack, the senses changed, walking with a stick and staggering off course, a frail, half-mad old man whose teeth all fall, while others say 'chee chee', his descendants 'chi chi' and his own wife spits 'thu thu'; before that despised birth, he asks to reach the lotus feet with anklets. The praise tells of Siva, who yoked the Veda horses with the reins, mounted the chariot with the sun for its wheel and burned the three cities with one arrow, worshipping Murugan at Kachi, and of the vel that struck Brahma, pierced the mountain and the sea and cut down the Asuras.
nuance: The scorn is given in sounds (செச்செச்செ, சிச்சிச்சி, துத்துத்து) set to the beat, the household's disgust heard rather than described. The poet asks for the feet before old age, not at the hour of death as in 28 or 68.

reading: The poet heaps names on himself: a mind of hatred and fault, without penance, wholly false, without refuge, a sinner standing in the rubbish of kin, without forbearance, empty of any bond to the one who holds all the tattvas and stands free of them, cruel, without the art of learning Murugan's boundless praise, block-witted, base, without a way; he asks whether he will reach Murugan by thinking even in dream of his arms, his vel, Kathirai, the golden hill and the other shrines and all of Kachi. The praise tells of the vel that made the roaring seas cry out, ended Surapadman's clan, eased the gods' distress so that Indra returned to his city, and saw Brahma punished, and of the feet with golden anklets.
nuance: The self-abuse (துரிசாளன், வெற்றன், கட்டைப் புத்தியன், மட்டன்) is a set piece, as in 29. Inside it is the formula of 314, the Lord who holds all and stands free (சகலமும் பற்றிப் பற்று அற நிற்கும் பொருள்): the poet's lack is that he has no bond to him.

reading: Before Death drives out and drags away alone the breath dwelling in this rag of a false body, a great hut that lets out urine and filth, built with limbs to hold all the deeds and given by a father and mother, the poet asks Murugan to come and gladly grant him the power to speak with love, in good and flawless words, of his fragrant red feet. The praise is of the Goddess: Siva who burned the three cities, and she who, frightened by the flooding river, embraced Kampar so that his body was marked, and who gives her feet to those who think of her lotus feet; Murugan is Gauri's son, lord of Indras at Thirukkottam.
nuance: சல மலம் விட்ட ... குடில் and தரவரு பொய்க்குள் கிடந்த கந்தல்: the body is a latrine-hut and a rag given by parents. The Kanchi legend of the Goddess embracing Ekambaresvara (கம்பர்) in the flood is named by its details. திருக்கொட்டம் is the Kamakottam of Kanchi. The battle lines on Sura taking many forms and the peacock are hard to divide.

reading: The poet asks for a birth in which, having sung great poems on the peacock, Murugan's arms, Valli and his red lotus feet with anklets, he will be honoured by many poets as a true poet, a master who knows the tattvas, a virtuous man of good qualities, and gain the golden feet; and whether the world's calling him forbearing and a renunciate who fears the false world will not bring him to the supreme consciousness. The praise is wholly of the Goddess: daughter of the mountain, whose womb bore the world, the Brahmin lady who keeps the thirty-two charities without lack, Sankari, Neeli, the peacock beauty who holds the poison in her throat, Digambari, 'our mother', Ambika, Tryambaki, Gauri: Murugan is lord of Indras at Thirukkottam.
nuance: An unusual plea: for fame as a poet and a name for virtue (புலவன் எனத் ... தலைவன் எனத் ... குண புருஷன் என), joined to release. புதுமை அல(ச்) சிற்பரம் பொருந்துகை may mean 'it is no wonder' or a 'new union with the supreme'. The thirty-two charities (முப்பத்திரண்டு அறம்) are here named outright, as in 318. Shares its closing line with 321.

title: காஞ்சீபுரம்
theme: Songs at Kanchipuram (காஞ்சீபுரம், 2 of 3), nearly all closing on Murugan as the beautiful lord of Kachi (கச்சிச் சொக்கப் பெருமாளே): in tight doubled-consonant rhythms the poet confesses bondage to women, the body of bone and skin, old age, the heirs dividing his goods and the burning of the corpse, and asks for the feet, pure devotees and the gift of Tamil; two songs are love laments for a girl sick for Murugan.
structure_note: Courtesans and women (323, 326, 328, 332, 335, 336); the body, birth and death (324 to 327, 330, 331, 333); short songs (329, 330); and two akam laments in another's voice (334, 337). Many lines are built from doubled consonants (த்த, க்க, ச்ச) for the rhythm, so word division is often uncertain.
source_issues: Song 323: unflagged garbles குலத்தைத்குத் திரத்தை (line 389) and குறத்தத்தைத் கறத்தத்தி (line 390), with stray த்.
Song 325: unflagged garble கொடிக்குக்டக் (line 427), probably கொடிக்குக் (with a stray ட்).
Song 326: பூணர்க்கச்சி (line 449) is probably புணர்க்கச்சி.

reading: The poet asks not to whirl in the confusion of desire for women's coral lips and dark hair, not to wander tending this pot of bone, semen, blood, fat and skin, and not to languish in suffering, but to praise and worship the golden feet with their garland of lotus and kadamba. The praise names the vel that pierced the Krauncha and the golden mountain, the lord of the cock banner, who gave Indra his golden heavenly city, at Kachi, where Siva of the konrai and matted hair has the Goddess of chastity at his side.
nuance: எலுப்பு, சுக்கிலம், அத்தம், தடி, தொக்கு: the body is listed by its parts (bone, semen, blood, fat, skin) and called a pot (கடம்). The third line (சுதத்தத்தச் சதத்தத்தப் பதத்தர்க்கு ...) is too dense to divide with confidence.

reading: Before the kin cry 'a little for me, a little for you' over the wealth and the gold plate, call the body-hut an illusion, lay it on the logs, burn it, bury it, and the poet falls to earth to be born again, he asks for the strength to escape the arrogant, threatening, word-twisting wicked and to sing Murugan's feet. The praise names the one who embraced Valli of the millet field, the vel that struck down the mango so that the serpent's hoods and the sea trembled, the life who gives fruit to devotees free of spreading, shrinking, trembling and bewilderment, and the one who circled the world on the green peacock for the fruit, at Kachi.
nuance: எனக்குச் சற்று உனக்குச் சற்று: the heirs' squabble at the deathbed is quoted, and the same words return in 325 as the poet's own craving. The plea is unusual in asking to escape wicked men (துட்டர்) rather than women. கனிக்குத் திக்கனைத்துச் சுற்றிட is the circling of the world for the fruit, as in 3 and 30.
