tamil: கலச வர்க்கத் தைத்த கர்த்துக் குலையற ...... இளநீரைக்
கரிம ருப்பைப் புக்கொ டித்துத் திறல்மத ...... னபிஷேகம்
னடல்ப டைத்தச் சப்ப டுத்திச் சபதமொ ...... டிருதாளம்
மபிந வச்சித் ரத்த னத்துத் திருடிக ...... ளுறவாமோ
தரிகி டத்தத் தத்த ரிக்கத் தரிகிட ...... எனவோதிச்
தசைகள் பட்சித் துக்க ளித்துக் கழுதொடு ...... கழுகாட
அடிந டித்திட் டிட்டி டித்துப் பொருதிடு ...... மயிலோனே
அருணை யிற்சித் தித்தெ னக்குத் தெளிவருள் ...... பெருமாளே.
reading: The poet heaps conceits on women's breasts, which defeat the lotus bud, the bubble, the golden pot, the tender coconut, the elephant's tusk and the chakravaka bird, and asks whether he should be kin to these thieving women with painted breasts. The praise is a battle in drum syllables with ghouls feasting and the peacock dancing in asura blood, and names Murugan the true guru made manifest on the green steed, who appeared at Arunai and gave the poet clarity.
nuance: திருடிகள், thieves, carries the charge. In the praise, மெய்ப்ரத்யக்ஷ நற்சற்குருபர ... அருணையில் சித்தித்து எனக்குத் தெளிவருள் makes Arunai the place where the guru appeared to the poet himself. The comparisons in the first half are dense and some, such as the burning of Kama's crown, are hard to place.

reading: A song of praise without a plea: it names Ganapati, the elephant-faced one who destroyed the elephant-faced asura and holds gram, sesame, lentils, plantains and many fruits in his belly, and Murugan his younger brother who fought the asuras and their hill with the vel. It names Siva who held the reins and led jackals as horses, who dances everywhere and wears the flayed elephant's hide, and ends with Saravana of the bright vel at Arunai of rich fields and pools.
nuance: நரிமிகுக் கிளைகளைப் பரியெனக் கடிவளக் கையில் பிடித்து எதிர் நடத்திடும் ஈசன்: the jackals turned into horses are the story of Siva acting for Manikkavasagar, a devotee's story in the praise of Murugan's father. The list of foods follows Ganapati's offerings in the opening songs.

reading: The poet piles up what women's eyes do: they widen and speak, work Kama's tricks, rival golden earrings, spread like the sea, glow with poison, meet arrows, wage war on the young, wander in stealth and deceit and defeat the humming bee, and he asks whether he will escape being ruined under women who embrace with bewildering eyes and wring out a man's life. The praise shows Murugan walking, his anklets ringing and his flower feet aching, in a changed form among lions, bears and tigers to the millet field, bowing at the hunter girl's small feet and embracing her, then destroying the asuras and dwelling at Arunai on the south side.
nuance: Each pair of verbs ends -வன (அகல்வன புகல்வன, கடியன கொடியன), a list of what the eyes do that sounds like a list of beasts. The praise reverses it: the god himself goes in disguise and bows at a woman's feet (சிறு பதயுக சததளம் பணிந்து).

reading: A voice laments that a girl, tormented by the distant sea's roar in her ears, by Kama and by the moon, her garment slipping on her bed of flowers, reviled by the townsfolk and the subject of many slanders, should wilt and faint day after day. The praise names Murugan the lord of Sonachala with twelve shining shoulders, whose unfailing vel destroyed Sura, the chest dear to the daughter of the heavenly world, and the master of the gods.
nuance: நாடோர்கள் ஏச ... நானா பவாதம்: gossip and slander are part of the girl's suffering, as in akam poetry. The second line (காலாளும் வேளும் ஆலால நாதர் காலால் நிலாவும் முனிந்து) is hard to divide, and who is speaking is not said.

reading: The poet describes courtesans who dance in the street and charm for love of coin, wasting some days with them until wrinkles come, then the body's ruin: disease, a staff, walking like a monkey, phlegm, lying on a mat, eyes changed, ears deaf, pain and pleasure forgotten, while townsfolk, kin, wife and children crowd round saying 'chi, this curse won't go'; he asks whether he will fade like that. The praise names Siva who burned Kama and the three cities and drank the poison, and Uma, Vishnu's sister and the poet's mother, who bore the great Kumara of wisdom; the vel dances as Sura, Meru, the seas, the mountains and the serpent's hoods are shaken; Murugan dances on the head of the Veda, and Arunachalam is the pillar of light that ran up and touched the sky.
nuance: காசாசைச் செயலாலே: the women's charm is for coin. The kin's verdict (சீசீ சிச்சிசி போகா நற்சனியன்) is the bitter end of the courtesan's life, and the song gives it in their own words. தூணோடிச் சுடர் ஆகாசத்தை அணைந்து: the hill as the column of fire that rose to the sky recalls the Annamalai story of Siva's endless form.

title: திருவருணை
theme: Songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 4 of 6): the poet confesses infatuation with women, the body's birth, decay and corpse, and the hour of Death, and asks for Murugan's feet, for release and for a place among his devotees; one song is a love-lament in a girl's voice and one a chant of the five syllables joined to the name of Arunachala; the praise returns to the hill of fire, the tower, Murugan as Siva's teacher and as the saint who defeated the Jains.
structure_note: Courtesan and love songs (414, 415, 417, 418, 424), with 420 and 427 keeping the feet in mind within the embrace; the course of a life from womb to pyre (416, 423) and the body as carrion (422); Death's coming (426); union with Siva (421); a girl's love-lament (413); praise with a short plea (419); and a mantra song (425).
source_issues: Song 414: one corrupt character in கி஡ணயி (line 6); here ஡ண stands for ரி, so கிரியில் (Sonagiri), not ரீ as in songs 12 and 88.
Song 418: நீடோ டி (line 6) has a stray space inside the vowel sign; read நீடோடி.
Song 421: line 3 reads ஒ ரு பமதாய் with a letter lost; probably ஒரு ரூபமதாய் ('one form').
Song 425: line 3 ends தி முலா after the beat marks, an unflagged fragment that fits neither the mantra rotation nor the following line.
Song 426: line 8 begins with four dots (....) instead of six; harmless.
Song 427: line 16 begins with the unflagged garble திநச்முடுக; the sense (the seven seas turned to dust) survives.

reading: In a girl's voice: in the groves the cruel horn of Kama sounds, the wind presses, his five flower arrows strike her on her bed, and one night seems as long as an age; she asks Murugan, lest her mind be ruined, to come and give her his kadamba garland where the bees roam. The praise names him the guru whom Siva with serpent, crescent, river and gems in his hair thought on, the one with six faces, kura flowers, the peacock, the hunter girl and Lakshmi on his chest, whose vel made Meru, Sura and the sea afraid, standing in the holy street of Arunapuri.
nuance: ஊரும் உலகும் பழைய பேருகம் விளைந்ததென ஓரிரவு: a single night of separation feels like an aeon, the lover's sense of time. The plea for the god's garland is the conventional request of the love-sick girl.

reading: The poet asks Murugan to come on the peacock so that he does not wander without virtue, ruined by women's voices skilled in song and their dark tied hair. The praise names him the warrior whom the deceitful asuras feared, Kumaresa at Sonagiri, the one who spoke a single word into the ear of the First One, and the younger brother of the elephant-faced god.
nuance: ஆதியர் காது ஒருச்சொல் அருள்வோனே: the teaching whispered into Siva's ear, here 'one word' without naming Om.

reading: The poet tells how women show off combed hair, darting eyes and coral mouths, speak sweetly and loosen their garments, and how he, cruel one, spent his wealth, youth, learning and mind on them until the world mocked him as an outcast and his understanding was ruined by the senses; he asks whether Murugan, master of the common stance at Arunai, will not think to keep his servant under his gaze. The praise names him the one who taught Siva the one hard-to-know thing, the young one born as six children in the Saravana pool where the heavenly women nursed him, the vel that made the seas cry out, and the one who guarded the millet and embraced the hunter girl.
nuance: பொருள் இளமை கலை மனமும் ஏகப் போக்கிய புலையன் இவன்: the loss is itemised, wealth, youth, learning and mind, and the world's verdict 'outcast' is quoted. அறுசிறுவர் ஒருவுடலமாகித் தோற்றிய: the six infants of the Saravana pool who became one body.

tamil: குழவியு மாய்மோக மோகித குமரனு மாய்வீடு காதலி
குனிகொடு கூனீடு மாகிடு கிழவனு மாயாவி போய்விட
பழயச டாதார மெனிகழ் கழியுடல் காணாநி ராதர
பலபல வாம்யோக சாதக வுடல்கொடு மாயாத போதக
எழுகடல் தநமுள மேருவு மிடிபட வேதாவும் வேதமு
இருளறு பாதாள லோகமு மிமையமு நீறாக வாள்கிரி
அழகிய மாபாக சாதன னமரரு மூர்பூத மாறுசெய்
அமரினை மேவாத சூரரை அமர்செயும் வேலாயு தாவுயர்
reading: The poet runs through a life, infant, youth in passion, householder loving his home, wanderer, bent old man, the life gone and the body dust with the firewood, and says he never knew this; he asks whether, beyond the six supports of the body and with a body trained in many yogas, he will now reach the undying home of the Lord of deathless knowledge. The praise is Murugan's battle: the seven seas, Meru, Brahma and the Veda and the sun put to flight, the old serpent and the underworld shaken, the mountain split in two, and Indra and the gods given back their city, at Arunai.
nuance: The first lines are a life in one breath, as in 9 and 110. பழய சடாதாரம் ... நிராதர: the six adharas of the yogic body and the supportless state beyond them; the plea moves from impermanence to yoga, but the words of the third and fourth lines are hard to divide.

reading: The poet confesses that, sunk in infatuation with women wearing ketaki flowers, with petty thoughts, no learning by listening, and deeds of fate bent on his ruin, he has become a great sinner wandering the earth in vain; he asks Murugan to come on the peacock with the vel to rule him and grant release. The praise names him the child who uprooted Taraka, destroyer of justice, so the gods returned to their homes, Vishnu's nephew, the one who dwells in the northern tower of Sonagiri, the hill that rose as fire and light, and the one who took up the sword against the asuras.
nuance: கேள்வியதிலாது, ஊழ்வினையினால்: lack of learning and fate are named together as causes, but the plea does not excuse him; he still calls himself பாதகன். சோதி அனலா உதித்த சோணகிரி: the hill as the light that rose as fire.

reading: The poet asks not to wander with women on whose breasts and spear-like eyes he dwells, and to be given the feet that shine as his home. The praise names Murugan the one who ran round the sea-girt land on the peacock and the lord praised by the Chola land on the hill of hot light.
nuance: ஊராக திகழ் பாதம்: the feet as a town to live in. நீடாழி சுழல் தேசம் வலமாக நீடோடி: circling the world on the peacock, as in 398.

tamil: கோடுசெறி மத்த கத்தை வீசுபலை தத்த வொத்தி
கோளுலவு முப்பு ரத்தை வாளெரிகொ ளுத்தி விட்ட
நீடுகன கத்த லத்தை யூடுருவி மற்ற வெற்பு
நீபமலர் பத்தி மெத்த வோதுமவர் சித்த மெத்த
ஆடலணி பொற்சி லைக்கை வேடுவர்பு னக்கு றத்தி
ஆதரவு பற்றி மெத்த மாமணிநி றைத்த வெற்றி
தேடிமையொர் புத்தி மெத்தி நீடுறநி னைத்த பத்தி
தேறருணை யிற்ற ரித்த சேண்முகடி டத்த டர்த்த
reading: The praise names Murugan the guru of Siva, who flayed the elephant and burned the three cities, and asks him, who pierced the golden mountain and trampled the other hill to ash, to come daily on the blue peacock to the minds of those who sing the kadamba with devotion. It names him the hero who embraces the hunter girl on his twelve shoulders, the Sivavel known in the minds of devotees, and the one who broke the gods' prison at Arunai.
nuance: The plea is not for the poet himself but for all who sing with devotion (நீபமலர் பத்தி மெத்த ஓதுமவர் சித்தம்): Murugan is asked to come into their minds.

reading: The poet describes a sulking woman with kumkum on her bow brow and angry eyes, at whose flower feet he bows until her bangles jingle and love returns, and their union, and asks whether even in that union he would forget Murugan's golden feet in his heart. The praise names Siva, three-eyed and compassionate, who dances beside the mountain's daughter, as the giver of Murugan, the hero who embraced the hunter girl, the one who fought the asuras in the sea, and the lord at Arunagiri who ends the fears of devotees.
nuance: புணரினும் நிற் பொற்பதங்கள் நெஞ்சினுள் மறவேனோ: the question means he will not forget; the feet are held in the very act the other songs flee. The lovers' quarrel (புலவி) and the bowing at her feet are classical akam, told as the poet's own.

reading: The poet asks that, enjoying union with Siva's consort and with his hunger stilled by the nectar of Siva-knowledge, the two becoming one form and all the worlds enjoyed, he may play at the Lord's side while Vishnu, Brahma and the gods say 'this is the one' and the Vedas chant, and that Murugan grant this with his vel and peacock. The praise names him the one who threw the fiery vel so that the asuras' heads and the seven seas were dust, the chest that embraced the hunter girl, and the lord of the great fire hill, asked to end the poet's poverty and disease.
nuance: சிவஞான அமுதே பசியாறி, இருவோர் ஒரு ரூபமதாய்: hunger stilled by knowledge and two becoming one form describe union with Siva, an unusually high plea. The ending asks for the end of poverty (மிடி) as well. A letter is lost in line 3, and who the 'two' are is not certain.

reading: The poet sees his body as what dogs, jackals, vultures, kites, demons and worms feed on gladly, a mire of filth and bones caught between the nets of birth and death, taking more forms than the sand of the sky could count; he asks that, calling his body and life Murugan's due, he be taken into service and joined to the devotees, and asks whether Murugan will not think of him today. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the vel that sets the worlds rejoicing while Vishnu and Brahma serve and sing, and Murugan as the lord whom the Sankara of Arunagiri, with Gauri at his side and Ganga, worships.
nuance: செனனவலை மரணவலை ரண்டும் முன்பின் தொடர்ந்து: birth and death as two nets, one before and one behind. The remedy is not solitary but the company of devotees (அன்பரோடே கலவி நலம் மருவி), and கடன் எனது உடலுயிரும் makes body and life a debt owed to the Lord.

reading: The poet traces his making from seed and blood in the womb, growing like a pill, the belly swelling and the body's heat rising until birth in the tenth month, then crying, nursing, crawling, toddling, learning only empty knowledge and sinking into infatuation with peacock-like women, and asks whether he will waste away in birth like this. The praise names Vishnu who destroyed the southern rakshasas and gave a kingdom to the one who came to him, the guru Siva who burned the three cities, Uma who woke all the worlds as his mother, the vel that set the seas on fire, and the coral-hued hunter girl, at Arunai.
nuance: கற்று வெற்றறிவு பெற்று: learning itself is listed among the stages that lead nowhere. The giving of a kingdom to a southern suppliant after the rakshasas' fall points to Vibhishana, though the name is garbled.

reading: The poet quotes his own flattery of women, breasts like pots and an elephant's brow, teeth like pearls, lips sweeter than fruit, hair like clouds, Lakshmi of the lotus, young vanji twig, peacock, and calls himself the dull-witted fool who coaxes, pleads and daily worships their feet; he asks when he will reach Murugan's feet. The praise names Siva who drank the poison, who took the form of the fierce Sarabha bird to stop the man-lion that tore Hiranya with its claws, and Uma his chaste consort as Murugan's mother, and Murugan as the old man who roamed the hunters' millet field, on the peacock at Arunapuri.
nuance: The flattery is given as direct speech, so the poet's folly is shown, not described: he worships the women's feet (தினமவர் தாடொழு) where he should worship Murugan's. வெஞ்சச் சிம்புள் சொருபமதானவர்: Siva as the Sarabha subduing Narasimha. திரிகிழவா: Murugan's disguise as an old man to court Valli.

tamil: செயசெய அருணாத் திரிநம சிவயத் ...... தி முலா
reading: The song chants 'Jaya jaya Arunadri' with the five syllables of Siva in each of their rotations, then asks whether, fixing his eyes on Arunadri and melting at 'Hara Hara Saranadri', the poet will drink the sea-nectar of the Siva-word at the holy feet. The praise names Murugan the vel that burned the asuras, the one who spoke into the two ears of the red Siva-light whose head and feet the two seekers could not find, the golden guru who showed the dance in the space of light that powders the two deeds, and the lord who delights in Arunadri, the hill of Siva.
nuance: The opening rotates the five letters in order, சிவயநம, மசிவயந, நமசிவய, யநமசிவ, வயநமசி, each joined to அருணாத்திரி, so the mantra and the hill are one chant. திருமுடி அடி ... இருவர்க்கு அடிதலை தெரியாப்படி: Brahma and Vishnu failing to find the ends of the column of light is the story of Arunachala, and Murugan is the one who taught that light.

reading: The poet pictures the lone Death on his buffalo, dark as a mass of night with fiery eyes and horns like black serpents, throwing the noose while he sits in anxious thought and his kin and sons weep at the hour ripe for death; he asks Murugan to come then with his lotus faces, smile, long eyes, earrings, vel and dancing peacock, and grant him a boon. The praise names him the one who drank the milk of the mountain's daughter, who taught the Agama to the bowing lords, who split Sura, who set the Jains gathered at Koodal kicking on the stakes, son of Ganga, easy to reach for devotees, at the great tower of Arunai.
nuance: The plea is the familiar one of 8 and 46, but the picture of Murugan coming is unusually full, face, smile, ornaments and anklets, as if the sight itself were the rescue. இளமுலையின் செழும்பால் குடுத்து and அமணர் ... கூடலில் ... கழுவில்: the milk of Uma and the impaled Jains of Madurai are Sambandar's story, here given to Murugan.

tamil: திகுடோ டிமி டிமிடோ டிமி டாங்குட டிந்தகமென் ...... றியல்பேரி
சிரமீள்பட குவடோ துகள் வான்பெற வாங்கியவண் ...... கதிர்வேலா
reading: The poet lists women's charms, voices like cuckoo, peacock, dove, parrot and bee, mountainous breasts, spear eyes, crescent brow, dark hair, bright teeth, moon face and swan gait, and seems to say that even if he sports with such women in bed he will not let go of Murugan's anklet-sounding lotus feet, the cock banner and his form beyond painting. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the vel that made the seven seas dust, Siva who gives the white ash to end the poet's sorrow, Uma who bore 'us' and bore Murugan, and Valli's lover who ends the poet's two deeds and malas, at the hill of fire.
nuance: If அன்தகையேனே is read 'I will not be held back from', the song makes the same vow as 420, keeping the feet in mind in the embrace. அடியேன் துயர் தீர்ந்திட வெண்தழல் மாபொடி அருள்வோர்: Siva's gift of holy ash for the poet's sorrow. Line 16 is corrupt.

title: திருவருணை
theme: Songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 5 of 6): the poet confesses a counterfeit asceticism worn for gold, the trade of flattering patrons, and his bondage to courtesans who cheat and sell, sets out the diseased and maya-bound body, and asks for the feet, for release and for the gift of song; three love-laments in a woman's voice ask Murugan to come; the praise turns on the vel against Sura, Valli and Devayanai, and Murugan standing in the streets and at the tower of Arunai.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (429, 438, 439, 442), with 434 and 437 confessing a life spent on women;the false ascetic (428) and the flattering poet (436); the body and its diseases (433, 437, 441); love-laments in a woman's voice (430, 432, 440); the self-abuse litany (435); and pleas for song (431, 441).
source_issues: Song 430: corrupt character in லு஡றிய (line 3), probably லூறிய ('oozing', of the serpent's poison).
Song 435: line 2 reads முமுடன், with a letter lost; probably முழுமூடன் or மூமூடன் ('utter fool').
Song 438: line 6 reads கின்ற்முடர் (probably கின்ற மூடர்) and line 18 தொணடர் (for தொண்டர்); neither is flagged.
Song 442: corrupt character in னு஡றாயிர (line 3), for நூறாயிர ('a hundred thousand').

tamil: தலையை மழித்துச் சிவந்த துணியை யரைக்குப் புனைந்து
சதிரொடு வப்பப் புனைந்து விரகொடு கற்கப் புகுந்து
கலையை மிகுத்திட் டணிந்து கரண வலைக்குட் புகுந்து
கனக மியற்றித் திரிந்து துவளு மெனைச்சற் றறிந்து
அலைகட லிற்கொக் கரிந்து மருவரை யைப்பொட் டெறிந்து
அருளொடு கைப்பற்றி வந்து மருண கிரிப்புக் கிருந்து
மலையை வளைத்துப் பறந்து மருவு புரத்தைச் சிவந்து
மதலை புனத்திற் புகுந்து நரவடி வுற்றுத் திரிந்து
reading: The poet confesses a counterfeit renunciation: head shaved, ochre cloth at the waist, matted hair grown and twisted, a tiger skin worn with flourish, tricks learned, penance known only as a word, ash smeared thick, while he stays caught in the net of the senses and wanders making gold; he asks Murugan to take a little notice of him as he wilts and in pity end his care. The praise names Murugan who cut down the tree in the sea, shattered the hill, entered the gods' world and took the hand of the elephant-reared bride, who came to Arunagiri and pities devotees who know, the son of Siva who bent the mountain and burned the cities with an idle laugh, and who entered the millet field in human form.
nuance: The plea is a confession, not a satire of others: the participles all lead to துவளும் எனை, 'me, who wilt'. He has worn both the shaved head (தலையை மழித்து) and the matted hair (சடையை வளர்த்து), every mark of the ascetic, and தவம் ஒரு சத்தத்து அறிந்து says he knew penance only as a sound. கனகம் இயற்றித் திரிந்து names the motive, gold. கொக்கு in the praise is taken as the mango tree that Sura became in the sea. சதிரொடு வப்ப and கதறு நிலைக்கைக்கு அமர்ந்த are obscure.

reading: The poet heaps abuse on courtesans: thieves who trade in their bodies, wicked and shameless, with bow-like brows and lifted breasts, who melt men's minds with laughter, frighten them with their eyes and fall on them, and who polish brass ornaments with ash to pass them off as gold; he asks to leave behind his delusion for them and bow single-minded at Murugan's golden feet. The praise is a battle scene in drum syllables, ghouls dancing with hands and drums and eating flesh as the demon armies fall to the vel, and ends with Guha who abides at Arunai.
nuance: திருட்டு வாணிப, 'thieving trade', names the commerce at once. பித்தளையில் பணி மிக நீறால் விளக்கியே குழையிட்ட புரட்டிகள்: the cheats wear brass ear-ornaments scoured with ash to shine like gold, so even their jewels deceive. ஒருமித்து, single-minded, is set against the divided heart the women produce.

tamil: தேதென வாச முற்ற கீதவி நோத மெச்சு
சீறும ராவெ யிற்றி லு஡றிய காளம் விட்ட
போதனை நீதி யற்ற வேதனை வாளி தொட்ட
போகமெ லாநி றைத்து மோகவி டாய்மி குத்த
மாதினை வேணி வைத்த நாதனு மோது பச்சை
வானவர் சேனை முற்றும் வாழம ராப திக்குள்
மேதினி யோர்த ழைக்க வேயரு ணாச லத்து
மேருவை நீறெ ழுப்பி நான்முக னார்ப தத்தில்
reading: A love-lament for a girl: the speaker names what torments her, the flowers swarming with bees, the cool moonlight that burns like poison from a serpent's fang, and the arrows of Kama the warrior, and asks Murugan to come and embrace this girl filled with longing. The praise names Murugan the peacock hero honoured by Siva who bears a woman in his hair and by Vishnu, the bridegroom of the parrot raised by the elephant in Indra's city, who stands in the streets of Arunachala for the world to see, and who reduced Meru to dust and set the vel's mark on Brahma.
nuance: பூவையை நீ அணைக்க வரவேணும: the speaker asks the god to embrace the girl, so this is akam poetry in the voice of a mother or companion, not the poet's confession. The moon that burns is a classical torment of the lovesick. வாரணமான தத்தை is Devayanai, raised by Indra's elephant. The last line (நான்முகனார் பதத்தில் வேல் அடையாளம் இட்ட) is unclear: the vel's mark may be set on Brahma's feet or on his station.

tamil: தோத கப்பெ ரும்ப யோத ரத்தி யங்கு
சூலை வெப்ப டர்ந்த வாத பித்த மென்று
பாத கச்ச மன்தன் மேதி யிற்பு குந்து
பாவ லற்கி ரங்கி நாவ லர்க்கி சைந்த
வேத மிக்க விந்து நாத மெய்க்க டம்ப
மேரு வைப்பி ளந்து சூர னைக்க டிந்து
கோதை பொற்கு றிஞ்சி மாது கச்ச ணிந்த
கோல முற்றி லங்கு சோண வெற்பு யர்ந்த
reading: The poet asks that his heart not be lost to women with great breasts, that colic, fever, wind and bile and the other diseases not come near him, and that Death, the sinner, not come on his buffalo and throw the noose to seize him; he asks Murugan to pity this poet and give him songs of fine words fit for the learned. The praise names Murugan the Veda, bindu and nada, the true kadamba-wearer called Virabhadra and Kanda, the vel that split Meru, cut down Sura and pierced the sea, the lover of the golden girl of the hills, who sits in the beautiful tall tower of Sonagiri.
nuance: The three things the poet fears come in order, women, disease, Death, and the remedy is the gift of song (பாடல் மிக்க செஞ்சொல்), the poet asking to be made a poet. Murugan is given Siva's fierce name வீரபத்ர. கோபுரத்து அமர்ந்த places him at the temple tower of Arunai.

reading: A short song in a lovesick woman's voice: struck by Kama's flower arrows, by the cruel young moon spitting fire and by the cuckoo whose call destroys her modesty, she asks whether it is right that she waste away in longing. The praise names the chest that embraces the maiden of heaven, the hero whose anklets are fragrant with the gods' crowns, the bright vel standing at Arunai to be seen, and the Lord who breaks the back of Death.
nuance: நானும் மயலில் இளைக்கும் தரமோ: the woman speaks herself. நாணம் அழிய உரைக்கும் குயில்: the cuckoo's call makes her lose her shame. The last line, காலன் முதுகை விரிக்கும், gives Murugan a victory over Death even in a love song.

reading: In a rhythm of long vowels, the poet speaks of women whose speech is milk, honey and syrup, and of the body, a hut bound by the noose, made of skin, wind and flesh and stained, and asks whether he must tire and die of the unending disease of maya. The praise is a string of vocatives: Lord of the world, the high one, Veda, master, lord of the hill of light, way of jnana, king of the heavens, meaning of the many Vedas, vel-bearer, child, lord of the hunter girl, the support of the six centres, the hero.
nuance: The song is built of paired long syllables (ஞாலா மேலா வேதா போதா), so meaning bends to sound and several splits are guesses. மாயா ஓயா நோய், the never-ceasing disease of maya, makes maya itself the illness. சோதிக் கிரி is Arunachala, the hill of fire, and ஆறாதாரா names Murugan the six adharas of yoga.

tamil: பூணர்முலை மடந்தை மாதர் வலையினி லுழன்ற நேக
புகழ்மறை யறிந்து கூறு மினியென தகம்பொ னாவி
மணமுணர் மடந்தை மாரொ டொளிர்திரு முகங்க ளாறு
வரிபர வநந்த கோடி முநிவர்கள் புகழ்ந்து போத
பணைமுலை யரம்பை மார்கள் குயில்கிளி யினங்கள் போல
பறைமுர சநந்த பேரி முறைமுறை ததும்ப நீசர்
அணிசுக நரம்பு வீணை குயில்புற வினங்கள் போல
அரிமகள் மணங்கொ டேகி யெனதிட ரெரிந்து போக
reading: The poet says that much of his life has gone wandering in the net of women, and that now, knowing the praise the Vedas give Murugan, he will count his heart, gold, life and goods as Murugan's; to end this dog's sorrow he asks Murugan to come gladly on the peacock with his consorts, his six faces shining like the sun on a gem hill, praised by countless sages. The praise shows heavenly women chanting the Veda like cuckoos and parrots, drums sounding as the vel destroys the demons' army in the sea, and Murugan who married Hari's daughter and burns away the poet's trouble on the hill of Arunai.
nuance: அகம் பொன் ஆவி பொருள் என நினைந்து: the offering of heart, gold, life and goods is the gift of the whole self, the servant's surrender. அரிமகள், Hari's daughter, is Valli. The opening lines (பொறியுடல் இறந்து போனது அளவு ஏது) are hard to divide.

tamil: புலைய னான மாவீனன் வினையி லேகு மாபாதன்
புகழி லாத தாமீகன் அறிவி லாத காபோதி
நிலையி லாத கோமாளி கொடையி லாத ஊதாரி
நினது தாளை நாடோ று மனதி லாசை வீடாமல்
சிலையில் வாளி தானேவி யெதிரி ராவ ணார்தோள்கள்
சிறையி லாம லேகூடி புவனி மீதி லேவீறு
அலைய மேரு மாசூரர் பொடிய தாக வேலேவி
அதிக தேவ ரேசூழ உலக மீதி லேகூறும்
reading: The poet heaps names on himself: an outcast, futile, a doer of great sins, angry without patience, a fool, without renown, dark-natured, without understanding, blind, his senses running off, an unsteady clown, a spendthrift who gives nothing, a ruin of his line; he asks Murugan to come and grant that he think of the feet every day with a longing that never ends. The praise names Rama, who fought until Ravana's arms were broken and took back Sita, as his uncle, and Murugan who sent the vel to powder Meru and Sura, rode the peacock among the gods and dwells at Arunai.
nuance: கொடையிலாத ஊதாரி, a spendthrift who never gives, is a pointed paradox. The plea does not ask that desire end but that it turn: ஆசை வீடாமல், thinking of the feet with a longing that is not let go.

reading: The poet describes poets who, to end their poverty, liken rich men to the wish-granting tree, the rain cloud and Pari, praise them as fit to give heaps of gold at once, make 'thieving poems' of ornate figures to get money, and then spend what they earn on golden women and fall slaves in the net of their fish eyes; he asks whether one should come to that. The praise names Murugan sitting on the peacock at the northern side of the golden, jewelled tower of Arunai where Agama devotees and pure Vedic men gather, and the son of Siva who shares his left side with the peacock-like Uma, whose vel pierced Sura.
nuance: திருட்டுக் கவிகள்: the poet calls praise-poems for patrons theft, an unusual confession about his own craft; the patron comparisons (கற்பகம், புயல், பாரி) are the stock ones of court poetry. The money won by false praise ends with the courtesans, so the two trades are joined. The praise lines on the tower (உத்தர திக்கு, கலபக் கற்கி) are hard to construe.

reading: The poet tells how he was caught in the net of women whose eyes are likened to the deer, poison, the carp, Kama's arrow, the sea, the vel, the sword and the blue lily, and names the body as a poison of flesh, an oozing filth, a bloated corpse swinging with the three gunas, impermanent rubbish; he asks whether this delusion will ever clear. The praise names Rama, who struck Vali from behind a sal tree and gave Tara to Sugriva after Ravana had imprisoned Janaki in the grove of sorrow, as his uncle, and Murugan, son of the pure Lord of Sonagiri, whose kadamba-garlanded shoulders crushed the hill and who cut down Sura.
nuance: குணத்ரயத்தொடு தடுமாறும் ஊசல்: the body is a swing tossed by the three gunas. நித்தத்துவம் அற்ற செத்தை, 'rubbish without permanence'. The line உபாதியை ஒப்பித்துத் துனிப்பவத்து அற is obscure; உபாதி may be the limiting adjunct of philosophy or simply affliction.

reading: The poet lists the courtesans' kinds: those who flatter to the face, the scheming, the low-priced, the cunning, the deceitful in speech, those who for love of coin sell their breasts to many, who melt men with laughter and 'aha', thieves and forms of illusion; he asks when, leaving his revelling with them, he will reach the holy feet. The praise shows Siva dancing to drum syllables, worshipped by his devotees, Agastya, Vishnu, Brahma and the Goddess who nurtured dharma rejoicing in Murugan the eternal Lord who stands at Arunai, who smashed Sura and resettled the gods, the Lord of devotees.
nuance: காசாசையில் முலை பலர்க்கும் விற்பவர்: the song names the sale outright. அறம் வளர்த்த கற்பகம் is the Goddess as nurturer of dharma, rejoicing with the others in Murugan.

reading: The poet describes women with cloud-dark hair, bow brows, arrow eyes and breasts like Meru, who walk dancing down the good street crying the price of their breasts, lure those who come with deceitful play, and snatch their life with a powder of infatuation; he asks whether such women can be kin. The praise has drums sounding as the vel leaves Sura's thousand heads bare, shakes Meru and wrecks the demons' island; it names Murugan the son of Sivakami, the Shakti who is first, middle and cause of many things, and the one who rejoices at Arunachala in his love for Valli, daughter of Vishnu.
nuance: முலை விலைகூறி: the women cry their price in the street. மயல் தூள் மருத்திடு suggests a love-powder or drug given to the men. The string of Shakti's names (ஆதி மத்தி பலகாரணத்தி ... ஈசசத்தி) is hard to divide, and the phrase on Vishnu searching out the Veda for Brahma is tentative.

reading: A love-lament: the speaker names the roaring sea, darkened, its fishes stirred, and the moon that rises full of poison out of the mare-faced fire beneath the sea, and asks Murugan to think how to ease the infatuation of the girl with rain-dark hair and vine waist, and to come on the emerald peacock and give release. The praise names the chest that holds Valli's sandal-smeared breasts, the Lord of Indra's city, of Senthil and of Arunai, the vel that pierced the seven hills, and the one who ended the fear of the suns, Hari, Hara and Brahma.
nuance: The torments are the classical sea and moon, with the moon rising from வடவை, the submarine fire. முத்தி தரவேணும: the girl's longing is to be ended by mukti, so the akam frame opens onto the plea for release.

reading: The poet lists the diseases of his body, wind, bile, scrofula, abscess, dry colic, leprosy, chills, thirst, diabetes, the great belly, phlegm, vomiting, retention of urine and countless more, says he can no longer bear to carry it about the earth, and asks for the attainment of Siva-knowledge so that his tongue may praise the Thiruppugazh, full of Siva. The praise names Murugan the son of the coral-haired Siva who gave the blazing discus to Vishnu for his unfailing devotion, the vel that killed Sura, the hill, the lion-faced and the elephant-faced demons, and the Lord at Arunachala with the hunter girl and the elephant's daughter.
nuance: சிவமார் திருப்புகழை எனுநாவினில் புகழ: the book names itself, and the cure asked for is not health but the power to sing it. சிவஞான சித்தி joins knowledge and its attainment. The discus given to Vishnu for his devotion is told only as தொலையாத பத்தி.

reading: The poet speaks of women who, with eyes swift as Kama's arrows, chatter 'come, go' with the cunning of a hundred thousand minds, and of himself as a clown wholly in thrall to their musk-scented breasts, reviled by earth and sky, a fool without conduct, wretched and vile; he asks whether there will be a day when Murugan rules him among his devotees. The praise names the emerald Narayana, who embraced the sixteen thousand women of the northern cowherds, as his uncle, the ever-young king of Sonachala, and the lone vel thrown so the world might live, the sea dry and the demons fall as ash.
nuance: நூறாயிர மனமுடை, 'with a hundred thousand minds', is the women's fickleness. The poet asks to be ruled together with the devotees (அடியவரோடு), not alone. Krishna's sixteen thousand women stand in the praise just after the poet's own confession, without comment.

title: திருவருணை
theme: Last songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 6 of 6): a life wasted by fate in women's craft that asks to reach the feet through Tamil song; a whole life traced from the drop in the womb to the pyre that leaves not a handful of ash; and a plea for the feet that are Jnana-Siva; the praise centres on Murugan coming on the peacock to the tower of Arunai, the hill of fire.

reading: The poet says that, as fate had it, his mind wavered in the craft of young women, his understanding turned and he wandered in deeds as a fool; he asks Murugan to come so that this displeasure ends and he may reach the feet in due order, thinking of them through the ancient great Tamil set to music. The praise names Kumaresa who fought the deceitful demons' crowns to the ground and whom all the worlds circle, fanned by the gods with chowries, who comes beautifully on the peacock to the tower of Arunai.
nuance: விதியதாகவே opens the confession by laying it to fate. முதிய மா தமிழ் இசையதாகவே மொழிசெய்து: the way to the feet is song in old Tamil. முனிவு தீர may mean the Lord's displeasure or the poet's own vexation.

reading: The poet traces a life from conception to the pyre: the drop in the womb, the whorl and the clot of blood, the growth month by month until birth in the tenth, the infant crying in its filth, at the breast and crawling, the decked child sent to learn, the youth following dancing women into lovemaking and spending his wealth, then disease and mockery, grey hair, the stick and a body bent like a monkey's, the wife taking charge of the goods, Death's noose dragging the life away, kin wailing each for their share, the drum, and the burning; he asks whether he should be this body, not worth even a handful of ash. The praise is a long battle in drum syllables, a catalogue of Siva's emblems and of Uma who bore Murugan, and his union with Devayanai and Valli, ending at the hill of fire, Arunai.
nuance: The plea runs as one sentence through every stage of life, each image piled on the last, until ஒருபிடி பொடிக்கும் இலை எனும் உடல், a body not worth a handful of ash. சந்தித்து அவரவர் பங்குக்கு அழுது: the kin weep, each for their share, and the wife has already taken the property (சம்பத்து ... அண்டைக் கொளுகையில்). In the praise Uma is given Siva's own emblems, the axe and deer in her hand and the dwarf Muyalakan under her foot (மழு உழை கரத்தி ... முயலக பதத்தி). Many lines of the embryo passage and of the battle are hard to divide.

reading: The poet describes women anointed with civet, rosewater and musk, with heavy breasts, scented cloud-dark hair and thread-thin waists, who lose all shame, and calls himself the fool who mixed with them and wandered, thinking what he sought was the goal; he asks for the feet that are Jnana-Siva. The praise names the feet on the peacock that turn devotees' deeds to ash, the son of Sivakami Uma who granted Kali her dance with Hara, the six-faced child of the river, who sported with Valli and married her, the nephew of victorious Raghurama, at ancient Arunapuri.
nuance: நாடியதுவே கதி எனா சுழலும் மோடன்: the error is taking the object of desire for the goal. ஞானசிவமான பதம்: the feet are not a means to knowledge but are knowledge and Siva. The line on Kali dancing with Hara appears to allude to their dance contest; how Uma's grace enters it is unclear.

title: திருக்காளத்தி
theme: Songs at Kalahasti (திருக்காளத்தி): the poet sets household life and the body that ends as carrion against Siva-knowledge and the golden feet, asks the Lord to rule him without bowing to others or clinging to the world, and asks, troubled in a body of five elements, for a steady mind; the praise names Murugan the guru on Siva's shoulders and Kalahasti as the southern Kailasa.

reading: The poet describes himself carried along in this body with the five cheats, wearied by household life, delighting in kin, cherishing his family, until he is laid in a pit as a corpse for vultures and dogs to eat and the body-hut decays; he asks Murugan to mark him, hold him on the shore of release's unfailing bliss, dry up the false roots of the world's maya, and give him Siva-knowledge and the golden feet. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva who burned the cities to dust and burned Kama of the cane bow, who struck down Sura so the eight directions feared, who embraced the girl in hunter's guise in the holy forest, and who takes in even the lowest who come for Siva's attainment at Kalahasti.
nuance: The fault confessed is not lust but the ordinary householder's life (சமுசாரம், சுற்றம், குடிபேணி), followed straight into the grave pit where vultures and dogs feed. சிவஞானம் பொற்கழல் joins knowledge and the feet as one gift. The opening lines (சரக்கேறித் தப்பதி, பரிக்காயம்) and குரக்கோணம் are obscure.

reading: A short song: the poet asks that, so he neither bows his head to others nor aims at the attachments of worldly men, Murugan, without making him suffer, set his peerless flower feet on him and rule him. The praise names Murugan the dancer, lover of the true principle, who dwells in the minds of those who think of him and gives his holy feet to the freed, the Lord of Kalahasti.
nuance: சிரத்தானத்திற் பணியாதே may mean 'without my bowing my head' to men, or ask for the feet to be set on the head (சிரத்தானம்); the reading depends on the split. கர்த்தத்துவ நேசா is obscure.

reading: The poet speaks of the human form assembled by the five in the world of moving and unmoving things that Brahma creates, of wandering in the attachments that bind and failing to cross women's deceit, and of being troubled as disease and deeds cover the body; he asks Murugan to protect him by grace and give him a mind that does not waver. The praise names Murugan, son of the anklet-wearing beauty at Siva's left, with the cock banner, the guru who crawled on the shoulders of Siva of the crescent, serpent, bow and trident, whose throat shines with the poison of the sea; it tells of the Sarabha that flew raging to crush the pride of Vishnu as the lion, and ends at the southern Kailasa, Kalahasti, where one did penance so the sin of punishing the sun would end.
nuance: பஞ்சவர் கூடித் திரண்டது ஓர் நர உரு: the body is made by 'the five', the elements, gathered together. கலங்கிடா மதி, an unshaken mind, is the whole request. The Sarabha story (சிங்கமதாகத் திரிந்த மால், சிம்புள்) and the closing lines on the sun (செங்கதிரோனைக் கடிந்த தீவினை) are told obliquely, and who did penance at Kalahasti is not clear.

title: சிதம்பரம்
theme: First songs at Chidambaram (சிதம்பரம், 1 of 5): two litanies of pure praise and short pleas for vision, Siva's nectar and the five syllables open the chapter; the rest confess bondage to courtesans who sell, take money in advance, cheat and leave disease and sores behind; the praise turns on Murugan as guru to his father, on Siva and Sivakami dancing, and on Murugan with Valli in the golden hall (கனகசபை, திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்).
structure_note: Praise litanies ending பெருமாள் காண் (449, 450); short pleas for vision and grace (451, 452, 457); courtesan songs (453 to 456, 458 to 463), several ending in the diseases the women leave (456, 460, 461).
source_issues: Song 453: corrupt character in கமுகென்பக்஡ணவம் (line 3); with ஡ண for ரீ it reads க்ரீவம் ('neck', likened to the areca palm).

reading: A song of praise only, each line ending 'behold the Lord': Murugan, the poet's own guru who dwells in the golden hall, the lotus-handed light, the Lord who plays among the devotees who seek him, the pure light worshipped by Brahma, sages, gods and Arunagirinathar, the nephew of Janaki's husband, son of Sivakami, bearer of the name Muruga, the lover of the nectar-sweet hunter girl in the forest, who lives with his consorts at Puliyur.
nuance: அருணகிரிநாதர் appears among the worshippers, a signature of the poet inside his own praise, and எனது குருநாத makes Murugan his personal guru. Puliyur is Chidambaram. The line on golden-hued Brahma (கனகநிற வேதன் அபயமிட) is unclear.

reading: A second litany ending 'behold the Lord': Murugan the brother of the elephant-faced one, the guru of the Lord of chaste Sivakami, the nephew of Rama, the bearer of the victorious vel, the rider of the peacock whose wings shake the mountains, the six-faced one with pearls on his chest, the child dancing to the drum, the king of poets who threw the vel so the Suras fell, and the Lord of pure Siva-knowledge who lives at Puliyur with Valli.
nuance: கத்தர் குருநாத: Murugan as guru to Siva, the Lord of Sivakami, without the story told. கவிராஜப் பெருமாள் makes him king of poets, and சுத்த சிவஞானப் பெருமாள் makes him Siva-knowledge itself. வித்துருப ராமருக்கு is obscure.

reading: A short song: the poet asks not to wander with his mind confused by the two kinds of deed, nor to roam with his heart in the seven hells, but, through understanding that thinks on the grace of the supreme guru, to be given Murugan's vision. The praise names Murugan the Sangam poet who gave Tamil that discerns, the son of Siva with golden anklets, easy to reach for those who walk the path of compassion, the Lord in the golden hall.
nuance: தெரிதமிழை உதவு சங்கப் புலவோனே: Murugan is himself a poet of the Sangam who gives Tamil. கருணைநெறி புரியும் அன்பர்க்கு எளியோன்: he is easy for those who practise compassion, not only for those who worship.

reading: The poet asks that, praising 'Guha, supreme guru' in his heart, Siva's nectar well up on his tongue and end his hunger, that the root of the two kinds of deed, the deceits and the diseases be torn out, that he chant 'namasivaya om' with joy, and that, knowing the space with neither day nor night to be the supreme state, he be given the golden feet as Murugan comes on the peacock. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the vel scattering Sura's forces and frightening the serpent, and Murugan who sweetly taught his father, the dancer of Kailasa, until his heart melted, the Lord in the golden hall.
nuance: நமசிவய ஓம்: the five syllables joined with Om. பகலும் இரவும் இலா வெளி, the space beyond day and night, names the state beyond waking and sleep. The teaching of Siva is told without naming Om (தந்தைக்கு உருக ... கொஞ்சி).

reading: The poet describes women with eyes like bees and carp, bow brows, cloud-dark hair, areca necks and breasts like an elephant's temples, who come down the street to cheat, call men with feigned love, embrace them and take their money; he asks that he not grieve and let his body-hut decay this way, but serve Murugan's devotees, hold the kumkum-scented feet and reach the shore. The praise is a battle in drum syllables in which the vel breaks the Suras, who had crushed the eight directions, the serpents and the hills, gives Indra back his place, and Murugan sits beside the hunter girl in the golden hall.
nuance: உன் அன்பருக்குச் செயல் தொண்டுபட்டு: service to the devotees is the remedy for service to the women. The line on drinking a sea (சத்திக் கடல் உண்டு) is obscure.

reading: The poet describes women with night-dark hair, moon faces, arrow eyes, breasts like an elephant's temples and anklets ringing, who speak like parrots and cuckoos and snatch the gold from a man's palm, and asks when his servitude to these cheats will end. The praise has conches, drums and Tamil bards sounding as the vel cuts off Sura's arms and head and sends him to Death's city, and names Kandavel who lives with the moon-faced Devayanai and the hunter girl in the golden hall.
nuance: அங்கை பொன் பறிக்கார பெண்கள்: women who snatch the gold from the hand. ஊழியம் செய்வது என்று போமோ: the poet names his state as servitude, the bondage that the service of the feet replaces. அண்டி மண்டையர் is obscure.

reading: The poet describes women with perfumed hair and breasts like white elephant tusks, who come to the bed like parrot, cuckoo and peacock, leave scars on breasts and arms and loosen their garments; he asks whether, in that infatuation, with his eyes and ears failing, he must lie with the wrongs he did before and see his body perish. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, vultures, kites and eagles crowding the field where the vel struck the deceivers, and the Lord of the devotees in the golden hall where the moon, Indra and the gods melt in praise.
nuance: முன்செய்த வஞ்சினங்களுடன் கிடந்து உடல் அழிவேனோ: the body is pictured dying in bed with its old deeds, the same bed as the embrace. வஞ்சினம் may mean wrongs or vows of hatred.

reading: The poet describes women smeared with sandal and kumkum, moon-faced and fish-eyed, who speak sweetly as though they knew a man already ('which town are you from?'), say 'come', and taste union with whoever shows gold in his hand; through them come suffering, sores with pus and worms, and colic, until the body dies and enters Death's city, and he asks for the knowledge to cross that sea and gain the feet. The praise shows gods, sages, Brahma, Vishnu, Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Arundhati and the women of every world praising the dance of Sivakami Sundari, mother of Kandavel, the vel that powders the demons' heads, and Murugan who bowed at Valli's feet in the millet field and sits in the golden hall.
nuance: நீர் எந்த ஊர் அறிந்தவர் போல: the courtesan's opening, feigning old acquaintance. துன்று பொன் அங்கையின் மீது கண்டவரோடு: union for whoever has gold in hand. The praise centres on Sivakami's dance, praised by the women of every world.

reading: The poet says he has come again and again, sprouting from seed, his body burning and his life worn away in the forest of his deceits, until he faded; he asks Murugan, pleased in heart, to come on the elephant with gods and devotees around him, scatter that forest, and appear before him with kadamba-garlanded shoulders, golden crown and lotus feet. The praise names the vel thrown at the angry demons when Vishnu, who swallowed the eight directions, fled in fear and begged for service at Murugan's feet, the lover of the hunter girl and of Devayanai, and the Lord of the dancer of the golden hall who burned the cities with a smile.
nuance: எந்தன் வஞ்சனைக் காடு: the forest of deceit is the poet's own, not the women's. வந்து வந்து வித்தூறி: births come one after another like seeds sprouting. The lines on the gods fleeing are hard to divide.

reading: The poet describes women with plaited hair, adorned necks and laughter, who grab a man's garland, madden him, bind him with coaxing, take gold until his wealth is gone and then drive him out with deceitful words, and asks whether he must wander, his desire for them satisfied and then turned bitter. The praise names the vel that crushed the demons and gave the gods back their place, Siva who burned the cities, flayed the elephant and struck off Daksha's head, and Murugan who poured the true meaning into Siva's ear, the beautiful Lord of Tiruchitrambalam.
nuance: பசப்பிப் பொன் தரப் பற்றிப் பொருள் மாளப் பறித்துப் பின் துரத்து: the courtesan's whole course in a line. சிவனார்தம் செவிக்குச் செம்பொருள் கற்கப் புகட்டி: Murugan teaches Siva, though Om is not named.

reading: The poet describes women who laugh with teeth bright as lightning, melt men and fall on them, snatch their wages in a moment, wink, wear fine cloth to show their waists, hide their breasts, give their lips' nectar, speak like cuckoos and embrace men on soft beds, and asks whether such women can be kin. The praise shows the gods hiding and crying 'Kanda, supreme', the vel slaying the demons with lions, chariots, horses and elephants while vultures and ghouls dance in blood, the son of Sivakami beside Siva who burned Kama and bears the skull, and Murugan who keeps the hunter girl in his heart and walks in Tiruchitrambalam.
nuance: செணத்தில் சம்பளமே பறிகாரிகள்: the women snatch a man's wages in an instant. திருச்சித்தந்தனிலே குறமானதை இருத்தி: Murugan holds Valli in his heart as the poet asks to hold the feet.

reading: The poet describes courtesans with parrot speech and peacock gait who cheat and snatch, take money in advance, cling until a man's debts cover him, and leave him with vomiting, colic, boils, hiccups, sorrow, cold and bile, and asks when this thief will gain a place in grace. The praise names the vel dancing while the hills burst and the guardians of the directions sing, the son of Uma, Siva's half, the wish-granting gem, the mother dear to devotees, the son who came as a merchant to deceive and win the hunter girl Valli, and the Lord of the hall where Siva dances.
nuance: முற்பணம் கைக்கொடும் தாரும்: 'give money in hand in advance', the courtesans' terms. In the praise Murugan comes as a merchant (செட்டியென்று எத்தி) to win Valli: the verb எத்தி, 'cheating', is the one used of the women (எத்தும் பறியர்), so by one reading the poet lets the god play the trick he condemns. Some of Uma's epithets are unclear.

reading: The poet describes the common women (பொதுமாதர்) who adorn and perfume themselves, laugh and call, embrace a man on the bed and take his gold, and the man who, after paying, wanders with sores that swell and eyes that fester, so that those who see him cover their eyes; he asks whether he must wander so. The praise names the vel that broke the hill and struck the demons' heads like balls into the sea while the gods rejoiced and showered flowers, the son of the Mad One who burned Kama and the cities, flayed the elephant and ruined Daksha's sacrifice, Murugan who rapped Brahma the creator on the head, and the Lord of the Chitrambalam with the hunter girl.
nuance: கண்டவர்க்குக் கண் புதைப்ப: the disease ends in the disgust of onlookers, the public shame that answers the private pleasure. படைத்துப் பொன்றுடைத் திட்பன் தனைக் குட்டும் படுத்தி: Brahma rapped on the head, from the story of Om, though Om itself is not named.

reading: The poet heaps names on courtesans: thieves who snatch wages, deceivers who intoxicate, the deaf, the blind, the stupid and the quarrelsome, who count and wrangle, ensnare with their eyes, preen and dance, and asks whether such women can be kin. The praise names the vel that broke the elephants, lions, chariots and horses of Sura when he came to ruin the sages, Brahmins and gods, the son of Siva who flayed the elephant, burned the cities with a laugh and cut off Brahma's head, and Murugan who married the daughter of the gods and the daughter of the hunters and entered the beautiful Tiruchitrambalam.
nuance: The plea is almost entirely a list of epithets in -இகள், each a separate insult, as in 429 and 438. Several (சிதடிகள், உதடிகள், சங்க்ய சங்கிகள்) are uncertain.

reading: The poet lists a woman's beauties, hair, brows, carp eyes, moon forehead, lips sweet as fruit, cuckoo voice, pearl teeth, areca neck, bamboo arms, golden necklaces and breasts like an elephant's temples, and asks whether his mind should be one that clutches at those who take even the last coin of their lovers. The praise names Vishnu who churned the sea for nectar, who shares himself with Lakshmi, who powdered the head of Lanka's king and holds the worlds in his belly, and Siva who burned the cities, and calls Murugan the son of Sankari, praised by Brahma, the Lord of the shining Ambalam.
nuance: The plea is almost all description, the catalogue of beauty that the closing question turns against. விண்டவர் தங்கள் தம்படியும் கவண்டிய: 'grabbing even the copper coin of those who part', but the split and subject of this line are uncertain.

title: சிதம்பரம்
theme: Songs at Chidambaram (சிதம்பரம், 2 of 5): the poet confesses his capture by women, their arts, their magic and their price, and once by the five senses and once by kin, wealth and learning, and asks for Murugan's feet, love and release; two songs ask to hold Murugan's form in mind even in the women's embrace. The praise centres on the hall (அம்பலம்) where Siva dances, Sivakami, and Murugan's place beside them.
structure_note: Songs on women (465 to 468, 473 to 475, 477, 478); the body as a bubble and the wish for release (469); the senses (464); a heap of self-abuse ending in a namo nama litany (470); a yogic song (471); a complaint that the Lord does not hear (472); and a song against kin, wealth and learning (476). 465 and 466 share a metre and opening, and 476 and 477 build each line on a repeated syllable or word.
source_issues: Song 474: one corrupt character in கமுக க்஡ணவர் (line 4), probably க்ரீவர், 'areca-like neck', with ஡ண for ரீ.
Song 478: unflagged garble வழ்ழைதொடை (line 9), probably வாழைத்தொடை; முன்னல்கமு (line 6) is also doubtful.
Song 464: சிறுகூரா (line 21) is unclear and may be corrupt.

reading: The poet calls himself a wretch who suffers the bewilderment, wavering and grief the bond of the five senses brings, with no steadiness or good quality, a fool and fickle, and asks that Murugan, recognising him as his old servant, give the lotus feet with golden anklets that Siva, wearing the serpent, the crescent, kurundu flowers, Brahma's skull and Ganga in his red hair, praises, sees with joy and worships. The praise shows the battlefield where jackals, dogs and red kites feast on heads, necks, tusks and bones, and the hall at Chidambaram where people come with austerity, japa and love.
nuance: The whole song runs in nasal-heavy syllables (தியங்குஞ்சஞ் சலந்துன்பங்), and the word divisions are often a guess. உன்றன் பழந்தொண்டு: the poet claims to be Murugan's servant of old. The feet asked for are those Siva himself worships (கும்பிடும் செம்பொன் சிலம்பு), so the son's feet are above the father's. The meaning of சிறுகூரா near the end is unclear.

tamil: பருவம் பணைத்தி ரண்டு கரிகொம் பெனத்தி ரண்டு
படருங் கனத்த கொங்கை மினல்கொந் தளித்து சிந்த
புருவஞ் சுழற்றி யிந்த்ர தநுவந் துதித்த தென்று
பொறிகண் சுழற்றி ரம்ப பரிசம் பயிற்றி மந்த்ர
உருவந் தரித்து கந்து கரமும் பிடித்து வந்து
ஒளிர்கொம் பினைச்ச வுந்த ரியவும் பலைக்கொ ணர்ந்து
செருவெங் களத்தில் வந்த அவுணன் தெறித்து மங்க
தினமுங் களித்து செம்பொ னுலகந் துதித்தி றைஞ்சு
reading: The poet describes women with breasts like elephant tusks, hair flashing like lightning, brows whirled like Indra's bow, carp eyes and practised touch, who destroy men with magic powder, and asks whether union with such deceivers is fitting. The praise shows Murugan taking a disguise in the forest to win and embrace Valli, sending the five syllables of Siva ahead in battle so the demon is struck down, and dwelling in the holy hall that the golden world praises daily.
nuance: மந்த்ர பொடிகொண்டு அழிக்கும் வஞ்சர்: the women's weapon is a charmed powder, a love-magic, which the praise answers with a holier spell: சிவம் அஞ்செழுத்தை முந்த விடுவோனே, the five syllables of Siva sent first against the asura. The line on Valli (ஒளிர்கொம்பினைச் சவுந்தரியவும் பலைக்கொணர்ந்து) does not divide clearly.

tamil: மதவெங் கரிக்கி ரண்டு வலுகொம் பெனத்தி ரண்டு
வளைசெங் கையிற்சி றந்த வொளிகண் டுநித்தி லங்கு
விதவிங் கிதப்ரி யங்கள் நகைகொஞ் சுதற்கு ணங்கள்
விடுசங் கையற்று ணர்ந்து வலம்வந் துனைப்பு கழ்ந்து
நதியுந் திருக்க ரந்தை மதியுஞ் சடைக்க ணிந்த
நகமங் கையிற்பி டுங்கு மசுரன் சிரத்தொ டங்கம்
சிதையும் படிக்கொ ரம்பு தனைமுன் தொடுத்த கொண்டல்
தினமுங் கருத்து ணர்ந்து சுரர்வந் துறப்ப ணிந்த
reading: The poet describes women with breasts like a rutting elephant's tusks under gem necklaces, with bangled hands, whose varied pleasing ways, smiles and coaxing he sees in excess, and asks not to be confused and deluded but, with doubt gone, to circle Murugan, praise him and receive the golden feet. The praise names Siva who wears the river, basil and moon and dances at Kailasa, and Vishnu who shot the arrow that shattered the heads and jewelled arms of the asura who tried to uproot that mountain, as Murugan's uncle, at the holy hall the gods worship daily.
nuance: The song is a twin of 465 in metre and opening (the breasts as an elephant's two tusks). The praise links two Ravana stories: the one who tried to pluck Kailasa in his hands (நகம் அங்கையில் பிடுங்கும் அசுரன்) is the one Rama's arrow destroyed. வலம்வந்து: the plea names the temple rite of circling.

reading: The poet describes women with moon faces, bow brows, carp eyes, cloud-dark hair, parrot speech and conch-white smiles, and lovemaking with them on the bed as Kama and Rati's pleasure, hair loosened, words faltering and eyes closing; he asks that even then Murugan grant him, alone as he is, the blissful moon faces and the beauty of the feet. The praise calls Sivakami the letter A, the life of all, who is also Hari and grows as a light in the poet's eye, and Murugan her son, whose vel destroyed the asura's army and before whom Brahma's head broke, the lord of Valli and Devayanai at the hall in southern Puliyur.
nuance: The plea seems not to ask to leave the bed but to be given Murugan's faces and feet there (மயல்கொண்டு அணைகீனும் ... அருள்வாயே), as 468 says outright. அகரம் திரு உயிர் பண்புற அரி என்பதுமாகி: Sivakami is the letter A and the life of letters, and also Hari, the Saiva teaching that Vishnu is a form of the Goddess. மறையன் தலை உடையும்படி may allude to Brahma's punishment.

reading: The poet describes women with moon-like earrings, Mandara-like breasts, champak-wreathed hair like cloud, carp eyes, crescent brows, kovai lips and conch necks, coaxing like heavenly dancers, and says that even if he sports with them on the bed in single desire, he will hold Murugan's twelve holy eyes and twelve strong arms. The praise shows Indra's world restored, sun and moon moving again and the Sura hosts dying, and Murugan teaching the mantra to Vishnu, Brahma, the sun, moon, Siva and Indra, with Valli, at the great hall of Chidambaram beside the Sivaganga tank that devotees call a pool of Tamil wisdom.
nuance: பஞ்சணை மீது குலாவினும் ... கொள்வேனே: unlike most songs, the plea does not renounce the women but vows to keep the Lord's form even in their embrace. மனு நூல் விளம்பிய: மனு is probably mantra, so this is Murugan as teacher of the gods. செந்தமிழ் ஞான தடாகம் ... சிவகங்கை: the temple tank is praised as a pool of Tamil wisdom.

tamil: காய மாய வீடு மீறிய கூடு நந்து
காசி லாசை தேடி வாழ்வினை நாடி யிந்த்ரி
வேயி லாய தோள மாமட வார்கள் பங்க
வேத கீத போத மோனமெய் ஞான நந்த
மாய வீர தீர சூரர்கள் பாற நின்ற
வாகை வேடர் பேதை காதல வேழ மங்கை
ஆயும் வேத கீத மேழிசை பாட வஞ்சே
ஆதி நாத ராடு நாடக சாலை யம்ப
reading: The poet calls the body a house of illusion, a nest that perishes like a bubble, a hut in which he daily seeks money and livelihood with his senses whirling and his mind astray, and asks not to suffer clinging to bamboo-shouldered women but to be given the single release that is complete in Vedic song, knowledge, silence, true wisdom and bliss. The praise names the vel that split the mountain, Valli's lover, the Vel of Senthil, the light where the Vedas, the seven notes and the five syllables sound, and the lord at the dance hall of the First Lord at Chidambaram.
nuance: காயம் மாய வீடு ... நந்து புற்புதம்: the body is a house of maya and a perishing bubble, an image the Naladiyar also uses. The goal is a single release (இன்ப முத்தி ஒன்று) in which Veda, knowledge, silence and bliss are all fulfilled. The song names both Senthil and Chidambaram.

reading: The poet heaps names on himself, man of vile qualities, ghoul-formed, dull and stupid, low in conduct, helpless, cruel, braggart, bound to the five elements, a waste born of a ruined womb, rotten, angry, shrouded by ill fortune, sinner, eunuch, drunkard who heeds no advice, and asks when Murugan will rule this dog of a servant. The praise names the serpent king of the netherworld, the Chola king of Manu's way and Indra praising the lord of Puliyur, and ends in a litany of 'namo nama' to the one who dances in the hall, gives the highest state by his sight, and burned the three cities.
nuance: The self-abuse is the longest yet, a run of rhymed names in -னை. The closing litany (சிவசிவ ஹரஹர தேவா நமோநம ... திரிபுரம் எரிசெய்த கோவே நமோநம) gives Murugan the acts of Siva, the dancer and burner of the three cities, or else turns to hail Siva himself; the text does not separate them. The serpent king (பாதாள லோகன்) is probably Patanjali of the Chidambaram legend; several of the abusive names are obscure.

reading: A yogic song: the poet asks whether, binding the fire at the root, driving it up to the crown, with bindu and sound crying out, mounting the white horse of mantra and attention, passing through the radiant hall, binding the bindu with the moon so it does not slip, burning the three cities to ash and striking down the tattvas, he will reach his Father's feet with sorrow burnt, eat wisdom, his body hard as diamond and golden, and praise Murugan. The praise calls Murugan the guru who spoke into the poet's ear the 'eight and two' he did not know, saying 'this is the lingam'; who, as a merchant, told the meaning to Siva who once sold bangles as a merchant in Sivakami's town; and who went to the forest as a merchant to win Valli, at the hall in Puliyur.
nuance: The plea is a map of the yogic ascent: fire (அங்கி) at the base, the cosmos above, bindu and nada, the moon, the burning of the three cities taken inwardly as the bonds, the tattvas falling, the body turned to diamond (குடில் வச்சிரங்களென). எட்டிரண்டு, 'eight and two', recurs six times; in Tamil numerals அ is eight and உ two, so the guru's teaching may be the letters of Om or Siva and Shakti, while elsewhere the phrase is the ten directions. செட்டி: Siva's bangle-selling and Murugan's courting of Valli are both played as merchant disguises.

reading: The poet says that, judging it evil to trust deceitful talebearers with poisoned minds, he sought Murugan's feet with love and cried 'our father, refuge', and asks whether this has not reached his ear, or whether his eyes are on his women; no one can defy his word, the burden is his, and the poet has no other helper, so let him come and appear as he did for the gods. The praise shows Murugan knocking Brahma on the head, embracing Valli and shaking the mountains and seas, the lord of Siva who dances in the hall at Puliyur.
nuance: உன்செவிக் கேறலைகொல் பெண்கள்மெற் பார்வையைகொல்: the poet chides the Lord, asking whether he is deaf or too busy looking at his wives, an intimacy of complaint. உன்றனக்கே பரமும்: the burden of saving him belongs to the Lord. The knock on Brahma's head (கஞ்சனைத் தாவி முடி முன்பு குட்டே) recalls the Om story without naming Om.

reading: A short song: the poet asks not to waver in mind over women with breasts like red pots until his body wastes, but to be given grace so that he melts in love. The praise names Murugan who holds the banner in his red hand, the poet who knows fine words, the son of Uma, growing in the hall.
nuance: செஞ்சொல்தெரி புலவோனே: Murugan is himself the poet who discerns fine speech.

reading: The poet runs through a woman's beauty, cloud hair, bow brows, carp-arrow eyes, moon forehead, areca neck, bamboo arms, mountain breasts, lotus hands, plantain thighs, drum waist and fine silk, and calls such women, dancing like peacocks, without good qualities; he asks whether he must be caught in their net and perish, and asks for Murugan's love. The praise names Sivai, the self-born, the beauty of all worlds, as his mother, the fiery vel thrown at the asura army, Vishnu who killed Ravana and holds the fourteen worlds as his uncle, and Devayanai and Valli, at Chidambaram.
nuance: The beauty is catalogued only to be set against இயல் குணமிலாத வியன் செயலார், women of display with no good nature. பொருள் சங்க மாதர் may mean women joined for money, but the division is unsure.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking in detail, hair loosening, garlands crushed, eyes troubled, sandal paste washed by sweat, lips tasted like jackfruit segments and voices cooing like doves and peacocks, and asks whether he, a dog, must be ruined and fall with his body wasting. The praise shows the battle in drum syllables, Sura's crown smashed and the seven seas dried by the vel, Murugan dancing, and Chidambaram of mango groves, cuckoos, plantain and cane, where Sivakami and the hunter girl bow to him.
nuance: The plea is only a question at the end of the scene (நாயென அழிந்து விழுந்து உடல் மங்குவேனோ): the ruin is the body's fading.

tamil: அத்த னன்னை யில்லம் வைத்த சொன்னம் வெள்ளி
அத்து பண்ணு கல்வி சுற்ற மென்னு மல்ல
முத்த னென்ன வல்லை யத்த னென்ன வள்ளி
முட்ட வெண்மை யுள்ள பட்ட னெண்மை கொள்ளு
தித்தி மன்னு தில்லை நிர்த்தர் கண்ணி னுள்ளு
சித்தி மன்னு செய்ய சத்தி துன்னு கைய
பத்த ருண்மை சொல்லு ளுற்ற செம்மல் வெள்ளி
பச்சை வன்னி யல்லி செச்சை சென்னி யுள்ள
reading: The poet asks that, free of the trouble called father, mother, house, stored gold and silver, the rich who seek them, learning and kin, he sing Murugan as best he can, and asks whether this complete fool's withering will not end while his heart fails to know him as the freed one, the swift one, the Lord, Valli's beloved. The praise names Murugan the child born from the eye of the dancer of Thillai, holding the red vel of power, worn by devotees who speak the truth, and embracing Devayanai, with green vanni, lilies and vetchi on his head and the green peacock.
nuance: கல்வி stands in the list of bonds with gold, silver and kin: learning too is a trouble (அல்லல்) to be shed before one can sing. Each line pair turns on repeated syllables (அத்தன், அத்தை, அத்து; முத்தன், முத்தன், முட்டன்), so several words (அத்து, பட்டன், முத்தன்) can be read more than one way.

reading: The poet speaks of women who show dark hair, bow brows, eyes like killing lilies, jasmine smiles and creeper waists, who show delusion and then show poverty, and asks whether Murugan, who can show the path that does not end at the burning ground, show good understanding and slowly wither karma, should let him suffer. The praise names Murugan the young lord of Thillai, which shows clarity, the ancient Veda and rich speech, Valli of the millet field, the one who shows grace and the path of learning, and the good lord of devotees who praise his feet.
nuance: The verb காட்டு, to show, runs through every line: the women show their charms and then poverty (நல்குரவு காட்டும்), the Lord shows the path past the cremation ground (இடுகாட்டின் எல்லை நடவாத வழி), and Thillai shows wisdom. The play joins காட்டு with இடுகாடு, the burning ground.

tamil: றுள் ளதுகில் நூலிடைக் காமபண் டார அல் குல்
reading: The poet runs through a woman's beauty from smile to anklets, her walk swaying in silk, and calls such women plunderers of gold like skilled thieves, and asks whether infatuation with them is fitting. The praise names Murugan who, so that troubling deeds and the gunas flee, holds the poet's heart as his own and rules it, who taught the seed of wisdom to delight his father, Valli whom the poet calls his own mother, the vel, and the lord who rejoices at the tower of Thillai with Devayanai, sung in clear Tamil.
nuance: பொற் சூறை கொண்டார்கள்: the women plunder gold like raiders. எந்தாதை மகிழ ... ஞானவித்து ஓது: Murugan teaching his father the seed of wisdom, the Om story without the word. என்னுடைய தாய்: Valli is called the poet's mother.

title: சிதம்பரம்
theme: Songs at Chidambaram (சிதம்பரம், 3 of 5), many sung at its towers (கோபுரம்): the poet confesses to women who demand money, plunder and cheat, catalogues the body and its diseases, imagines his death and cremation, and asks for the feet, wisdom and the company of devotees; the praise turns on Siva's dance at Puliyur, Murugan as Siva's teacher, and the gopurams of the temple.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (479, 481 to 484, 486, 489, 491, 492); the body and its diseases (480, 485, 487); death and cremation (490) and countless births (493); and an akam song in the voice of a lovesick girl's companion (488). The towers are named: south (480), west (481 to 484), north (485), all four (486).
source_issues: Song 486: one corrupt character in காலினு஡புர (line 7), probably காலின் நூபுர, 'the anklets of the feet', with ஡ for ஊ; also the unflagged garbles காரிர் பாருமை யாசி வாபத (line 12) and யீண (line 20).
Song 487: one corrupt character in புற்றெழுதலு஡சல் (line 3), probably ஊசல், with ஡ for ஊ.
Song 492: unflagged garbles சிவகா மிககொரு (line 17, probably சிவகாமிக்கு ஒரு) and சுக்முழ் கி (line 24, probably சுகம் மூழ்கி).
Song 479: unflagged garble போதக் மீதென (line 12).
Song 488: வருகொவே (line 14) is probably வருகோவே.

reading: The poet describes women who grab a man's side, press shoulder to shoulder, bite his lips, loosen their ornaments, say 'give money', wink and talk, coax with feigned love and then pick quarrels, and calls himself the fool who wanders in the blame of these tricksters; he asks for grace to reach the supreme and Murugan's feet. The praise shows Murugan crushing the Suras with a club, Devayanai on a golden couch and Valli of the millet field, and Siva who danced to the drum's beat beyond the knowing of Brahma and Vishnu, at the tower of the Tiruchitrambalam.
nuance: தாபணமே என: the women's demand for money is quoted in their own words. பசப்பிப் பின் பிணக்கைக் கூறிய: feigned love followed by the made-up quarrel is the courtesan's way of ending a spent man's welcome. The plea's last words (பரத்துற் றண்பதத்துப் போதக் மீதென) are garbled.

reading: The poet calls the body a hut of bone, rheum, marrow, brain, phlegm, water, hair and skin, crammed with pus, worms and flesh, its nerves like tubes, where the tricksters of the senses dwell; he says the desires for women and for land, with evil and fated deeds and time, have gathered in it, and asks not to spread in sorrow but to be given the feet that rise to the release of Sadasiva and the supreme world. The praise shows the battle in drum syllables, the Suras drowned with their chariots and horses as food for the vel, Siva dancing, and Murugan on the peacock with Valli at the southern tower.
nuance: ஆசை பெணாசை மணாசைகள்: the familiar triad of cravings (woman, land, gold) appears with gold folded into ஆசை. தீவினை ஊழ்வினை காலமொடு: deed, fated deed and time are named together as the forces that keep him in sorrow.

reading: The poet describes women whose breasts are like elephants ready for war, with hearts as dry as the cane waste from the mill, who seem like lovers while thinking only of whose wealth they can take, and whose long eyes are a net like the spears of Death's messengers; he asks for grace not to be joined in lust with these tricksters who cast down the lustful drowned in love's sea. The praise shows Murugan as a lion against the Suras on the blue peacock, Vishnu who shot Ravana's crowns as his uncle, and Brahma and the gods worshipping at the western tower in Puliyur.
nuance: ஆலைக் கோதினில் ஈரமிலா மனம்: their hearts have no more moisture than the crushed cane thrown from the mill. ஆருக்கே பொருளாம் என நினைவதனாலே: their thought is only whose money it will be. The eyes are காலத் தூதர் கை வேல், Death's messengers' spears, so the courtesan and Death are drawn together.

tamil: காதைக் காதி மெத்த மோதிக் கேள்வி யற்ற
தேமற் பார வெற்பில் மூழ்கித் தாப மிக்க
மாதைக் காத லித்து வேடக் கான கத்து
வாரிக் கேயொ ளித்த மாயச் சூரை வெட்டி
வீதித் தேர்ந டத்து தூளத் தால ருக்கன்
மேலைக் கோபு ரத்து மேவிக் கேள்வி மிக்க
reading: The poet describes women whose eyes reach to the ears and wound like carp, with cloud-dark hair, who play proudly in the shade of groves and stir lust that heeds no counsel, and asks to be given the path that escapes the burning evil of drowning in their breasts. The praise shows Murugan walking through the hunters' forest for love of Valli until his fragrant feet reddened, cutting down Sura who hid in the sea, and Puliyur where the dust of chariots in the streets hides the sun's chariot, at the western tower praised by learned Vedic priests.
nuance: வாசத் தாள் சிவப்ப வருவோனே: the god's feet redden from walking to Valli, a tender picture against the battle praise. கேள்வி அற்ற காமப் பூசல்: lust is a quarrel deaf to instruction.

reading: The poet lists women: greedy plunderers, skilled deceivers, collectors who take a toll, killers with their eyes, gamblers in speech, coral-lipped and cruel, who pain the heart while seeming close and hide enmity within, and asks that he, a dog wandering in maya, be saved by Murugan coming with golden shoulders, twelve hands, the kadamba garland and six faces, and giving inner wisdom. The praise shows the vel thrown at Taraka, Rama whose golden foot turned a stone into a fair form as he went to the forest, Devayanai joined as promised, and Valli, at the western tower of Thillai.
nuance: சூறைகள் கொள்ளும் ஆயக்காரிகள்: the women are toll collectors who plunder, a picture of love as a tax. கல்லிலே பொற்றாள் படவே அது நல்ல ரூபத்தே வர: the stone that became a woman at Rama's touch is Ahalya, named only by the deed.

reading: The poet lists the arts by which women give infatuation, flowered hair, anklet feet, rhythm of hands, sly talk, scented smiles, contrary speech, swan gait, breasts and their cloth, and their haughty price in coin, and says he sinks daily in their sea of lust; he asks for grace to join Murugan's devotees, the silent jnanis. The praise names Vishnu who came when the elephant cried 'root of the four Vedas' as his uncle, Sivakami as his mother, the three thousand Vedic priests of Puliyur who worship daily by sacrifice, and Murugan on the peacock at the western tower, tall as Meru.
nuance: The plea's remedy is company: மோன ஞானிகளுடனே சேரவும், to join the silent knowers. மேன்மை மூவாயிர வேதியர்: the three thousand Brahmins of Thillai, the temple's hereditary priests. The elephant's cry is the Gajendra story, as in 25.

reading: The poet catalogues the body, bone, skin, hair, nerves, pus, worms, brain, a sea of blood, a pot of filth, and its diseases, fatigue, anaemia, wind, rib pain, colic, asthma, hernia, fever, diabetes, phlegm, deafness, hunchback, cholera, blindness, lameness, dumbness and scrofula, and confesses that, taking this flawed dwelling as permanent, he wanders by ruinous deeds; he asks for the feet, wisdom and love. The praise names the Goddess who rides the old golden bull, Siva who pressed Ravana down under his foot when he lifted the mountain, and Valli, at the northern tower in Puliyur.
nuance: குடிப்புக்கு ஊனம் இதே சதமாம் என எடுத்து: the fault is not having a diseased body but taking it for a lasting home. Siva's name is given in the five syllables (சிவாயநமோ).

reading: The poet describes women with dark hair, swinging earrings, dancing ornaments and ringing anklets, who walk like peacocks and speak words sweet as milk, women for a price, and calls himself the fool who, loving them, drowns in ruinous deeds and sinks into the seven hells; he asks for Siva's son's feet. The praise shows Murugan on the peacock with the vel, the seas and islands shaken and the asuras reduced to rubbish, Uma, Vishnu's sister who never leaves Siva's side, and Murugan with Devayanai at the four towers of Puliyur, land of wisdom.
nuance: விலைமாதர்: the women are named by their price. ஞான பூமியதான பேர்புலியூர்: Chidambaram is called the land of wisdom. The plea's last line (காரிர் பாருமை யாசி வாபத) is garbled.

reading: The poet lists the body's diseases, wind, bile, colic, abscess, stone, phlegm, cough, scrofula, blindness, deafness, dumbness, piles and dropsy, calls it a body eaten by the ninety-six tattvas, and confesses wandering in many guises, gripped by the poison of desire for wealth; he asks whether, instead of building houses, falling into infatuation and dying with his voice gone, his mind will not think of the pure space where the peacock dances, which gives release. The praise names Siva of the five syllables, helper of pure devotees, with green Uma, as Murugan's father, Murugan as the younger brother of Vinayaka who taught the supreme one the primal meaning, and the lord of Valli at the golden crystal tower of Puliyur.
nuance: தொண்ணூற்றாறு தத்துவர்கள் உண்ட காயம்: the ninety-six tattvas are pictured as eaters of the body. மயிலாடு சுத்தவெளி: release is a pure space where the peacock dances, the Lord's vehicle become the image of the goal. பரப்பிரமன் ஆதி உற்ற பொருள் ஓதுவித்த: the Om story, with Siva as the supreme one taught, though the phrase may be divided otherwise.

reading: In the voice of a lovesick girl's companion or mother, the singer says the girl, an innocent doe, is ruined by the cuckoos calling in every grove, the cold north wind, Kama's fragrant arrows, the gossip of women who follow her, the flower bed and the bell of the returning bull, and asks Murugan, knowing her plight, to give her his honeyed garland. The praise shows the elephant that frightened Valli into Murugan's arms, Siva who dances in the hall at Perumpatrappuliyur among cane fields, Murugan who comes on the peacock to end devotees' sorrow, and the vel that rolled Sura over.
nuance: This is akam poetry with no confession of the poet's own: the signs of evening (the bull's bell, the cold wind) and the women's gossip (மாதர் வசை) are classical. The garland asked for (மது மாலை) is the lover's token that would make the love public.
