nuance: The rhythm is a chain of short past-tense verbs (பொறுத்தார் பரித்தார் சிரித்தார் எரித்தார் ...), each act of Siva one beat. The song closes on முருகோனே, not பெருமாளே.

reading: The poet asks whether he will reach the true reality that is beyond the reach of those on the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga, that the divisions of sects cannot approach, beyond Parasakti and beyond turiya, the single flame of supreme jnana pervading all, the stainless state of sayujya and the bliss-form beyond words. The praise names Murugan, who gave the poet grace to sing the glorious Thiruppugazh of the Kumara whose vel rolled Sura over, and Kathirkamam hill in Ilam, where black monkeys tear open jackfruits and play among plantains and mangoes.
nuance: The goal lies past every path the Saiva system names: சரியை, கிரியை and யோகம் fall short, சமயபேதம் cannot come near, and the state is above துரியம். திருப்புகழை ஓதற்கு எனக்கு அருள்வோனே: the book names itself as Murugan's gift. ஈழம் places Kathirkamam in Lanka. சுகசெர்ரு பத்தை is a garble, probably சுகசொரூபத்தை.

reading: The poet describes women with heavy pearl-hung breasts, honey-sweet song-like speech, flower-arrow eyes, dark hair and makara earrings, and asks whether he, the lustful man caught in them, will come to forget even the feet that made him forget desire. The praise names Vishnu who crushed the ten-headed one in the city the sun feared to cross, and Murugan at fierce Kathirkamam on the triangular hill of gems, caught in Valli's feet, waist and spear-like eyes on the millet hill.
nuance: The song is built on a mirror: the poet is caught (அகப்பட்ட) by women's eyes, and Murugan ends caught (அகப்பட்ட) by Valli's spear-eyes. ஆசையை மறப்பித்த கால்களை மறக்கைக்கும் வருமோ may instead ask whether he will ever forget his desire; the division is uncertain.

reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love: wounded by Madana's flower bow and burned by the full moon above the walls, weeping pearls from both eyes through the night, she is wasting away in deep infatuation, and the speaker asks Murugan to come and give her life. The praise names his jewelled chest that delighted in the hunter girl, his form of gold and ruby, Murugan near to his devotees, the first of release, the hero on the green peacock whose vel broke Sura.
nuance: An akam lament in another's voice (இவளை வாழ்விக்க வரவேணும்), not the poet's confession. The torments are the classical ones, Kama's bow and the moon at night, with the tears as pearls (முத்தம்).

reading: A short song that judges rather than confesses: those who wander under women's power, who roam without thinking of great austerity, and who do not recite and bow so that evil leaves them will shine in the fire of hell. The praise names Murugan the light of nada, of good qualities, the vel who embraces two women, the Kumara of Sivajnana, the flawless lord of Kathirkamam.
nuance: தீநரக மீதில் திகழ்வாரே: 'they will shine in hell's fire' is ironic, the verb of glory used for the damned. The song speaks of others in the third person, unusual in a book of first-person pleas.

tamil: முதிரு மார வார நட்பொ டிலகு மார வார மெற்றி
முடிவி லாத தோர் வடக்கி லெரியு மால மார்பி டத்து
வெதிரி லாயர் வாயில் வைத்து மதுர ராக நீடி சைக்கும்
விளையு மோக போக முற்றி அளவி லாத காதல் பெற்ற
கதிர காம மாந கர்க்கு ளெதிரி லாத வேல்த ரித்த
கயலு லாம்வி லோச னத்தி களப மார்ப யோத ரத்தி
அதிர வீசி யாடும் வெற்றி விடையி லேறு மீசர் கற்க
அகில லோக மீது சுற்றி யசுரர் லோக நீறெ ழுப்பி
reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love: tormented by the roaring sea, by the moon that rises burning from the poison of the northern fire, by the sweet raga of the cowherds' bamboo flute and by her mothers' unending scolding, she has come to boundless love, and the speaker asks Murugan to come and embrace her. The praise names the god of Kathirkamam with the matchless vel and the bright peacock, the husband of the one of the sky (Devayanai), who gave the bull-riding Isa the hard word of jnana, and who scattered the demons' world to ash so the gods' world might live.
nuance: The sea, moon and flute are the evening torments of separated lovers in classical akam; the cowherd's flute is the Kural's image (1228). அரிய ஞான வாசகத்தை அருள்வோனே is the teaching of Siva, without Om being named. விகட மாதை, 'the bold girl', may describe her daring in love.

tamil: வருபவர்க ளோலை கொண்டு நமனுடைய தூத ரென்று
மயலதுபொ லாத வம்பன் விரகுடைய னாகு மென்று
கருவியத னாலெ றிந்து சதைகள்தனை யேய ரிந்து
கழுமுனையி லேயி ரென்று விடுமெனும வேளை கண்டு
பரகிரியு லாவு செந்தி மனையினுட னேயி டும்பன்
பதிகள் பல வாயி ரங்கள் மலைகள்வெகு கோடி நின்ற
அரவுபிறை பூளை தும்பை விலுவமொடு தூர்வை கொன்றை
அரகரசி வாய சம்புலத குருபரகு மார நம்பு
reading: The poet pictures Yama's messengers coming with the palm leaf, seizing him by the waist-cloth, following him with abuse ('a wicked rogue, a cheat in his infatuation'), striking him with weapons, cutting his flesh and pouring out his dark blood until they say 'lay him on the stake', and asks Murugan to come quickly before him at that hour. The praise names the Kumaresa of Senthil, of Idumban and of Palani, who came to Kathirkamam for devotees to see after standing in thousands of shrines and countless hills, the son of the matted-haired Siva who wears serpent, crescent, vilvam and konrai, the guru who came to rule those who trust him.
nuance: Death's men here are torturers rather than a summons: the abuse, the cutting and the stake (கழுமுனை) belong more to pictures of hell than to the deathbed songs. The Kathirkamam shrine is presented as the place Murugan came to after all his other shrines.

reading: The poet lists the arts of women who glare with sword-like eyes, sway their breasts, loosen their clothes, laugh, let down their hair, embrace on the bed and bite the lips until shame is gone, and asks whether, caught in the net of these sinners, he must lie diseased on a mat, pale, hungry and thirsty like a dog. The praise names Rama, who killed Tataka with one arrow, guarded the sacrifice and broke the great bow, as uncle; Murugan as guru of the father who plucked Brahma's head and burned Kama; the hero on the peacock that shook the serpent's thousand heads and split the mountain; and the lord with Uma who lives in dharma.
nuance: The consequence of lust is disease and degradation in this life (நோய் பிணி கிடத்து பாய்மிசை வெளுத்து), not hell. The closing அருக்கொணா மலை is not Kathirkamam, and may be Thirukkonamalai (see 650).

title: திருக்கோணமலை
theme: The one song at Thirukkonamalai (திருக்கோணமலை) in Lanka: the poet confesses drowning in desire for women who sell their bodies, mocked by the world and sick in a body of filth, and asks to be saved by singing Murugan in verse; the praise makes Murugan the meaning that comes alive in the verses of the sages and Tamil poets.
source_issues: Song 650: one corrupt character in மயலு஡றி (line 259), probably மயலூறி.
Song 649, filed under Kathirkamam, closes on அருக்கொணாமலை and may belong to this shrine.

reading: The poet confesses that, drowning in desire for women who glitter with girdles and jewels on bodies put up for sale, he became the great lustful man the world laughs at, toiling and exhausted, and asks Murugan, the one life who lets him cross over by telling him in verse, not to let him suffer in disease in this cage of filth, but to look with grace on the dog who seeks and praises him and give him the grace of his feet. The praise names the son of Sivakami's lord, the six-faced teacher, the one who comes as the meaning in the verses of Vasishtha, Kashyapa, the yogis, Agastya, Idaikkadar and Keeran, who comes to the gopuram gateway at Thirukkonamalai, and whose vel powdered the sea of seven births.
nuance: விலைக்கு மேனி: the women's bodies are 'for a price', so the courtesan's trade is named. உனைக் கவிக்குள்ளாய்ச் சொலிக் கடைத்தேறவே: the way out is to put the god into verse. வகுத்த பாவினில் பொருட்கோலமாய் வரு: Murugan is the meaning-form that comes in the poems of the sages and of Tamil poets such as Idaikkadar and Nakkirar (கீரன்). The words about parrots and பூதி at the gopuram gate are obscure.

title: காசி
theme: Songs at Kasi (காசி) on the Ganga: a sinner and gambler who never wore the holy ash asks to see the feet and gain jnana; a life traced from conception in the womb to the women who ruin it; and a body gone hollow like a wood-apple, with Murugan as the victor over the Jains.
source_issues: Song 653: one corrupt character in மயலு஡றி (line 338), probably மயலூறி.

reading: The poet confesses that he is a sinner on earth, a fool steeped in gambling, a thief of the mind's discipline, a vain man burning with desire who thought only of ways to keep spear-eyed women, a man of two deeds who never wore the true holy ash that the lovers of the full Sivajnana scriptures wear, and asks Murugan to smear it on him, let him see the red feet and grant the awakening of jnana. The praise names Vishnu who came when the crocodile seized the elephant, Siva who burned the three cities to ash, and Murugan who recited the Saiva scripture before the righteous, the jnana-speaking Kumara of the forest girl, at Kasi.
nuance: பூசு மெய்த்திரு நீறிடா இருவினையேனைப் பூசி: the verb is repeated, 'me who did not smear it, smear', so the poet asks the god to put the ash on him himself. காரணக்குறியான நீதியரானவர்க்கு முன்னாகவே நெறி காவியச் சிவநூலை ஓதிய may refer to a particular telling of a Saiva text before an assembly; the allusion is not clear.

reading: The poet traces his making: the union of a man and a woman, the seed growing within by Brahma's will, the embryo taking shape like a grub, a ball, a palm fruit, a tender coconut and a pot by the way of deeds, ten months passing until it comes head down into the world, the parents calling it their child, the milk, the crawling and the toddling; then he asks whether he must perish through big-eyed women. The praise tells of Narasimha bursting from a pillar to tear Hiranya's body for the boy who said Hari was there, names Narayana of the conch and discus asleep on the serpent at Srirangam as uncle, and Parameswari at Siva's side as mother, at Kasi on the Ganga.
nuance: The growth of the embryo by stages of size (பந்து, பனைபழம், இளநீர், குடம்) and the tenth month head down (திங்கட் பதுசெல வேதலை கீழுற) is a formula the book repeats (see 520). The whole of the plea is the life story; the fault is named only in its last words, the women.

reading: A short song: the poet asks that, with his body become like a wood-apple eaten by an elephant and pervaded by infatuation, wearied daily like the boorish, he not be let to wither, but be given grace. The praise names Murugan the crest-jewel who won the debate when the Jain lords went to the stake, the hero on the peacock, son of Umapati of the dark throat, at Kasi by the Ganga.
nuance: வேழம் உண்ட விளாங்கனி: the proverbial wood-apple that the elephant leaves whole outside and empty within, an image of a body hollowed while it looks intact. அமணீசர்கள் கழுவேற வாதில் வென்ற is Sambandar's victory at Madurai, so Murugan is again identified with Sambandar (639, 641, 666).

title: மாயாபுரி
theme: The one song at Mayapuri (மாயாபுரி): a short and obscure song that seems to read the letters சி, அ and ம as Sivajnana, scattered desire and the fall into maya, and asks for grace not to dwell on maya.
source_issues: Song 654: the song names no shrine; its placement under Mayapuri rests on the heading alone.

reading: A short, obscure song. It seems to say that living by tasting the letter சி is Sivajnana, that scattering and wandering is the desire for action, and that falling as the letter ம draws near is great maya, and asks for grace not to cling to it in thought. The praise, also hard to divide, names a Lord who poured compassion so that the suns in the sky might enter, with the letter அ again in its first line; no shrine is named.
nuance: சிகரம், அகரம், மகரம் can be read as 'the letter சி', 'the letter அ', 'the letter ம'. In the doctrine of the five letters (சிவாயநம) சி stands for Siva and ம for malam, which would fit சிகரம் with சிவஞானம் and மகரம் with மாயை; but சிகரம் can also mean a summit, and the reading is a guess. The shrine's name Mayapuri may be played on in மாயை.

title: வயிரவிவனம்
theme: The one song at Vayiravivanam (வயிரவிவனம்) on the Saraswati river: a plea for the jnana to bow at the feet of those who keep Murugan's feet in mind, with Murugan as the guru who told Brahma the first word.

tamil: அருவரை யெடுத்த வீர னெரிபட விரற்க ளூணு
அலைகட லடைத்த ராமன் மிகமன மகிழ்ச்சி கூரு
பருதியி னொளிக்கண் வீறும் அறுமுக நிரைத்த தோள்ப
பதமல ருளத்தி னாளு நினைவுறு கருத்தர் தாள்கள்
சுருதிக ளுரைத்த வேத னுரைமொழி தனக் குளாதி
சுரர்பதி தழைத்து வாழ அமர்சிறை யனைத்து மீள
மருமலர் மணக்கும் வாச நிறைதரு தருக்கள் சூழும்
வளமுறு தடத்தி னோடு சரஸ்வதி நதிக்கண் வீறு
reading: The poet asks Murugan to grant him the jnana to bow at the feet of those who think daily in their hearts of his flower feet. The praise names him son of the Mother who dwells with Hara, whose toes crushed the hero who lifted the mountain, nephew of Rama who bridged the sea, six-faced and twelve-armed in the sun's light, the jnana guru who told Brahma, the speaker of the Vedas, to say the first word within his own speech, the vel that freed the gods, at Vayiravivanam on the Saraswati amid fragrant groves and blue-lily pools.
nuance: The plea is twice removed: not for the feet, but to bow at the feet of those who hold his feet in mind (கருத்தர் தாள்கள் பணிய), service of devotees as the form of jnana. சுருதிகள் உரைத்த வேதன் உரைமொழி தனக்குள் ஆதி சொலு: the challenge to Brahma to speak the first word is the Om episode, but Om is not named.

title: வெள்ளிகரம்
theme: Songs at Vellikaram (வெள்ளிகரம்), the 'silver town' (வெள்ளிநகர்) among paddy fields near Valli's hill: the poet confesses his infatuation with women and his body ruled by the five senses, and asks for the silence beyond words, for the instruction that melts the heart, and for words to proclaim Murugan; the praise turns again and again on Valli and on Murugan himself made a lover.
structure_note: 656 and 657 share a closing line on the blooming lotus of Vellikaram; 658 to 663 are a run of short songs tightly built on doubled ல்ல and ள்ள, with shared refrains (658, 659: அடையலர் செல்வம் அளறிடை செல்ல; 660, 661: வெய்ய சைய வில்லி சொல்லை வெல்ல வல்ல; 662, 663: வெள்ளிமணி மாட மல்குதிரு வீதி). Women (658 to 661, 663), the senses and silence (656), proclaiming the god (657, 659, 662), and 664, a praise song of Murugan the madal-riding lover, Kannappa and Krishna.
source_issues: Song 664: two corrupt characters, in உலு஡கல (line 533, probably உலூகல, 'mortar') and வயலு஡டிடை (line 537, probably வயலூடிடை).
The heading is வெள்ளிகரம், while the songs name the town வெள்ளிநகர் (658 to 664) and வெள்ளிகரம் (656, 657).

reading: The poet tells how, in this body swarmed by the five that follow Brahma's ordaining, in the wave-girt world, battered by the five quarrelsome ones and stumbling, a servant in distress, he asks that heart, word and body reach their end, the world's infatuation leave him, and, with himself gone, to gain Murugan's feet, Murugan tell him the one thing that marks the bound of silence. The praise pictures Valli's breasts, face and ears like vallai leaves, names Murugan who wrote his emerald form on the madal and stood in Valli's field, the guru of self-born Siva of the silver mountain, at Vellikaram of the blooming lotus.
nuance: எனது அற நினது கழல் பெற: the feet are gained when 'mine' ends. மவுன எல்லை குறிப்பது ஒன்று புகல்வாயே asks to be told the one word that points to silence, a paradox the book returns to. The ஐவர் are the five senses, pictured as quarrelsome masters. The opening (அடல் அரி மகவு விதி) is hard to divide.

reading: The poet asks whether the golden feet can be gained except by words that make all the world know Murugan's emblems: the dancing peacock that broke the peaks, the fresh kadamba, the small sword-like vel, the lotus faces, the fighting cock in his hand, and his name as Valli's husband of the Aivana hill. The praise names him the incomparable son of Siva, the guru of the discourse beyond words, the beautiful one under the old nelli tree where the cowherds pass with their herds, the great life of Siva who wears Ganga, the moon, konrai and vilvam, at Vellikaram.
nuance: The plea makes proclaiming the god the only road to his feet (மொழியின் அல்லது ... பெறலாமோ), while the praise calls him the teacher of a discourse beyond words (நிர்வசன ப்ரசங்க குருநாதா): speech is the poet's way, wordlessness the god's teaching.

reading: The poet tells of desiring women whose jasmine-white teeth and sweet speech, ear-rings, slender waists and breasts draw him into a union that brings worry, and asks Murugan instead to give gently his red feet, adorned with a garland of clear verse and fragrant flowers. The praise names Valli, born of the lone spotted doe with which the ascetic sage played, whose millet Murugan slowly ate in the field on Valli's hill, and Murugan of the beautiful silver town who destroys the assemblies of those who preach false paths and makes enemies' wealth sink in the mire.
nuance: The plea offers a garland of verse (கவிமாலை) for the feet, the poet's song set against the union. அவநெறி சொல்லும் அவரவை கொல்லும் may again point to the defeat of the Jains, though no sect is named. The doubled ல்ல and ள்ள rhythm makes several words hard to divide.

reading: The poet asks whether his heart, cunning and melting at women's eyes that push at their ear-rings and their jasmine smiles, will not learn, while life remains in the world, to say with learning and understanding that Murugan is the treasure Uma gave. The praise names Valli's bridegroom, the hero of the old emerald peacock that measured the world's bounds, the warrior who threw the vel to split the hill, the life of the silver town amid fields.
nuance: உலகு உயிர் உள்ள பொழுதே: the time to learn to praise is now, while life lasts. The heart that melts (உருகிட) for women is the same heart the poet would have melt in praise.

reading: The poet tells how, giving his wealth into the hands of a deceitful, clever woman, his gems, grain, silver, learning and wealthy kin all vanished, and of the indescribable misery of the mire to which the five senses lead, and asks the true Lord to give his red feet. The praise names Murugan infatuated by the parrot speech of Valli, daughter of the generous spotted doe, the life of the silver town where white conches climb in the dark fields as the farmers slowly reap the paddy, and the Lord able to overcome the word of the fierce bowman of the mountain.
nuance: கையில் அள்ளி பொருள் ஈய: the wealth goes by the handful into the woman's hand, so the courtesan's trade is named, and with it go not only goods but learning and kin. The refrain வெய்ய சைய வில்லி சொல்லை வெல்ல வல்ல probably names Siva, whose bow was the mountain, and may refer to Murugan's teaching of Siva; the allusion is not certain.

reading: The poet asks whether he will take delight in the words of a creeper-like woman who mocks him while making him infatuated with her painted breasts, slender waist, deceitful eyes that push at her ear-rings, and dark hair full of jasmine. The praise names Murugan the beloved son infatuated with divine Valli, daughter of the spotted doe on the stony hill of millet, true to the true and false to the false, the life of the white silver town.
nuance: மெய்யர் மெய்ய பொய்யர் பொய்ய: Murugan is real to those who are real and unreal to the false, an epithet that answers the woman's deceit (கள்ள விழி) in the plea. எள்ளல் செய்யும்: the woman mocks the man she infatuates.

reading: The poet calls himself one without a way to salvation, who in his need went to people who will not share even a sesame seed's worth, unlike those ashamed to say 'there is none' and who never refuse from what they have; who cannot put Murugan's names into verse, does not understand the boundless first cause, and is a liar who tends a sagging body; and asks by what power the pure feet will rule him without letting him go. The praise names the vel that struck the dark mountain so the demons died and the gods lived, the lord of the creeper of Valli's hill, the Kumaresa on the peacock wearing vellil and kadamba, at the silver town of jewelled mansions.
nuance: இல்லையென நாணி உள்ளதின் மறாமல் describes the true giver, ashamed to say 'none', who does not refuse from what he has, the Kural's ideal (223). Whether the poet confesses begging from misers (பகிராரை ... நாடி) or his own failure to share depends on how the line is divided.

reading: The poet, a lone dog who ran like a boy after the slow beauty of thin-waisted women and fell into the sea of infatuation, asks that, to be saved, Murugan once speak to him the instruction that makes the heart melt and seek, and give him the joyous play that is neither being nor non-being, beyond delusion. The praise names the lord who rules the whole earth, Valli's bridegroom on Valli's hill, whose vel set the seven seas aflame and felled the demon lords with their mountain, at the silver town.
nuance: உள்ளதும் இலாது அல்லது: the bliss asked for is beyond both 'is' and 'is not', the language of the Siddhanta and Vedanta for the Lord. உபதேசம் is the guru's instruction, asked for directly. The division of மல்லதவிரோத is uncertain.

tamil: வதன சரோருக நயன சிலீமுக வள்ளி புனத்தில் நின்று
இதவிய காணிவை ததையென வேடுவ னெய்திடு மெச்சில் தின்று
இளையவ மூதுரை மலைகிழ வோனென வெள்ள மெனக் கலந்து
கதைகன சாபதி கிரிவளை வாளொடு கைவசி வித்தநந்த
கயிறொ டுலு஡கல முருள வுலாவிய கள்வ னறப் பயந்து
விதரண மாவலி வெருவ மகாவ்ருத வெள்ள வெளுக்க நின்ற
விளைவய லு஡டிடை வளைவிளை யாடிய வெள்ளிநகர்க் கமர்ந்த
reading: A song of praise in long, intricate lines: it pictures Murugan in Valli's millet field, her lotus face and arrow eyes, the god who lost his strength and, infatuated, mounted the palmyra horse, the lustful one who is our Lord; names him son of the pure Siva who ate the meat the hunter tasted first and offered with 'see, these are sweet'; and tells of his uncle as Krishna, delighting Yashoda, rolling the mortar he was tied to, growing until he pierced the sky as Mahabali feared, at the silver town where conches play in the fields.
nuance: மாலாய் மடலேறும் காமுக எம்பிரானே: Murugan himself takes the lover's last resort, riding the madal, and is called 'the lustful one' and 'our Lord' in one breath, as in 641 and 656. The hunter whose spittle-tasted meat Siva ate is Kannappar, the type of love that ignores rule. Several phrases (வாராய்பதி காதங் காதரை ஒன்முரும், நூறாயிர பேதஞ் சாதமொழிந்த) are obscure.

title: திருவல்லம்
theme: The one song at Thiruvallam (திருவல்லம்): the body as a walking hut of skin, flesh and bone, and a plea for the strength to proclaim Murugan before the devotees before the senses carry the life away.
source_issues: Song 665: one corrupt character in குடிலு஡டே (line 546), probably குடிலூடே.

reading: The poet pictures the body as a hut of desire and skin, flesh and fluids, with bones driven in as pegs, walking on two legs, and asks that, lest the life, like a fierce elephant, run loose along the paths of the senses when its time of speed comes, Murugan give him the strength to recite 'Vel, Kanda' faultlessly before the devotees who fall at his feet. The praise names Vishnu who played the flute and who came before an eyelid could blink when the elephant, in distress, cried 'Moolam, rule me', and Thiruvallam, Siva's ancient town round which Brahma, the directions, earth and sky revolve, where women come to dance.
nuance: The body is a hut (குடில்) built of skin, flesh, water and bone pegs (என்புறு கீல்), a builder's inventory of the body. The life as an elephant on the paths of the senses is answered in the praise by Gajendra, the elephant saved when it called. The plea is for speech, the strength (விறல்) to praise aloud among devotees.

title: வேலூர்
theme: Songs at Vellore (வேலூர்), a rich town of mango, honey and sugar presses: the poet confesses bondage to courtesans who welcome givers and drive off the rest, and to women who destroy young men, and asks for the feet and a truthful worship; the praise tells Sambandar's victory over the Jains at Madurai as Murugan's own.
source_issues: Song 666: two corrupt characters, in தேனு஡றல்கள் (line 581, probably தேனூறல்கள்) and வேலு஡ர் (line 586, probably வேலூர்).
Song 667: one corrupt character in வேலு஡ர் (line 605, probably வேலூர்).

reading: The poet lists the courtesans who show delight when men who give much wealth come and drive away those who do not give even after union, illusions who feign friendship and make men fools, show their breasts and their beauty to anyone as if in love, wandering prostitutes without compassion, and asks on what day he will leave their ways and join Murugan's feet. The praise tells how, in the Pandya land of Madurai, Murugan smeared holy ash on the king who leaned to the Jains, straightened his hump, sent the palm leaf up against the river's current, and, praised by the queen, destroyed the Jains to the root; and names Vellore, where mangoes fall, honey flows and sugar presses run day and night.
nuance: அதிகராய்ப் பொருள் ஈவார் நேர்படில் ரசனை காட்டிகள், ஈயார் கூடினும் அகல ஓட்டிகள்: love measured to the gift. The praise tells the Madurai episode of Sambandar in full (the ash, the hump, the leaf against the stream, the queen, அழகி), all as Murugan's deed. Two words have corrupt glyphs.

tamil: சேலால மொன்று செங்கண் வேலாலும் வென்று மைந்தர்
தேன்மேவு செஞ்சொ லின்சொல் தானோதி வந்த ணைந்து
கோலாக லங்கள் கண்டு மாலாகி நின்ற னன்பு
கோள்கோடி பொன்ற வென்று நாடோ று நின்றி யங்கு
மாலாலு ழன்ற ணங்கை யார்மாம தன்க ரும்பின்
வாழ்வான கந்த முந்த மாறாகி வந்த டர்ந்த
மேலாகு மொன்ற மைந்த மேனாடர் நின்றி ரங்க
வேய்போல வுந்தி ரண்ட தோள்மாதர் வந்தி றைஞ்சு
reading: The poet tells of women whose eyes defeat the fish and the spear, who set out first to ruin young men's prosperity and minds, come with honeyed words and embrace them, and bring a sorrowful pleasure that never ends, and asks that, infatuated by their show, his love not wane and his limbs not waste, but that he be given grace to worship daily with keen truthfulness, having overcome countless evils. The praise names Murugan who rode the peacock and defeated the great Sura, who threw the vel at the hill while the gods stood in pity, and Vellore, where women with bamboo-like shoulders come to worship.
nuance: தீராத துன்ப இன்பம்: the pleasure the women give is itself a sorrow. கூர்வாய்மை கொண்டு இறைஞ்ச: worship asked for is worship with truthfulness. கோள்கோடி பொன்ற வென்று may mean overcoming the planets, or slanders; the opening lines of the praise on Kama's cane bow are hard to divide.

title: விரிஞ்சிபுரம்
theme: Songs at Virinchipuram (விரிஞ்சிபுரம்), also named Thiruvirinchai and Karapuram in the songs: the poet confesses the courtesans who play their lovers against each other and take his wealth, his neglect of rites, austerity and giving, and the five elements he cannot cast off; he asks for the feet, for love that melts, and for the formless state, and the praise names Murugan as teacher of Siva and as the Tamil child who impaled the Jains.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (668, 669, 671); a song on the feet beyond the sects (670); and a song on the formless state and Murugan as first guru (672). Songs 668, 669 and 671 end at Karapuram (கரபுரம்), 670 and 672 at Thiruvirinchai.
source_issues: Song 670: one corrupt character in புண்ட஡ணகம (line 8), probably புண்டரீகம (஡ண for ரீ).
Songs 668, 669 and 671 end at Karapuram (கரபுரம், கரபுரி), not Virinchipuram; 670 and 672 name Thiruvirinchai. Karapuram may be another name of the shrine.

reading: The poet describes women who keep one man on the bed in a small house, set another circling at their door, send a third rushing about the street, set lovers against each other until they draw knives and fight in the room, and think it all fitting so long as they make a living; deluded by them he abandoned the path of austerity, chariyai, kiriyai and tapas, threw away his wealth and wandered scorned, and asks grace that his sorrows end, good qualities come and he think always with love of the golden feet. The praise names the vel that ended the cruel demons who imprisoned the ascetic sages (புலவர்), Valli of cuckoo speech, and Murugan who impaled the shaven-headed Jains, at Karapuram of areca, plantain and cane.
nuance: The opening is a sharp comic sketch of a courtesan managing four men at once (ஒருவரை ... ஒருவரை ... ஒருவரை), her motive given as உயிர்பிழைப்பது, earning a living. The loss is named in Saiva terms: சரியையில் கிரியையில் தவமும் அற்று. கழுவின் உச்சியில் வைத்திடுவோனே identifies Murugan with Sambandar at Madurai. Who the imprisoned புலவர் are (gods or poets) is not clear.

reading: The poet pictures lovemaking on the bed, the hair loosened, eyes closing, cooing voice, sweat on the face, prattle and anklets on both feet, and asks Murugan to think of ruling even the sinner whose mind will not let go of that desire. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva whose bow is a mountain, the lord riding the peacock, who came to Madurai so the Jain thieves went to the stake, the nephew of Vishnu whose lotus foot made the stone Ahalya a woman again, at Karapuri where long valai fish leap at the areca palms.
nuance: பதகனையும் ஆள நினைவாயே: the plea asks only to be thought of, the 'even' (உம்) marking the poet as least worthy. The Madurai impalement again gives Murugan Sambandar's deed. Ahalya's release by Rama's foot is told as Vishnu's.

tamil: நிகரில் பஞ்ச பூதமு நினையு நெஞ்சு மாவியு
நிகழ்த ரும்ப்ர பாகர நிரவ யம்ப ராபர
சகர சங்க சாகர மெனமு ழங்கு வாதிகள்
தனிமை கண்ட தானகிண் கிணிய தண்டை சூழ்வன
மகர விம்ப சீகர முகர வங்க வாரிதி
வழிதி றந்து சேனையு மெதிர்ம லைந்த சூரனு
சிகர துங்க மால்வரை தகர வென்றி வேல்விடு
திசைதொ றும்ப்ர பூபதி திசைமு கன்ப ராவிய
reading: The poet asks for the lotus feet with tinkling anklets that are seen in solitude, beyond the five elements, the thinking heart and the life, which the Veda names as radiant, partless and beyond, and which the disputants of the five sects, roaring like the sea, do not know. The praise tells of the sea boiling and crying out, the way opened in the sky, Sura and his army killed so Indra and the gods could return home, and the vel that shattered the high peak, and names Murugan the son of Chandrasekhara at Thiruvirinchai, worshipped by the kings of every quarter and by four-faced Brahma.
nuance: சமய பஞ்ச பாதகர் அறியாத: the feet are what the sect-disputants cannot know; the knowing is தனிமை கண்ட, in solitude. The run நிகழ்தரும் ப்ரபாகர நிரவயம் பராபர நிருப reads as Sanskrit names of the Absolute but its division is uncertain. திசைமுகன் பராவிய திருவிரிஞ்சை: the town's name is tied to Brahma (விரிஞ்சன்).

reading: The poet asks whether, instead of holding in his mind with love Murugan's golden hands, faces, pearl-hung chest, radiance, flower feet, cock and peacock, and instead of giving in dharma even a handful of food to those who come in real hunger, he must wander deluded, embracing women who speak sweet friendship as if old acquaintances, give amorous play and snatch his wealth. The praise names the vel that cut down the dark demons until the vultures were full, Murugan who made Brahma, Vishnu, Varuna, Agni, Yama and Indra stand firm, the noble one who gave grace before Siva, the dancer with the poisoned throat, tiger skin and serpents, and the lord at Karapuram who daily tells the meaning of the Vedas to the sages.
nuance: The neglect confessed is twofold: contemplation of the Lord's form and feeding the hungry (பசியில் வருமவர்க்கு அசனம் ஒருபிடி படையாதே). உரிய பொருள் பறித்திடுமானார: the women take what rightly belongs to him. உத்தமவேள் may mean Murugan taught before Siva the dancer, as elsewhere in the book.

tamil: மருவு மஞ்சு பூத முரிமை வந்தி டாது
மயல்கொ ளிந்த வாழ்வு அமையு மெந்த நாளும்
உ ருகி யன்பி னோடு உ னைநி னைந்து நாளும்
உ ருவ மொன்றி லாத பருவம் வந்து சேர
அரிவி ரிஞ்சர் தேட அரிய தம்பி ரானும்
அருளு கென்ற போது பொருளி தென்று காண
திரியு மும்பர் நீடு கிரிபி ளந்து சூரர்
செயல மைந்த வேத தொனிமு ழங்கு வீதி
reading: The poet confesses that he does not know how to cast off the five elements as filth not his own, lives in delusion, and has not come by the proper way; he asks that, melting with love and thinking of Murugan daily, he reach the stage that has no form and does not even speak of 'the world', and be given the paired high feet. The praise names Murugan the first guru, whom Siva, the Lord whom Vishnu and Brahma could not find, bowed to and asked 'grant it', and to whom Murugan showed 'this is the meaning'; the vel that split the mountain; and Thiruvirinchai, whose streets resound with the Veda.
nuance: உலகம் என்று பேச அறியாத உருவம் ஒன்றிலாத பருவம்: the goal is a state without form in which the world is not even named. The myth of Murugan teaching Siva is told with Siva bowing at his feet (அடிபணிந்து பேசி), though Om is not named. மலம் இது என்று போட: the elements of the body are to be thrown off as impurity.

title: திருவாலங்காடு
theme: Songs at Thiruvalangadu (திருவாலங்காடு), where Siva danced with Kali: the poet confesses scheming women, the body as a nest of Death, the tattvas that make up the body, and Death's messenger with the noose, and asks for the feet, the supreme state and the gift of Tamil praise; one song, sung at Thiruvothur, confesses praising unworthy patrons and names Murugan as Sambandar.
structure_note: Women (673); the body and Death (674, 676); the tattvas of the body and the bond (675); the poet's trade of praise and Sambandar's miracles (677). Song 677 names Thiruvothur (திருவோத்தூர்), not Thiruvalangadu.
source_issues: Song 677 is grouped under திருவாலங்காடு but names திருவோத்தூர் (Thiruvothur) on the சேய்நதி.

reading: The poet heaps abuse on women with poison-sharp eyes and scheming minds, makers of blame, whose breasts show nail-scratches, who feed men a ghoulish food, who are wanton singers and charmers falling on deluded lovers, and asks that before his ruined mind delights in them on moonlit terraces he be granted the feet that flowers honour. The praise names Murugan's chest garlanded with flowers where bees hum 'thanathana' like the Veda, the hero Guha who rides the ram, who played with Valli's shoulders in the millet field, at Thiruvalangadu where Nataraja, the Lord of the world, danced with Kali.
nuance: பேய் அமுது ஊணிடு may refer to the charge that courtesans feed men a love-philtre; the reading is a guess. தகர் ஏறு, riding the ram, is a rarer mount than the peacock. காளியொடு ஆடிய: the shrine's dance contest of Siva and Kali. Several compound epithets in the first half (கீலகலாவிகள், காளிமவீணிகள்) are hard to divide.

reading: In a world where people celebrate sons and gold as their firm support, the poet asks that before the life that lives in this mean nest of a body, packed with fierce Death, is taken, and before people say his thought of praising Murugan has gone and speak scorn, the deeds swelling in his heart leave him and Murugan give his feet and rule him. The praise names Vishnu, who held up the hill as an umbrella, guarded the calves and swallowed the world, as uncle, Murugan who went infatuated to Valli and said 'rule me', and the grace that gives a fearless heart to those who bow with love, linked to the dancer who danced at Alangadu for the gods' life.
nuance: புதல்வரும் ... பொன்தான் என்று: the false supports named are sons and gold. புன்கூடு, the mean nest, is the body; கூற்றம் பொதிதரு, Death is already packed inside it. The line on the Alangadu dancer and 'the fruit of the song' (பாட்டின் பயன்) is obscure; it may allude to a poet-saint's songs at the shrine.

tamil: புவிபுனல் காலுங் காட்டி சிகியொடு வானுஞ் சேர்த்தி
பொறிபுல னீரைந் தாக்கி கருவிகள் நாலுங் காட்டி
பவவினை நூறுங் காட்டி சுவமதி தானுஞ் சூட்டி
படிமிசை போவென் றோட்டி அடிமையை நீவந் தேத்தி
சிவமய ஞானங் கேட்க தவமுநி வோரும் பார்க்க
திருவளர் மார்பன் போற்ற திசைமுக னாளும் போற்ற
குவடொடு சூரன் தோற்க எழுகடல் சூதந் தாக்கி
குவலயம் யாவும் போற்ற பழனையி லாலங் காட்டில்
reading: The poet lays out how the body is made: earth, water, wind, fire and sky joined, the new mind yoked, the ten senses and organs, the four inner instruments, and the paths, until the body comes, bearing a hundred deeds of becoming and its own understanding, with Pati and the bond (pasa) shown; he asks Murugan to drive him off this world of illusion, come and raise his servant, and show the supreme state. The praise names the dancer who dances so that sages may hear and see Siva-knowledge, Lakshmi's lord and Brahma praising, the peacock ride that saved earth and sky, the vel that defeated Sura with his mountain and struck the seven seas, and Murugan who honours the hunter girl's feet at Palayanur Alangadu.
nuance: The first half is a short tattva doctrine: the five elements, the ten பொறி-புலன், the four கருவிகள் (the inner instruments), and பசுபதி பாசம், the Lord and the bond, before the plea for பரகதி. சுவமதி and புகல்வழி நாலைந்து (perhaps twenty paths) are not clear. பழனையில் ஆலங்காடு names the shrine's village Palayanur.

tamil: வடிவது நீலங் காட்டி முடிவுள காலன் கூட்டி
மகனொடு மாமன் பாட்டி முதலுற வோருங் கேட்டு
படிமிசை தாளுங் காட்டி யுடலுறு நோய்பண் டேற்ற
பரிவொடு நாளுங் காத்து விரிதமி ழாலங் கூர்த்த
முடிமிசை சோமன் சூட்டி வடிவுள ஆலங் காட்டில்
முருகவிழ் தாருஞ் சூட்டி யொருதனி வேழங் கூட்டி
இடியென வேகங் காட்டி நெடிதரு சூலந் தீட்டி
இலகிய வேல்கொண் டார்த்து உ டலிரு கூறன் றாக்கி
reading: The poet asks that before the dark-bodied messenger sent by Death throws his noose, and son, uncle, grandmother and kin hear of it, and life departs with the mind confused, Murugan show his feet on earth, remove the old deeds and sins that brought the body's disease, guard him daily, and rule him with the command 'sing the supreme praise in expansive Tamil'. The praise names Murugan the son of the dancer with the moon on his head at Alangadu, who brought the elephant to win the hunter girl he longed for, and whose vel split Sura in two and ended the gods' distress.
nuance: விரிதமிழால் அம் கூர்த்த பரபுகழ் பாடு என்று ஆட்கொள்: the poet asks to be ruled by a command to sing, the song itself as the form of grace. நோய் பண்டு ஏற்ற பழவினை: disease is traced to old deeds. ஒருதனி வேழம் கூட்டி: the elephant that frightened Valli into Murugan's arms.

tamil: தவர்வாட் டோமர சூலந் தரியாக் காதிய சூருந்
சருகாக் காய்கதிர் வேலும் பொருகாற் சேவலு நீலந்
துவர்வாய்க் கானவர் மானுஞ் சுரநாட் டாளொரு தேனுந்
துணையாய்க் காவல்செய் வாயென் றுணராப் பாவிகள் பாலுந்
பவமாய்த் தாணது வாகும் பனைகாய்த் தேமண நாறும்
படியாப் பாதகர் பாயன் றியுடாப் பேதைகள் கேசம்
செழுநீர்ச் சேய்நதி யாரங் கொழியாக் கோமளம் வீசுந்
reading: The first half praises Murugan as the great one who lives without lack with his companions, the vel that burned dry Sura, the seven seas and seven hills, the fighting cock, the peacock, Valli of the hunters and Devayanai of heaven, and the poet asks whether he too must sing endless songs to sinners who do not know that Murugan guards as a companion. The praise names the little one who, with the holy word flowing with honeyed nectar and with the white holy ash, made the male palmyra bear fragrant fruit that fell to the ground and sent to the stake the Jains who read no Veda, wear only mats and pluck their hair, at Thiruvothur by the red river.
nuance: The plea is about the poet's trade: பாவிகள் பாலும் தொலையாப் பாடலை யானும் புகல்வேனோ, singing to unworthy patrons. The praise gives Murugan two of Sambandar's deeds: the male palmyra made to fruit at Thiruvothur (பனை காய்த்து ... பழமாய்ப் பார்மிசை வீழும்படி) and the impalement of the Jains; திருநீற்றால் அமராடும் may refer to his curing the Pandya with ash.

title: பாக்கம்
theme: Two songs at Pakkam (பாக்கம்) on the body: food for crows, dogs and vultures at the pyre, carried by Death's trident, and the hut that wanders town to town in craving; the poet asks for the learning to string Murugan's names together and for the senses driven out so he can enter the house of release.

reading: The poet speaks of his body, dark as a cloud, with kin as many as the sea, food for crows, dogs, vultures and ghouls in the long fire of the burning ground, and of Death with his sharpened trident stabbing and carrying off the life, and asks Murugan to call him, grant him grace and give him the knowledge of texts to string his names into words. The praise names the vel that sent the demons fleeing to every quarter and freed the gods from prison, and Murugan, the jnana-master who spoke words full of devotion for those who wear the holy ash, at Pakkam where poets look on him with clusters of verse.
nuance: காக்கைக்கு நாய் கழுகு பேய்க்கு அக்கமான உடல்: the body is already apportioned to scavengers. The plea is for skill in verse (நாமமொழி கோக்கைக்கு நூலறிவு), again the gift of song. சாவருளி is unclear: it may be 'grant (escape from) death' or a different division. நீறுபுனைவார்க்கு ஒக்க ஞானபரனாய்ப் பத்தி கூர் மொழிகள் பகர் may point to Sambandar's hymns.

tamil: பாற்றுக் கணங்கள் தின்று தேக்கிட் டிடுங்கு ரம்பை
பார்த்துத் திரிந்து ழன்று ஆக்கத் தையுந்தெ ரிந்து
வேற்றுப் புலன்க ளைந்து மோட்டிப் புகழ்ந்து கொண்டு
மாற்றற்ற பொன்து லங்கு வாட்சக்கி ரந்தெ ரிந்து
மாற்பொற்க லந்து லங்க நாட்டச்சு தன்ப ணிந்து
பாற்சொற்ற டம்பு குந்து வேற்கட்சி னம்பொ ருந்து
பாக்குக் கரும்பை கெண்டை தாக்கித் தடம் படிந்த
reading: The poet asks whether, rather than carrying this hut of a body that flocks of vultures will feed on, wandering from town to town, eyeing others' prosperity and standing in longing until he wilts, he will drive out the five senses, praise Murugan, and enter the house and rejoice. The praise names Vishnu, who bears the shining disc, sword, conch, mace and bow, whose hands the sea-waves wash, and who sleeps on the serpent bed in the milk sea, as uncle, at Pakkam where fish strike the areca and the cane.
nuance: வீட்டில் புகுந்திருந்து மகிழ்வேனோ: வீடு is both home and release, so the end of wandering from town to town is the house of liberation. ஆக்கத்தையும் தெரிந்து ஏக்கற்று: craving is aroused by seeing others' wealth.

title: திருவேற்காடு
theme: Two songs at Thiruverkadu (திருவேற்காடு): the poet confesses the women's eyes, breasts and waist that keep him taking bodies, and his lust as a great sinner, and asks when the round of births will end and whether Murugan will look on him, join him to the devotees and give him one word, as he rescued Nakkirar.
source_issues: Song 680: one corrupt character in வயலு¡ரா (line 10), probably வயலூரா.
Song 681: two corrupt characters in வேதபு ¡£சுரர் (line 21), probably வேதபுரீசுரர் (¡£ for ரீ).

reading: Through eyes dark as poison that wage war, breasts and a slender waist, the poet, without support, takes body after body, and asks Murugan to say when that time will end. The praise names Murugan the child of the milk-fragrant mother, the lord of Vayalur, nephew of Vishnu, with the hunter girl and the heavenly maiden on either side, giver of the Veda and of nada, at Velangadu.
nuance: அநேகம் காயம் ... காலம் தான் ஒழிவது ஏது: desire is tied directly to rebirth, the many bodies. The second half of the plea (சாலந்தாழ்வுறு மால ஏலங்கோர் பிடியாய) is hard to divide. வேலங்காடு is Verkadu.

reading: Infatuated with women of dark hair, spear eyes, milk-sweet speech, thread waists and tender-coconut breasts, the poet calls himself a lustful great sinner and asks: will Murugan not look on him by grace, not join him to his devotees, not sharpen his grace; and as he once rescued Keeran, who excelled on the old sea-girt earth through the poets' words, will he not give him one word. The praise names Murugan as the one whose angry word destroyed the sects built on false causes, the Siva-faith and the yoga of the great, the life of devotees, the son of Vedapurisvara at Thiruverkadu, and the bridegroom of Indra's daughter.
nuance: The plea is a run of questions ending in அலையோ (பார்ப்பாய் அலையோ, சேர்ப்பாய் அலையோ, கூர்ப்பாய் அலையோ). கீரரை ஆர்ப்பாய்: Nakkirar, whom tradition says Murugan freed from captivity, is the precedent for the poet's request for one word (ஒர் சொல்). The praise lines on sects (மத ஏற்பாடிகளே அழிவே உற) are uncertain in division.

title: வடதிருமுல்லைவாயில்
theme: Songs at Vadathirumullaivayil (வடதிருமுல்லைவாயில்): the poet asks whether grace will leave him long in darkness, confesses courtesans who take a man home by a trick and rob him, and asks not to fall into the snare of women's eyes; the praise names Murugan as Siva's guru, the Goddess of the burning ground, and Siva the Masilamani who defeated Kali.
structure_note: A plea for grace (682), a courtesan song (683) and a song on women's eyes (684). Song 682 is badly garbled.
source_issues: Song 682: several words look garbled (குணவல் வாசிவனே, பரிசெல்ரவி, மோடமடர், நகாகன), and the praise is hard to read.

reading: The poet, calling himself without understanding, asks whether Murugan has the grace to remove his distress so he may reach the shore of this sea-girt earth, whether he will leave him long in the house of darkness, whether there is no grace for him, for he does not know what is fitting, and when the day will come that ends the hut of the body. The praise is a tangle of names: the Goddess at Arunachala, Murugan as Siva-guru, the son of Parameswari who plays with ghosts in the cactus forest of the burning ground, the nephew of Vishnu, the son of the one who danced at Thillai, at Vadamullaivayil of jasmine groves.
nuance: The plea is a series of anxious questions (அருள்வல்லையோ, இடுமோ, அருளில்லையோ). குடில் இல்லமே தரு நாள் எது may ask when the body-hut will cease to be given, that is, when birth ends; the reading is tentative. Many words of the praise (குணவல்வா, பரிசெல்ரவி, மோடமடர்) look garbled.

reading: The poet describes women with moonlike faces who face men coming from afar, flirt, fall on their shoulders as if old lovers, take them home by a trick, give their lips while they plunder the wealth, then fall silent and pick quarrels, and asks whether he, a fool and sinner whose mind has failed in delusion for these deceitful wanton women, will gain salvation. The praise names the vel thrown from the peacock at Sura, the nephew of Krishna who climbed the mortar to steal butter from the hanging pots in the herders' villages, and Siva the Masilamani, the first Lord who defeated Kali in contest and whose dancing feet the sea king, Brahma and Vishnu worship.
nuance: The courtesan's cycle is told in order: approach, false intimacy (முன்னாளில் இணங்கிய மாதர் போல்), a trick to bring him home, plunder while the lips are given, then silence and quarrels. மாசிலாமணி is the name of the Siva of Thirumullaivayil.

reading: The poet asks that he not fall into the snare of women who walk the street outdoing swans and peacocks, speak like cuckoos and shoot eye-arrows like Kama, false maidens with jewelled breasts, but that Murugan rule him in joy through the snare of loving knowledge of his feet, without the evil eye. The praise names Murugan the guru of the father who wears the crescent, vanni, serpent and konrai, the nephew of Rama whose arrow sent Ravana's heads to the sky, the vel that made the mountain leap, and the lord of supreme knowledge at northern Mullaivayil where sages do penance.
nuance: கண்ணி is played twice: the women's snare (கண்ணியில் விழாமல்) and a 'snare' of knowledge of the feet (பதஞான கண்ணியில்), so the remedy is a better binding. கண்ணுறு வராமல் may mean free of the evil eye. சொல்லுமுனிவோர் தவம்புரி names sages doing penance at the shrine.

title: திருவலிதாயம்
theme: One short song at Thiruvalithayam (திருவலிதாயம்): the poet asks not to wander deluded by women but to be given a mind able to honour Murugan's feet.

reading: A short song: the poet, a dog of a servant, asks not to wander thinking of the delusion of young women with fragrant jasmine hair, but to be given a mind able to honour the two good feet. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Vishnu, the husband of Valli, who dwells at Thiruvalithayam, lord of the great sages.
nuance: இனவல்ல மானமனது அருளாயோ: the request is for a mind, not for release, a mind able (வல்ல) to honour the feet. நாயடியன், the dog-servant, is the poet's self-abasement.

title: திருவொற்றியூர்
theme: Two songs at Thiruvotriyur (திருவொற்றியூர், Adhipuri): the poet asks for knowledge before the world mocks him as a maniac of love, and not to be born again in a woman's womb but to reach the Siva-state; the praise names Murugan the guru whom Nataraja praises.

reading: The poet, plunged in lovemaking with women of dark hair and carp eyes, their breasts scented with musk and sandal, asks for the grace of knowledge before the world laughs at him in every way as a madman reciting Kama's arts. The praise names Murugan the guru-king whom Nataraja praises and whom Brahma, Vishnu, gods, sages and Siva-yogis extol, the son of Siva who holds the skull, shares his body with a woman and is golden-bodied, at Adhipuri.
nuance: The fear named is public mockery (உலகோர்கள் ... நகைகள் கூறி), not Death or hell. நடராஜர் பரவு குருராஜ: Siva the dancer praises Murugan as guru. ஆதிபுரி is Thiruvotriyur.

reading: In a dense run of Sanskrit names of the Lord as self-luminous form, cosmic form and true bliss, the poet asks whether, not born again in the womb of women, and gaining the grace of the light of compassion, he will reach the blameless Siva-state and be rid of all troubles. The praise names Murugan with the cock banner, nephew of Vishnu with the discus, Kumara, Guha, Siva-Subrahmanya, death to the demons, the son of the first Siva at Thiruvotriyur by the sea, who dwells in the hearts of the great tapasvins of yoga.
nuance: மாதர் வயிறு இடையூறு கருவிற் பிறவாதபடி: release is asked as never again entering a woman's womb. The opening compounds (சொருபப்பிரகாச விசுவரூப ப்ரமாக நிசசுக) read as Sanskrit epithets, but their divisions and the sense of துலியப்பிரகாச are uncertain.

title: திருமயிலை
theme: Songs at Mylapore (திருமயிலை): the poet confesses the eyes, speech and breasts of women and of the courtesans who sell love, the bad company and the deceit of his life, and his failure to think of the feet, worship or keep silence, and asks to join the devotees and see Murugan; the praise names the Goddess in long litanies, Murugan as guru who whispered into Siva's ear, and Sambandar raising the merchant's daughter at Mylai.
structure_note: Women and courtesans (689, 692, 696, 697); the poet's faults and his longing for the devotees (690, 691, 694, 695); a love-song in a girl's voice (693); and a dense song on the poison and the Lord's state (688). Songs 691 and 696 carry long litanies of names.
source_issues: Song 694: one corrupt character in சால §ம்முடு (line 5); the word cannot be restored.
Song 697: two corrupt characters in ஒத்தவ ¡£வார் (line 1), perhaps ஒத்தவரீவார் (¡£ for ரீ); line 6 has மிக்முழ்கி, perhaps மிகமூழ்கி.

reading: The song opens with the great poison that came terrifying Brahma, Vishnu and the gods, and names the Lord of all whose instruments it fitted; the poet asks Murugan, son of Siva, to come in an instant to give him his own state. The praise names the vel thrown in the war of gods and demons, sounds the battle in drum syllables, and names Murugan, son of the Himalaya's daughter, who comes dancing on the peacock, our supreme guru dwelling at Mylai.
nuance: The first eight lines are a run of Sanskrit-derived words (அதகரண விதன பரிபுரண ... நிமிர சமிரமய) whose division is uncertain; they seem to speak of Siva holding the poison and of the Lord's pervasion. நினது பதவி தர வருவாயே: the plea is for Murugan's own state. Lines 11 to 12 are drum syllables.

reading: A short song: the poet asks whether he too must perish, stopped by women's spear-like eyes, nectar-like speech and mountain breasts. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva of Kailas, who dwells at Mylai by the waves of the sea, the lord of his devotees.
nuance: The three charms come in three short lines (விழியாலே, மொழியாலே, முலையாலே), and the plea is only a question, with no request.

reading: The poet asks that he not grow weak and his mind waste by the deceitful deeds of a great sinner without dharma, but be given the joy of living each day, worshipping the red feet and joined to grace. The praise names the vel that frightened the demons' armies, the son of the pure Abhirami, the hero whose shoulders the hunter girl longed for, and Kanda at the great city of Mylai.
nuance: அறமிலா அதிபாதக வஞ்சத் தொழில்: the confession is of conduct, not of women. The plea asks for a daily life (தினமுமே மிக வாழ்வுறும் இன்பம்), not release.

tamil: ளிவர வுருகிலி அயர்கிலி தொழுகிலி ...... உ மைபாகர்
reading: In a long run of negatives the poet confesses that he does not think of the feet that end the two deeds that bring sorrow in birth, does not melt in grace, does not tire, does not worship, does not proclaim Murugan as the child Uma's lord delights in, is not filled, does not lessen his folly, does not know true insight and does not dwell in the silence where speech ends; afflicted by women, he asks whether a day will come when grace joins him to the devotees. The praise names Murugan who spoke sweet words to the hunter girl, Saravanabhava, the meaning at the end of the Vedas, the one of A, U and M and the syllables of the mantra, whose vel destroyed the demons, at Mylai of beauty and learning.
nuance: The confession is built from a dozen verbs ending in -கிலி (நினைகிலி, உருகிலி, அயர்கிலி, தொழுகிலி ...), a list of what devotion does by what the poet fails to do. வசனம் அறவுறு மவுனம்: silence beyond speech is among the things lacked. அகர உகர ... மகர names the parts of Om; the following சிகர ... யகர may be the syllables of the five-letter mantra, and the line is hard to divide.

tamil: இணையதில தாமி ரண்டு கயல்களென வேபு ரண்டு
இலகுசிலை வேள்து ரந்த கணையதிலு மேசி றந்த
பணைமுலையின் மீத ணிந்த தரளமணி யார்து லங்கு
பயிலுநடை யாலு ழன்று அவர்களிட மோக மென்ற
கணகணென வீர தண்டை சரணமதி லேவி ளங்க
கறுவிவரு சூர னங்க மிருபிளவ தாக விண்டு
மணிமகுட வேணி கொன்றை அறுகுமதி யாற ணிந்த
மலையரையன் மாது தந்த சிறுவனென வேவ ளர்ந்து
reading: The poet describes the price-women, eyes like paired carp rolling to their earrings to wage war and sharper than Kama's arrows, breasts hung with pearls, coming like Rati, and asks whether he should wander after their gait and fall into the pit called desire. The praise names Murugan who rides the peacock with anklets ringing, whose vel split Sura in two, and who grew as the child of the mountain king's daughter, half of Siva, and came to live at Mylai.
nuance: விலைமானார், women with a price, names the trade, and மோகம் என்ற படுகுழி makes desire the pit the poet walks into following their gait.

tamil: களபமணி யார முற்ற வனசமுலை மீது கொற்ற
கனிமொழிமி னார்கள் முற்று மிசைவசைகள் பேச வுற்ற
வளமையணி நீடு புஷ்ப சயனஅணை மீது ருக்கி
வரியளியு லாவு துற்ற இருபுயம ளாவி வெற்றி
துளபமணி மார்ப சக்ர தரனரிமு ராரி சர்ப்ப
சுருதிமறை வேள்வி மிக்க மயிலைநகர் மேவு முக்ர
அளகைவணி கோர்கு லத்தில் வனிதையுயிர் மீள ழைப்ப
அருவரையை நீறெ ழுப்பி நிருதர்தமை வேர றுத்து
reading: In the voice of a woman in love with Murugan, the singer asks not to waste away each night on the flower bed, seeking to ride the madal, through the arrows Kama shoots at her sandalled breasts, the slander that the women speak, and the moon circling like fire, but that Murugan come and embrace her with his shoulders on the bed. The praise names Vishnu who holds the discus and sleeps on the serpent as uncle, the hero of the green peacock at Mylai of Vedic sacrifice, and the Kumara who sang the song of grace that called back to life the girl of the merchant clan.
nuance: This is akam poetry, not the poet's confession: the classical torments of the lovesick girl, the gossip of women (இசைவசைகள்), the moon as fire, and the madal. அளகை வணிகோர் குலத்தில் வனிதை உயிர் மீள அழைப்ப அருள் பரவு பாடல் சொற்ற: Sambandar's raising of the merchant's daughter at Mylapore, given to Murugan, sung at the very shrine where the tradition places it.

tamil: கடிய வேக மாறாத விரத சூத ராபாதர்
கபட வீன ராகாத இயல்பு நாடி யேநீடு
குலவு தோகை மீதாறு முகமும் வேலு மீராறு
படியி னோடு மாமேரு அதிர வீசி யேசேட
பரவை யாழி நீர்மோத நிருதர் மாள வானாடு
வடிவு லாவி யாகாச மிளிர்ப லாவி னீள்சோலை
மணிசெய் மாட மாமேடை சிகர மோடு வாகான
reading: The poet calls himself a cruel man who, not seeking a nature unlike that of wicked gamblers who break their vows, fools who make strife, hunters of deeds and deceivers, speaks great perversity and does not keep the path, and asks that, rather than dying daily in this hut of the body, he see Murugan come on the peacock with six faces, the vel and twelve shoulders. The praise tells how Murugan shook the earth and Meru, set Sesha's hoods dancing, struck the mountain and the sea, and killed the demons so the gods regained their land, at Mylai of jack groves, lotus ponds, fields and jewelled mansions.
nuance: The list of vile people (சூதர், பாழ்மூடர், வினைவேடர், கபட ஈனர்) is the company the poet has resembled. The plea asks for a vision of the Lord's form (நேர்காண வருவாயே). One corrupt character in line 5 obscures a word.

reading: The poet asks whether, instead of wandering with worldly people on this sea-girt earth without praising Murugan, he will have a great day when, crying daily with full heart 'Son of Siva, lord of the three gods, gem of Uma, Guha', he is joined by grace to the devotees who worship. The praise tells how Indra and all the gods were humbled and the demon lords oppressed them, and how Murugan's vel split the proud Sura in two, at Mayilapuri.
nuance: The contrast is between two companies: உலகோரொடு திரிவேன், wandering with the worldly, and உன் அடியாராய் வழிபாடுறுவாரொடு, the worshipping devotees. The names to be cried out are given in the plea itself.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking at length, the breasts scented with musk and sandal, the garment slipping, the sweating face, the earrings, the bangles, the loosened hair, the anklets, the drinking of the lips, and asks whether a day will come when he, a man of deeds sunk in the whirlpool of the deep sea of the two deeds, gains grace and lives. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess, Parai, Abhinavai, Sivai, Sambhavi, Uma, Bhairavi, Tripurai, Bhagavati who holds sun and moon, the mountain's daughter, Gauri, Mohini, who never leaves Siva's side, and names Murugan her son who rides the peacock and throws the vel, at Mylai.
nuance: இருவினை ஈண்டும் ஆழ்கடல் இடர்படு சுழி: the two deeds are a deep sea with a whirlpool. இருகதி பெற may mean the two goals or a great goal; the sense is uncertain. The litany of the Goddess (பரை அபிநவை சிவை சாம்பவி) is longer than the praise of Murugan.

tamil: உ ரை செயு முத்தம வீரா நாரணி
உ றுஜக ரக்ஷணி நீரா வாரணி ...... தருசேயே
reading: The poet confesses that, deluded by peacock-like women with moonlike faces and unfading lust, he became the servant of those sunk in the sea of desire and of misers holding great wealth, his mind sinking like an ox, and asks, with many epithets of Murugan, whether he will gain the jewel of his grace. The praise sounds the drum in syllables, names Murugan the hero who, while Siva danced, spoke the guru's teaching with the ears covered, the son of Narayani Uma who protects the world, the master of the end of the Vedas, and the life of Mylai.
nuance: நீள்நிதி தரு வியலுத்தர்கள்: the poet's servitude is to misers as well as women, perhaps as a poet begging patrons. காதே மூடிய குருபோதம் உரைசெயும்: the teaching given to Siva is told as spoken with ears covered, the secret of the ear-whispered instruction, though Om is not named. The lines asking for the jewel (மாமணி ... பெறுவேனோ) are hard to divide, and two characters are corrupt.

title: திருவான்மியூர்
theme: One song at Thiruvanmiyur (திருவான்மியூர்): the poet confesses he wandered in union with women of no virtue instead of seeking Murugan, and asks for the lotus feet; the praise names Murugan as the expert who gave knowledge into Siva's two ears.

reading: The poet describes women with mountain breasts, thread-thin waists, carp eyes and moon faces who have no virtue, and confesses that, a base man, through desire for their arms he wandered in union without seeking Murugan, and asks for the shining lotus feet so that he does not perish on this famed earth. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Narayana, the expert who gave the treasure of knowledge into Siva's two ears, death to the demons, and the son of Siva worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu and Indra, at Thiruvanmiyur of jewelled mansions.
nuance: அரன் இருகாதிலே உதவு நிபுணா: the teaching of Siva is placed in his ears, without naming Om. மடிவாய் இறாத வகை may ask that he not die before reaching the feet; the phrase is hard to divide. ஆலமயில் அமுதேசர் may name the shrine's Siva.

title: கோசைநகர்
theme: One song at Kosainagar (கோசைநகர்): the poet asks not to wander in desire for women's bodies but to think each day of the feet whose anklets resound with the hundred crore Vedas.

reading: The poet asks that he not wander with great desire for the women's bodies where all of Kama's arts and play are born, but that grace come so that he thinks every day of the great lotus feet whose anklets cry out with a hundred crore Vedas. The praise names Siva, who wears the cool moon, the serpent, arugu grass, the feather and Ganga in his matted hair, the sharp vel given for Siva's glory, the death of the demons, Valli and Devayanai on either side, and Murugan beloved of devotees at Kosainagar.
nuance: நாத சதகோடி மறை ஓலமிடு நூபுரம்: the anklets of the feet sound the Vedas, so the feet are where scripture itself cries out. The opening names the woman's body plainly (திரிகோணம்) as the place where Kama's arts arise.

title: பெருங்குடி
theme: One song at Perungudi (பெருங்குடி) that tells a whole life in a row of verbs, from ten months in the womb to the burning, and asks whether the poet will end this birth that ends in fire.
source_issues: Song 700: one corrupt character in வயலு¡ரா (line 14), probably வயலூரா.

reading: The poet tells a life as people live it: mothers bore them ten months in the womb; they were born, lay, sat, crawled and walked; for a while they embraced fine women and were deluded, carried the burden of the household with their work, settled, declined, died and were burned; he asks whether he will not end this birth that ends in burning. The praise names Mukunda, who in Lanka, with the monkey and his fire and the long sea trembling, came forth, as uncle, the lord of Tamil Vayalur whose fierce hand threw the vel that shook the mountain, at Perungudi of groves, cane and plantain.
nuance: The first half is a list of plural past verbs (சமைந்தனர் பிறந்தனர் கிடந்தனர் இருந்தனர் தவழ்ந்தனர் நடந்தனர் ... இறந்தனர்), so the life is everyone's and passes in a breath; only the last line turns to the poet. The household burden (க்ருகபாரம் சுமந்தனர்) is part of the round, not its remedy. The line on Lanka (இலங்கையில் இலங்கிய இலங்களுள் இலங்கு அருள்) plays on the sound இலங்கு and is hard to read.

title: மாடம்பாக்கம்
theme: Two songs at Madambakkam (மாடம்பாக்கம்) on the courtesans: their charms one by one, and the whole cycle of the bargain, the bed, the robbery, the beating and the new man; the poet asks to be ruled at the lotus feet, and the praise names Murugan as the light of the Agamas beyond maya and as teacher of Siva.
source_issues: Song 702 ends with இளைய நாயகனே, not பெருமாளே, and names no shrine except தமனியப்பதி (the golden town); its placement under மாடம்பாக்கம் is not confirmed by the text.

reading: The poet lists the charms of the price-women one by one, earrings, bangled hands, voice like the yazh, smile, scented hair, honeyed lips, wide eyes, anklets, rose water and breasts, and asks Murugan whether he will not think to rule him at the lotus feet with anklets, so that he does not tire, sunk in infatuation through their wiles. The praise names Murugan as the light hard to reach that the Sivagamas proclaim, the form of nada, tantra and kala, the one sought by the four Vedas, beyond maya, who brings the stilling of the mind, the hero whose vel cut down Sura, and the teacher who, when Siva said 'tell it', spoke the dawn of the bliss of knowledge, at Madaiyampathi.
nuance: The first half repeats ஆலே, 'by', after each charm, a catalogue that ends in விலைமாதர் பாவகங்கள், the price-women's feigned feelings. The praise is unusually doctrinal: சிவாகமங்கள், நாத தந்த்ர கலா, மாயாதீத, மனோலயம். கூறென அரனார் முன் ... ஞானசுகோதயம் புகல் தேசிக: Murugan teaching Siva, without naming Om.

reading: The poet tells the courtesans' whole routine: setting the price, hiding the breasts, loosening the hair, darting eyes, twisting speech, standing out in the open, accosting rough men and following them, saying 'isn't it wrong to turn back after taking the betel?', taking them to bed, then snatching all their wealth, quarrelling and beating them away, and taking up a new man with new stories; he asks whether Murugan will rule him, a great sinner unshaken even after seeing their ways, who lacks the knowledge to approach the fragrant feet even for a moment. The praise names Siva, struck with a bow, who cut off Brahma's middle head and begged with it and burned the triple city with a smile, with Uma at his side, sounds the battle in drum syllables, names Rama who cut Ravana's ten heads and twenty arms with one arrow, and Murugan who comes on the peacock, the young lord of a golden town amid pearl-strewn fields.
nuance: The routine runs from விலையறுக்கவும், fixing the price, to புதிய பேருடனே கதைகள் செப்பவும், the next customer, a full cycle of the trade. குணங்கண்டும் துளங்கா: the poet's fault is that seeing it all does not shake him. The song ends with இளைய நாயகனே rather than பெருமாளே and names the town only as தமனியப்பதி, the golden town.

title: கோடைநகர்
theme: Songs at Kodainagar (கோடைநகர்): two twin songs trace a life from the womb through play, women and the search for wealth to the edge of hell, two short akam songs plead for a lovesick girl, one catalogues the brutes who fall into Yama's pit, and others ask for the feet at the hour of death and for the yogic stilling of breath that ends dying.
structure_note: 703 and 704 are twins, in the same metre and with the same closing plea. 705 and 706 are akam songs in another voice. 707 has no plea at all, only a list of sinners and their end. 708 is a death song and 709 a yogic one.
source_issues: Song 703: unflagged garble பாழவெளநேரகெய் தாம (line 7); the twin song 704 has பாழ்நரகெய் தாம, so read பாழ்நரகு எய்தாமல்.
Song 707: corrupt character in வயலு¡ரா (line 21), clearly வயலூரா; also சொங்கள் (line 11) may be a garble for சொம்கள் or சொத்துகள், 'property'.

tamil: ஆதிமுத னாளி லென்றன் தாயுடலி யி ருந்து
ஆசையுட னேபி றந்து நேசமுட னேவ ளர்ந்து
பூதலமெ லாம லைந்து மாதருட னேக லந்து
போகமதி லேயு ழன்று பாழவெளநேரகெய் தாம லுன்றன்
சீதைகொடு போகு மந்த ராவணனை மாள வென்ற
தேவர்முநி வோர்கள் கொண்டல் மாலரிபிர் மாவு நின்று
கோதைமலை வாழு கின்ற நாதரிட பாக நின்ற
கூடிவரு சூரர் தங்கள் மார்பையிரு கூறு கண்ட
reading: The poet tells his life from the first day as an embryo in his mother's body, born with desire, raised with love, grown into a handsome man who played, roamed the earth, mixed with women and sought wealth thinking it needful, and asks to be given love to reach the flower feet before he falls into ruinous hell. The praise names Murugan nephew of Narayana who killed Ravana for carrying off Sita, son of the one whom gods, sages, Vishnu and Brahma could not find in their search, and the lord who came to dwell at Kodainagar.
nuance: The plea is a life in stages (ஆகமலமாகி நின்று, பிறந்து, வளர்ந்து, ஆளழகனாகி, மாதருடனே கலந்து, பொருள்தேடி), each a step toward the hell it ends in. What it asks for is love (அன்பு) that reaches the feet, not release as such. கோதைமலை in the praise is unclear to me.

tamil: சாலநெடு நாள்ம டந்தை காயமதி லேய லைந்து
சாதகமு மான பின்பு சீறியழு தேகி டந்து
பாலனென வேமொ ழிந்து பாகுமொழி மாதர் தங்கள்
பார்மிசையி லேயு ழன்று பாழ்நரகெய் தாம லொன்று
ஆலமமு தாக வுண்ட ஆறுசடை நாதர் திங்கள்
ஆனைமடு வாயி லன்று மூலமென வோல மென்ற
கோலமலர் வாவி யெங்கு மேவுபுனம் வாழ்ம டந்தை
reading: A twin of 703: the poet tells of lying long in the woman's body, coming to earth in pains near death, the birth rites, crying, crawling and playing, being called a child, then lying on the heavy breasts of sweet-voiced women, seeking wealth and wandering, and asks for love to reach the one flower foot before he falls into hell. The praise names Siva who drank the poison as nectar, Narayana who answered the elephant's cry of 'Root' in the pond, Valli whose lips' nectar Murugan drank, and the vel that felled Sura, at Kodainagar.
nuance: சாதகமுமான பின்பு: the birth rite (jatakarma) is one stage among the others. The elephant crying மூலமே is the story of Gajendra, as in 25.

reading: A short akam song in the voice of someone pleading for a lovesick girl: Kama, who did not die though the rider of the bull burned him to ash, wounds her with his fragrant arrows, and the flute with its seven-note holes torments her; it asks Murugan not to let this deer-like girl, wasting into enmity, hurt, end and longing, perish, but to come, look on her and join her, or else give his unfading kadamba garland. The praise names the Kumara of the peacock who circles the fourteen worlds, the deathless, ageless lord of Kodai, who fought until great Sura fell uprooted, the hero of the vel.
nuance: The song is a chain of short rhyming words (வாராய் பாராய் சேராய்; தேவா சாவா மூவா நாதா), so the splitting is often a guess. Asking for the god's garland when he will not come is a standing akam motif of the Thiruppugazh. I read the voice as a mother's or companion's; it is not said.

reading: A short akam song: a lovesick girl, or one speaking for her, asks Murugan to come and embrace her with his twelve arms so that she does not perish from the sea that roars around the world, the slander the women speak each day, and the moon that burns like poison. The praise names the chest that embraced the hunter girl, the peacock hero who stands at Kodai, and the lord who pierced the mountain so that Death took fright and loosed the fetters of the gods.
nuance: The torments are the classical ones: the sea's roar, the town's gossip (வஞ்சியர் உற்று உரைக்கும் வசை) and the moon that burns like the poison (ஆலம்). The speaker is not named.

reading: The song lists the brutes (குண்டர்கள்) who fall into the pit where Yama torments: those who make friends and then betray, who forget the good done them, who break their vows, who revile the great, who obstruct giving when they see it, who abandon their oaths, who long to live forever, who wreck justice and dharma, who swell with pride, who suffer in maya, and who seize the property of the gods. The praise names Rama, whose arrow pierced the seven trees and Vali and brought down Ravana's Lanka, as uncle, Murugan of Vayalur with its towers and peacocks, and the lord of Kodai praised by gods and devotees.
nuance: There is no plea and no confession: this is a moral catalogue in the manner of the didactic books, and Yama's pit is its only sanction. ஈவது கண்டு தகைந்த, blocking another's giving, and ஓதிய நன்றி மறந்த, forgetting a good done, are Kural sins. வயலூரா in the praise names another shrine.

reading: The poet pictures the kin who gather weeping, Yama come with his terrible heavy trident and noose, the bier and the fire, and asks that he not perish thus in ruin but that Murugan, in grace, set him, a man in bonds, at the golden feet. The praise names the vel that fought until Sura fled into the sea, the hero who gave a garland to the honey-girl in the forest, the one who goes singing at Koodal, and the lord of Kodai with its rice fields and groves.
nuance: பாசத்தேனை: the poet calls himself the one in bonds, so Yama's noose (பாசம்) and his own bondage share a word. கூடற் பாடிக் கோவைப் பாவைக் கூடப் பாடித் திரிவோனே may refer to Murugan singing at Madurai, or to a kovai poem; I can't identify it.

tamil: வாசித்த நூல்ம தங்கள் பேசிக்கொ டாத விந்து
மாசிக்க பால மன்றில் நாசிக்கு ளோடு கின்ற
யோசித்த யாரு டம்பை நேசித்து றாத லைந்து
யோகச்ச மாதி கொண்டு மோகப்ப சாசு மண்டு
வீசப்ப யோதி துஞ்ச வேதக்கு லால னஞ்ச
வீரப்ர தாப பஞ்ச பாணத்தி னால்ம யங்கி
கூசிப்பு காவொ துங்க மாமற்றி காத ரிந்த
கோழிப்ப தாகை கொண்ட கோலக்கு மார கண்ட
reading: The poet asks whether, with the bindu that read books and argued creeds cannot give made steady as the light of truth, and the breath that runs in the nose turned into the hall of the skull, he will not by yogic samadhi end this dying again and again in a world crowded by the demon of delusion, the life leaving through every pore. The praise names the vel that dried the sea and frightened Brahma, the potter of the Vedas, the Murugan who, dazed by Kama's five arrows, fell at the hunter girl's feet, the son of the destroyer of the cities, and the lord of the cock banner who came to dwell at Kodai.
nuance: A rare yogic plea: knowledge from books and sects (வாசித்த நூல் மதங்கள்) is set against the bindu-light, and the breath is to be turned (மடைமாறி) into the skull (கபால மன்றில்). The middle lines (யோசித்த யாருடம்பை நேசித்துறாது அலைந்து) are hard to divide, and whether the dying through the pores is ordinary death or the yogi's departure is not clear.

title: திருப்பேரூர்
theme: Songs at Tiruporur (the heading reads திருப்பேரூர், the songs திருப்போரூர்): three confessions of bondage to women, one naming the courtesans' messengers, betel and greed, end in a plea for grace or for the feet, and a fourth song is a litany of epithets for Murugan, the sun that clears the darkness of ego.
structure_note: 710 to 712 are confessions about women; 713 is praise alone, a chain of Sanskrit epithets.
source_issues: Chapter heading reads திருப்பேரூர், but the songs name திருப்போரூர் (710, 711), போரி மாநகர் (712) and சமர மாபுரி (713); the heading should probably be திருப்போரூர்.

reading: The poet tells how women with honeyed speech feign great infatuation, send hundreds of messengers in a day, call a man home, laugh and flirt, embrace him, bend to give betel and bite it halfway, drink the saliva of his lips as honey and play many games, all meaning to snatch his wealth through his infatuation, and asks for grace so that his desire for these sinful women leaves him. The praise names the hero who, carrying off the hunter girl, won with one sword against the hunters who surrounded him, the nephew of Vishnu who sent his discus by thought to the elephant seized in the lotus pond, and the lord of Tiruporur with its chariots, walls and towers.
nuance: நீள்பொருள் பறிப்பார்: the whole performance, messengers and betel included, is aimed at wealth, which is what makes these courtesans in the Kural's sense. The sword fight with the hunters is a less common detail of the Valli story.

tamil: உ ருக்கார் வாளி கண்கள் பொருப்பார் வார்த னங்கள்
உ ருச்சேர் நீண்ம ருங்குல் பணைத்தோ ளோதி கொண்ட
அருக்கா மாதர் தங்கள் வரைக்கே யோடி யின்ப
அசட்டால் மூடு கின்ற மசக்கால் மாயு மிந்த
எருக்கார் தாளி தும்பை மருச்சேர் போது கங்கை
இருக்கா லேநி னைந்து துதிப்பார் நாவி னெஞ்சி
செருக்கா லேமி குந்த கடற்சூர் மாள வென்ற
தினைக்கோர் காவல் கொண்ட குறத்தேன் மாது பங்க
reading: The poet calls himself a great sinner whose heart runs to the women with arrow-eyes, mountain breasts, crescent foreheads and cloud-dark hair, and wears their net of pleasure, and asks for grace so that he is spared the disgrace of dying in the dullness and folly that cover him. The praise names Murugan son of the lord who wears erukku, thali and thumbai flowers and the Ganga, who dwells in the tongues and hearts of those who praise him in Vedic verse, whose vel destroyed Sura in the sea, and Valli's partner at Tiruporur.
nuance: அசட்டால் மூடுகின்ற மசக்கால் மாயும் இந்த அவத்தால்: what the poet fears is a pointless death in stupor, more than the women themselves. இருக்காலே நினைந்து may mean 'by the Rig Veda' or 'with the verses'.

tamil: சீரு லாவிய வோதிம மான மாநடை மாமயில்
தேனு லாவிய மாமொழி மேரு நேரிள மாமுலை
தாரு லாவிய நீள்குழல் வேய ளாவிய தோளியர்
சாம வேதியர் வானவ ரோதி நாண்மலர் தூவிய
காரு லாவிய நீள்புன வேடர் மால்வரை மீதுறை
காண ஆகம வேதபு ராண நூல்பல வோதிய
போரு லாவிய சூரனை வாரி சேறெழ வேல்விடு
போதன் மாதவன் மாதுமை பாதி யாதியு மேதொழு
reading: The poet describes the women he roams beside, swan-gaited and peacock-graceful, moon-faced, honey-tongued, with breasts like Meru, carp eyes and bamboo shoulders, and asks that by Murugan's grace he fall at the feet on which Sama Vedic priests and gods strew fresh flowers. The praise names Murugan who embraced the girl guarding the field on the hunters' hill, the cause who spoke the Agamas, Vedas and Puranas, the compassionate one whose vel churned the sea to mud against Sura, worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu, Uma and Siva, at Porur.
nuance: The description of the women is a catalogue of conventional likenesses, part for part, and takes half the song. வினாமிக is obscure to me.

tamil: திமிர மாமன மாமட மடமை யேனிட ராணவ
தினக ராசிவ காரண பனக பூஷண ஆரண
குமரி சாமளை மாதுமை அமலி யாமளை பூரணி
குருகு காகும ரேசுர சரவ ணாசக ளேசுர
பமர பாரப்ர பாருண படல தாரக மாசுக
பசித பாரண வாரண துவச ஏடக மாவயில்
சமப ராமத சாதல சமய மாறிரு தேவத
சகல லோகமு மாசறு சகல வேதமு மேதொழு
reading: A song of praise alone: Murugan is the sun that destroys the darkness of ego in the poet's dark and foolish mind, the sun of the three worlds, the son of Siva and nephew of Narayana, the child given by Uma under her many names (Kumari, Syamala, Amali, Yamala, Purani, Narayani), Guha, Saravana, the jewel desired by the hunters' daughter, the lord of the six sects and their gods, worshipped by all worlds and all Vedas at Samarapuri.
nuance: ஆணவ திமிரமே அரி சூரிய: the one doctrinal phrase makes Murugan the sun that removes anava, the first of the bonds. சமய மாறிரு தேவத சமய நாயக reads as lord of the six sects. Many of the compound epithets in the middle (பமர பாரப்ர பாருண, பசுர பாடன பாளித) are Sanskrit I can't divide with confidence. சமர மாபுரி translates the shrine's name, போர் being battle.

title: உத்தரமேரூர்
theme: Songs at Uttaramerur (உத்தரமேரூர், வடமேரு): the poet asks to know by inner knowledge the feet that all the gods and sages fail to know, to be rid of the body built of skin and phlegm, to be looked on despite a life spent chasing women and wealth and singing for worthless men, and to be freed from the sea of desire; one praise recalls Siva claiming Sundarar as his slave.

tamil: சுருதி மறைக ளிருநாலு திசையி லதிபர் முநிவேர்கள்
சொலவில் முடிவில் முகியாத பகுதி புருடர் நவநாதர்
அரிய சமய மொருகோடி அமாரர் சரணர் சதகோடி
அறிய அறிய அறியாத அடிக ளறிய அடியேனும்
வரைகள் தவிடு பொடியாக நிருதர் பதியு மழிவாக
மடிய அலகை நடமாட விஜய வனிதை மகிழ்வாக
நரிகள் கொடிகள் பசியாற உ திர நதிக ளலைமோத
நளின வுபய கரவேலை முடுகு முருக வடமேரு
reading: The poet lists those who seek and cannot know the Lord's feet, the Vedas, the guardians of the eight directions, the seven rishis, the three lights, the nine Naths, the star-worlds, the priests, a crore of sects and hundreds of crores of gods, and asks that he, a servant, be given the knowledge that knows within knowledge, so that he may know them. The praise is a battle: mountains turn to powder, the sea to mud, Sura dies, ghouls dance, dogs, jackals and crows feed on rivers of blood, and even Yama bows, as Murugan rides the peacock, lord of the gods at Vada Meru.
nuance: அறிய அறிய அறியாத அடிகள் ... அறிவுள் அறியும் அறிவு: the feet that all knowing fails to know are to be known by a knowing within knowing, given by grace. The long list of seekers is there to set off the poet's 'even I' (அடியேனும்).

tamil: தோலெ லும்பு சீந ரம்பு பீளை துன்று கோழை பொங்கு
தூல பங்க காயம் வம்பி லேசு மந்து நான்மெ லிந்து
ஆல முண்ட கோன கண்ட லோக முண்ட மால்வி ரிஞ்ச
ஆன னங்கள் மூவி ரண்டு மாறி ரண்டு தோளு மங்கை
வால சந்த்ர சூடி சந்த வேத மந்த்ர ரூபி யம்பை
மாயை யைந்து வேக மைந்து பூத மைந்து நாத மைந்து
வேலையன்பு கூர வந்த ஏக தந்த யானை கண்டு
வீர மங்கை வாரி மங்கை பாரின் மங்கை மேவு கின்ற
reading: The poet speaks of the gross body built of skin, bone, pus, nerves, rheum and phlegm, rolled into a lump, which he carries uselessly and wastes in, and asks whether, his sickness and sorrow gone, he will think of the feet praised by Siva, Vishnu, Brahma, the Vedas and Agamas, and of the six faces, twelve shoulders and victorious vel.
