tamil: அரிமரு கோனே நமோவென் றறுதியி லானே நமோவென்
அரகர சேயே நமோவென் றிமையவர் வாழ்வே நமோவென்
பரிபுர பாதா சுரேசன் றருமக ணாதா வராவின்
பகர்தலி லாதாளை யேதுஞ் சிலதறி யாவேழை நானுன்
கரதல சூலாயு தாமுன் சலபதி போலார வாரங்
கரிபரி மேலேறு வானுஞ் செயசெய சேனா பதீயென்
குரல்விட நாய்பேய்கள் பூதங் கழுகுகள் கோமாயு காகங்
குடதிசை வாராழி போலும் படர்நதி காவேரி சூழுங்
reading: The poet sets out a litany of homage (நமோ), to Hari's nephew, the one without end, the six-faced Vel, Hara's son, the life of the gods, and says his desire is for the feet; he calls himself a poor man who knows nothing and asks to receive Murugan's teaching of pati, pasu and pasam. The praise shows Chamundi drunk and roaring like the sea as she dances, the rider of elephant and horse hailing Murugan 'victory, victory, commander', and dogs, ghouls, vultures, jackals and crows feasting on the field where Sura fell, at Vayalur by the Kaveri.
nuance: பதி பசு பாச உபதேசம் is the Saiva Siddhanta triad named outright as the content of the teaching asked for. ஆடம்பர நாளும் பகர்தல் இலாது may contrast showy daily recitation with the poor man's plea, but the division of that run of syllables is uncertain. The rider of elephant and horse who hails the commander is probably Indra.

reading: With the refrain காட்டி ('showing'), the poet lists what women show: breasts, Kama's state, clothes and jewels, alluring eyes, sweet voice, feigned affection to anyone, wet smiles and their arts, until they show the net of their snare; he asks whether that showing of ruin is not enough. The praise plays on வேலை (vel, sea, sport): Murugan fed fire to the forest of Sura's armies, rides the peacock, sent the vel into the sea, wed the virtuous hunter girl of the hill country, and freed the gods, at Vayalur.
nuance: The song is built on one verb: the women 'show' everything, and the plea turns the verb on the poet's own ruin (ஈடழிதல் காட்டல் அமையாதோ), which may mean 'is it not enough to have shown me my ruin?' or 'will this showing of ruin not stop?'. சேர மலை நாட்டில் may place Valli in the Chera hill country or simply mean the hill land where they gather.

reading: In a long, dense rhythm the poet describes lovemaking in detail, nails, kisses, loosened hair and bird-cries on the bed, and the women who cast the net of their eyes to seize wealth; he asks when Murugan will cut away the grief of Kama's arts and protect him, held in boundless Siva-knowledge, so that he praises in Thiruppugazh. After a battle in drum syllables, the praise names the Kumara of Vayali, Hari's nephew, the six-faced one, and the lord who could tell without error the path of release to the father who dances on the northern peak.
nuance: பொருட் கவர கட்டுப் பொறிச்சியர்கள், 'trappers who bind to seize wealth', marks the women as courtesans. The remedy is the book itself: திருப்புகழை உற்றுத் துதிக்கும் வகை. வடகுவடில் நடனமிடும் அப்பர்க்கு முத்திநெறி தப்பற்று உரைக்க is Murugan as Siva's teacher, here of the path to mukti rather than of Om.

tamil: உ றவு சொலவல துரகிகள் விரகிகள் ...... பிறைபோலே
உ ணர்வு கெடும்வகை பருவிக ளுருவிக ...... ளுறவாமோ
reading: The poet heaps up epithets for courtesans in rhyming -igal endings: they price their breasts, know many arts, bite lips, join fools for their money, carry eyes like swords that even Yama would find excessive, torment the world, speak of kinship and deceive, and he asks whether they are fit for kinship. The praise is a battlefield of ghouls and demons where Uma bows and the goddess of victory dances, and names Murugan the guru who threw the vel in a moment, lord of the way of knowledge, at Vayali near Trisirapuram.
nuance: மடையர் பொருள் பெற மருவிகள், those who join fools to get their money, and உறவு சொலவல துரகிகள் விரகிகள், skilled at talk of kinship and deceit, are the stock charges. The rhyme-chain (அசடிகள் கசடிகள் ... கபடிகள் முகடிகள்) is itself the rhetoric: abuse by sound. த்ரிசிரி கிரி is Trichy's rock, which places Vayali.

reading: The poet asks whether it is by him that he is born and dies, praises, calls, walks, sits, enjoys women's houses, tires, burns the disease of attachment, thinks and bears, and ends: who am I here? The praise names Murugan the king who drew fibre from stone, the lord who gave him the word that is nectar to the ear, the vel seen as in a mirror, not dwelling in the minds of the unlearned, son of the gracious Siva who destroyed Daksha, king of the hunter girl and of Vayal town, the one lord over the three.
nuance: The repeated என்னால் ('by me') ends in இங்கு நான் ஆர், 'who am I here?': agency is taken from the self, and even the visits to women are listed among acts not the poet's own. கல் நார் உரித்த, drawing fibre from stone, is the softening of a stony heart. கர்ணாமிர்தப் பதம் தந்த கோவே points to the word given the poet at Vayalur. Whether the question is surrender or bewilderment is not said.

reading: The poet compares a woman's parts, eyes to the sea and arrows, brow to bow and crescent, lips to fruit and coral, breasts to elephant and hill, waist to creeper and drum, hip to a serpent's hood, and says that by her body, dress and proud walk he whirls in a sorrow where even one day apart is hard; he asks whether he will not escape it. The praise has crows, jackals and ghouls feeding on the demons whose guts were torn out, the gods resettled, and Murugan who loves the daughter of the fierce hill hunters, at Vayalur among fragrant screwpine groves.
nuance: The plea names a lover's grief rather than a courtesan's fraud: ஒருநாள் பிரிவது அரிதாய்ச் சுழல்படும் ஒழியாத் துயர், the unending sorrow of one who cannot bear a day's parting. எழில் பாத்திரம் இவள், 'she is a vessel of beauty', gives the woman one direct line.

reading: The poet describes golden women like Lakshmi in the lotus, whose camphor-scented breasts, lightning waists, moon faces, dark hair circled by humming bees, bangled shoulders and mango-slice eyes bewilder young men versed in the whole of Kama's quarrelsome lore, and asks whether he must suffer again through them. The praise names the vel that shattered demons, chariots and elephants, the hero praised by ghouls in the forest, the lord of Indra's daughter and the hunter girl, at the beautiful temple of Vayali where the Ganapati of unfailing grace and the holy Lord also dwell.
nuance: கலகக் காம நூலை முழுதுணர் இளைஞோர்: the young men are learned in the manual of love, so learning itself is part of the trap. அருளில் சீர் பொய்யாத கணபதி and திருவக்கீசன் point to the shrine's own deities: Vayalur has a Ganapati called Poyyā Ganapati and a Siva called Agnisvara, which is my identification from the names.

reading: The poet asks not to perish among impatient men of endless argument, among those who deal in mantra-magic, in the ritual works and rules of conduct that sectarians take up, or even in the chariyai, kiriyai and yoga practised by those devoted to the embodied Lord, but to be given jnana that does not waver. The praise names Murugan as the vel that ended the Diti-born demons' torment of the world, the precious lord of Siva of Thiruvotriyur with the red flame and blue throat, and the supreme beyond maya, bindu, nada and shakti, the god of Mélai Vayali.
nuance: The list descends from quarrelling logicians to sectarians and then to the Saiva paths themselves: சரியை க்ரியா யோக நியமத்தின் மாயாது. The first three paths, usually steps toward jnana, become places one can be lost in. சலனப்படா ஞானம், knowledge that does not waver, is set against all of them. மாயை விந்து நாதம் வரசத்தி மேலான பரவத்து puts Murugan above the tattvas of the Siddhanta scheme.

reading: With the refrain அலமல ('enough, enough'), the poet renounces the body of blood, worms, water, filth, hair and flesh, its ornaments, perfumes, six-flavoured food and bed, wife, children, mother and kin, all worldly learning but the Siva-lore of the four Vedas, and every tie but with those who think of the Lord; he asks for the knowledge that reaches the shore of the sea of grace. The praise has drums, ghouls and gods crying 'Hara, Siva', names Murugan the nephew of the child who crawled with the mortar and broke the marutha trees, and places him at Viralimalai with its tiger caves and at Vayali where carp leap in the paddy.
nuance: The renunciation is ordered from the body outward to food and bed, kin and learning, and keeps only one tie, உனை நினைபவர் உறவு, kinship with those who think of the Lord. The infant Krishna dragging the mortar between the marutha trees (மருது முறிபட உருளும் உரலொடு தவழ்) is told in its unmistakable details.

reading: The poet gives the questions of courtship, 'is that a cuckoo's voice, a spear for eyes, a creeper waist?', and the lovemaking with women in their sea of pleasure whom he befriends instead of thinking them enemies, and asks whether, by the grace of Murugan who equals the Pati above pasu and pasam, he will not know the truth. The praise is obscure: it seems to recall Karna, king of Anga and son of the sun, facing the one in a eunuch's guise, and names Murugan the son of Hara and the peacock at Vayalur where the Kaveri carries akil and sandal, lord of the gods of Amaravati.
nuance: பகையே என நினையாது உற நண்பு கூரும்: the error is taking enemies for friends. The plea asks for மெய் உணர்தல, knowing the real, through the Pati of the Siddhanta triad. இரவிசேய் எனும் அங்கராசன் is Karna; மயல் பேடிகை may be Arjuna disguised as Brihannala, but how the lines join is not clear to me.

tamil: கோவை வாயி தழுக்குந் தாக போக மளிக்குங்
கோல மாலை வளைக்குந் தோளி னாலு மணத்தங்
ஆவி கோடி யவிக்குஞ் சேலி னாலு மயக்குண்
ஆசி லாத மறைக்குந் தேடொ ணாதொரு வர்க்கொன்
சேவி லேறு நிருத்தன் தோகை பாக னளிக்குந்
தேடொ ணாத பதத்தன் தீதி லாத மனத்தன்
காவி டாத திருச்செங் கோடு நாடு தனக்குங்
காதி மோதி யெதிர்க்குஞ் சூர தீரர் ப்ரமிக்குங்
reading: The poet speaks of women's kovai-fruit lips, breasts, garland-bearing shoulders, combed and scented hair and carp-like eyes that wither a crore of lives, and asks that, deluded, he not wear himself out daily but be given today the dancing feet that even the faultless Veda cannot find. The praise names Siva, dancer on the bull, consort of the peacock-like Uma, whose feet Vishnu could not find, of fire's colour, as Murugan's father, says Murugan loves Thiruchengodu and Vayali among the lilies, and calls him the one who stops Death's play.
nuance: The feet asked for are ஆடல் தாள்கள், dancing feet, and the Veda cannot reach them (ஆசிலாத மறைக்கும் தேடொணாது), as Vishnu could not find Siva's feet in the praise: the plea and the praise share one motif.

reading: The poet recalls how Murugan, intending him for his lotus-like feet, came to him on the great hill of Viralimalai crowded with konrai and magizh trees, called 'come', cut away the stain of his mind's desire and gave him the nectar of jnana, and vows never to forget that love. The praise names Murugan the guru of Siva, who burned Kama with his forehead eye, bears the heavenly river in his hair and wears a forest snake as an earring, and the lord of Vayalur, whose vel cut off Sura's head.
nuance: This is autobiography, not confession: வா என அழைத்து என் மனது ஆசை மாசினை அறுத்து ஞானமுது அளித்த வாரம் இனி நித்தம் மறவேனே. The call is placed at Viralimalai (அவிராலி மாமலை), though the song is sung at Vayalur, which tradition makes the place of the first call. The pledge is gratitude, not a request.

tamil: திருவு ரூப நேராக அழக தான மாமாய
சிகரி யூடு தேமாலை யடவி யூடு போயாவி
கருவி ழாது சீரோதி யடிமை பூண லாமாறு
கருணை வாரி கூரேக முகமும் வீர மாறாத
சருவ தேவ தேவாதி நமசி வாய நாமாதி
சதம கீவல் போர்மேவு குலிச பாணி மால்யானை
மநு நியாய சோணாடு தலைமை யாக வேமேலை
reading: The poet calls himself a sinner of bad conduct, his life pierced by women of beautiful form and deep delusion, and thanks Murugan who ruled him in a dream so that he would not fall into the womb but sing his glory and take up service; he vows never to forget the peacock, the sea of compassion, the faces, the hero's anklets, the kadamba and the vel. The praise names Siva, god of gods, of the name Namasivaya, half woman with the mountain's daughter, as father, Vishnu whose foot measured the fourteen worlds as uncle, and the god of Mélai Vayali in the Chola land ruled by Manu's justice.
nuance: கனவில் ஆள் சுவாமீ: the Lord took the poet as his servant in a dream, a second piece of the poet's own story beside 911. கருவிழாது சீரோதி அடிமை பூணலாமாறு gives the purpose: not to fall back into the womb, to sing and to serve. The line on Indra's thunderbolt and elephant is partly corrupt, and whom it names (Devayanai, raised by Indra's elephant?) is not clear.

tamil: புக்க அனல்வய மிகஏ டுயவே ...... உ மையாள்தன்
reading: In a run of either-or questions, the poet asks whether a woman's hair is black sand or cloud, her brow a bow or the crescent, her eyes arrows or does, her lips fruit or coral, her breasts pots or hills, her waist a creeper or a drum, her feet flowers or shoots, and confesses wandering vainly in that infatuation; he vows not to forget even once the jewelled-anklet feet. The praise makes Murugan the one who came in the form of the Kaundinya lord of Brahmapuram, learned in Tamil and Veda and praised as Uma's son, when the Buddhists and Jains were ruined, the southern king took the ash and the palm leaf survived the fire, and names him Hari's nephew and Shakti-Ganapati's younger brother, at Vayalur.
nuance: The questions (அறலோ முகிலோ, சிலையோ பிறையோ) are the conventional comparisons put as a lover's doubt, so the confession is made from inside the poetry it renounces. பிரமாபுரம் வாழ் கவுணியர் பெருமான் is Sambandar of Sirkazhi of the Kaundinya clan; the ordeal by fire (அனல் ... ஏடு உயவே) and the Pandya's ash are his story, credited to Murugan.

reading: The poet describes courtesans who half-hide at the door, send small messengers to men of desire, press faces and nails, loosen their garments on the flower bed and wear young men down day after day, then swear 'this is the price, this is the truth' and turn harsh when the money given runs out, and asks whether having joined them is not enough. The praise tells of the churning of the sea with the mountain as churn and Vasuki as rope, Vishnu at one end and Vali at the other, and Lakshmi rising with the nectar, and names Murugan the bridegroom of the noble one who cuts the chain of deeds, at Vayalur.
nuance: விலை ஈதே கடிய சத்தியமாம் எனவே சொலி: the woman names her price and swears to it, the trade and the oath in one line. அவர் கொடப் பணம் மாறிட கடுகடுத்திடுவார், growing harsh when the money given changes, is the stock end. Vali among the churners is an unusual detail. The last lines (மறு ஒர் எட்டுடன் ஆயிரம்) are obscure.

title: வயலூர்
theme: Last songs at Vayalur (வயலூர், 2 of 2): the courtesans' showing and the dangerous beauty of women, answered by a litany of the Goddess's names and by the longest plea of the group, which sets the 'small pleasure' of union against the three impurities removed and the sea of Siva's release.
structure_note: 915 repeats the காட்டி refrain of 901; 916 turns from women to a long list of the Goddess's names; 917 is a very long song in which the confession, the doctrinal plea and the battle in drum syllables each run to many lines.
source_issues: Song 915: corrupt character in வயலு¡ரா (line 12), probably வயலூரா.

Song 917: corrupt characters in வுந்த§முழ்கி (line 18, probably வுந்திமூழ்கி) and in பக்ஷ¢த்து, ரக்ஷ¢த்த (line 63, probably பக்ஷித்து, ரக்ஷித்த); unflagged garble ப்ரைமைதரு (line 29, probably ப்ரமைதரு).

tamil: மேகலை நெகிழ்த்துக் காட்டி வார்குழல் விரித்துக் காட்டி
மேனியை மினுக்கிக் காட்டி நாடக நடித்துக் காட்டி
ஆகம முரைத்துக் காட்டி வாரணி தனத்தைக் காட்டி
ஆதர மனத்தைக் காட்டி வேசைகள் மயக்கைக் காட்ட
மோகன விருப்பைக் காட்டி ஞானமு மெடுத்துக் காட்டி
மூவுல களித்துக் காட்டி சேவலை யுயர்த்திக் காட்டு
வாகையை முடித்துக் காட்டி கானவர் சமர்த்தைக் காட்டி
மாமலை வெதுப்பிக் காட்டி தானவர் திறத்தைக் காட்டி
reading: With the refrain காட்டி ('showing'), the poet lists what courtesans show, the loosened girdle, spread hair, rolling spear eyes, shining body, staged drama, invitations to their houses, Kama's rules recited, breasts, laughter with anyone and pretended feeling, and asks whether he will perish by the desire they show. The praise uses the same verb for Murugan: he showed love, drew out and showed jnana as the guru who taught the old Tamil sage, gave the three worlds, raised the cock banner, made the peacock dance, heated the great mountain, and guarded the gods' heads, at Vayalur.
nuance: The one verb carries both halves: the women 'show' to deceive (விரகாலே, வேசைகள் மயக்கைக் காட்ட), and the Lord 'shows' jnana (ஞானமும் எடுத்துக் காட்டி). மூதமிழ் முனிக்குக் கூட்டு குருநாதா is Murugan as Agastya's teacher of Tamil.

reading: The poet says women's eyes are crueller than a sword's edge, poison, Yama's tread and arrows, and lists their nectar mouths, white smiles, sweet 'come, sit', rosewater, saffron, sandal and musk, breasts, hips and navel, the hut where maya dwells, and asks whether he will cease to be bewildered on seeing such harlots. The praise is a litany of the Goddess, Kali, Tripurai, Sundari, Nili, Gauri, Sankari, Sivai, Kundali, Chandika, Ambika, Tryambaki whom Lakshmi, Saraswati, Rati, Arundhati and Indra's queen worship, Vishnu's sister, and names Murugan her son, who removes the sorrow of those who think of the vel and peacock, at Mélai Vayalur.
nuance: மாயை குடிகொள் குடம்பை, the nest where maya lives, calls the woman's body the dwelling of illusion. The praise gives most of its length to the Goddess's names, so the song is as much hers as her son's, as in 32.

reading: Over many lines the poet describes perfumed women who roam the streets and take young men's wealth with their lives, and a long scene of lovemaking, lips tasted like nectar and honey, marks of nail and teeth, the bird-cries learned from Kama's art, and the lovers' points of the moon from foot to crown, an experience 'one cannot leave even for a moment'; knowing this union a small pleasure, he asks when, the three impurities cut and the mind made one, he will reach the boundless space and light, the manifest Siva-tattva and the sea of release. The praise, after drum syllables, shakes peaks, seas, the eight elephants and the serpent Sesha, fills the field with blood, vultures and jackals, and names the Saravanabhava of Vayali who taught Agastya the Tamil of verse, music and drama.
nuance: புணரும் இது சிறு சுகம்: the poet judges union a small pleasure, after describing it at length as one that 'cannot be left for a moment' (ஒரு பொழுதும் விடலரிது). The lunar kalas waxing and waning on the body (குமுத பதி கலை குறைகலை நிறைகலை) come from the love manuals. The plea runs through Siddhanta terms: திரிமலம் அற்று, கருத்து ஒருமை உற்று, சிவ தத்வ ப்ரசித்தி, முத்திச் சிவக் கடல். The division of several lines in the plea is unsure.

title: திருத்தவத்துறை
theme: Songs at Thiruthavathurai (திருத்தவத்துறை, Lalgudi) on the Kaveri: two courtesan songs whose pleas ask to leave the women's delusion and to be raised among the devotees, with praise of the vel that taught Siva and of the shrine's goddess who fosters dharma.
source_issues: Song 919: corrupt character in ய¨டையை (line 4), probably யுடையை.

reading: The poet describes courtesans who gather and tie up their dark hair for others to see, roll eyes that reach their ears, grow deceit in their minds, make the wealth in lustful men's hands their kin, bare breasts like full pots and put a price on anyone's heart, and asks for grace to leave their delusion. The praise shows ghouls dancing to drums and vultures circling, Siva on the bull dancing like a spun top, and names Murugan the hero of Thiruthavathurai on the Kaveri, who crushed the demons and cut the gods free.
nuance: காமுகர் அன்பு புகுவித்த கைப்பொருள் உறவாகி: the women's kinship is with the money, not the man, and யாரையும் நெஞ்சை விலைப்படுத்திடு, pricing anyone's heart, says the trade reaches the heart itself.

reading: The poet speaks of women in pearl garlands with bent waists and fine garments who fill men of wealth with infatuation and stand daily in the streets with cuckoo voices, and asks whether, so that he does not whirl in their net but lives praising the anklets, Murugan will not speak the word that raises him, a sinner of low quality, to the high state in the assembly of devotees. The praise names the vel that spoke true jnana into the ear of Siva who dwells in the hearts of great ascetics, mansions where the fame of the Thiruvasagam spreads, the Kaveri's floods and heaped paddy, Seyppathi, and the goddess of eternal auspiciousness who fosters dharma, at Thiruthavathurai.
nuance: அத்தமுளோர் தமையே மயல் நிரப்பி: the women choose men of wealth. The plea is for a place in the சபை of devotees, a social salvation. The line on the Thiruvasagam spoken by the great one among Tamil scholars seems to refer to Manikkavasagar's work, but its syntax is unclear to me. அறம் வளர்த்த நித்ய கல்யாணி names the goddess as the one who fosters dharma.

title: பூவாளூர்
theme: The one song at Poovalur (பூவாளூர்) in the rain-fed land of the Kaveri's channels: a catalogue of murderous, money-asking courtesans, and praise that makes Murugan the child-saint who defeated the Jains of Madurai and saved the Pandya king and queen.
source_issues: Heading: the source gives the shrine as பூவாளுர் beside பூவாளூர, and the song's last line has பூவா ளுருறை (line 24), probably பூவாளூருறை.
Song 920: corrupt character in தீக்ஷ¢த (line 22, probably தீக்ஷித); unflagged garble மர்மு தேவிகள் (line 5, probably மூதேவிகள்).

reading: The poet lists courtesans whose eyes are Death's arrows, saw-blades and poison, murderous sinners who recite the Kama-shastra, question any lover, are vessels of pleasure, ask for coins, are shapes of illusion, and charge with breasts like elephants, and asks whether he should waste time with them; he asks for the day Murugan will say 'come' and rule him with love. The praise is Sambandar's story: the mouth still wet with the Goddess's milk sang, the palm leaf went against the current, eight thousand Jains lost the debate and mounted the stakes, the Tamil land that had abandoned the ash was saved, and the king whose hunch was straightened and his queen were made to live at Alavai; Murugan is that child of jnana, at Poovalur.
nuance: காசு கேட்டிடும் மாயா ரூபிகள, those who ask for coins, mark the courtesans. In the praise every detail is Sambandar's: பால் அறாத் திருவாய் (the infant fed by the Goddess), ஏடு நீர்க்கு எதிர் போய் (the leaf in the Vaigai), இரு நாலாம் ஆயிர சமண் (eight thousand Jains), கூன் நிமிர் இறையோன் (the Pandya cured of his hunch). The queen is not named; tradition calls her Mangaiyarkkarasi. நீறிடாத் தமிழ்நாடு, the Tamil land without the ash, is the poet's word for the Jain period.

title: திருப்பராய்த்துறை
theme: The one song at Thirupparaithurai (திருப்பராய்த்துறை): women who make the poet called vile and a body drowning in disease, and the plea that the Lord come to dwell in his breast; the praise centres on Murugan correcting Brahma's pride and giving the initiation of knowledge.
source_issues: Song 921: corrupt characters in முக்கண ¡றிவாக (line 21, perhaps முக்கணர் அறிவாக) and தீ¨க்ஷ (line 22, probably தீக்ஷை).

reading: The poet describes fragrant women whose small feet ring with anklets, whose breasts stand like two hills and whose eyes redden like Kama's arrows, lovers and deceivers who spin him about until he is called vile, and asks whether there will be a day when, with yoga growing and the body that whirls in the water of disease removed, Murugan sits within his breast. The praise names the vel that wore down the mountain and made Sura tremble, and the wondrous one who changed the pride of Brahma, maker of the world, and spoke the initiation of ancient knowledge, at Paraithurai.
nuance: நீசன் எனும்படியாக்கி: the women's harm is a loss of name as well as of self. நீ அகலம் தனில் வீற்றிருப்பது asks for the Lord enthroned in the breast. வேதன் அகந்தையை மாற்றி ... தீக்ஷை செப்பிய is the binding of Brahma and the teaching that followed, though Om is not named. The opening of the praise (தீர்க்க புத்திர முதல்வோனே, praised by the cloud-dark Vishnu, with a body of diamond) is obscure to me.

title: தென்கடம்பந்துறை
theme: The one song at Then Kadambanthurai (தென்கடம்பந்துறை) on the Kaveri: women's eyes that outdo every standard of comparison and the gold given to them, against a plea to reach the red feet at dawn and dusk; the praise lists the shrines and hearts Murugan dwells in and the river born from Agastya's water-pot.

reading: The poet sets women's eyes against the sea, Kama, the bee, the carp and kendai fish, Yama, the lotus, poison and the vel that pierced the hill, eyes that roam here and there, redden at the corners and are packed with deceit, and asks whether, having given much red gold to such women, he will settle at dawn and dusk, free of ties, so that mind, speech and body draw near Murugan's red feet. The praise lists the kadamba garland, the twelve shoulders, the six faces, mantra and tantra, Palani, Parangundram, Senthil and the hearts of true devotees, Siva with serpent, Ganga and moon who bows to him as guru, and the shrine on the river that came from the sage's water-pot on the Kudagu hill.
nuance: செந்தனம் தந்து, giving red gold, makes the women courtesans. த்ரிவித கரணங்களும் ... குறுகும்வகை: the three instruments of mind, speech and body are to approach the feet together. குடகு, the sage's கமண்டலம் and the river point to the Kaveri born from Agastya's water-pot; the part played by சங்கரன் in that line is not clear to me.

title: கருவூர்
theme: Songs at Karuvur (கருவூர், also Karuvai, Garbhapuram and Vanji): pleas for Siva-jnana and for the experience of the Pati beyond pasu and pasam, a confession of the elemental body and its pride of 'I', love scenes the poet asks to leave, and a song on kings in their pomp who do not know their death, with the Mahabharata in the praise.
structure_note: Doctrinal songs (923, 925, 926), love scenes (924, 927, 929), and 928, which has no first-person plea and speaks of kings. Several Karuvur songs also name Vayali (925, 927, 928, 929).
source_issues: Song 924: corrupt character in மி¨ச்முழ்கி (line 6, probably மிசைமூழ்கி); unflagged garble உற்ழுறல் (line 4).
Song 928: corrupt character in வயலு¡ர்க் (line 23, probably வயலூர்க்).
Song 929: the line துவயலி நின்றன வ்யாத்தமும் (line 7) is garbled.

reading: A short song: the poet asks to be made wise in understanding and excellent in mind, settled, and given the supreme yoga of Siva-jnana. The praise calls Murugan treasure, the eternal, his own thought, the good meaning, the refuge, the lord beyond words, at Karuvur.
nuance: No women and no death: the whole plea is positive, for மதி, மனம் and சிவஞான பரயோகம். சொற்பர வேளே, the lord beyond words, sets the goal past speech.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking: breasts like tender coconut, a pool of nectar and a pot of juice, held in both hands, the waist bending, hair slipping, lips sweet as sugar, face pressed to face, sinking into the bed, and asks to be ruled so that this deed ends. The praise names the anklets and golden shoulders with vetchi flowers that dance in the poet's eyes, Vishnu who set up the flagged chariot for Arjuna as uncle, the hunter girl's bridegroom, and the one who wounded the demon of the sea-hill, at Karuvai.
nuance: The plea is one phrase, சுகிக்கும் வினை அற ஆளாய், 'rule me so that the deed of enjoying ends', after a long description. நரனுக்கு அமைத்த கொடி இரதம் is Krishna as Arjuna's charioteer.

reading: The poet calls himself a dog who stumbles daily in the world with this body of flesh adorned from head to foot, and asks to be brought, leaving pasu and pasam, into the contemplation of the Pati, the full and partless one known by knowledge, and into that experience. The praise names Murugan son of the lord of the mountain, the rising sun of the east, master of the three Tamils and all the agamas, nectar of melting hearts, brother-in-law of Brahma, the compassionate true guru, beautiful at Karuvur in the west and at Vayali.
nuance: பசு பாசமும் விட்டு அறிவால் அறியப்படு பூரண நிட்கள பதி: the Siddhanta triad with its standard terms (பூரணம், நிட்களம்), ending in அநுபூதி, direct experience. கமலாலயன் மைத்துன is Brahma's brother-in-law, since Murugan's consorts are Vishnu's daughters and Brahma Vishnu's son; that reasoning is mine.

reading: The poet says this body of daily disease is made of earth, water, air, fire and space, yet it seeks to rule the world and win a great crown, runs about wearing ornaments and the foolish manhood that says 'I', and never sees that it is false or knows to desire true jnana; he asks to be joined by any means to Murugan's devotees and given high jnana and the life of the holy feet. The praise has drums sounding to the directions, Sura's host scattered and the serpent's hundred heads bowed by the vel, Siva who gave half his body to Shakti and burned the cities as father, and Valli's beloved, at Karuvur.
nuance: The body is analysed into the five elements (பிருதிவி, அப்பு, வாயு, தேயு, ககனம்) before its ambitions are listed, so the pride of rule and of 'I' (நானெனும் மடவாண்மை) rests on a heap of elements. எத்திற் கொடு நின் அடியாரொடும் உய்த்திட்டு: the means of rescue is the company of devotees. கோகுல சத்தி may call the Goddess the one of Gokula; I am unsure.

tamil: முட்டம ருட்டி யிருகுழை தொட்டக டைக்க ணியலென
முத்தமி ரத்ந மரகதம் வைத்தவி சித்ர முகபட
கட்டிய ணைத்து நகநுதி பட்டக ழுத்தி லிறுகிய
கட்டமு யக்கி னநுபவம் விட்டவி டற்கு நியமித
வெட்டிய கட்க முனைகொடு வட்டகு ணத்து ரணமுக
வெற்றியை யுற்ற குறவர்கள் பெற்றகொ டிக்கு மிகமகிழ்
கிட்டிய பற்கொ டசுரர்கள் மட்டற வுட்க வடலொடு
கெட்டவ ருற்ற துணையென நட்டருள் சிட்ட பசுபதி
reading: The poet describes women whose eyes reach their earrings, breasts covered with jewelled cloth and scented with akil, embraces with nail-marks on the neck in which words stop and life faints, and asks whether, having left that experience, he will not be granted with love a disciplined contemplation. The praise names the warrior of many weapons who delights the hunters' daughter, the Kumaresa of Vayali, the vel ringed by dancing ghouls, and the six-faced lord of Garbhapuram, son of Pasupati who stands as refuge for the ruined.
nuance: நியமித கற்பனை is my best reading of what is asked, a regulated or ordained contemplation, but the line may divide otherwise, and விட்ட may mean the poet has left the embrace or wants to. கெர்ப்பபுரம் is Karuvur in Sanskrit, கரு = கர்ப்பம்.

reading: The poet pictures kings in their pomp, bowed to by ministers, princes, commanders and lesser kings, crowned with command, riding palanquin, elephant and horse under the white umbrella, fanned with whisks, proud on cotton beds, delighting in horns, flutes, songs and the dances of Konkan women, and says they do not know the death that Brahma writes. The praise tells the Mahabharata: the Pandavas lose to Sakuni's dice and go into exile, twelve years and a year in hiding, recover the cattle, are refused their share, and win the land when Krishna drives Arjuna's horses; Murugan is his nephew, Guha of Vayalur, who freed the gods, at Vanji.
nuance: There is no first-person plea: the whole first half describes others, and the judgment comes in one line, அயன் எழுதும் யம கோட்டியை உணராரே. The praise is apt to it, a story of a kingdom lost and won. யம கோட்டி is unclear: it may mean Yama's decree or the death written by Brahma.

tamil: முகிலள கஞ்சரி யாக்குழை யிகல்வன கண்சிவ வாச்சிவ
முளைபுள கஞ்செய வார்த்தையு நிலையழி யும்படி கூப்பிட
துயரொழு குஞ்செல பாத்திர மெலியமி குந்துத ராக்கினி
துவயலி நின்றன வ்யாத்தமும் வயலியல் வஞ்சியில் மேற்பயில்
சகலம யம்பர மேச்சுரன் மகபதி யுய்ந்திட வாய்த்தருள்
சருவுக்ர வுஞ்சசி லோச்சய முருவவெ றிந்தகை வேற்கொடு
அகிலமு மஞ்சிய வாக்ரம விகடப யங்கர ராக்கத
அமரர டங்கலு மாட்கொள அமரர்த லங்குடி யேற்றிட
reading: The poet describes lovemaking, hair slipping, eyes reddened, smiles, sweat, cries and lotus hands raised to the brow, and the body, a vessel of flowing sorrow, wasting in the women's embrace, and vows not to forget night and day the form in which Murugan stands at Vayali and the form at Vanji. The praise names the all-pervading lord born in Saravana for Indra's sake with six faces, the vel that pierced Krauncha, the peacock, the cock crying out against the demons, and the one who restored the gods' cities and freed them.
nuance: The plea does not ask to escape; it vows memory of two shrine forms, Vayali and Vanji (Karuvur), held in the heart night and day. The opening of that line (துவயலி நின்றன வ்யாத்தமும்) is garbled.

title: நெருவூர்
theme: The one song at Neruvur (நெருவூர், Neruvai): the poet, lacking every virtue of the devotees who serve the guru and the Lord's servants, asks not to wander among priced women and vows never to forget the feet; the praise is a sequence of Krishna's deeds.

tamil: உ ரலி னொடுதவழ் விரகுள இளமையு ...... மிகமாரி
reading: The poet sets himself against the virtuous company who worship the guru, the devotees and the devotees' servants as equal to the Lord, and calls himself one without their conduct, worship, falling at the feet or weeping, without goodness, patience, skill, sense or steadiness; he asks not to stumble on the hill of priced women's breasts, wander in the forest of their hair and drown in the sea of their eyes, and vows not to forget in dream or waking the lotus feet given him at Vayali. The praise is Krishna's: the dark child who crawled with the mortar and broke the marutha trees, lifted the hill as an umbrella against the rain for the cattle, came through the trap of the underground chamber, and humbly drove Arjuna's chariot to break the hundred kings, and calls Murugan his nephew, at Neruvai among paddy and lotuses.
nuance: அடியவர் அடியவர் அடிமையும் ... நிகரென வழிபடு: the devotees honour even the servants of servants as the Lord, and the poet's list of what he lacks (நலமிலி பொறையிலி ... நிலையிலி) is the standard self-abuse set against them. In the praise எளிமை, the humility of Krishna as charioteer, is named as a virtue. The opening run about the snake-bearing devotees is hard to divide, and நிலவறை, the underground chamber, is my reading of an allusion I cannot place exactly.

title: திருவெஞ்சமாக்கூடல்
theme: The one song at Thiruvenjamakkoodal (திருவெஞ்சமாக்கூடல்): a short plea in three similes, the bee, the monkey and the ball, for grace that ends the mind; the Lord is seen by his servants and hidden from the stubborn.
source_issues: Song 931: unflagged garble மந்திபோற்ள (line 2), probably மந்திபோற்; ஏசித் (line 4) may be a corrupt தேசித் (teach).

reading: A short song: the poet asks to seek grace like a bee seeking nectar, to strike down the disease of time like a monkey, to play with the bond like a ball, and, his mind ended, to be taught and given grace. The praise names Murugan the one his servants see, the lord of the high vel dwelling in the forest shrine, not to be found by the stubborn, at Venjamakkoodal.
nuance: சிந்தை மாய்த்து: the mind is to be ended, not calmed. The three similes are compact and their sense is uncertain: the bee is clear, but what the monkey and the ball stand for (காலப் பிணி சாடி, பாசத்துடன் ஆடி) is my guess. தொண்டரால் காணப் பெறுவோனே against மிண்டரால் காணக் கிடையானே: devotion sees what stubborn pride cannot.

title: திருப்பாண்டிக்கொடுமுடி
theme: Songs at Thiruppandikkodumudi (திருப்பாண்டிக்கொடுமுடி): a short plea to escape the sea of births made by the two deeds, and a love scene in which the poet is drawn to women like a needle to a magnet.
source_issues: Song 933: corrupt character in வயலு¡ரா (line 10), probably வயலூரா.

reading: A short song: the poet asks whether, instead of drowning in the sea of births made by the two kinds of deeds and tossing in suffering, he will by the radiance of grace's compassion firmly reach the goal. The praise calls Murugan hard for Hari and Brahma to know, easy for his devotees, the wondrous lover, the teacher who gave grace to Siva as guru, the Kumara of Kodumudi.
nuance: அரியயற்கு அறிதற்கு அரியானே, அடியவர்க்கு எளிய: hard for the gods, easy for devotees, a pairing of the hymns. குருவெனச் சிவனுக்கு அருள் போதா keeps the teaching of Siva in a single phrase.

reading: The poet describes falling to women with glory-lily hands and bangles as a needle falls to a magnet, their sandal-scented hair like dark cloud, spear eyes reaching their earrings, and the touching of garments and holding of breasts, and asks whether he will not give up those embraces. The praise names Murugan of Vayalur, who grants men and the king of gods what each desires, the lover who bowed to the small feet of the deer-like girl in the bamboo-fringed millet field, and the lord praised in bards' words to whom the lord of Pandikkodumudi with serpent-bound hair is drawn as to a supreme guru.
nuance: ஊசி காந்தத்து உறவென வீழ்ந்து: the needle drawn to the magnet makes desire a force the poet does not choose. மான் சிற்றடி தொழு மதிகாமி: Murugan bowing to Valli's small feet reverses the usual direction of worship. The last lines on Siva of Kodumudi are hard to divide.

title: சேலம்
theme: The one song at Salem (சேலம்): an akam love poem in which a girl, pierced by the moon's fire, the wind, the cuckoo and the flute, wastes in longing, and the singer asks Murugan to come and embrace her.

reading: In another's voice, the singer says that because the moon pitilessly throws fire, the wind strikes, the cuckoo calls in the cool grove and a flute sounds alone, the girl's carp-like eyes droop, and asks Murugan not to let her fade and fail but to come and hold her to his jewelled chest so that she may live content. The praise names the vel that pierced the mountain through, the Kumara of the three Tamils, son of the radiant lord, who rode the peacock to destroy Sura's kin, the younger brother of the elephant-faced Ganapati, at Salem.
nuance: No confession: the speaker is the girl's mother or friend, and the girl's love is for the god. The machinery of akam longing is all here, the moon as fire, the wind, the cuckoo and the lone flute, as in 24; சிலைபொரு கால், the wind, may compare it to a bow or bring it from a hill. மாதுக்கு இரு கயல் சோர: the drooping eyes are the one physical sign given.

title: ராஜபுரம்
theme: The one song at Rajapuram (ராஜபுரம்) in the Kongu land: the poet lists his own honours as a court poet and asks whether one so gifted should praise base sinners as equal to the legendary patrons; the praise is of Vishnu who saved the elephant.

tamil: சங்கு வார்முடி பொற்கழல் பொங்கு சாமரை கத்திகை
சந்த பாஷைகள் கற்றவன் மந்த்ர வாதிச துர்க்கவி
பங்கி பாலச ரச்வதி சங்க நூல்கள்வி தித்தப்ர
பண்டை மூவெழு வர்க்கெதிர் கண்ட நீயுமெ னச்சில
வெங்கை யானை வனத்திடை துங்க மாமுத லைக்குவெ
விண்ப ராவஅ டுக்கிய மண்ப ராவஅ தற்குவி
கொங்க ணாதித ரப்பெறு கொங்கி னூடுசு கித்திடு
கொங்கு லாவுகு றக்கொடி கொங்கை யேதழு விச்செறி
reading: The poet sets out his credentials, conch and crown, golden anklet, whisks and umbrella, palanquin and elephant, many crores of rhythmic languages, mastery of mantra, the four kinds of verse, the title of king of poets, a child Saraswati, the expounder of prabandhas laid down by the Sangam books, and asks whether it is fitting for such a poet to praise some sinners of the five great sins as 'you who equal the ancient one-and-twenty patrons'. The praise tells how the elephant, terrified by the crocodile in the forest pool, cried 'Root!' and Vishnu came on Garuda, names Murugan his nephew, the hero of the Kongu land and lover of the hunter girl, at Rajapuram.
nuance: The boast is the argument: the honours (சத்ர, சாமரை, கவிராஜ) are the regalia a court poet earns, and the poet lists them to say they are too good to be spent on பஞ்ச பாதகர். பண்டை மூவெழுவர் are the three sets of seven patrons of Tamil tradition. Whether the poet speaks of himself or in a typical bard's voice is not said.

title: விஜயமங்கலம்
theme: A single song at Vijayamangalam (விஜயமங்கலம்) in Kongu: a frank picture of lovemaking, ending not in a plea but in a vow never to forget Murugan's feet even while serving women.
source_issues: Song 936: corrupt glyphs in சா¡£ரம் (line 3, probably சாரீரம், 'voice'), பாலு¡று (line 6, பாலூறு), வயலு¡ரா (line 18, வயலூரா) and க்¡£தேசி (line 22, perhaps கீத தேசி or க்ரீ-; the raga word is uncertain).

tamil: உ ரக கங்கணப் பூதேசர் பாலக ...... வயலு¡ரா
reading: The poet describes lovemaking with a woman whose eyes redden in love's quarrel, whose garlands slip, whose voice hums like a bee, whose breasts bear nail marks and whose lips flow with honeyed nectar, until his life sinks into her navel; he says that even if he melts and becomes the servant of women doing their bidding, he will not forget Murugan's feet from now on. The praise names him nephew of the discus-bearing Narayana who lived as a child in the cowherds' village, son of the skull-bearing lord of ghosts with serpent bracelets, the lord of Vayalur who threw his vel when the hunters cried out and told the Kura girl to stop grieving, and the lord of Vijayamangalam, where bees sing the desi melody over lotus pools.
nuance: The turn is unusual: மங்கையர்க்கு ஆளாகி ஏவல் செய்திடினும் நின் கழல் சீர்பாதம் நான் இனி மறவேனே makes no request to be freed from women, only a vow that service to them will not erase the feet. The lines on Vishnu (உலக கண்டமிட்டு ஆகாச மேல் விரி சலதி கண்டிட சேராய மாமவருடன் மடிந்திட) are hard to divide, and the hunters' cry and Valli's grief seem to point to the battle at Valli's hill without naming it.

title: சிங்கை - காங்கேயம்
theme: Two songs at Singai (சிங்கை, given with Kangeyam, காங்கேயம்): pleas to be freed from trusting women and wandering shamelessly after them, with praise of the vel, of Valli, and of Siva's dance that bowed Kali's head.

reading: The poet says that, drawn by women's hair where bees hum among cool lilies and by their pearl-hung breasts like hills, he came trusting as refuge a poisonous deed and a desire for a woman; he asks Murugan today to destroy his evil deeds and come on the peacock. The praise names the vel fragrant with lotus, konrai, thumbai and magizh flowers, the vel that fought while goblins feasted on corpses, the chest that embraced the Kura girl of fine speech, and the lord at Singai of shining champak groves.
nuance: தஞ்சமென வந்து நம்பி: he sought the woman as a refuge (தஞ்சம்), the word devotion reserves for the Lord. The line ending கதிர்வேலா is used twice in the praise, which may be a slip in the source.

reading: The poet asks whether he must wander shamelessly at every crossroads, heart withered, with the belly as his only aim, and asks for grace so that, no longer roaming under the sway of women, his deeds may leave him and his mind be glad. The praise names Murugan son of Siva with the crescent on his hanging matted hair, who danced to the drum syllables until Kali, the woman of battle, bowed her head, the one who married the hunters' daughter, threw the vel at the asuras, and is son of Kampar and of the lord of Kailasa, at Singai.
nuance: சந்திதொறு நாணமின்றி: shame lost at every crossroads is the confession; உந்தி பொருளாக may mean living for the belly or for the women's navel. மங்கை ரணகாளி தலைசாய points to Siva's dance contest with Kali, in which she yielded; கம்பர் names Siva of Kanchi.

title: பட்டாலியூர்
theme: Three songs at Pattaliyur (பட்டாலியூர்) in Kongu: the killing eyes of women and the wish to serve before grey hair comes, a rejection of sectarian argument and even of mantra and yantra lore in favour of the highest state, and a long praise of the shrine's fierce goddess.
structure_note: 939 catalogues women's eyes and praises the goddess Bhairavi; 940 asks for service while youth lasts; 941 turns away from the debates of the six faiths.
source_issues: Song 941: corrupt glyphs in சுக்¡£பர் (line 13, Sugriva) and வயலு¡ரா (line 16).

tamil: உ னதடி நிழலிற் சேர வாழ்வது ...... மொருநாளே
reading: The poet lists what women's eyes do: they strike the earrings, outrage the lotus, put even Yama's men to flight, cut a man as nectar mixed with poison, practise Kama's arts, melt even sages with cunning glances, speak of a desire to steal wealth and quarrel as if the age were ending; he asks whether a day will come when, instead of falling into the pit of infatuation these eyes give, he lives in the shade of Murugan's feet. The praise calls him the life of Vayalur on the emerald-feathered peacock, and then names the goddess at length, the trident-bearing Malini, the refuge, the lion-rider, the Mohini of those who drink liquor, the Kali whose goblins dance at the drum-beaten cremation ground, the Bhairavi of Pattaliyur.
nuance: Every line of the first half ends in a verb of the eyes (மோதுவ, சீறுவ, மீளுவ, நாடுவ), so the whole plea is built as one sentence about them, ending in உயிர்வதை நயனம், eyes that torture life. The praise gives more space to the goddess, a cremation-ground Kali and Bhairavi worshipped with liquor (மதுபானம் பருகினர்), than to Murugan; several of her epithets (சாதகி, யாமளி, வித்தாரி) are obscure.

tamil: கத்தூரி யகரு ம்ருகமத வித்தார படிர இமசல
கட்டார வடமு மடர்வன நிட்டூர கலக மிடுவன
கொத்தூரு நறவ மெனவத ரத்தூறல் பருகி யவரொடு
கொக்காக நரைகள் வருமன மிக்காய விளமை யுடன்முயல்
அத்தூர புவன தரிசன நித்தார கனக நெடுமதி
அச்சோவெ னவச வுவகையி லுட்சோர்த லுடைய பரவையொ
பத்தூரர் பரவ விரைவுசெல் மெய்த்தூதர் விரவ வருடரு
பச்சோலை குலவு பனைவளர் மைச்சோலை மயில்கள் நடமிடு
reading: The poet describes women whose breasts, rubbed with musk, agil, sandal and camphor and hung with pearl chains, strain against the bodice, and asks that he not drink their lips as honey and melt like wax in a smith's furnace; while youth is strong, before his hair turns white as a crane, he asks to be shown the way of humble service at Murugan's feet. The praise names Vayalur within golden walls, recalls the story of Paravai in the pain of separation and the true messenger who hurried to her, calls Murugan the supreme guru, and ends at Pattali where peacocks dance in groves of green palmyra.
nuance: கொக்காக நரைகள் வரும் முன்: the plea sets a deadline, service while the body is still young. குற்றேவல் அடிமை is humble service, the book's word for devotion. The lines on பரவை and the மெய்த்தூதர் recall Siva going as messenger to Paravai for Sundarar; how Murugan is tied to that story (as the one who grants it, or as Siva's own form) is not clear.

tamil: சங்கைக்கத் தோடு சிலுகிடு சங்கிச்சட் கோல சமயிகள்
சண்டைக்குட் கேள்வி யலமல மண்டற்குப் பூசை யிடுமவர்
மங்கைக்குப் பாக னிருடிக ளெங்கட்குச் சாமி யெனவடி
மந்த்ரப்ரஸ்த் தார தரிசன யந்த்ரத்துக் கேள்வி யலமலம்
வெண்பட்டுப் பூணல் வனகமு கெண்பட்டுப் பாளை விரிபொழில்
கொங்கைக்கொப் பாகும் வடகிரி செங்கைக்கொப் பாகு நறுமலர்
கும்பிட்டுக் காதல் குனகிய இன்பச்சொற் பாடு மிளையவ
reading: The poet says 'enough, enough' to hearing the clamour of the six faiths arguing their many arts of knowledge, to hearing of the wealth of those who make worship for gain, and even to hearing the mantra, its arrangements, the darshanas and the yantras of the Saiva texts that the consort of Himavan's daughter taught the sages; he asks that, no longer wandering in vain, he be given the highest state. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Rama, who sent Sugriva's army to Lanka, the lord of Vayalur with its areca groves, and the young one at Pattali in Kongu who bowed to the forest girl, likened her breasts, hands and hair to the northern mountain, flowers and cloud, and spoke sweet words of love.
nuance: The refusal reaches past the sectarians to the Saiva scriptures themselves: சிவநூலின் மந்த்ரப்ரஸ்தார தரிசன யந்த்ரத்துக் கேள்வி அலமலம். The highest state (பரகதி) is set above hearing even Siva's own mantra lore. The praise ends with Murugan himself humbled in love, bowing to Valli (கும்பிட்டுக் காதல் குனகிய).

title: திருமுருகன்பூண்டி
theme: A single short song at Thirumuruganpoondi (திருமுருகன்பூண்டி): a plea for the feet through ripened penance and prayer, with praise of Murugan as beyond the six faiths.
source_issues: Song 942: unflagged garble தக்ருர்வாய் (line 5); the ருர் sequence elsewhere in this run stands for ூர், so the word may be தக்கூர்வாய் or similar.

reading: The poet asks that, having pleaded many times for what is needful and come to know it, he ripen by touching penance and prayer and be granted Murugan's feet. The praise calls him hard for the six faiths to see, Siva's son, and the lord of Thirumuruganpoondi.
nuance: தவசெபமும் தீண்டிக் கனிவாகி: penance and japa are what ripen the soul for the feet. The line சவதமொடுந் தாண்டித் தக்ருர்வாய் is garbled and unread, and சிவகுமரன் பீண்டிற் பெயரானே may say that the town bears his name.

title: அவிநாசி
theme: Three songs at Avinasi (அவிநாசி) in Kongu: a plea to the guru to end death and birth, courtesans who take coins, and old age with the coming of Death's messengers; Murugan is also praised in the person of Sambandar.
source_issues: Song 945: நீனைத்தினம் (line 23) is probably a misspelling of நினைத்தினம்.

reading: A short song: the poet asks Murugan to become his true guru and rule him so that he neither dies nor is born again, and to give him the steadfast great life. The praise calls him the Kura girl's husband, Guha, Kumaresa of the Word, the one who declares the four, at Avinasi.
nuance: இறவாமல் பிறவாமல்: release is named as the end of both death and birth. அறநாலைப் புகல்வோனே may mean he who speaks the four Vedas or the four aims of life; the text does not say which.

reading: The poet describes courtesans of the street who take coins as their share, rosewater-scented, flower-crowned, lotus-mouthed, who greet with folded hands and are idle, and says that even if he sinks in love into their beds he will not forget the lotus feet that the gods bow to. The praise seems to identify Murugan with Sambandar, who made a girl from bones and sang Tamil at the Sangam so that the Jains were impaled, and names the vel that burned the demons and restored Indra to Amaravati, at Avinasi in Kongu.
nuance: பங்குக் கைக் காசுகொள் வேசியர்: the coin taken as their share marks these as courtesans. As in 936, the plea is a vow not to forget the feet even in their beds. அங்கத்தைப் பாவை செய்தாம் ... கழு ஏறிட points to Sambandar's raising of Poompavai from her bones and to the impaling of the Jains at Madurai; the opening lines of the praise are obscure.

reading: The poet pictures old age, phlegm rising, black hair grey, eyes dimmed, gait faltering, mother, wife and children disgusted and kin mocking with abuse, and asks that before Death's messengers come in anger with noose and trident to drag him away, Murugan come on the peacock and give his paired feet; he asks also to think of him daily in rich Tamil and that Murugan dwell in his mind as his life's companion. The praise names the vel that split Sura in the sea into the cock and the peacock, Kumaresa who told the hidden meaning to Hara, whose feet Brahma and Vishnu searched for, and Avinasi, where Brahmins who give dharma worship daily.
nuance: The plea moves from the body's decay to the household's contempt (வசைக்குறும் சொலினால் மிகவே தினம் நகையாட) to the messengers, then asks for the feet before they seize him (பிடிக்கு முன்). அரற்கு அரும்பொருள் தான் உரை கூறிய is the teaching of Siva without naming Om.

title: திருப்புக்கொளியூர்
theme: Three songs at Thiruppukkoliyur (திருப்புக்கொளியூர், the old name of Avinasi): Murugan as the guru of the Siva-yogis, a praise that recalls Siva's acts for Sundarar, and the poet himself besieged by Kama's army at evening.
source_issues: Song 946: corrupt glyph in வயலு¡ரா (line 12).
Song 947: corrupt glyph in வயலு¡ரிலி (line 12).

reading: The poet says he will not forget the wondrous feet of Murugan, the true guru who, to ripe Siva-yogis of disciplined conduct and silence who eat only greens and with devotion pass beyond the thirty-six tattvas to the supportless state of release, gave in that very moment the teaching of jnana, so that their deluding faults fell away. The praise names him the fierce hero with twelve arms, the lord of Vayalur where blue lilies and pearl-bright pools spread fragrance, the golden-bodied lord of Avinasi, who gives grace to truth so that the false Kali age departs, at Pukkoliyur.
nuance: ஆறாறு தத்துவ மேல் வீடு பற்று நிராதார நிலை: the thirty-six tattvas of Saiva doctrine are passed, and release is held as a state without support. The teaching acts instantly (அக்கணமே). The song asks nothing for the poet beyond not forgetting the feet.

reading: The first half pictures Indra's white elephant and Indra living in the shade of the kalpaka tree in his splendid city with the gods around him, and asks the Kumara of lordly form to appear and rule the poet, the life of Vayalur. The second half recalls Siva's acts for his devotee Sundarar: the thousand gold coins sought from shrine to shrine for the woman of Kamalalayam, the Lord coming as a Brahmin in the forest to untie a packet of rice for the tired singer, and at Avinasi the child called back from the crocodile's mouth; Murugan is the Lord whom that lord of Pukkoliyur praises.
nuance: The song is almost wholly praise and its hero is Sundarar (தொண்டர்), served by Siva as friend and helper (சகாயன்). செறிப்பித்த கராவதின் வாய் மக அழைப்பித்த is the boy swallowed by a crocodile at Avinasi and restored at Sundarar's song. The first half is hard to construe, and its link to the plea எனை ஆள் is uncertain.

tamil: தெறிக்கக்கணை யேவு வீர மாமனும் ...... உ ந்திமீதே
reading: The poet pictures evening as a battle: Kama, called by the cuckoo, rides the chariot of the breeze with flower arrows and the moon as his hanging garland, the sea as his war drum, and draws his sugarcane bow; caught in the arts of fragrant-haired women he is dying, and asks whether this pleases the compassionate one and when he will reach the jnana that is the Name by which it is crossed. The praise names Murugan the lover of the millet-field girl, son of the lord with the crescent in his hair, the vel that took Sura's life, and nephew of the heroic Rama who dammed the sea and made Ravana's crowns fly, at the festival town of Pukkoliyur.
nuance: The akam convention of evening as the hour when love's pain grows, usually given to a woman, is here the poet's own, armed as Kama's march (படை கூடி மேலெழா அணி வகுத்து). கடக்கப்படு நாமமான ஞானம்: the knowledge that crosses it is a Name, presumably Murugan's.

title: §ப்ருர்
theme: Two songs at Perur (பேரூர்) in Kongu: a plea for the one word of jnana that cures the incurable disease, and for desire, town and name to end as they do for yogis who have been taught.
source_issues: Chapter heading §ப்ருர் is corrupt; the songs' own text (949, 950) shows the shrine is Perur (பேரூர்).
Song 949: corrupt glyph in §ப்ருர்ப் (line 4).
Song 950: corrupt glyphs in §ப்ரு (line 16), and the unflagged garble பர்ரு ராசூழ் in the same line.

reading: A short song: the poet asks for the one word whose rule is the knowledge of the soul, to cure the disease that does not end. The praise calls Murugan the son of the lord of the world's people, the child, the king of hills, great in battle, at Perur.
nuance: தீராப் பிணி, the disease that will not go, is probably birth itself; ஓர் வாக்கு is a teaching word, an upadesa. சீவாத்தும ஞான ஊராட்சி, the 'town-rule' of the knowledge of the soul, is an odd figure and its sense is a guess.

reading: The poet asks that, as the yogis who have been taught see no span of life, no ill-omened day and no wasted day, his desires too should truly end, together with town, name and all else, so that he can say to women with poisoned sword-eyes 'who am I, who are you'; he asks Murugan to be his mother and give grace to him, a dog. The praise names him the life of Indra and Brahma, beyond all, the lord of Vayalur, the vel that pierced the mountain, the bearer of the cock-banner riding the green peacock, and the lord at Perur, ruled by the Lord who danced there.
nuance: நானார் நீயார் எனுமாறு: the end of desire is pictured as no longer recognising the women at all. வாணாள் கோணாள் வீணாள் காணார், yogis who see neither lifetime nor bad days nor wasted days, sets them outside time. பட்டி ஆள்பவர் கொட்டியாடினர் is Siva of Perur, Patteeswarar, and his dance. Much of the plea's syntax is uncertain.

title: கொடும்பாளுர்
theme: A single song at Kodumbalur (கொடும்பாளூர், கொடும்பை in the text): a plea to leave the clamour of sects and arguments and know the knowledge that cannot be pointed to, with praise of Murugan as the merchant riding the peacock.
source_issues: Chapter heading spells the town கொடும்பாளுர் for கொடும்பாளூர்.

reading: The poet asks whether, leaving attachment to the countless arts of argument, the rites and quarrels of the six sects who divide and clamour, and the learning of scholars bound to this Kali age, he can know the knowledge that cannot be pointed to, abide a little in it, and receive the word of grace. The praise names Murugan the chest embraced by the young green creeper of the Kuravar called killers, the one before whom the cruel Krauncha and the demon perished while the sea, the encircling mountains and the ten directions shook, and the merchant (செட்டி) who rides the golden horse that is the peacock, at Kodumbai.
nuance: குறியாத அறிவை அறிந்து: the knowledge sought is one without a mark or sign, set against தர்க்கப் பலகலை, the arts of disputation. The epithet செட்டி, the merchant, recalls the story of Murugan coming as a trader; the text names only the title and the peacock as his horse. அரவியிடம் தப்பி is obscure.

title: கீரனூர்
theme: A single song at Keeranur (கீரனூர்): the courtesans' arts of luring and pricing, and the churning of the milk sea in praise of Vishnu as Murugan's uncle.
source_issues: Song 952: corrupt glyph in லக்ஷ¤மி (line 17, லக்ஷுமி).
Chapter heading reads கீரனூர் but the song's last line has கீரனுருறை, probably கீரனூருறை.

reading: The poet lists what courtesans do: laugh with charm, melt men with song and dance, call anyone at all, wound with Kama's eyes, stand at the doorway in the street, name a price, sway their breasts, loosen and tie their hair, let their garments slip, speak desire, fall on a man and leave him in great sorrow; he asks whether kinship with women who learn these arts of deceit is fit for him. The praise tells the churning of the milk sea, Meru as the churning stick and the serpent as rope, Vali holding half and the gods the other half, until Lakshmi, the Parijata and many powers rose, and names Murugan nephew of the green Achyuta who gave out the nectar, the bearer of the vel at Keeranur, a town of mansions and groves like Kubera's Alaka.
nuance: விலைகூறி: naming a price is the plainest courtesan charge, and தோதக வித்தைகள், arts of deceit, are something learned. In the churning, பாதி வாலி பிடித்திட gives Vali the place usually held by the demons.

title: குளந்தைநகர்
theme: A single short song at Kulandai (குளந்தைநகர்): fear of dying in the pit of women's delusion, and trust that no one but Murugan can give the boon.
source_issues: Song 953: குறமகண் (line 7) is probably குறமகள்.

reading: The poet asks that, falling under the sway of women with wave-like hair, bow-brows, poison eyes and drum-like waists into the wide pit of delusion, he not give up his life to Death in fear and suffering; if Murugan does not grant the boon, who else will? The praise names him the one who circled the earth on the peacock, the groom of the Kura girl, and the lord of the temple at Kulandai.
nuance: வரம் தராவிடில் பிறர் எவர் தருவாரே: the plea rests on there being no other giver. The circling of the earth recalls the contest for the fruit.

title: தனிச்சயம்
theme: Two songs at Thanichayam (தனிச்சயம்) in Kongu: the poet's own lovemaking and a wish that this birth end, with Murugan as the one who commanded him to sing the Thiruppugazh; and old age with its contempt and the hour of dying.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking frankly, giving betel, embracing, making bird-cries, kissing the neck, biting the lips and toiling without shame until his life is exhausted, and asks whether this birth of union, in which virtue is lost, will not end. The praise names Murugan who commanded him to sing the good Thiruppugazh with its lordship, poetic gift and authority of a guru, the one with the cock-banner, the most able of the able who teaches Siva and Agastya the grammar and literature of the three Tamils, at Thanichayam in the west.
nuance: The book names itself: குறித்த நற் றிருப்புகழ் ... எனைப் பணித்து அருள்வோனே, Murugan as the one who set the poet to sing. அறத் தவித்து: the union is the loss of dharma, and the plea is that the birth itself, not only the habit, end.

reading: The poet pictures the body's ruin in old age: its once-proud form shrivels, black hair whitens like cotton, the ears go deaf, the eyes blind, the teeth loosen, cough and phlegm rise, the head reels with bile, the body rots worse than a bloodless worm, mind, deeds and speech run out of bounds, the wife who came reviles him, all call him unclean, sense fails and the pulse is barely there; on that day of the soul's distress he asks for grace. The praise is a battle in drum syllables where ghouls drink blood from skulls and kites pull entrails, and names Murugan the lord of Vayalur and of Thanichayam in Kongu.
nuance: The decay is listed from the outside in, ending in துடிப்பதும் சிறிது உளது இலது, a pulse barely there or gone. அவத்தை here is the soul's distress at death. தடச்சிகண்டியில் in the last lines is unclear.

title: மதுரை
theme: Twelve songs at Madurai (மதுரை, also Koodal and the City of the Golden Lotus): courtesans and the wish for the feet, jnana that silences the sects, and praise that draws on Madurai's own stories, Siva's sports for Manikkavachakar and Sambandar's victory over the Jains.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (959 to 963, 966); thanksgiving for jnana and the love that melts the bones (956); short pleas for jnana and compassion (964, 965); praise songs (957, 958); and 967, which recasts the book's opening song.
source_issues: Song 956: corrupt glyph in புண்டா£க (line 3, புண்டரீக).
Song 960: corrupt glyphs in ரா¡£ணமயி (line 23); the line வேத மீண கமலக் கணர் மெய் பச்சை ரகுராம ... is hard to recover.
Song 967: unflagged garble ரத்முரும் (line 6, probably ரதமூரும், 'drives the chariot').

reading: The poet asks whether his bones will not melt in love as he names Murugan's shoulder that killed the demons, the vel that pierced the hill, the golden-anklet lotus feet, the kuthalam flower on his crown, the chest that took the forest girl and the six faces, and marvels at the jnana Murugan gave, in which the clamour of the sects, the arts, the five elements and the restless instruments of mind all fell silent. The praise tells how Ganapati, who loves chickpeas, candy, honey and millet dough, wrote the Bharata with one tusk on Meru when asked, and how Murugan circled the world on the peacock faster than the wind while Ganapati circled his father, and names him worshipped by the gods at Madurai.
nuance: The song is thanks rather than plea: தந்த ஞானம் இருந்தவாறு என், how wonderful the knowledge given. என்பெலாம் உருகு அன்பு, love that melts the bones, is a phrase of Saiva devotional poetry. The praise gives both sides of the fruit contest.

reading: The poet asks for grace to live and flourish in the state of reaching Murugan's paired feet. The praise calls him the younger brother of the elephant-faced one, the six-faced one, the guru who taught the Veda to Hara and to Brahma, the hero who cut down the demons, and the one who made his peacock dance to delight Uma and Chokkar of Madurai, whom none in heaven or earth, not Vishnu or Brahma, can know, and who calmed the gods' fear with the vel.
nuance: ஆதி அரனுக்கும் வேத முதல்வற்கும் ஆரணம் உரைத்த: here Murugan teaches both Siva and Brahma, not only binding Brahma for his ignorance.

reading: The poet seems to compare Murugan's coming to the sun's procession that lights the world and the moonlight that ends the dark, and asks that, singing the feet that grant honour, he may speak rich Tamil so that devotees rejoice, and be given boons. The praise names Murugan who delights when devotees bow saying 'Arahara, Sundara, Arumuga', son of Uma the creeper of the mountain, the beloved of the Kura girl, Saravana with kumkum on his chest, who grew up in golden Madurai.
nuance: The opening images (பரவு நெடுங்கதிர் உலகில் விரும்பிய பவனி, இருளை விடிந்தது நிலவாலே) have no clear subject and the reading of the first half is a guess. செந்தமிழ் உரைசெய அன்பரும் மகிழ: the gift sought is song that gladdens devotees.

tamil: பணத்தை நோக்குவர் பிணமது தழுவுவர் ...... அளவளப் பதனாலே
பறிப்பர் மாத்தையி லொருவிசை வருகென ...... அவரவர்க் குறவாயே
அலட்டி னாற்பிணை யெருதென மயலெனு ...... நரகினிற் சுழல்வேனோ
அமர்த்தி யாட்கொள மனதினி லருள்செய்து ...... கதிதனைத் தருவாயே
தகப்ப னார்க்கொரு செவிதனி லுரைசெய்த ...... முருகவித் தகவேளே
சயத்த யோத்தியில் வருபவ னரிதிரு ...... மருமகப் பரிவோனே
செலுத்தி யீட்டிய சுரபதி மகள்தனை ...... மணமதுற் றிடுவோனே
திருத்த மாய்ப்புகழ் மதுரையி லுறைதரும் ...... அறுமுகப் பெருமாளே.
reading: The poet describes courtesans who abuse some men and praise others, give one the betel from their mouths and another a helping hand, look only at money and embrace even a corpse in measure with it, give potions in the bedroom, embrace saying 'Karthigai is coming' and take a man's goods, say 'come once in Masi', call men while thinking of their property, finish with one and drive him off; he asks whether he must whirl like a yoked threshing bull in the hell called infatuation, and asks to be lifted from these pits, set among Murugan's devotees, ruled and given the goal. The praise names him the one who, like a guru learned in shastra and Veda, told the Saiva path into his father's ear, nephew of Rama who killed the demon who stole Janaki, husband of Indra's daughter, and the one who impaled the Jains, at Madurai.
nuance: பணத்தை நோக்குவர் பிணமது தழுவுவர்: they embrace even a corpse if the money is right, close to the Kural's image of the courtesan's embrace. The festival calls (கார்த்திகை வருது, மாத்தையில்) show the gifts expected at feasts. The remedy is company: உனடியவர் உடன் எனை அமர்த்தி. பல சமணரைக் கழுக்கள் ஏற்றிய identifies Murugan with Sambandar at Madurai.

reading: The poet describes a courtesan's display, fragrant hair, rolling spear-eyes, pearl smile, swinging chain, glittering body, the sari let fall to her feet, a walk like a peacock's dance, the net cast for men whom she makes beg and then gives disease and suffering, and asks when Murugan will seat in devotion to his garlanded feet one who leapt into their share, lost his mind and churns in the sea of sinful birth. The praise recounts Siva's Madurai sports: honouring Vathavurar as guru and revealing the jnana feet, turning jackals into horses for the king, dancing on the Vaigai bund and eating the woman's puttu, and calls Murugan the son of that madman; it also names the vel that ended the asuras and the green peacock like Rama.
nuance: நோய் பிணி கொடுத்து: the women give disease, a rare explicit charge. The praise is Madurai's own legend: வாதவூரனை, நரியின் குழுவை வாசியாம் என, வைகையாறின் மீது மண் எடுத்து, மாது தரு பிட்டு, Manikkavachakar's story. Several words in the last lines are corrupt.

reading: The poet describes women whose brows are bows, eyes arrows and breasts rutting elephants, whose coral lips and betel he thought pleasure to drink and eat, melting in their embrace with kumkum and sandal soaked in sweat, and asks whether even he, the rogue despised by all who took these women as his strength, will bow to Murugan's feet. The praise tells of Rama with Sita in the Dandaka forest killing Khara and Trisiras, Kumbhakarna and the ten-headed one with his bow, names Murugan the nephew of that Mukunda and the son of Uma, Gauri, Shankari, and the lotus-faced one born on the reed bed of the north, at Tamil Madurai.
nuance: பலருக்கும் கடை என்றனை இகழவும் ... வண்டனும் உனதடி பணிவேனோ: the self-abuse sets up the question whether even such a one can still bow. முழையுடல் சிதற and சங்கிலி மண்டப are obscure.

reading: The poet asks that, instead of dying on the breasts of oiled and garlanded women, wandering in delusion, roaming the world for wealth, hiding and becoming a thief and running in darkness, he chant and melt in clear jnana, study the Siva Purana books, and be given Murugan's feet. The praise names Siva, who from the letter A and the elements became the one form and the first, and danced in the hall before the gods while his consort sang, and calls Murugan his son, born as the maker of Tamil who, so that the Vedas, the six faiths, the three worlds, dharma, the tattvas and yoga might be kept, cured the Pandya Maran's hunchback and fever at Alavai.
nuance: திருடனாகி: the search for money to spend on women ends in theft. The praise says outright that Murugan was born as Sambandar (தமிழ்செய் மாறர் கூன் வெப்பொடு அன்று தவிர), who cured the king Koon Pandiyan of his hunch and fever.

reading: The poet asks whether he must wander every day, infatuated by women's songs and bangled hands, breasts like elephants on a golden hill, cuckoo speech, thread-thin waists, plantain thighs, moon faces and the trickery of spear-eyes. The praise names Murugan nephew of Vishnu who sleeps on the serpent in the sea, helped the elephant, became Vamana and wears the tulasi garland, the son born from the sparks of the eye of Siva clad in elephant hide with poison in his throat, at Koodal, the wonder-city of poets of the three Tamils.
nuance: கோவிற் பொறியால் வரு: Murugan born from the sparks of Siva's eye, stated plainly. The plea is a list of the woman's parts, each one a reason for wandering (உழல்வேனோ).

tamil: கலைமேவு ஞானப் பிரகாசக் கடலாடி ஆசைக் ...... கடலேறிப்
பலமாய வாதிற் பிறழாதே பதிஞான வாழ்வைத் ...... தருவாயே
மலைமேவு மாயக் குறமாதின் மனைமேவு வாலக் ...... குமரேசா
சிலைவேட சேவற் கொடியோனே திருவாணி கூடற் ...... பெருமாளே.
reading: A short song: the poet asks that, having bathed in the sea of the light of jnana found in the arts and crossed the sea of desire, he not stray in the many deluding disputes, and be given the life of knowledge of the Lord. The praise names Murugan who dwelt in the house of the Kura girl of the mountain, the hunter with the bow, bearer of the cock-banner, at Koodal.
nuance: பதிஞான வாழ்வு: the life sought is knowledge of Pati, the Lord. Two seas are set against each other, the sea of jnana to bathe in and the sea of desire to cross. திருவாணி கூடல் is unexplained.

reading: A very short song: the poet asks to be given the understanding of kindness to living beings, with truth and justice as its nature and discipline as its support. The praise calls Murugan the one of the sound of nada, the sea of jnana and the flawless nectar, at Koodal.
nuance: பூதத் தயவான போதம்: compassion to all creatures is asked for as a kind of understanding. The opening நீதத்துவம் can be split as நீதி தத்துவம் or otherwise, so the first line is uncertain.

reading: The poet lists courtesans as schemers, bed-quarrellers, goblins, women with mutilated noses, proud and fat, idle women who flatter, eat, dance and sing, who run down the street feigning modesty, coax and speak as if on a man's side, plunder and hook men for desire of wealth, and asks that their hold scatter and that Murugan place him on the one way that joins the nectar of grace and grant that he climb to his feet. The praise is a battle in drum syllables in which the vel destroyed the Suras, names Murugan who daily played with the millet-guarding daughter of the deer, and who whispered a meaning into the ear of Chokkan of south Koodal, the burner of the three cities with the woman as his half.
nuance: The plea is a list of feminine epithets ending in -கள் (காரிகள், மூளிகள், வீணிகள், பேசிகள்), a set form of the book. குனகிகள் பக்ஷம் போல பேசிகள், those who talk as if on your side, is the courtesan's double dealing. சொக்கன் காதில் ஓர் பொருள் places the teaching of Siva in Madurai.

reading: The poet asks Murugan, who gave grace to the word of the three-eyed Lord who chants him as the shakti, the hill and the seed of release, and whose feet the thirty-three classes of gods worship, to grant him the Sivam that dwells in devotees' hearts, the treasure held by the green-cloud Vishnu who loosed the arrow at the ten heads and drove the chariot to Arjuna's victory. The praise is a dance in drum syllables in which Murugan, equal to his dancing father, grants the nine siddhis, at the City of the Golden Lotus.
nuance: The song rebuilds the book's opening song 6 phrase by phrase: முத்து ... சத்தி ... முத்தி, the three-eyed one who chants, the thirty-three gods, the arrow at the ten heads, the chariot driven for a devotee, the green cloud. Here the treasure asked for is named as சிவம் in devotees' hearts. கனக பத்மபுரி is Madurai of the golden lotus tank. The phrase division of the first half is uncertain.

title: ஸ்ரீ புருஷமங்கை
theme: Three songs at Sri Purushamangai (ஸ்ரீ புருஷமங்கை): pleas against women's eyes and the waste of wealth on them, and for the supreme of Vedanta beyond the senses and the mind's maya, with praise of Rama and Krishna as Murugan's uncle.

reading: The poet asks that he not, infatuated by the breasts of women whose eyes are Kama's arrows, fail to bow with justice and love to the feet of the First Guru and so waste in mind and body; that he stand apart from the work of the five senses, which stand like hunters, and the four inner instruments, and understand and receive grace; and that Murugan come and end his craving, defeat the maya of thought and grant the supreme reality at the end of the Veda. The praise tells Rama's story, Tataka's death, the guarding of Vishvamitra's sacrifice, the breaking of the bow, marriage to Janaki and giving up the crown for a mother's word, names Murugan his nephew, and pictures his peacock dancing so that Adisesha's heads shake, at Sri Purushamangai.
nuance: வேடர் என நின்ற ஐம்புலன் நாலு கரணங்கள்: the senses are hunters and the inner instruments (mind, intellect, ego, thought) are named as four; release is standing apart from their work (தொழில் வேறுபட நின்று). வேதமுடிவின் பரம்பொருள் is the supreme of Vedanta.

சேரவெ யிலங்கு துங்க வாவிக ளிசைந்தி ருந்த
reading: The poet speaks of women with loosened hair and swinging earrings who stir desire, whose breasts stand firm against lovers, and whose eyes are a net in which his great understanding was lost; with a heart tossed in love, he asks Murugan to come, stand before him and give grace to end his trouble. The praise names Kanda on the one peacock with the vel and anklets, son of Uma, holder of the cock-banner, the life of Senthil, and the lord of Sri Purushamangai with its chariot streets, fragrant groves and high pools.
nuance: கண்கள் வலையாலே பேரறிவு குந்து: the eyes are a net that takes away understanding. மந்தி தந்தி வாரண அனங்கன் is a string of comparisons whose sense is unclear. The praise names Senthil though the song is placed at Purushamangai.

reading: The poet says that, pained by the five arrows of Kama in spring, he went to women standing in every street, came at the right hour, fell at their feet, talked much friendship, drank the nectar of their honeyed mouths and sank into their cool breasts, and worked until the wealth he had sought ran to waste; he asks whether he must wander without any goal. The praise names Murugan nephew of Krishna, who drove the cattle, measured the earth, slept on a banyan leaf and stirred the milk and curd in cowherd homes, the one whose chest shines with the deer-girl of the hunters, at Sri Purushamangai, where the Vedas sound.
nuance: தேடிய தனங்கள் பாழ்பட: money earned and wasted on the women of the street is what leaves him with no goal (சேர்கதி அதின்றி).

title: இலஞ்சி
theme: Four songs at Ilanji (இலஞ்சி): pleas that Murugan come on the peacock with Valli at the hour of Death, and that the poet be kept from women's embraces and given the feet; the last is a love-lament for a girl wasting at evening.
structure_note: Two courtesan or lovemaking songs (972, 973), a death-hour plea framed by a portrait of Valli (971), and an akam song in another's voice (974).
source_issues: Song 972: corrupt character in கடலு¡டே (line 6, for கடலூடே); and கிளியோனே (line 18) stands where the sense (ஆனைக்கு இளையோனே, younger brother of the elephant) needs இளையோனே.

reading: The first half paints the hunter girl, her eyes, sweet speech, young breasts and elephant-like gait, and asks Murugan to come seated on the peacock with her, clearing the karma of birth, when cruel Death arrives. The praise tells of the Veda lamenting as the little anklets on his feet are worshipped, names him nephew of Vishnu of Srirangam and twelve-armed lord of the hills, and ends at Ilanji where Tamil shines.
nuance: The plea itself is only the last line of the first half: பவவினை களைந்து வரு கொடிய அந்தகன் அலவருவாயே, come when Death comes; everything before it describes Valli (எயின்மாது), so the song asks for the divine couple together at death. The opening run of syllables (கரங்க மலமின தரம்ப ...) is hard to divide, and the river with crocodiles and waves that hails him 'Kumara' is not clearly identified.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking in detail, earrings shaking, bangles slipping, hair falling loose, sandal paste rubbed away and the waist-cloth slackening as he drowns in the sea of passion, and asks that at that very moment Murugan grant him the vision of his moon-like faces, seated on the blue peacock, and his anklet-bearing feet. The praise names the goddess Sivakami, who dances united with Siva, the one who walked as messenger for Sundarar's song, and calls Murugan the younger brother of the elephant-faced god, the vel against Sura, the meaning of the Veda, and Visakha of Ilanji wedded to the girl of the millet field.
nuance: The plea does not ask to escape the embrace but to see Murugan in the middle of it (மூழ்குற்றிடு போது ... அருள்வாயே). சுந்தரர் பாடல் உகந்து இரு தாளைக் கொண்டு நல் தூது நடந்தவர் is Siva going on foot as Sundarar's envoy, named here through the goddess who shares his body.

reading: The poet asks that, whirling, wilting and swooning at the spear of women's eyes, he not desire their shoulders, cross the bounds and so waste away and die, and asks for the feet adorned with kadamba, thandai and anklets. The praise names the vel that struck the golden hill, the bridegroom of Indra's daughter, the chest that wedded the girl of the millet field, and the lord who came in the pool as a treasure and dwells at Ilanji.
nuance: The plea is built of doubled verbs (சுழன்று சுழன்று துவண்டு துவண்டு), the body acting out its own ruin. The last line plays on இலஞ்சி three times: the pool (the Saravana pond where he was born), இலஞ்சியம (a treasure or refuge), and the shrine.

reading: Speaking for a lovesick girl, the singer tells how the evening, the garland, Kama's flower arrows and the burning north wind have stripped her beauty and worn her thin, and asks Murugan to come today, before the tender creeper gives way, so that the love of the breasts once joined may grow. The praise names Murugan who made Death tremble with the vel, walked in the forest and, shame cast aside, pleaded his love to the forest girl, the lord of Ilanji amid groves and paddy, who conquered Sura when even the sun feared him.
nuance: This is an akam song, not the poet's own confession: the girl is spoken of in the third person (கோமள வஞ்சி தளராமுன்). Each image is a pun repeated three times, மாலை (evening and garland) and வாடை (north wind, fading, the wind's blast). The praise answers the girl's longing with Murugan's own: he too pleaded with the forest girl (காதல் இரங்கு குமரேசா).

title: திருக்குற்றாலம்
theme: Three songs at Thirukkutralam (திருக்குற்றாலம்): the courtesans who dance for money and pull the ladder away, the diseased body bound for Yama's town and hell, a plea for the Absolute beyond Veda and knowledge, and the poet who writes on women's breasts as poets write on palm leaf; the shrine is set above a list of famous temples and among devotees and siddhas.
source_issues: Song 975: corrupt character in ம¨டொக்க (line 7), probably மூடொக்க.
