nuance: The whole plea is a cosmic dance with every figure joining (ஆட repeated), ending மயிலும் ஆடி நீ ஆடி வரவேணும். வனச மாமியார், நெடிய மாமனார: Lakshmi and Vishnu as mother- and father-in-law, since Murugan's wives are counted Vishnu's daughters. ப்ரபுட தேவ மாராஜன் names a king, the only patron named in this chapter. கேர்டுதி is corrupt.

tamil: குருதி மூளை யூனாறு மலம றாத தோல்மூடு
குமிழி போல நேராகி அழியு மாயை யாதார
பருகு காய மேபேணி அறிவி லாம லேவீணில்
பரவு நாட காசார கிரியை யாளர் காணாத
எரியின் மேனி நீறாடு பரமர் பாலில் வாழ்வான
எழுமை யீறு காணாதர் முநிவ ரோடு வானாடர்
அலகை பூத மாகாளி சமர பூமி மீதாட
reading: The poet confesses cherishing without sense the body, a hut covered with skin over blood, brain, flesh, excrement and phlegm, a bubble on pit water that bursts, food for vultures, dogs, ghouls and crows, sinking in the world in vain, and asks Murugan to tell him the abode of supreme wisdom that ritualists who strew flowers and shoots in showy rites cannot see. The praise names him child of Uma, wife of the ash-smeared Siva, delighting as sages and gods praise him in song, whose vel powdered serpent, Meru and seas while ghouls and Kali danced on the battlefield.
nuance: குழிநீர் மேல் குமிழி போல: the body as a bubble on standing water. The ritualists are dismissed as நாடக ஆசார கிரியையாளர், rites like a stage play. The closing question repeats 1049's formula word for word.

tamil: சரியு மவல யாக்கையு ளெரியு முரிய தீப்பசி
சகல சமய தார்க்கிகர் கலக மொழிய நாக்கொடு
றரிய துரிய மேற்படு கருவி கரண நீத்ததொ
அவச கவச மூச்சற அமரு மமலர் மேற்சில
விரியு முதய பாஸ்கர கிரண மறைய வார்ப்பெழ
விகட மகுட பார்த்திப ரனைவ ருடனு நூற்றுவர்
திரியு மொருப ராக்ரம அரியின் மருக பார்ப்பதி
திமிர யுததி கூப்பிட அவுணர் மடிய வேற்கொடு
reading: The poet, staggering day and night to quench the hunger-fire burning in his sagging body, asks: when the quarrels of logicians of every creed are ended and one worships the lotus feet with the tongue, and becomes a form of knowledge beyond turiya and beyond all instruments, thrilled, the breath stilled, will Kama's flower arrows strike those pure ones? The praise recalls the Kurukshetra war in which the hundred fell by Arjuna, and Krishna who went once as envoy, Murugan's uncle, and the vel that made the ocean cry out and shattered the hill.
nuance: சகல சமய தார்க்கிகர் கலகம் ஒழிய: the quarrel of the creeds' debaters must end before worship. The question is rhetorical: Kama's arrows (ரதிபதி விடு பூக்கணை) cannot touch one who has passed beyond the instruments, so the plea is for that state. ஒரு தூது திரியும் அரி is Krishna's embassy to the Kauravas.

tamil: மகளு மனைவி தாய்க்குல மணையு மனைவர் வாக்கினில்
மருவு முயிரை நோக்கமு மெரியை யுமிழ ஆர்ப்பவ
உ கமு முடிவு மாச்செலு முதய மதியி னோட்டமு
உ ருகு முரிமை காட்டிய முருக னெனவு நாக்கொடு
புகல வரிய போர்ச்சிலை விரக விசைய னாற்புக
புரவி கரிகள் தேர்ப்படை மடிய அரசை மாய்த்துயர்
மிகவு மலையு மாக்கடல் முழுது மடிய வேற்றுரு
reading: Before Yama binds him, while daughter, wife, mother's kin and all who come wail and cry out inside and outside the house and Death's men with fire-spitting eyes shout, the poet asks to praise Murugan's anklets with his tongue, calling him the Murugan who showed his claim on those who dwell as the ages and their end, the moon's course, being and non-being. The praise recalls Arjuna whose bow destroyed the horses, elephants and chariots of Dhritarashtra's sons and Krishna who relieved the earth's burden, and the vel that pierced Sura when he took the form of mountain and sea.
nuance: The deathbed is crowded with named kin (மகள், மனைவி, தாய்க்குலம்) whose wailing is useless against Yama's men. The second clause of the plea is hard to split; its sense of Murugan as one whom even beings beyond time melt toward is a guess. ஡ stands for ஊ in உடலூடே.

reading: The body is a hut of guts, water, fat and excrement on many bones, set up as a home for cruel disease, with life said to be in it; before Death's men come to fight for it, the poet asks whether Murugan will not give him the flawless truth so that his mind may ripen and praise his feet. The praise names Kanda who, becoming a vengai tree in the forest of the hunters, loved and secretly united with the Kuratti, and the Lord of the ancient gods who gazed at his endless form.
nuance: மதியும் மூத்து: the mind ripening, as if wisdom were a matter of maturing, not escape. The vengai tree and களவு belong to the Valli story. வடிவிலாப் புலமதனை நாட்டிடு is obscure.

reading: The poet marvels at the word of grace Murugan spoke that killed his five senses and instruments and turned death away from him: a word common to all and the one first source, the meaning of the Vedas beyond day and night, the end of all meaning, great open space, the endless goal, inconceivable, nectar to drink. The praise names the vel that made the ocean cry out, the mighty peacock, the son of Parvati who drank at the breasts of the Krittika women, and the Lord of the ancient gods of lotus, milk sea and mountain.
nuance: Unusually the plea is in the past tense: கருணை வார்த்தை இருந்தவாறு என், 'how was that word of grace!', marvelling at a teaching already received. மரணம் மாற்றிய: the word has turned death away. பெருவெளியதாய் names the teaching as vast space.

reading: The poet confesses that he does not sing or seek the vel that withered the great mango tree rising from the salt sea, to reach liberation, does not fall at the ringing feet full of compassion, nor even at the feet of those who fall at them, does not give without delay even a handful of bran to those who ask, and so dies without having lived; he asks Murugan to grant him worth and liberation forever. The praise tells how the elephant gripped by the crocodile cried 'Narayana, Gopala, save!' and Vishnu came on Garuda and crushed its head, and calls Murugan his nephew and protector of Indra's world.
nuance: The confession is a list of omissions, each worse than the last: not singing, not falling at the feet, not falling even at the devotees' feet (வீழ்வார் கால் மீதினும் வீழேன்), not giving even bran (தவிடின் ஆர்ப் பதம்). வாழாதே சாவது: to die without having lived.

reading: The poet asks whether he must go round without being saved, not wearing or seeking the feet that darkness cannot enter of the boundless reality that is sun, moon, earth, sky, water, fire, wind, the stars, the days of the week, the twenty-seven asterisms, the seven worlds, the Veda and the light beyond it, Brahma, Vishnu and, above them, Sivam. The praise recalls the eighteen days in which the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra fell while Partha was protected by Krishna, Murugan's uncle, and names Murugan of the vel and kadamba on his peacock.
nuance: The list climbs from the elements and time (கிழமை, பதினாலு ஆறு ஏழாம் நாள், the 27 stars) through the gods to மேலே சிவமான தொலைவிலாப் பொருள். இருள் புகாக் கழல்: feet no darkness enters. The line naming Krishna is corrupt (஧த்ருர் கோமான்).

reading: As youth passes and the body goes, drums sound, the house rings with 'ko ko', the child cries, the wife cries, the mother falls crying 'my life', and the funeral journey enters Death's town, the poet asks Murugan to come on that day and say to Death 'go' and to him 'return'. The praise names the hero who routed the asuras amid the hunters' cries in the millet field, the babbling child-guru who taught even his father, the six-syllabled one, with form and without.
nuance: தாதையும் ஓதும் குதலை வாய்க் குருபர: the child who with a babbling mouth taught even his father, the teaching of Siva. சடாக்ஷர is the six-syllable mantra of Murugan. The plea's last words (வாரா வானாள் போநாம் நீ மீள்) are hard to split, and பா஡ண is corrupt, perhaps பூரண.

reading: The poet, who sang verses on women who say 'come to the house', asking whether their eyes are sword, vel, carp or deer, their dark curling hair cloud, forest or Mayon's form, their coral mouths milk, honey, syrup or the gods' nectar, asks whether he, a dog, must perish without being saved. The praise shows Murugan running as Parvati watches melting, crying to Sura 'don't go, turn back' as the asuras wail and the ocean burns, the vel that pierced the Krauncha hill, and calls him treasure of the one under the banyan.
nuance: The confession is about the poet's own craft: the string of 'is it this or that?' comparisons is the love poetry he wasted on courtesans (கவி பாடா நாயேன்), as in 1039 he wasted praise on patrons. ஆல் கீழ் வாழ்வார் is Siva seated under the banyan.

reading: The poet says women's eyes like Death's vels have killed the way, path and dharma of Vedic recitation, his courage, shining knowledge and fortune have left, and he has become a mound water cannot climb, where weeds spring up in what falls; he asks the hero to look and rule him so that he does not go in vain. The praise calls Murugan son of the one who felled Death, whom Vishnu could not see, treasure of those who daily recite his flawless feet with full mouths, and the vel that drove the asura chiefs into the sea.
nuance: நீர் ஏறாதோர் மேடாய்: a raised patch the water never reaches, where only weeds grow, the poet's barren life. மறலி சாய்த்தவர், the one who felled Death, is Siva. Several splits in the plea are uncertain.

reading: Before quarrelsome Death destroys all the lust that, through women's cruel eyes in lovemaking, drew him with delight into this rotting hut that runs with blood, the poet asks Murugan to come in compassion on the golden peacock, its beauty pouring. The praise names the vel that split the hill the sun circles, the hero who chased the asura chief across the conch-filled sea, the son of the Lord who burned Rati's husband, and the lotus face too beautiful to draw.
nuance: இரதி பதியை எரி செய்தருளும் இறைவர் குமர: Murugan as son of the Lord who burned Kama, set against the lust of the plea. எழுத அரிய, the beauty that cannot be drawn.

reading: The poet asks when there will be a day free of the trickery of those who say 'your sorrow will end and your poverty go; you will easily get the nectar drink, the wish-cow and the magic pill; to end our wasting hunger give us curd and rice, anklets, bracelets and necklaces and gold plates to melt'. The praise names the vel that pierced the high hill and the asuras' chests and split the ocean's belly, the hero on the peacock who broke the gods' fetters, possessed of knowledge, strength, virtue, splendour and beauty.
nuance: The speakers are not named. They promise wonders (அமிர்த சுரபானம், சுரபி, குளிகை, the alchemical pill) and ask for food and gold, which suggests false wonder-workers rather than courtesans. இவ்விரகு தவிர்வது ஒருநாளே asks for release from this deceit.

reading: Since ornaments, wealth, jewelled clothes, old servants and wife will not come with him on the hard journey when life leaves, and kin of good heart will gather only to lay the body on firewood, the poet asks Murugan, before that cruelty, to grant that he, his servant, speak of his feet so that they are pleased. The praise calls him the matchless one of Arunai and Palani, the old one and the young lord, who embraced the hunters' peacock-like girl after worshipping her with both hands.
nuance: பகரில் ஒருவர் வருக அரிய பயணம்: no one comes on that journey. கிழவ இளைய pairs 'old' and 'young' as epithets. இருகை தொழுது புணர்: Murugan worships Valli with folded hands before union. அடிமை அடிகள் குளிர மொழிவது may also mean that the feet speak coolly to the servant.

title: பொதுப்பாடல்கள்
theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 6 of 21), sung in pairs that share a meter and a closing line: the poet fears the hour when Death's noose falls and kin carry the body to the fire, sees the body from womb to decay, renounces house, kin and wealth as passing, and confesses his bondage to women; the praise turns on the freeing of the imprisoned gods, Siva's dance in the burning ground, and Murugan as teacher of Siva and of Tamil to Agastya.
structure_note: Paired songs share a meter and a refrain: 1068-1069 (the gods freed from prison), 1070-1071 (the plea to sing Murugan's love for Valli, ending 'praised by the three worlds'), 1072-1073 (red feet and anklets), 1078-1079 (Siva dancing in the burning ground, Murugan the companion of the hunters' parrot), 1080-1081. 1074 is mostly praise of Siva's attributes; 1075 is an akam plea for a lovesick girl.
source_issues: 1069: corrupt glyph in வழ஧முடி (flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS).
Across the chapter a stray space after the vowel உ splits words at line starts (உ யிர்போமுன், உ யர்கால், உ ழல், உ சந்த, உ கந்த); read as one word.
1072: புலவோனெ for புலவோனே; 1075: வருவொனே for வருவோனே.
1077: கொண்முவா is probably கொள் மூவா; the line is unclear.

reading: Before his children, father and wife crowd round wailing, before Death with his cruel eyes casts the noose from his strong hand to bind him, the mind fails and life goes, the poet asks Murugan to give his red-gold feet as a pillar to lean on and show grace. The praise names him bridegroom of the girl of the cool hill where monkeys leap, the warrior who fights the crowding asuras as the gods praise, and the ever-young lord who embraces with love women with moon-like foreheads.
nuance: தம்பம் உனது செம்பொன் அடிகள்: the feet as a pillar (ஸ்தம்பம்) to hold when the body is shaken. The closing epithet, the ever-young lord who embraces women for their delight, turns the language of the poet's own confession into praise of the god's love.

reading: The poet traces the body from its birth in one mother's womb, a shape of legs and arms clothed in skin over oozing flesh and blood, wandering full of illusion, to the wheezing and pitiable old age that ends in death, and asks that before then he be given the life of saying 'Muruga' with love in his heart. The praise tells how the demons laid waste the gem-rich golden city of the king of the gods who rides the rutting elephant, set it on fire, and carried the gods off to prison, and how Murugan set them free.
nuance: The whole remedy is a name: முருகா எனச் சொல் பகர் வாழ்வு, a life of saying 'Muruga'. The city is Indra's Amaravati and the elephant his Airavata, though neither is named here; 1069 names them.

reading: The poet, born in a womb, beautiful in youth, babbling the learned books while his black hair turns white without understanding, asks to be taught the true knowledge that the pure, undying Vedic brahmins praise, who plunge into the fire rite twice a day and once more and bathe in water. The praise, sharing its close with 1068, tells how the demons took the crown of Amaravati, seized Indra of the thousand eyes with his elephant Airavata, ruined the land of the wish-granting tree and imprisoned the gods, whom Murugan freed.
nuance: கலைநூல் பிதற்றி: book learning is mere prattle while the hair greys. The knowledge sought (இயல் போதகம்) is the one the fire-tending brahmins praise, so the song sets learning against teaching rather than rite against devotion. A corrupt glyph sits in the line about the crown, and how முருகாய் மனக்கவலையோஆட divides is unclear.

reading: The poet asks whether he will end the bewilderment of carrying this pot of the senses and swarming in distress without telling, with love, of how Murugan once went to the millet field of the hunter girl who guarded it and rejoiced upon her young breasts. The praise recalls Rama, who brought the monkey hordes and ground Lanka and its demons to dust, and names Murugan lord of the gods, praised by devotees in the bliss beyond birth and death and by the three worlds.
nuance: The plea is not to escape Valli's story but to sing it: telling of Murugan's love for her (நின் திறம் புகலாது) is the cure for the confusion of the senses (இந்த்ரிய கடம், the body as a pot). The middle of the praise, with the angry cloud-hued one, the three-eyed one and a fierce elephant, is hard to divide.

reading: The poet calls himself one with no love that melts the heart, no nobility, character or shame, nothing to be saved by, and asks whether he will end as a quarrelsome scoundrel who speaks insolently in anger, without clearly knowing with love how Murugan went to embrace the breasts of the girl of the bowmen's hill. The praise recalls the one who arrogantly lifted the hill where Siva stays and had his heads cut off, and names Murugan, whose feet the gods of the eight directions, the sun and Indra serve, praised by the three worlds.
nuance: The self-abuse is specific: not lust but anger and insolent speech (சினத்தில் மண்டி மிண்டு உரைக்கும் வம்பன்). The one who lifted Siva's hill is Ravana; who cut his heads (Rama, as in 1070) and how that clause joins the praise of Murugan is unclear.

reading: The poet asks not to rejoice as if they were permanent in the house he lives in, his prattling children, kin, home town, wives, youth, wealth, wide lands and hills, but to be granted to worship Murugan with a shining lamp. The praise names him nephew of the cloud-hued one who climbed the kurundu tree, bridegroom of the hunter girl of the monkey-haunted hill, the scholar who knows the Veda and cool Tamil, and the lord of red feet and anklets.
nuance: The remedy for clinging is a concrete rite, worship with a lamp (விளங்கு தீபம் கொண்டு உனை வழிபட). Murugan as the scholar of both Veda and Tamil (வேதம் தண்டமிழ் தெரிதரு புலவோன்) sets the two side by side.

tamil: உ லந்த காயங் கொண்டுள முறுதுய ...... ருடன்மேவா
உ கந்த பாதந் தந்துனை யுரைசெய ...... அருள்வாயே
reading: Trusting that the wife he joined and the sons who delight his eyes would never fail him, the poet took his pleasure in the world and fell into misery, with a wasting body and grief in his heart; he asks instead for Murugan's beloved feet and the grace to speak of him. The praise names him nephew of Hari who joined the lady of the blossoming flower, bridegroom of the hunters' creeper-like girl, and lord of red feet whose anklets and bells ring in every direction.
nuance: Companion to 1072: the same closing line, and the same turn from family to the feet, here as the disappointment of trust (கலங்கிடார் என்று, 'they will not falter') rather than a list of things that pass.

tamil: உ சந்த சூரன் கிளையுடன் வேரற ...... முனிவோனே
உ கந்த பாசங் கயிறொடு தூதுவர் ...... நலியாதே
reading: Most of the song is praise of Siva, who wears the bull, the elephant-skin cloak, ash, the sacred thread, tiger skin, axe and deer, swaying ear-ring and garland of skulls on his crown, and of Murugan as the guru whom that Lord lovingly approached, who in anger uprooted Sura with his kin. The plea asks that when the poet is spent, so that Death's messengers with their noose and rope do not torment him, Murugan come on the great peacock to end his sorrow.
nuance: ஈசன் பரிவுடன் மேவிய குருநாதா: the long list of Siva's emblems builds up to Murugan as Siva's own teacher, the teaching of Om though the syllable is not named here. The plea is only two lines, for the hour of death.

reading: Praising Murugan as the life of Siva who burned the three cities in an instant, the rider who drives the peacock to terrify the asuras, the six-faced lord whose vel pierced the great mountain, and the younger one who comes after the elephant-faced, big-bellied god, the singer asks whether Kama's arrows may strike the young girl who lies pale with longing. The praise ends with Murugan who embraced the hunters' daughter, nephew of Hari asleep on the serpent, lord of the whole earth who ends the deeds of devotees and the sorrows of the gods.
nuance: An akam plea in the voice of someone who speaks for a lovesick girl, a mother or a friend, set inside a frame of praise; the poet's own confession is absent. பசலையொடு அணையும் is the classical pallor of love-sickness.

reading: The poet describes the common women whose Meru-like breasts are adorned with civet, agil, sandal, pearls and gem chains, with lovely blue-lily eyes and nectar speech, in whose beds he melts under their sway in helpless passion, and asks Murugan to rule him, his slave who is perishing. The praise names Murugan nephew of the cloud-hued one who gathered the frightened cows with his flute and who drove the churning of the roaring sea while the mountain whirled, and lord of the one on the bee-haunted lotus.
nuance: பொதுவின் மடமாதர்: women common to all, but neither money nor deceit is named, so the song stays with passion. The praise joins Krishna's flute and the churning of the ocean as feats of Vishnu, sung in drum syllables (குமுகுமு, நெறுநெறு, மொகுமொகு). The last epithet makes Murugan lord of Brahma.

reading: The poet speaks of women with moon faces and eyes that rival their ear-rings, who ensnare the first understanding, and of the karma of plunging into union with them that he, a dog, has drawn on himself; he asks for the love that praises with joy the feet that give wisdom and the higher state, so that the sorrows of his mind wither. The praise names Murugan the chest where the hunter girl's breasts rest, the one who crushed the asuras and freed the gods, the beautiful Kumara who drank the milk of the six mothers, son of Uma, and lord of Hari, Hara and Brahma.
nuance: வழிவழி அடிமை, hereditary service, appears in the plea, but whether the poet asks for that knowledge to widen or is complaining that it has been driven out is unclear from the split. அரி அர பிரமர் தம்பிரானே puts Murugan above the three gods.

reading: Not wishing to stay in this hut of a body that comes with cruel diseases, hiccups and vomiting, bent and dulled, the poet says he has escaped from the other faiths that will crumble and come to Murugan, and asks him to set his feet on his head in a little friendship and rule him, so that he gains the true thing. The praise shows Siva, the ancient one, dancing in the bare burning ground with demons clapping and dancing round to the drum's beat and his chaste consort matching him, and names Murugan his Kumara, companion of the hunters' parrot.
nuance: பரசமயத்துத் தப்பிப் போந்தேன்: the poet speaks as a convert from other sects. அடி ... தலைமேலே ... பூண்டு: the feet set on the head, the Saiva image of the guru's initiation. பதிவ்ரதை ஒத்த names Uma as the chaste wife who keeps time with Siva's dance.

reading: In this world circled by the sun, wound round by the two kinds of deeds and worn out, the poet sees how the stinking body is treated: kin say 'take it quickly', drop their attachment, go to the burning ground and lay it in the fire by rule; he asks whether Murugan will not burn away this bundle of peril and rule him. The praise, paired with 1078, shows the Bhairavas, the damaru's sound and the serpent as Siva dances in the high burning ground while the tall one keeps time with his hands, and names Murugan his son, companion of the hunters' parrot.
nuance: The plea turns the cremation fire into a figure for grace: kin burn the body by rule, and the poet asks Murugan to burn (காய்ந்து) the bundle of his troubles. Whether உறவோரும் means kin or is a variant of துறவோரும் (renouncers) changes the scene, and தத்துக் கத்தை is obscure.

tamil: குடமென வொத்த கொங்கை குயில்மொழி யொத்த இன்சொல்
வடவரை யுற்று றைந்த மகதெவர் பெற்ற கந்த
இடமுடன் வைத்த சிந்தை யினைவற முத்தி தந்து
தடவரை வெற்பி னின்று சரவண முற்றெ ழுந்து
reading: The poet asks Murugan to come and rule him, removing the sorrow of his mind with release and making him know song. The praise names him the one who keeps in mind the love of the hunter girl with pot-like breasts and cuckoo speech, younger brother of the elephant born of the great god of the northern mountain, and the victor in battle who rose from the Saravana pool.
nuance: A short song where praise outweighs plea. இசை அறிவித்து may mean 'teach me music' or 'make known (your) glory'; how இடமுடன் வைத்த சிந்தை divides is unclear.

tamil: மடவிய ரெச்சி லுண்டு கையில்முத லைக்க ளைந்து
சடமிக வற்றி நொந்து கலவிசெ யத்து ணிந்து
படவர விற்சி றந்த இடமிதெ னத்து யின்ற
குடமுனி கற்க வன்று தமிழ்செவி யிற்ப கர்ந்த
reading: Before he weakens, having eaten the spittle of women, thrown away the capital in his hand, whirled toward another birth, and still dared to make love when his body was withered and aching, the poet asks Murugan to rule him. The praise names him nephew of the green cloud who chose the hooded serpent as his bed, the one who spoke Tamil into the ear of the pot-born sage, and Kumara trusted by the hunter girl.
nuance: கையில் முதலைக் களைந்து: the money lost is the capital itself, not just income. குடமுனி கற்க அன்று தமிழ் செவியிற் பகர்ந்த: Murugan as the teacher of Tamil to Agastya.

title: பொதுப்பாடல்கள்
theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 7 of 21): the poet confesses the sea of lust and the women whose bodies he lists part by part, sees the body as a bag of gut, blood and worms, and fears Yama on his buffalo and the cremation fire; he asks for the feet, for song, and for the one Thing where speech and mind end, and rejects begging from patrons and the clamour of rival sects. The last five songs share a closing couplet on Murugan riding the peacock against the demons' elephants, chariots and horses.
structure_note: Pairs by meter and refrain: 1082-1083 (the sport with the millet-field girl), 1084-1085, 1086-1088, 1089-1090 (death and the gods freed from prison), 1091; then 1092-1096, whose praise is a long description of the peacock ending in the shared couplet கலபகக மயில் கடவி நிருதர் கஜ ரத துரக கடகமுடன் அமர் பொருத பெருமாளே. 1087 is an akam plea in a mother's voice.
source_issues: 1089: corrupt glyph in லு஡ட்டு, read ஊட்டு (flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS).
1090: corrupt glyphs in வுடலு஡டே (read உடலூடே) and மறவோ஡க்கு, where ஡ stands for ர் (read மறவோர்க்கு) (flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS: 2).
1086: லளிதவிர் is probably a misspelling of லலித; the line is hard to divide.
Across the chapter a stray space after the vowel உ splits words at line starts (உ டலெழு, உ ரையடி, உ ருகி, உ லகனே, உ றவின்முறை); read as one word.

reading: Sunk in the sea of lust that swelled from dark infatuation, seeking fish-eyed women as if they were wealth, the poet fears the last day when Dharma comes on his buffalo with the tightened noose, and asks that before he is bound, he who thinks of Murugan as his help be given songs of verse and music. The praise names the hero who fights until enemies flee, the lord whose golden shoulders bear the Tamil songs and Vedas sung on earth, who rode the peacock round the world making the hill dust, and who joins the millet-field girl in sport.
nuance: Yama is called தருமன், Dharma, the judge, rather than கூற்று. The plea is for இயல் இசை, verse and music: the gift of song as the poet's defence at death. பகர் தமிழ் பாடல் செழுமறை சேர் பொற்புயம: songs of Tamil and Veda as garlands on Murugan's shoulders.

reading: The poet sees the body formed of earth, sky, wind and fire, where blood and semen join in the bag of skin with its foul gut, and asks that he not wander in this illusory birth suffering disease, but be given Murugan's holy feet bright with kadamba. The praise names the vel that ground Sura's army in the sea to dust, the lord of the three Tamils who chose many arts, the one who ran alone in play over the hill that the matted-haired one sought, and the one who embraces the doe-like girl.
nuance: குருதியிலே சுக்கிலமது கூடி: the embryology of blood and semen, with the elements, makes birth itself the illusion (மாயப் பிறவி). The line on the 'bright sea' (கதிர்விடு வேலை) may name a shrine; the episode of the solitary play on the hill is not clear.

reading: The poet confesses melting over the sandal-smeared, bodiced breasts of doe-eyed women whose eyes are like strife-making swords with poison set in them, and speaking words of helpless rapture; rather than perish so, he asks for the rising wisdom that speaks only of the grace of Murugan's two feet. The praise names him nephew of the old Mayan who sent the discus at the cry of the elephant seized by the crocodile in the pool, the grace of the huntress's breasts, and Murugan near to devotees whose vel broke the mountain.
nuance: The cry of the elephant (பகடு வாய் விட்ட மொழி) is Gajendra's, as in 25. உதய ஞானம்: wisdom that rises like the dawn, and whose content is the feet's grace.

reading: Listing the courtesans' eyes skilled in killing, their ear-rings, gait, oiled hair, teeth, breasts, slight waist, lotus face, back, forehead mark and parrot speech, the poet asks whether he should give his mind to these. The praise is a chain of names: master of arts, fierce Murugan, scourge of the wicked, the young, the golden, son of the mad one, praised god of the green peacock, the world, first of release, lord of siddhi, nephew of Vishnu, the One, the bright form garlanded with vetchi.
nuance: Both halves are lists: the plea strings body parts with -இலே, the praise strings names with -னே, so the song sets the catalogue of women against the catalogue of the god. பித்தர் புதல்வனே, son of the madman, is Siva as பித்தன்.

reading: Not content with the song of the anklets that fall at women's feet crying for refuge, as if the waist would break under breasts soaked in agil paste and musk, the poet asks to be granted to chant 'namah, refuge' to Murugan, who loves the girl of the forest dwellers who guards the millet on the hill. The praise names the lord who does not fear even at the end of the aeon, when the seven seas flood all the worlds, Brahma of the lotus and Mal, and the god on the great vermilion-faced elephant, perish and Hara dances with his consort.
nuance: The cosmic dissolution (ஊழி முடிவு) is the setting of the praise: only Murugan stands unafraid when the gods go under. நம சரண் is a Sanskrit formula of surrender. Many compounds (பகலிரவு உண்டான இருவரும், லளிதவிர்) are hard to divide, and the identity of 'the two who made day and night' is unclear.

reading: In a mother's voice, the singer asks that before her precious lightning-like girl wastes away, tormented by quarrelsome Kama's heavy flower arrows, the humming of bees drunk on honey, the sea's waves and roar, the moon that burns like the sun, and slipping conch bangles, Murugan dispel the darkness and embrace her with his red-garlanded shoulders. The praise shows the sun circling the world crying 'protect' and seeking Murugan, the vel that tore through Sura's head and shoulders, and the lord who once explained to the great one dancing with demons and ghosts.
nuance: Akam convention throughout: the moon that burns (கலைமதி அங்காயும் வெயில்), the sea's roar and slipping conch bangles (சங்கு ஆளும்) are the classical tormentors of a girl in love. What Murugan taught Siva in the last line (அறமும் மறம் தோயும் அறிவு நிரம்பு) is obscure.

reading: The poet sees the body as blood, water, skin, gut and bone, holding a life full of illusion, cruelty, anger and harsh lust, and asks that before Death comes with his long noose to take it and his mother cries out, he be given the art of joyfully chanting Murugan's grace, calling him Guha who rose from the lotus. The praise names the hero whose vel left great Sura's mind ruined and fleeing, and the one who once recited the ancient Veda that gladdened the Supreme who drank the poison and dances, praised by sun, moon and the one who dug up the earth.
nuance: பழமறை அன்று ஓதும்: Murugan reciting the ancient Veda to Siva, the teaching story, without Om being named. The one who dug the earth (படியை இடந்தான்) is Vishnu as the boar.

reading: Before everyone at home says 'take it, take it' of the body that heaps up both kinds of deeds and is ruined, weeps at the burning ground and lights the fire at its head, and before the riders of the dark, twin-horned buffalo tie their rope tight and call him, the poet asks Murugan to show him his pair of anklet-bound feet. The praise names him bridegroom of the hunter girl who drove off parrots, Kumara of the forehead eye that set old fire to the enemies' homes, the Murugan who listened in order to the Tamil song that set forth the Vedas, and the one who freed the gods.
nuance: அருமறைகள் கூட்டி உரைசெய் தமிழ்ப் பாட்டை அடைவடைவு கேட்ட: Murugan as the listener to Tamil song that carries the Vedas, perhaps the hymns of the Saiva saints, though none is named. The forehead eye burning the enemies' homes is Siva's burning of the three cities; பகருநுதல் நாட்ட makes Murugan its son.

reading: Before his kin are struck with grief, the body is laid on a high fire in the long forest of the dead, and Death binds his rope and strikes to bind the life, the poet asks for the mind to praise Murugan's feet with joy and eager longing. The praise names him the bridegroom who honours the feet of the girl with crescent brow and carp eyes, born in another form as child to the hunters to guard the millet, the one who gave knowledge to Siva of the matted hair with arugu, crescent, aththi and the Ganges, and the one who freed the gods.
nuance: பிடியின் அடி போற்று மணவாளா: Murugan himself praises the feet of Valli, the she-elephant, reversing the poet's plea for Murugan's feet. பிறிது உருவில் வாய்த்து: Valli as a goddess born in another form among the hunters. அறிவீவாய்: the teaching of Siva.

reading: Describing the union that women give, hair scattered, eyes closing, bangles jingling, sweet speech trembling and breasts pressed, the poet asks not to lose his mind in the cruel deceit of such women but to be given Murugan's two fragrant feet, the god who circled the world on his peacock in an instant. The praise names Rama whose arrow dried the sea, Krishna who fought the twin marutha trees, Hari who sleeps on the serpent with Lakshmi, Murugan's vel that scattered the demons, and the husband of the hunter girl, master of all arts.
nuance: கலவி தரு மகளிர் கொடுமை எனும் உறு கபடம்: the scene ends in a judgment of deceit. The world-circling ride on the peacock is the race for the fruit, alluded to in passing.

reading: The poet confesses singing to patrons, stuffing their names among titles like sinless, peerless, pure, steadfast, refuge-giver, Kama, Vijaya and Murugan, and telling each that his hand rivals the lotus, gem, conch, rain cloud, wish-cow and wish-tree, while they would not give a millet's worth; he asks for an end to the poverty of wandering from door to door, and for the one Thing where speech and mind cease. The praise describes the peacock, shining like gold, silver and emerald mountains, its shadow cast like the Vimala and Yamuna, spreading over Pothigai, and Murugan riding it against the demons' elephants, chariots, horses and armies.
nuance: The poet's confession is of a court poet: the names of the god (முருகன் among them) wasted on men. மொழி ஒழிய மனம் ஒழிய ஒரு பொருள்: the remedy for begging is a silence where speech and mind end. The peacock lines are hard to divide.

reading: The poet describes the body of gut, faeces and urine, flesh, fat, blood and pale mire, with countless worms writhing and blood oozing until it stinks, which women perfume with civet and adorn with shining jewels as they come to delude the world, and asks for the understanding in which love pours, deeds end, mind ends and darkness ends. The praise likens the peacock to a mountain, to the discus that rends enemies, to the conch, and to the cloud that grew to measure the sea-girt world, and closes with Murugan riding it against the demons' armies.
nuance: The peacock is described with the emblems of Vishnu, discus, conch and the cloud that grows to measure the world (Trivikrama), so the mount takes on the uncle's form. The plea is a chain of endings (வினை ஒழிய மனம் ஒழிய இருள் ஒழிய).

reading: The poet sets against a crore of rival faiths, clamouring with sharp arguments, blind to the one Thing, his plea that the mire of the two deeds go, the instruments of the mind be shaken off, death and wound end, and melting and drinking the word he gain daily the sight of wisdom to know Murugan's musk-fragrant lotus feet. The praise shows the peacock at the end of time, when the stars scatter like sparks and the seven nether worlds, the mountains and the elephants of the quarters melt, running to the sky's summit like the black smoke of the submarine fire that drinks the seas.
nuance: பரசமயம் ஒரு கோடி குருடர் தெரிவரியது ஒரு பொருள்: the sects are blind to the One, as in 1078, where the poet has left them. The praise sets the peacock in the cosmic dissolution, as 1086 does for Murugan.

reading: The poet tells of women whose diamond and emerald-adorned eyes, as if Kama and Death had joined to worship slaughter, carry poison to take young men's lives, and of how following their unfathomable ways he found no path out of the seven births; he asks Murugan to grant a little of his eyes' grace to take this suffering blind man as his servant. The praise tells of Ganesha, whose belly is filled with puffed rice, aval, lentils and the three fruits offered at his feet, and who wrote the whole story of the Kurus with his one tusk on the northern peak as the sage spoke, and of Murugan's peacock that circled the sea-girt world in a moment.
nuance: The praise turns to Ganesha as the scribe of the Mahabharata (குருநாடர் கதை முழுதும் எழுதும் ஒரு களிறு) before naming Murugan's swift peacock, perhaps the race for the fruit between the brothers. மறலி விறல் மதனன்: Death and Kama joined in the women's eyes.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking in full, the women's eyes closing, speech trembling, bangles jingling, sweat on the brow, the garland scattered and hair loosened, drinking their lips and plunging into the sea of passion on the bed, and vows that even then he will not forget Murugan's feet. The praise shows Siva's dance, the back of Muyalakan cracking, the nether worlds struck as one foot rises, the moon shaken from his crown and all worlds reeling, and Murugan dancing beautifully in ways that delight that Lord, before the shared close of the peacock against the demons.
nuance: Unusually, the plea is not to be saved from women but a vow: அவசமுறுகினும் அடிகள் மறவேனே, 'even when I am lost in passion I will not forget your feet'. Whether the dancer delighting Siva at the end is Murugan or the peacock is not certain.

title: பொதுப்பாடல்கள்
theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 8 of 21): the poet confesses bondage to courtesans who sell themselves and take a man's wealth, the frank pleasures of love, the begging of patrons with verse, and the body as a tree or hut that dies and is burned, and asks for teaching (போதகம்), a melting heart and the Lord's feet; the praise turns on Siva's matted hair and his dance, Sambandar's victories over the Jains, and the fire-column of Annamalai.
structure_note: The songs come in runs that share a metre and a closing line: 1097 to 1099 end அமரர்சிறை மீளவிட்ட பெருமாளே, 1100 and 1101 with the worlds' gods worshipping Kanda (அண்டர் அண்டம் தொழும்), 1102 and 1103 the vel sent from the hand, 1105 and 1106 காமவேள் மைத்துனப் பெருமாளே, 1107 and 1108 share their last two lines, as do 1109 and 1110. Confessions of women (1098 to 1104, 1107, 1108); the poet's trade of praising patrons (1105); quarrelsome disputants (1106); death and the pyre (1109, 1110); and 1097's body-tree and 1111's inner light.

reading: The body is pictured as a great tree: rooted by the two kinds of deed in the soil and water of seven births, sprouting troubles, spreading maya as branches, desire as tender shoots and darkness as leaves, budding with loss and ripening the fruit of death; before its shade falls and it perishes in the heat, the poet asks Murugan for sweet teaching. The praise names him son of the fierce hero who struck down the moon, sun, gods, Indra, Brahma and Vishnu gathered at Daksha's sacrifice, rider of the peacock over the eight mountains who freed the gods from prison.
nuance: The tree is worked out stage by stage (வேர், முளை, உலவை, குழை, இலை, நனை, பழம்), so that each phase of growth is a phase of ruin: the buds are loss (இழவு) and the ripe fruit is death (மரணம்). போதகம், teaching, is what the poet asks for here and in 1099. The Daksha lines name the gods at the sacrifice and an எதிர் வீர உக்ரர் who struck them, Siva in his fierce form.

reading: The poet describes women who dress up and preen on the long street, beguile passers-by with their eyes, name a price for their breasts, coax them into their fine houses and onto flowered beds, and after love by Kama's rules melt the heart and take whatever wealth there is, and asks whether he must wander bound by desire for them. The praise names Murugan nephew of Krishna, who drank curd and ghee in the cowherds' homes and cried when Yasoda bound him to the mortar, bridegroom of the hunter girl, and the vel who won the Tamil debate by setting the palm leaf afloat against the flood.
nuance: முலையை விலை கூறி விற்று and நிதியம் உளதே பறிக்கும் name the sale and the taking of money outright. மதனனுடை ஆகமம், 'Kama's scripture', makes the art of love a rival rule. The palm leaf sent up the river (ஏடு ... வருபுனலில் ஏறவிட்டு) in a Tamil debate is the story of Sambandar against the Jains at Madurai, and the song credits it to Murugan.

tamil: உ டலுயிர தாயிருக்க உ னதெனதெ னாமறிக்கை
reading: The poet tells how women with lotus faces and budding smiles embrace a man on the bed, give him their lips and say 'don't forget me; while body and life are one there is no yours and mine, I cannot bear a moment apart', and asks for teaching that will end the deceit of that union. The praise names Murugan nephew of the Mayan whose feet danced on the serpent's crowned, jewelled hoods, born in the Saravana pool, the peacock hero who circles the world-mountain, the six-faced one who is the life of the path of knowledge.
nuance: The deceit is in the women's words of total union (உடல் உயிரதாய் இருக்க உனது எனது எனாமறிக்கை), which the poet quotes; தோதகம், fraud, is set against போதகம், teaching, in a rhyme. The dance on the serpent's hoods is Krishna's on Kaliya, told without naming him.

reading: The poet calls himself a wicked thorn without merit, with a seething, loveless heart, who never comes to praise, carries the hollow where the five senses lurk, wanders seeking food, a stubborn, troubled wretch who is servant to women with kinsuka-red mouths, and asks when he will bow and praise Murugan's lotus feet with their anklets. The praise lists the Ganga, snakes, moon, lotus, thumbai and konrai in Siva's red matted hair, the green creeper at his side who bore Murugan, and names him the death of the clan of the cruel Jains, whom the worlds worship as the learned Kanda.
nuance: The first half is almost all self-abuse, a run of nouns ending in -அன் (கண்டகன், பங்கிலன், அன்பிலன், சஞ்சலன், தொழும்பன், தழும்பன்). குண்டர் is the usual word for the Jains, so குலகாலா again points to Sambandar's victory credited to Murugan. Several words (அங்கதன், பண்டன், பொதும்பு) depend on how the syllables split.

reading: The poet speaks of the life that shrinks on the day Death punishes, and of women who, seeking only money, offer refuge with sweet words while knowing their own deceit, measure their love and deal falsely, and asks whether he must wander joyless, with no love for Murugan, in desire for them. The praise names Siva, who came with love to break Sundarar's bonds and claim him as his servant, who wears thumbai, konrai, bones, the Ganga and the moon in his hair, and Murugan the Kanda of fitting words who delights devotees' hearts.
nuance: தனந்தனை நாடி and இன்சொல் வஞ்சம் make the women's motive money and their means sweet speech. சுந்தரன் பந்தமுஞ் சிந்த வந்து ... தொண்டன் என்று அன்று கொண்டிடும் is the story of Siva claiming Sundarar as his servant at his wedding, the model of being taken into service. The run of syllables in the first lines is hard to split.

reading: The poet describes lovemaking at length: drinking lips sweeter than the gods' nectar, the girdle loosed, falling into the pool of the navel, struggling on the bed with loveless women, breasts like golden pots, ornaments scattering, sword eyes reddening, sweat under the moon, and asks how a mind sunk in that sea of pleasure will ever reach the shore. The praise names Murugan the hero who married Devayanai, daughter given by Indra of the four-tusked white elephant and Puloma's daughter, and who sent the vel from his hand so that the sea, the mountain and the mango tree trembled and the gods were freed.
nuance: The plea is a single question, எனவிதங் கரைசேர்வேன், 'how will I reach the shore', turning the sea of pleasure (இன்ப வாரி) into the sea of birth. அன்பொன்றிலாரொடு, 'with women who have no love', is the only judgement passed on the scene. The lines on the lotus-seated reciter of the Vedas are not clear to me.

reading: The poet describes union with young women, flowers falling from their bee-haunted hair, cloth slipping, lips drunk, bodies entwined like anril birds until two hearts become one, and asks when Murugan will let him pass beyond the deeds those women bind him in and melt for him instead. The praise names him nephew of Vishnu who measured and swallowed the earth, bridegroom of Devayanai of Indra's golden city, who dwells in the hearts of those who love him and split Sura's body with the vel.
nuance: The plea asks not for the melting to stop but for it to change object: உன்றன் மேல் உருக, 'to melt for you', answers the lovers' melting (அழிந்து) in the first half. The anril pair, a stock image of inseparable lovers, here describes the union the poet would leave.

reading: The poet tells how he is undone by women whose breasts, red mouths, poison-dark eyes like Kama's arrows, dark hair and honeyed speech overwhelm him, and asks whether his senses, swinging to and fro, will never think of any way to go and rest without saying 'Om namo Kanda'. The praise names the fragrant trees of Valli's millet field, Murugan whose crown touched the cool feet of that faultless girl, and the teacher whom Siva with the goddess at his side worships.
nuance: ஓநமோ கந்த என்று உரையாதே makes the failure a failure to say the mantra; ஊசலாடும் புலன், the swinging senses, is the image of the state. சீத பாதம் படுஞ் சேகரா has Murugan bowing his head to Valli's feet, the lover's humility, and தேவி பாகம் பொருந்து ஆதிநாதன் தொழுந் தேசிகா makes him Siva's preceptor. The list of trees in the praise is partly obscure to me.

reading: The poet boasts that he is a poet who sings swift verse and kovai, crushes a crore of trash poets in debate, and asks whether he will ever give up standing before patrons, praising them as the rain cloud, the parijata tree and the Meru of giving, and saying 'listen' while he recites ornate and expansive verse. The praise names Vishnu on the serpent bed in the sea and Brahma, for whom Siva was a light beyond reach; Siva the death of Death; and Kama with his cane bow and fish flag who shot at Siva for Uma, whose cousin Murugan is.
nuance: The poet names the kinds of verse he trades in (ஆசு, கோவை, சித்ர, வித்தாரம்), so his skill is the very thing he would give up. The patrons' praises (புயல், பாரிசாதத் தரு, த்யாக மேரு) are the stock hyperboles 1125 calls false. காமவேள் மைத்துனன: Kama is Vishnu's son and Murugan Vishnu's nephew.

reading: The poet asks not to be worn down by dog-like disputants who call good words evil and argue the Vedas against those who come to real austerity, and asks Murugan, who rode the blue peacock and fought cruel Sura, to give him the true meaning so that he may lovingly chant his feet every day without fear. The praise names Vishnu on the serpent in the sea and Brahma, Siva who kicked Death's chest, and Kama, Murugan's cousin, whose flower arrows sank the chaste goddess in a sea of love.
nuance: வேதர்க்கமிட்டு ஓயும் நாய் ஒப்பவர் compares sectarian disputants to dogs. நீதிப் பொருள், the righteous meaning, is set against their argument, and அச்சமற்று makes freedom from fear the fruit. The first lines' syntax is uncertain.

reading: The poet lists the pleasures of concealing women, sleeping on their breasts, nail marks, the navel, the night's plunge into the great sea of delight and the nectar of their lips, and asks Murugan to end them all and give him the bliss of a mind dissolved in silence. The praise pictures Siva with the thousand-mouthed Ganga, hooded snakes, the moon, kura, vilva, konrai and other flowers in his long matted hair, and Murugan as the son given by the goddess who embraces him.
nuance: மவுன ... மனோலய சுகம், the bliss of the mind's dissolution in silence, is a yogic goal set against the sea of sexual bliss (இன்ப ... மகோததி): one absorption is to replace the other. பஞ்சர between them is unclear to me (a cage, or Kama's five arrows).

reading: The poet speaks of women whose sword eyes, sharper than the vel, war on young men's lives, who pretend love with deceit in their hearts and take great wealth, and asks not to whirl in their power but, knowing the nature that has no end and passing beyond misery, to have a mind to worship Murugan's feet. The praise names Siva, who drank the poison from the sea so Vishnu, Brahma, the Vedas and the gods might live, danced with ghouls in the fire, rode the bull and wears the snake, crescent and river, and Murugan the son of the goddess who embraces him.
nuance: அளவி வந்து அணுகு மாநிதி கவர்ந்திடு மாதர: love is a pretence to take money. The last two lines repeat 1107's, so the two songs close as a pair.

reading: The poet pictures the hut of the body full of disease and evil, children crying, wife and household, until Death's messenger comes and fate closes over his deeds, and asks that before his life is lost Murugan think of him with love so that he may praise him every day in the three Tamils. The praise names the vel that pierced the chests of the wicked Suras, the child of the dancer, Muruga of pure Tamil knowledge, coming on the peacock, who keeps his devotees like stored treasure and never changes.
nuance: முத்தமிழினால் ஓத makes the praise he wants to sing Tamil praise, and the epithet சுத்த தமிழார் ஞான முருகோனே joins Tamil and knowledge in Murugan. வைத்த நிதி போல், 'like a hoarded treasure', is the image of how he keeps devotees, shared with 1110. Some lines (on the household, and the flower Brahma placed) are hard to construe.

reading: The poet pictures his funeral: kin and children close by, women devoutly covering the body with silk and garlands, the bier lifted, the mourners calling and then plunging into the water to wash off their grief, the body burned; and asks that before his life departs Murugan give him a life of praising his golden feet every day with inner love. The praise names Murugan son of the three-eyed Mahadeva who is all things, the vel that dried the sea and killed Sura, who rides the peacock among men, gods and sages and keeps his devotees like stored treasure.
nuance: The funeral is told from outside, as a sequence the dead man cannot see: silk, garland, bier, the plunge into water, and grief gone. The plea's timing, ஆவி பிரியாமுன், 'before life parts', is the book's common hour-of-death plea, here asking for a whole life of praise rather than rescue at the end.

reading: The poet asks for an inner vision: a lotus that neither water nor earth touches, spreading in length and breadth as a form of light, joined with love like a flower and its fragrance, in a ground of light that sun and moon do not reach, where he may dance for joy that Murugan is the peacock's rider; he asks for the shining vel and the garland. The praise names the peacock whose dance shakes the thousand-hooded serpent and scatters gems like stars, the cock banner, and Murugan the child of the light of Arunai that Vishnu and Brahma searched for and could not find.
nuance: சூரியனுடன் சோமன் நீழல் இவை அண்டாத சோதி, a light that sun and moon do not touch, is the language of yogic inner sight (as in the Tirumanthiram), here joined to bhakti: the vision ends in dancing. அருணஞ்சோதி points to the fire-column at Annamalai; who searched in the last line (ஆனைமுகவன், the elephant-faced one?) is unclear, and the whole song's syntax is uncertain.

title: பொதுப்பாடல்கள்
theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 9 of 21): the poet asks for the yogi's ascent through the body's centres to silence, for the knowledge and mantra Murugan taught Siva, and for his feet at the hour when Death's men come and kin and wealth fall away; he confesses courtesans who want silk and money, his wandering for food, and his trade of praising worthless patrons, and the praise ends in a litany of the goddess's names.
structure_note: Eight songs (1116 to 1123) share a clipped metre of doubled consonants and one closing line, முத்தா முத்தீ யத்தா சுத்தா முத்தா முத்திப் பெருமாளே, and 1112 and 1113 share பத்திசெய்வா னாடர் பெருமாளே. Yogic and doctrinal songs (1112, 1116, 1124); death, kin and wealth (1113 to 1115, 1117); women (1119, 1121, 1122, 1126); begging and praising patrons (1118, 1120, 1123, 1125). 1124 is an extended praise with a battle in drum syllables, and 1126's praise is a list of the goddess's names.
source_issues: Song 1112: one corrupt character in வா஡ணச (line 5); the sense needs வாரிச, lotus, so ஡ண probably stands for ரி or ரீ.

reading: The poet asks whether, dropping desire as if it were burnt, he will reach the bliss of knowledge free of the world's customs and sorrows, see the pure, supportless space beyond words and the inner instruments, climb through the blossoming lotus-wheels of the six centres to the moon above, and attain the sealed silence that is other than the thirty, the thirty-six and the thirty. The praise tells how Brahma ran crying, mountains toppled, the seven seas dried and crores of asura lords and Sura himself died by the vel, and names the twelve-shouldered hero who embraces the shoulders of the wife who guarded the millet.
nuance: The plea is a full yogic programme in Tirumular's vocabulary: கரணாதீதம் (beyond the instruments), நிராதார வெளி (the supportless space), சடாதாரம் (the six centres), மதி (the moon at the crown), and முத்திரையா மோனம் (silence as the seal). முப்பதும் ஆறாறும் முப்பதும் counts the tattvas as the Tirumanthiram does (thirty, thirty and thirty-six) and places the goal beyond them. The corrupt word in line 5 is most likely வாரிச, lotus.

reading: The poet pictures his kin, brother-in-law, uncle's daughter, mother and children, grieving without end as his body burns in the fire and those who set it there leave, and asks that before the fixed day comes and Death's messenger brings his torment, his heart may melt and he may gain knowledge and live chanting Murugan's feet. The praise names the gods Vishnu and Brahma who sought him, Siva on the bull, and Murugan with the long-plumed peacock for his horse, the six-faced one whose feet are ringed by the six-syllable mantra.
nuance: நாளும் இட்டு ஒரு தூது ஏவு: Death fixes the day and sends a single messenger. பக்ஷமுமேலாய் ஷடக்ஷர சூழ் பாத, feet surrounded on both sides by the six syllables, points to the mantra சரவணபவ, though the line is not named.

reading: The poet pictures himself, like a bird caught in the snare of the tattvas' workings, stammering as he falls to the ground and parts with life, and asks that at that time Murugan come quickly on the green victorious horse with his devotees who have reached that pure state, so that this lowly one's poverty may end. The praise names the younger brother of the wise elephant god with the coral belly, the peacock that circles the eight mountains and directions, the guru who gave grace to the three-eyed, matted-haired lord of Kanchi, and the bridegroom of the chaste hunter girl.
nuance: The plea asks Murugan to come at death with his devotees (பத்தரொடு தொக்கு), so that the dying man joins their company. கச்சியப்பர்க்கு அருள்செய் குருநாதா seems to name Siva of Kanchi as the one taught; it might instead recall the Kandapuranam's poet Kachiyappar. The bird image (ஒட்டில்பட்ட குருகு) is uncertain in its first word.

reading: The poet lists children, wife, brothers, elders, money in boxes, gems, pearls, ornaments and servants, all of whom grieve and leave at the pyre, and asks for the one day when, no longer melting for what is false, he may have the mind to strew flowers and praise Murugan's gracious feet. The praise names Siva who wears the crane's feather, the river and the moon in his red matted hair, and Murugan who gives clear siddhi, release and Sivam, and whose vel killed the asura of the mango tree.
nuance: The list of kin and possessions is the Tirumanthiram's argument that none of them follows the dead. சித்த முத்திச் சிவமும் அருள்வோனே puts siddhi, mukti and Sivam among Murugan's gifts. The lines on what they do at the pyre are hard to construe.

reading: The poet describes the body of the five elements running its course, filling and belching, and himself wandering while pretending, like those who make a show of devotion, and asks for the knowledge beyond the reach of the bond. The praise names the vel that went for the gods, split the mountain and pierced Sura in the sea, and Murugan who gives the meaning to those without earlier merit, the pure, freed one, lord of release.
nuance: பாசத்தால் எட்டா அப்பாலைப் போதம், the knowledge beyond what the bond can reach, is the plea in Siddhanta terms. அப்பாவித்துத் திரிவேன் seems to confess a pretended devotion. The clipped metre leaves most word splits open, and the reading is a sketch.

reading: The poet pictures Yama's men with red, fiery eyes and crescent swords binding him with the noose and dragging him off in anger, while kin and parents stand round saying 'we won't keep you, go', and asks who will be his kin at that time. The praise names Murugan who removes clinging attachments, who bowed at the golden feet of the girl in the green millet field, and who dwells in the minds of those who hold to true knowledge.
nuance: அக்காலத்துக்கு உறவு ஆர்தான், 'who then is kin?', is the whole plea; the praise answers it by naming Murugan as the remover of attachments (பற்று ... களைவோனே). The kin's words, ஒட்டோம் விட்டுக் கழியீர், as I read them, turn the dead out of the house.

reading: The poet confesses seeking wealth as a merchant seeks honey and singing a few songs to those who had come into fortune, like men of petty knowledge, and asks whether, leaning instead on those who have attained, he will be allowed to praise Murugan's good feet a little. The praise names the vel that fought and cut down Sura while the gods stood round, and Murugan who removes the past sins of those who serve his feet without fail.
nuance: The contrast is between the patrons (திக்காமல் பாடுற்றார்) to whom he sings for pay and the devotees (பெற்றார்) he would lean on instead; the same confession as 1105 and 1123. Most word splits are uncertain.

reading: The poet speaks of women whose devotion is for silk and green palm-leaf ear ornaments, who look with cruel glances, and of his consorting with them while friends and strangers in the neighbourhood mock him, and asks whether a sinner like him may reach Murugan's feet. The praise appears to name the lord of Kaazhi and the Sakti's grace, and Kumaresa who guarded the millet field.
nuance: The women's devotion (பத்தி) is for silk and ornaments, gifts the man must pay for. காழி, Sirkazhi, with சத்தி may allude to Sambandar's birthplace and the milk the goddess gave him; the praise is too clipped to be sure.

reading: The poet pictures the body as a torn, leaking hut put together from numbered parts, and himself running to this land and that for its food until worn out, and asks whether he must be stuck in that. The praise names Murugan who crushed Sura, the child of the six lights and the holy ash, with red flowers on his chest, the lord of the freed.
nuance: பத்தே ழெட்டீ ரெட்டேழ் ரட்டால் counts the body's parts as numbers, like the Tirumanthiram's numbered body (159); what the numbers stand for is not given. பைப்பீறல் கூரை, a torn-bag roof, is the hut of the body. The reading is a sketch.

reading: The poet confesses that for women with coral lips and false talk of pleasure, mad with taking their lies as truth, he seeks money for their hands, running south, to Kasi, east, west, to every direction and to the islands, and asks whether he must be ruined so. The praise names Murugan who became supreme for those who discipline themselves and meditate on him, and who went to the simple forest girl and became a vengai tree on the hill.
nuance: The distances (தெற்கு, காசி, கீழ், பச்சிமம், தீவு) measure how far money for the women drives him. முற்பால் வெற்பில் கணியானாய் recalls the story in which Murugan stood as a vengai tree before Valli. தப்பா முப்பாலை may name the Kural; the line is not clear.

reading: The poet speaks of women who talk like golden mynahs, pass off false love as true through fruit-red mouths, let their cloth slip from mountain breasts and press for money in hand with hard hearts, and asks whether he must be caught by their eyes and bound by long desire. The praise names Murugan who dwells in the hearts of those who serve his feet with words, whose vel struck Sura as the mango tree, and the child kissed by the mountain's daughter.
nuance: பொய்க்காமத்தே மெய்க்காம, false love as true love, is the deceit; காசுக்கே கைக்குத்திடு makes the payment explicit. கட்கே பட்டு, struck by the eyes, makes the eyes the snare.

reading: The poet confesses that he has sought food for the body all over the earth, praised unkind and thieving men with words of desire, like men of crooked knowledge, and asks for good words to sing Murugan's feet. The praise names Murugan who went to the deer-like girl in the millet field on the hill, held her feet and begged refuge for her golden shoulders, and the child kissed by the goddess whom Siva keeps at his side.
nuance: The plea asks for words (நற்சொல்) to replace the words already spent on patrons. Murugan holding Valli's feet as a suppliant (பாதத்தாள் பற்றிப் புகல்வோனே) mirrors the poet's own begging, turned to love. முக்கோணத்தானத்தாள, the lady of the triangle, names the goddess by the yantra.

tamil: அபரிமித சுருதியும டங்குந்த னிப்பொருளை எப்பொருளு ...... மாய
அணுவையணு வினின்மலமு நெஞ்சுங்கு ணத்ரயமு மற்றதொரு ...... காலம்
நிகர்பகர அரியதைவி சும்பின்பு ரத்ரயமெ ரித்தபெரு ...... மானும்
நினதுவழி யடிமையும்வி ளங்கும்ப டிக்கினிது ணர்த்தியருள் ...... வாயே
தகுதகெண கெணசெகுத தந்தந்த ரித்தகுத தத்ததகு ...... தீதோ
முரசதிர நிசிசரரை வென்றிந்தி ரற்கரச ளித்த ...... பெருமாளே.
reading: The poet asks Murugan to teach him sweetly the silent mantra that he gave to Siva, who burned the three cities, when Siva praised him with devotion as king, guru and Kumara: the one entity in which the fifty-one letters from a, all the arts, the many tattvas and the endless Vedas are contained, the bliss known by those who know, the end of the fourth state, the atom within the atom, beyond impurity, mind, the three qualities and time, filling all things, beyond comparison; and to make his old servitude shine. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, ghouls and Bhairavas dancing, vultures and rivers of blood, in which Murugan conquered the night-walkers and gave Indra back his kingship.
nuance: The guru story is told as Siva's own act of devotion (நிருப குரு பர குமர என்று என்று பத்திகொடு பரவ), and what Murugan gave is called a மவுன மந்திரம், a silent mantra; Om is not named. The long description of the absolute (துரிய முடிவு, அணுவை அணுவினின், நிறைவு குறைவு ஒழிவற) is Vedanta and Siddhanta vocabulary, and நினது வழியடிமை asks for hereditary service. The battle lines are rhythm.

tamil: உ பய அங்கமு நிலையா கிடவொரு ...... கவியாலே
உ ளது கொண்டுயி ரவமே விடுவது ...... தவிராதோ
reading: The poet lists the men he goes to, deceitful, cruel, hard-eyed, ignorant, loveless, sunk in delusion and births, cut off from grace and bound for hell, and asks whether his habit of praising them in verse as Vishnu who swallowed the worlds, as Kama or as the tree of the gods, and wasting his life on what they give, will ever end. The praise names Murugan who drinks at Valli's breasts, nephew of Rama who shot the arrow at the sea, who circles the eight directions on the peacock in a moment, son of Uma and of Siva who burned the three cities with a smile and dances in the hall, and who freed Indra's city.
nuance: The patrons are condemned in a long list of plural nouns before the confession comes; the poet's fault is the false praise (உலகம் உண்டவர் மதனார் இமையவர் தரு எனும்படி மொழியா), which compares the base to gods. உயிர் அவமே விடுவது, wasting life, is the cost.

reading: The poet confesses unending desire, eyes roving over women from foot to crown, the demon of desire covering him, without conduct and vile, running every day, and asks whether, instead of perishing so, the teaching of knowledge will come with love so that he may sing and dance daily of Murugan's twelve shoulders, six faces, kadamba garland and blue peacock. The praise is a litany of the goddess's names, Varahi, Kapali, Malini, Mahamayi, Yamalai, Kali, Uma, Bhavani, Narayani, mother of the worlds at Sonachalam and more, whose son is Visakha, who sent the vel against Sura.
nuance: ஆசா பசாசு, desire as a possessing demon, and ஆசார ஈனன், one without conduct, are the confession's key words. The cure is ecstatic devotion (பாடி ஆடி). The goddess's names mix Saiva, Sakta and Vaishnava titles (வாராகி, காளி, நாரணி, அம்பவானி) and place her at சோணாசலம், Annamalai.

title: பொதுப்பாடல்கள்
theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள்), not tied to a shrine: most confess the lure of courtesans and their eyes, a few turn to old age, the funeral and Death's servants, one sets ritual pomp aside for a union where 'you and I' fall away, and one thanks Murugan for the grace that made the poet sing the Thiruppugazh; the praise draws on Siva's and the goddess's epithets, Vishnu's avatars and the war with Sura.
structure_note: Courtesans and lovemaking: 1128, 1130, 1132, 1135, 1136, 1137, 1138, 1141. Age, death and the funeral: 1131, 1133, 1139, 1140. 1127 sets temple ritual beside non-dual release; 1129 is a song of gratitude rather than plea; 1134 asks for the teaching of knowledge. 1130 and 1133 give most of their praise to the goddess, Murugan's mother.
source_issues: Song 1129: unflagged garble லொ முவர் (line 15), probably ஒரு மூவர், the three spared at Tripura; the same garble recurs in 1141 (வொ முவர், line 15).
Song 1133: corrupt மா஡ண (line 14), probably மாரீ, and ஓ ஧ட்மு (line 22, flagged), probably ஓடு மூ (பிரமாவோடு மூவகையர்).
Song 1137: corrupt தத஧முழ்கி (line 9, flagged), probably ததி மூழ்கி (மகோததி, the great sea); unflagged கொநல்மு (line 15), probably கொடு மூ (மூவிலைவேல், the trident).
Song 1135: சியொதனன் (line 17) for சுயோதனன் (Duryodhana).
Song 1138: பிடுங்தித் (line 14) for பிடுங்கித்.

tamil: ஆராதன ராடம் பரத்து மாறாதுச வாலம் பனத்து
ஆறார்தெச மாமண் டபத்தும் வேதாகம மோதுந் தலத்து
நீராளக நீர்மஞ் சனத்த நீடாரக வேதண்ட மத்த
நீவாவென நீயிங் கழைத்து பாராவர வாநந்த சித்தி
வீராகர சாமுண்டி சக்ர பாராகண பூதங் களிக்க
வேதாமுறை யோவென் றரற்ற ஆகாசக பாலம் பிளக்க
வாராகர மேழுங் குடித்து மாசூரொடு போரம் பறுத்து
வானாடர சாளும் படிக்கு வாவாவென வாவென் றழைத்து
reading: The poet asks not to be bewildered by the pomp of worship, invocations and mantras, palm-leaf texts, pillared halls, places where Veda and Agama are chanted and fuel burned in sacrifice, but to be called by Murugan himself, 'come', and given, regularly and without difference, the state where 'you' and 'I' cease, the siddhi of bliss and release into supreme bliss. The praise is a battle where Chamundi and the ghosts rejoice, Brahma cries out, the sky cracks, the mango tree is cut at the root and the seven seas are drunk, and Murugan calls the gods back to rule their heaven.
nuance: The opening list (ஆராதனை ஆடம்பரம், ஆவாகன மாமந்திரம், வேதாகமம் ஓதும் தலம், எரிதாம் இந்தனம்) is ritual the poet does not want to be lost in (மருளாதே); against it stands நீ நான் அற வேறின்றி நிற்க, a non-dual union. Several compounds in the first half (சவாலம்பனத்து, வேதண்டமத்த) do not split securely, so the exact list is uncertain.

tamil: ஆலா லத்தைய ழுத்திய வேல்போல் நற்குழை யைப்பொரு
ஆளா மற்றவர் சுற்றிட மீளா மற்றலை யிட்டறி
கோலா லக்கண மிட்டுவ ராதார் நெக்குரு கப்பொருள்
கூடா நட்புமு ரைத்திடு கேடா விட்டகல் மட்டைகள்
பாலா மக்கட லிற்றுயில் மாலோ ரெட்டுத லைக்கிரி
பார்மே லிக்கனு டற்பொறி யாய்வீ ழச்சுடும் வித்தகர்
மேலா யத்தொடு திக்கடை மேவார் வெற்பொட ரக்கரை
மேனா டர்ச்சிறை விட்டருள் மீளா விக்கிர மத்தொடு
reading: The poet describes courtesans whose eyes are like a vel steeped in poison, who surround men and will not let them go, name a price for their arts of pleasure, and stay only if they get a share of wealth, offering false friendship; he asks whether he must suffer the fear and misery of such clowning. The praise names Siva who burned Kama when Uma came near, Murugan dwelling among devotees, the vel that struck the mountain and the demons, and the lord who freed the gods from prison and imprisoned Brahma.
nuance: விலைகூறி and பொருள் கூறாகப் பெறில் நிற்கவும் name the bargain outright: the women stay only for a share of the money. கூடா நட்பு, 'friendship that does not join', is a Kural phrase for false friendship; the women are also மட்டைகள், worthless husks.

tamil: ஆதேச வாழ்வி னிற்ப்ர மித்தி ளைத்துயி ...... ரழியாதே
ஆபாத னேன்மி கப்ர சித்தி பெற்றினி ...... துலகேழும்
ஏடேவு ராஜ தத்தி னைப்ப ணித்ததும் ...... இடராழி
ஏதேம மாயெ னக்க நுக்ர கித்ததும் ...... மறவேனே
மாலாய வாளி யைத்தொ டுத்த ரக்கரி...... லொ முவர்
சேராத சூர னைத்து ணித்த டக்கிய ...... வரைமோதிச்
சீராவி னால றுத்த றுத்தொ துக்கிய ...... பெருமாளே.
reading: A song of thanks: the poet says he will never forget that Murugan gave him unfailing wisdom and understanding of the books he studied, kept him from perishing in a passing life, carried him across the sea of desire, set him in the state beyond speech and mind, and made him, a base man, famous for singing the wondrous Thiruppugazh with honey in every direction, freeing him from the three impurities, the three qualities and bubble-like births. The praise names Siva who drew Meru as a bow with the serpent for string and Vishnu as arrow and burned the three cities, Devayanai daughter of Indra, and Murugan's sword that cut down Sura and his clan.
nuance: The song names its own book: அற்புதத் திருப்புகழ் தேனூற ஓதி. The plea of other songs is here a list of graces already given (கொடுத்ததும், அளித்ததும் ... மறவேனே). வாசாமகோசரம், beyond word and mind, and மலத்ரயம், குணத்ரயம் are Saiva doctrinal terms. ஏடு ஏவு ராஜதத்தினைப் பணித்ததும் may refer to some royal command or honour; its sense is uncertain.

reading: The poet describes courtesans with poisoned eyes who call a man in with sweet looks, show their breasts, rouse desire and bargain over the price, laugh from the street and snatch whatever wealth comes, and asks whether he, a rogue whose mind melts at their talk, must waste away. The praise is almost all to the goddess: speaker of the Veda, with crescent-moon locks, who kept dharma with two measures of grain, wearer of the tiger skin, rider of the bull, younger sister of Vishnu, whose great treasure Murugan is.
nuance: விலைபேசி and வருபொருள் கண்டு ஏற்கவே பறிக்கும் name the trade. The goddess's epithets run in a string ending in -ச்சி (குலத்தி, பேச்சி, இடைச்சி, சடைச்சி ...). இருநாழி படிகொடு அறம் காத்த points to the story, told of Kanchi, of the goddess who kept the charities with two measures of grain; I offer it as a likely allusion.

reading: The poet pictures death: troubles crowd round, the false hut of the body is laid out, kin and sons gather and lament with many words and then leave, and red-eyed Yama strikes and drags the life away; before that, he asks, may he be freed of his deeds and praise in ever-new words the victory of Murugan's vetchi-garlanded shoulders? The praise names Murugan as the one who taught his father, with crescent and Ganga in his red matted hair, the meaning of knowledge, and as god-emperor of Vishnu with his discus and Brahma the tall potter.
nuance: The kin weep and then go (அவர் ஏக), a single beat that empties the house before Yama (சமன்) arrives. The plea is not for rescue but to praise (புகழ் செப்பப் பெறுவேனோ) before the end. அப்பர்க்கு அறிவொக்கப் பொருள் கற்பித்திடுவோனே is the story of Murugan teaching Siva, here without naming Om. குயவன், potter, for Brahma the maker is unusual.

reading: The poet tells how at night Kama shoots his flower arrows and women's eyes, carp-like, deer-defeating, nectar and poison together, net young men's lives, and how, drinking their lips and embracing them, he sinks into the whirlpool of union; he asks for the good undying feet so that he does not drown. The praise names Vishnu who shot the arrow through Ravana's ten heads and twenty shoulders, Murugan as guru to Siva who pitied three in the walled cities, and the lord pleased by the songs of devotees who melt day and night.
nuance: சுழி மிதுன வாவி, the eddying pool of coupling, makes union a drowning, so the remedy is feet that do not perish (அழியா மன் நல் பதங்கள்). தெளிமருவு காரணத்து அமர்ந்த may name a place or a cause; I cannot tell which.

reading: The poet traces a life of unceasing sorrow driven by the burning belly, toil for food, the years passing, hair greying, the name 'old man', faltering steps and failing eyes, and asks whether he will perish without reaching the abode of the Dancer's raised foot. The praise is a litany of the goddess's names (Abhirami, Nili, Suli, Gauri, Mayi, Sivai, Ambikai, who burned the three cities and shares Siva's side), whose son Murugan is, Valli's bridegroom, lord praised by Hari, Hara, Brahma, Indra and the gods.
nuance: நடன் குஞ்சித வீடு is release imagined as the lifted foot of Siva's dance; the song asks for it from the son, not the father. விடிவது என்று, 'when will it dawn', is the old man's question. Two lines are corrupt (see source issues).

reading: The poet asks not to melt under the sway of young women whose sharp eyes are like Kama's battle, but to sink into the dust of Murugan's feet with their koothalam garland until the mind dissolves, and to receive the teaching of a knowledge beyond word and mind. The praise tells the story of Prahlada at length, the boy who answered his Brahmin teacher with Narayana's name and the man-lion who tore his father from the pillar, and names Vishnu as uncle and Siva as father.
nuance: மனோலயம், the dissolving of mind, comes from immersion in the dust of the feet (பாததூளியின் முழுகி), and the plea ends in வாசாமகோசர ... ஞானோபதேசம். The Prahlada story is told in Prahlada's own words (இரணிய ரூபா நமோ, அரி கரி நாராயணா).

reading: The poet describes lovemaking in frank detail, the swaying waist, ringing anklets, scattered jewels, scented flowers on the bed, and asks whether, after melting in a union said to equal Kama's own, he must wander the earth exhausted. The praise names Siva who burned the cities with a laugh, kicked Death, destroyed Kama and wore the sea's poison, and Vishnu who brought Duryodhana down in the Bharata war, with a battle in which jackals feast.
nuance: மதராஜன் மருவிய கலவி தனக்கு ஒப்பாம் is the boast inside the confession: the pleasure is called equal to Kama's, and its end is weariness (களைத்து).

tamil: இலகிய வேலோ சேலோ ஒளிவிடு வாளோ போதோ
எனவிழி கூறா வாரா அரிவையர் தேர்ளு டாடா
பலபல கோளாய் மாலா யுழலும தானால் வீணே
பரிவுட னாடாய் வீடா யடிமையு மீடே றாதே
அலைகடல் கோகோ கோகோ எனவுரை கூறா வோடா
அழகிய வேலால் வாளால் நிலவிய சீரா வாலே
மலைமிகு தோளா போதா அழகிய வாலா பாலா
மறைதொழு கோவே தேவே நறை செறி பூவே நீரே
reading: The poet tells how he praised women's eyes as vel, carp, sword, flower, Death's messenger, deer and poison, wandered deluded to the end, spoke deceit and became a materialist, and asks whether he will die without his service being fulfilled. The praise is a battle in which the sea cries out and Murugan drives off the demons with vel and sword, the lord of the peacock and son of Indra's fortune, worshipped by the Veda.
nuance: லோகாயதனாகி: the poet names the materialist school as one of his falls, beside false speech (படிறு சொல்). The list of eye-comparisons (வேலோ சேலோ ... எமன்விடு தூதோ) is the opening's whole substance. The plea's lines (நாடாய் வீடாய் அடிமையும் ஈடேறாதே பணிதியில் மூழ்கா) do not split securely, and I read them only roughly.

tamil: உ ளமுரு கியபத்த ருறவே மறவே ...... னெனவோதி
உ ணர்விலி பெறமுத்தி தருவாய் துகிர்வாய் ...... மடமாதர்
reading: The poet opens by naming Murugan as the peacock-rider born of peacock-like Uma and the child of six mothers, confesses that he never melted in devotion, is caught between his two deeds and is without understanding, and admits that though the pleasure of union with women is slight, he cannot, cannot give it up; he asks for release. The praise pictures Sura as a golden mountain, a sea, primeval darkness, Yama with trident and fiery eyes, the fire at the end of the age, a flesh-eating king challenging gods, Hari, Brahma and the seven worlds, and names Murugan as the king who threw the vel at him.
nuance: சுகம் அற்பமாகினும் ... விடவோ இயலாது இயலாதே is a rare admission: the poet grants the pleasure is small and still cannot leave it. The demon's challenge is in his own voice (அறையோ அறையோ), and the cries of the worlds answer (முறையோ முறையோ). Two words are corrupt (see source issues).

reading: The poet describes in detail a night with a woman, from bowing at her feet and her offered smile and betel to the bed, the loosened cloth, the nail marks, the babbling and the reddened eyes, and asks whether he must wear himself out in such union. The praise is a battle in which the demons of the sea lose their crowns, the mango tree is cut, the Krauncha hill is smashed, and the vel is worshipped by the short sage who loves the mountain, ending with the green peacock.
nuance: The scene is told as a sequence (பணிந்திட்டு, இருத்தி, அணைமேல் வீழ்ந்து, உடுத்த பொற்றுகில் அகல ...) and the plea is one line at the end (நொந்தெய்த்திடலாமோ). பருப்பதப்ரிய குறுமுனி is Agastya, here a worshipper, not named as Murugan's pupil.

reading: The poet asks that before Death comes saying women, sons, kin, life and clan are ended and his body of blood, water and bone is put on the fire, Murugan remove the grief of his anxious senses and his place among base men who rise by shouting down rivals with quarrelsome books, and give him a life of worshipping his feet with love. The praise names Siva who rides the bull with moon in his locks and deer and axe in his hands as the father who graced his younger son, and Murugan who split the mountain and came on the peacock.
nuance: கலகக் கலை நூல் பல கொண்டு எதிர் கதறி ... வென்று உயர் கயவர் is a sharp picture of learning used to win debates, which the poet counts as baseness. Death is காலன், and the body is the hut grown from blood, water and bone (குடில்).

tamil: உ லகிலுள பலரரிசி வாய்மீதி லேசொரியு ...... மந்தநாளில்
உ பயபத மிசைகுலவு சீரேறு நூபுரமும் ...... அந்தமார்பும்
reading: The poet pictures his funeral day, kin wailing, the town giving up hope, drums rising to the sky and many dropping rice into the dead man's mouth, and asks Murugan to come then with his six faces and twelve arms on the peacock, with Vedas sounding, gods raining flowers and his old devotees gathered, to rout Death's army and take him, a prattling dog-like servant. The praise names the victory where Kali and the ghosts feasted, Murugan's wandering in Valli's forest where he became a young tree, and his birth from the mother on Siva's side who bore him without bearing.
nuance: The funeral is told with its rites (பறை, திமிலை, முழவு, அரிசி வாய்மீது), and the plea answers it with a procession of its own, Murugan's arrival. மறலி படை யமபுரமும் மீது ஓட வே பொருது makes the rescue a battle against Death. மாதா பெறா, the mother who bore without bearing, is Uma, since Murugan came from Siva's eyes.

tamil: உ தடு கன்றிகள் நாணா வீணிகள் ...... நகரேகை
உ ணவை யுண்டுடை சோர்கோ மாளிகள் ...... கடல்ஞாலத்
பகழி குன்றவி லாலே நீறெழ ...... வொ முவர்
reading: The poet heaps abuse on courtesans as lustful, deceitful, shameless, drunk on liquor till their clothes slip, wicked sinners, goddesses of misfortune who bring poverty and false shapes of illusion, and asks for a state in which he is not tossed about in the pleasure of union. The praise names Siva who burned the flying cities with Vishnu as arrow and granted his feet to three who kept him in mind, and Murugan who cut the mango tree and joined the hunter girl in a grove where cuckoos and anril birds call.
